Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

1.1 Engineering Materials (ACiE0101)

A. Properties of Engineering Materials

Every engineering material is judged by four groups of properties: physical, chemical, mechanical and thermal. The course syllabus lists them in this order, so the group names themselves are exam material.

1. Physical Properties

Physical properties tell you how heavy a material is, how much of it is solid, and how it handles water, weather and fire. The syllabus lists melting/freezing point, boiling point, density and electrical resistivity here; for the exam, the density-related properties matter most.

Mass density (ρ) is the mass packed into one cubic metre of material, in kg/m³. These values are asked directly as one-mark MCQs:

MaterialDensity (kg/m³)
Water1000
Steel7850
Plain concrete2400
RCC2500
Brick masonry1900–2000
Cement1440
Timber (sal)≈ 800
Bitumen≈ 1040

Bulk density applies to loose granular materials such as sand and aggregate. It is mass divided by total volume, voids included, so it is always lower than the density of the solid grains themselves.

Specific gravity (G) compares a material's density with that of water at 4 °C. It is a pure ratio with no units: steel 7.85, granite ≈ 2.65, burnt brick 1.8–2.0, OPC 3.15.

Porosity (n) is the share of a material's volume that is empty space.

n = Vv / V × 100 %

Glass and steel have almost no voids. A porous material is weaker, insulates better, and absorbs more water.

Water absorption is the weight of water a material takes in during 24 hours of immersion, expressed as a percentage of its dry weight. Good building stone absorbs less than 5%; a stone absorbing more than 10% is rejected.

Permeability is the ability to let water pass through connected pores. Darcy's law gives the seepage flow:

Q = k · i · A

where k is the coefficient of permeability, i the hydraulic gradient and A the cross-sectional area.

Durability (weathering resistance) is the ability to survive repeated wetting–drying, freezing–thawing and chemical attack without deteriorating.

Fire resistance. Brick and concrete stand up to fire well. Timber burns, but its surface chars at roughly 0.6 mm per minute, and that char layer shields the wood beneath — so heavy timber sections hold strength longer than exposed steel.

2. Chemical Properties

Chemical composition decides how a material behaves. Cement gets its character from four compounds (C₃S, C₂S, C₃A, C₄AF). Iron and steel are iron–carbon alloys. Most building stones are dominated by silica (SiO₂) — quartz and granite are examples.

Corrosion resistance. Steel rusts only when it has both moisture and oxygen; remove either and rusting stops. Stainless steel resists rust because its chromium forms a thin passive oxide film — the chromium content must be at least about 10.5%.

Acid and alkali resistance. Limestone and marble are calcium carbonate, so acids dissolve them. Silica-rich stones resist acids well.

Reactivity with water. Quicklime slakes vigorously — CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ — and releases heat. Cement also reacts with water (hydration) and releases heat.

3. Mechanical Properties

Strength is resistance to failure. Each loading mode has its own strength: concrete is strong in compression (20–60 MPa) but weak in tension; mild steel carries 400–550 MPa in tension. The flexural strength of concrete (modulus of rupture) ≈ 0.7√fck N/mm².

Elasticity is deformation that fully disappears when the load is removed. Below the proportional limit the material follows Hooke's law. Steel: E ≈ 2×10⁵ MPa. Concrete: E ≈ 5000√fck MPa.

Plasticity is deformation that stays after the load is removed, without rupture. Fresh mortar, wet clay and mild steel beyond yield are plastic.

Ductility is the ability to stretch a long way in tension before breaking. Mild steel, copper and aluminium are ductile. It is measured by percentage elongation — Fe 415 bars must give at least 14.5%.

Brittleness is the opposite: sudden fracture with almost no warning deformation. Cast iron, glass, concrete and brick are brittle.

Toughness is the total energy a material absorbs before fracture under impact or shock. Charpy and Izod tests measure it, and it equals the total area under the stress–strain curve.

Hardness is resistance to scratching, indentation and abrasion. Mohs scale runs from talc (1) to diamond (10). Brinell, Rockwell and Vickers are the standard indentation tests.

Stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation — how little a member deflects under load. For an axially loaded bar, stiffness = EA/L.

Creep is slow, continuous deformation under a sustained load. It matters in concrete, plastics and timber; ordinary-temperature steel shows practically none. In concrete, creep grows with higher stress, younger age at loading and higher temperature.

Fatigue is failure under many repeated load cycles at stresses well below the ultimate strength. For steel, the endurance (fatigue) limit is about half the ultimate tensile strength.

Malleability is the ability to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets. Gold is the most malleable metal, then copper, then aluminium.

Wear (abrasion) resistance matters for floors and road surfaces; the Los Angeles abrasion test measures it.

4. Thermal Properties

Thermal conductivity (k) is the rate at which heat flows through a unit area for a unit temperature gradient, in W/m·K. Metals conduct strongly: copper ≈ 400, aluminium ≈ 200. Brick ≈ 0.7, concrete ≈ 1.5, wood ≈ 0.15. Glass wool insulates because its k is only ≈ 0.04.

Coefficient of thermal expansion (α). Steel expands 12×10⁻⁶ per °C and concrete 10–14×10⁻⁶ per °C — nearly the same, which is why reinforced concrete works as one material. Brick expands less (5–8×10⁻⁶); aluminium much more (23×10⁻⁶).

Specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of a material by 1 °C. Water's value (4.186 kJ/kg·K) is the highest of any common material, which is why water works as a coolant and thermal mass.

Thermal spalling. Under fire, the surface layer of a stone expands suddenly and flakes off. Sandstone behaves badly this way.

B. Stones

Geological classification

Igneous rocks cooled from molten magma and are the hardest group. They are subdivided by cooling depth: plutonic rocks cooled deep below the surface and have coarse grains (granite, diorite, gabbro, pegmatite); hypabyssal rocks cooled at shallow depth (dolerite, microdiorite); volcanic rocks cooled at the surface and are fine-grained or glassy (basalt, trap, pumice, obsidian).

Sedimentary rocks are layers of weathered material deposited by water, wind or ice — so they are stratified. Examples: sandstone (silica binder), limestone (calcium carbonate), shale, gypsum, dolomite, laterite.

Metamorphic rocks formed when heat and pressure changed earlier rocks: granite → gneiss, sandstone → quartzite, limestone/dolomite → marble, shale → slate or schist.

Physical and chemical classification (course values)

ClassificationGroupCharacterExamples
PhysicalStratifiedSplit along bedding planesSandstone, limestone, shale
Unstratified (massive)No layers, solid massGranite, marble, basalt
FoliatedSplit in one directionSlate, schist, gneiss
ChemicalSiliceousSilica is the main ingredientGranite, quartzite, sandstone, basalt
CalcareousLime is the main ingredientLimestone, marble, dolomite
ArgillaceousClay/alumina is the main ingredientSlate, laterite, kaolin

Requirements of good building stone

  • Crushing strength ≥ 100 N/mm² for load-bearing (structural) stone — granite 100–140 MPa, basalt 150–190 MPa. Weaker stones such as marble (≈ 70 MPa) and limestone (≈ 55 MPa) serve flooring, facing and other non-structural work.
  • Specific gravity 2.4–2.8. Heavier stones are stronger; light stones suit domes and ornamental work.
  • Water absorption < 5% after 24-hour immersion (IS 1124). A stone absorbing more than 10% is rejected outright.
  • Wear (Los Angeles abrasion) < 30% for road aggregate; Dorry hardness value > 17.
  • Toughness index > 13 (impact test, IS 5640).
  • Acid test: weight loss in 1% HCl over 7 days should be ≤ 5%.
  • The stone should be free from cracks, cavities and soft seams, with uniform colour and texture.
  • Fire resistance by family: argillaceous (clay) stones best, siliceous fair, calcareous poor.

Tests on stones

TestIS codeWhat it tells you
Compressive strengthIS 1121 Pt-1Load capacity; 40×40×40 mm cube, loading rate 14 N/mm²/min
Water absorptionIS 1124Porosity behaviour; 24-hr immersion
Attrition / Deval—Wear resistance of road stone
Los Angeles abrasionIS 2386 Pt-4% wear for pavement stone
Impact testIS 5640Toughness — aggregate impact value (AIV)
Acid testIS 1126Durability against atmospheric attack
Smith test—Presence of earthy matter (water turns muddy)
Crystallization / freezing–thawingIS 1125Durability against salt and frost
Dorry (coefficient of hardness)—Hardness rating

Course quick-facts: Smith test = dirt (clay) content; Brard's test = frost resistance; gneiss gives the highest crushing strength among common stones (NEC course key — classic texts often quote granite at 100–140 MPa and basalt/trap at 150–190 MPa, so gneiss is the exam answer here); pumice (igneous) serves as lightweight construction material; silica shows no cleavage; marble's minimum hardness value = 3.

Dressing and uses

Dressing is shaping a quarried stone to the required size and face. The operations, from rough to fine: pitching, hammer dressing, chisel dressing, boasting, sawing, grinding, rubbing, polishing.

Uses: rubble and ashlar masonry, foundations, facing work, road metal, railway ballast, concrete aggregate, flooring, lintels.

C. Bricks

Fig 1.1 — Modular brick 190×90×90 mm with frog (frog laid up, mortar-filled for bond)

Manufacturing — four stages

  1. Preparation of clay: unsoiling → digging → weathering (exposed through the monsoon) → blending → tempering (wet mixing, traditionally in a pug mill).
  2. Moulding: hand moulding (ground-moulded or table-moulded) or machine moulding (stiff-mud, dry-press). Moulds are made of shisham wood and sized slightly larger than the brick.
  3. Drying: 2–10 days in shade. Slow drying prevents cracks.
  4. Burning: in clamps or kilns at 900–1200 °C.

Clamp burning is the temporary, economical way: 3–4 weeks, uneven quality, about 60% good out-turn — suitable for third-class bricks. Kiln burning (Bull's trench, Hoffman, tunnel kilns) gives uniform quality with less fuel; the Bull's trench kiln is the most common in Nepal, with 80–90% out-turn.

Stages of burning: dehydration (up to 150 °C) → oxidation (150–600 °C, water and organic matter driven off) → vitrification (600–1000 °C; the clay needs at least 850 °C to vitrify) → slow cooling (fast cooling cracks the brick). Over-burning makes bricks brittle and bloated; under-burning leaves them soft and porous.

Classification (IS 1077, course values)

ClassMin compressive strengthMax water absorptionTypical use
1st class10.5 N/mm²< 15%Exposed and load-bearing work
2nd class7.0 N/mm²< 20%Plastered work
3rd class3.5 N/mm²< 25%Temporary works (clamp burnt)
4th class——Over-burnt "jhumb" bricks, used as aggregate

A first-class brick gives a clear metallic ringing sound when struck, has rectangular faces and uniform colour. The minimum strength for building work per NBC/IS 1077 is 3.5 N/mm²; load-bearing masonry commonly uses ≥ 7 N/mm² bricks.

Fig 1.2 — English bond: header and stretcher courses alternate (queen closer gives the ¼-brick lap)
Fig 1.3 — Flemish bond: each course alternates header and stretcher (closer at quoin gives the lap)

Shapes and sizes

Special shapes serve edges and openings: bull-nose, coping, cornice, plinth, hollow, perforated, paving (frog-less), fire-clay (refractory), acid-resistant, sand-lime, and fly-ash/AAC blocks as modern alternatives.

Standard modular size (IS 1077): actual 190 × 90 × 90 mm; nominal 200 × 100 × 100 mm including a 10 mm mortar joint. The traditional Indian non-modular brick is 230 × 110 × 70 mm, and NBC 109:1994 (Masonry: Unreinforced) specifies the Nepal Standard brick as 240 × 115 × 57 mm with a 10 mm vertical mortar joint (brick length = 2 × width + 1 joint). One cubic metre of modular-brick masonry contains 500 bricks; handmade bricks run about 560/m³ and machine-made about 530/m³.

Frog is the 10–20 mm deep depression on one face. It holds mortar and keys the courses together, and it carries the maker's stamp. Frog area ≈ 1/10 of the brick face. Bricks are always laid frog up so the mortar fills the depression completely.

Constituents of brick earth

ConstituentIdeal %What it doesIf too much
Silica (SiO₂)50–60Holds shape, prevents shrinkage and crackingBricks become brittle and weak
Alumina (Al₂O₃)20–30Gives plasticity for mouldingShrinkage and warping, cracks on burning
Lime (CaO)≈ 10 (well ground)Binds the particles, reduces shrinkageFlaking, puffing; lumps blister the brick
Iron oxide (Fe₂O₃)5–6 (course value: < 7)Red colour and imperviousnessDark blue-black colour
Magnesia (MgO)≈ 1Reduces shrinkage, yellow tintDecay of the brick
Alkalis< 1—Efflorescence

Harmful constituents: lime lumps, organic matter (black core), pebbles and grit, pyrites (white spots and efflorescence).

Defects in burnt bricks: bloating (spongy swelling from carbonaceous matter + sulphur), black core (bituminous matter), chuffs (rain on hot bricks), checks/cracks (lime lumps or fast drying), lamination (entrapped air).

Efflorescence

Efflorescence is the white deposit of soluble salts (sulphates of calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium) that appears when moisture carries the salts to the surface and they crystallize on evaporation. Remedy: use well-burnt bricks, salt-free water and sand, brush and wash the surface; soaking and hydrating the salts before use prevents it.

D. Tiles

Composition of good tile clay (course values): sand 40%, silt 30%, clay 30%; fine sand content should not exceed about 40%.

Types: ceramic floor tiles, porcelain/vitrified tiles (absorption < 0.5%), mosaic/terrazzo, paver blocks, quarry tiles. Roofing tiles are waterproof clay burned at about 1300 °C — flat, pan, Spanish (barrel), Italian, Mangalore, corrugated, half-round. Salt-glazed stoneware tiles serve as drain tiles; glazed tiles finish walls.

Quality limits: vitrified tiles absorb < 0.5%, ceramic wall tiles 10–20%, frost-resistant tiles < 3%. Maximum warping along tile sides is 2%. Glazing gives smoothness, imperviousness and an attractive finish.

Tests: water absorption, modulus of rupture, crazing resistance, abrasion.

E. Cement

Raw materials and manufacture

Cement needs a calcium source (calcareous: limestone, chalk) and a silica–alumina source (argillaceous: clay, shale). Limestone supplies lime (CaO 60–65% of cement); clay supplies silica 17–25%, alumina 3–8% and iron oxide 0.5–6%. Gypsum (2–5%) is added while grinding to control setting.

The wet process mixes with more water and gives better homogeneity; the dry process uses less fuel and is what modern plants use. Both burn the raw mix in a rotary kiln at 1400–1500 °C (the course quotes 1400 °C in MCQs; the general range may appear as 1400–1700 °C). The product is clinker, ground with gypsum into cement.

Bogue's compounds

Fig 1.4 — Bogue compounds of OPC (typical %)
CompoundNicknameTypical %Role
C₃S — tricalcium silicateAlite40–50Early strength (up to 7 days); fairly high heat of hydration
C₂S — dicalcium silicateBelite25–40Later/ultimate strength (28 days–1 yr); low heat; best chemical resistance
C₃A — tricalcium aluminateCelite5–11Reacts first, gives initial set and flash set; highest heat; weakest against sulphate attack
C₄AF — tetracalcium aluminoferriteFelite6–10Least cementing value; gives the grey colour

Heat of hydration, highest to lowest: C₃A > C₃S > C₄AF > C₂S. Total heat of OPC ≈ 500 J/g. Gypsum retards the flash set of C₃A — that is its whole job.

Types of cement

  • OPC 33 / 43 / 53 (IS 269 / 8112 / 12269): the grade number is the 28-day minimum compressive strength in MPa.
  • Rapid hardening (IS 8041): more C₃S and finer grinding; 1-day strength equals OPC's 3-day strength. Used for precast work, cold-weather concreting and road repairs. Specific surface ≈ 3250 cm²/g vs 2250 for OPC.
  • Low heat (IS 12600): low C₃A and C₃S, high C₂S; heat ≤ 270 kJ/kg at 7 days and ≤ 314 kJ/kg at 28 days. For mass concrete such as dams.
  • Sulphate resisting (IS 12330): C₃A ≤ 5%. For marine works, canals and sewage works.
  • Quick setting: initial set ≈ 5 min, final ≈ 30 min. For underwater grouting and running-water works.
  • High alumina (CAC): bauxite + limestone. Fast setting, high early strength, resists acids and sulphates; expands slightly on setting, so never combine it with OPC.
  • White cement: iron oxide < 1% (no ferrite phase), made from pure limestone and kaolin. Decorative work.
  • Portland Pozzolana (IS 1489): fly-ash or calcined-clay based; lower heat, better durability. Blast furnace slag cement (IS 455): marine works.
  • Others: air-entraining, expansive (shrinkage-compensating), hydrophobic, coloured (pigment 5–10%).

Choosing by situation (course quick-facts): blast-furnace slag → bridge abutments; high-alumina → refractory work (avoid steam curing); PPC → seawater works; sulphate-resisting → canals and sewage; rapid hardening → precast and road repair; low heat → mass concrete.

Hydration products

When cement meets water it forms C-S-H gel (calcium silicate hydrate, ~50–60% of the product, also called tobermorite gel) — this is what actually gives strength. Calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)₂ (~20–25%) makes the pore water alkaline (pH ≈ 12.5), which protects reinforcement from rust, but it is leachable and reacts with sulphates and CO₂. C₃A plus gypsum first forms ettringite; if ettringite forms late (delayed ettringite) it expands and cracks the concrete.

The Vicat needle test defines the setting limits — see the figure:

Fig 1.5 — Vicat needle test (IS 4031-5): OPC initial set ≥30 min, final set ≤600 min

F. Lime

Classification (IS 712)

ClassNameClay contentBehaviour / use
AEminently hydraulic> 25% (course: 25–30%)Sets quickly, even underwater; structural masonry; must be slaked and screened
BSemi-hydraulic12–25%Sets slowly underwater; lime mortar for masonry and plaster
CFat / high calcium< 5%Slakes vigorously; never sets underwater; whitewashing and finishing plaster
DMagnesium / dolomiticMgO > 5%Slakes slowly; used with pozzolana
EKankar limehydraulicGround from kankar nodules (impure limestone)
FSiliceous dolomitic—Used with pozzolanic materials

Hydraulicity comes from the clay content: feebly hydraulic 5–10% clay, moderately 10–25%, eminently 25–30%. The source of hydraulic lime is kankar. Poor (lean) lime has more than 30% clay and serves only inferior work.

Slaking and setting

Slaking is quicklime's reaction with water: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, releasing about 1,150 J/g (≈ 64 kJ per mole of CaO); the volume grows 2–2.5 times. Quicklime must always be slaked before use, otherwise it expands later inside the work. Lump lime is quicklime straight from the kiln; excess water turns hydrated lime into milk of lime.

Setting of fat lime happens by carbonation: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ — slow, taking weeks. Setting of hydraulic lime happens by hydration of its silica and alumina compounds — fast, and it works underwater. Hydraulic lime sets initially in about 120 minutes and cures in 7 days; the ball test checks expansion and disintegration after 6 hours.

Lime is produced by calcining calcium carbonate at about 800 °C.

Uses: mortar, plaster, whitewash, soil stabilization, lime-pozzolana mixes, and as a raw material in steel, sugar and paper manufacture.

G. Timber

Fig 1.6 — Log cross-section: pith → heartwood → sapwood → cambium → bark

Classification

Exogenous trees grow outward by adding rings — these give all structural timber. They divide into conifers (softwoods: needle leaves, resinous, lighter — pine, deodar, chir, kail, spruce, walnut) and deciduous (hardwoods: broad leaves, denser and stronger — teak, sal, sisau, oak, rosewood). Most hardwoods are tropical; most softwoods are temperate.

Endogenous trees grow inward in bundles — bamboo, cane, palm. They are not true trees and yield no sawn timber.

Structure of the trunk

From centre outward: pith (medulla — the dead central core) → heartwood (duramen — dark, dead, the strongest and most durable part) → sapwood (alburnum — light-coloured, living, weaker and perishable) → cambium layer (where growth happens) → bark (protective skin). Medullary rays run radially, carrying food across the trunk.

Each annual ring is one year of growth: light, soft spring wood formed early in the season plus dark, hard autumn wood formed late. Count the rings to get the tree's age.

Fig 1.7 — Timber defects: knot, shake (crack with grain), warp (cup, cross-section)

Defects — four groups

GroupDefects
Natural (growth)Knots (branch bases — the most common), shakes (cracks: heart, star, cup/ring — frost or wind), rind gall, burls, upsets (fibre damage), wane, bark pockets, druxiness (white fungoid spots), foxiness (red/yellow decay tint)
Conversion (sawing)Box-heart, half-heart, twisted fibres; quarter (rift) sawing vs plain (tangent) sawing — radial sawing is strongest, tangential weakest
Seasoning (drying)Shrinkage cracks and checks, splits, warping (cup, bow, spring, twist, diamond), honeycombing, case-hardening, collapse, blue stain
Fungi and insectsDry rot and wet rot (fungi), termites/white ants, marine borers (Teredo), beetles (pin holes)

Seasoning

Seasoning removes moisture from felled timber. Freshly felled wood can hold up to 100% moisture (of its dry weight); well-seasoned timber holds 10–12% (furniture) or 12–15% (building work). Seasoning prevents warping, shrinkage and rot; fungi attack only wood above about 20% moisture.

Natural (air) seasoning takes 60–90 days and costs little. Artificial seasoning takes only 4–5 days and controls the result — kiln seasoning is the most common industrial method. Other artificial methods: water seasoning (salt water replaces the sap and makes the timber insect-resistant), chemical/boiling, electrical (high-frequency).

Preservation and tests

Preservatives: ASCU (arsenic + copper + chrome — the common general one), creosote oil (railway sleepers), coal tar (marine piles), Wolman salts (all-round), charring and tarring (traditional), Abel's, Sloe's, Celry and Bethell's (full-cell) processes, and Rueping/Lowry (empty-cell). Bethell = pressure creosoting.

Tests: moisture content (oven-dry method or moisture meter), specific gravity, compression and tension along and across the grain, toughness (FPL tester), cleavage.

Market forms (course values): plank < 5 cm thick; board < 5 cm thick and > 12 cm wide; batten > 5 cm and > 12 cm; baulk > 5 cm and > 20 cm; deal 5–10 cm thick, < 25 cm wide; strip 5 × 10 cm. Teak serves boats, willow makes cricket bats. Strength is maximum parallel to the grain.

H. Metals and Alloys

The iron family — by carbon content (course values)

MaterialCarbon %Character and uses
Pig iron3–4%Product of the first extraction (blast furnace); brittle. Sub-types: Bessemer (from haematite ore), foundry/grey (high fuel, high temperature), forge/white (low fuel, low temperature), mottled (between foundry and forge; ornamental)
Cast iron2–4%Remelted pig iron; strong in compression (150–400 MPa) but weak in tension; brittle; not weldable. Columns, struts, sanitary fittings, pipe and manhole covers, machine bases
Wrought iron< 0.15%Most pure; slag fibres give ductility; weldable and rust-resistant. Electromagnets, roof coverings, chains, railings, ornamental work

Steel products and other metals

TMT/CTD bars: Fe 415, 500, 550, 600 — thermo-mechanically treated to give a strong outer rim with a ductile core, and a superior bond with concrete.

Alloy steels: stainless (Cr ≥ 10.5% plus Ni), weathering steel (COR-TEN — Cu and Cr), high-tensile prestressing steel (≈ 2% Mn).

Aluminium: density 2.7 g/cc, protected by its own oxide film, good conductor. Duralumin (≈ 4% Cu) serves curtain walls, doors, windows and cables. Copper is an excellent conductor and ductile — wiring, pipes, roofing. Zinc protects steel by galvanizing (sacrificial coating).

Common alloys (course list)

InvarSteel + Ni (very low expansion)German silverNi + Cu + Zn
MonelNi + CuGun metalCu + Zn + Sn + Pb

Malleability = hammered into sheets; ductility = drawn into wires. Removing impurities from ore = concentration of the ore; the dust from iron manufacture = inorganic sludge.

I. Paints, Varnishes, Distempers

Functions

Paint protects the surface from weather and corrosion, improves appearance, and special grades add fire retardance or anti-fouling action.

Ingredients (course definitions)

IngredientJobExamples
BaseThe body of the film — opacity and durabilityWhite lead, red lead, zinc white
Vehicle / liquid mediumDissolves the base and carries the filmLinseed oil
PigmentColourIron oxide, chrome yellow
Solvent / thinnerReduces consistency for brushingTurpentine, naphtha, petroleum spirits
DrierSpeeds drying by helping oxidationLead acetate, red lead, litharge, cobalt naphthenate
Filler / adulterantBulk and economyBarium sulphate

Course quick-facts: red lead serves as base, pigment and drier, and is the corrosion-resistant pigment; priming coat on steel = red lead, on wood = white lead; radiator paint = bronze paint; fire-resistant paint = asbestos paint; Duco = trade name for cellulose paint.

Types

  • Oil paint — the general-purpose paint.
  • Water paint / distemper — chalk + glue; interior walls only.
  • Emulsion (plastic) paint — water-based acrylic/vinyl; washable; covers ≈ 10–14 m²/L per coat.
  • Enamel — varnish + pigment; glossy, hard surface.
  • Cement paint — exterior; needs damp curing; alkaline-resistant.
  • Bituminous paint — waterproofing and pipe protection.
  • Aluminium paint — reflects heat; tanks and radiators.
  • Epoxy / polyurethane — industrial floors and chemical resistance.
  • Luminous paint — glows in the dark.

Application sequence

On plaster: surface preparation (clean, fill cracks) → putty filling → primer → first and second top coats, with sanding between. On timber: knotting → priming → stopping (filling) → undercoats → finishing. Emulsion on dry plaster needs no primer. Nepal practice: wood gets 3 coats (1 primer + 1 under + 1 finish enamel); walls get putty + 1 primer + 2 emulsion coats.

Coverage rules of thumb: distemper 1 kg / 8–10 m²; emulsion 1 L / 10–14 m²; enamel 1 L / 8–10 m².

Paint defects

DefectCause
BlisteringMoisture or strong sun swelling the film
BloomingDull patches — moisture during drying
Flaking / peelingPoor adhesion of the film
ChalkingBinder breakdown — powdery surface
Sagging / runsCoat applied too thick
WrinklingThick coat drying fast on top
CissingWet or greasy surface repels the paint
GrinningUndercoat shows through the top coat
SaponificationAlkali in the substrate attacks the oil binder
CrazingHairline cracks in small areas; cracking runs through the full layer
AlligatoringOne layer slides over another
Fading, flashingColour loss; glossy patches

Varnish and French polish

Varnish is a transparent protective film of resin (copal, lac, rosin) + solvent + drying oil + drier for timber. Types: oil varnish (most durable), spirit varnish (shellac in methylated spirit — dries fastest, most brilliant, but water-sensitive), turpentine varnish, water varnish. Enamel's liquid medium is varnish. French polish is many thin shellac coats rubbed to a gloss on wooden furniture. Lacquer = cellulose nitrate.

J. Asphalt, Bitumen, Tar

MaterialSourceKey points
BitumenRefining crude petroleumBlack-brown, thermoplastic; soluble in carbon disulphide (CS₂) and trichloroethylene
TarDestructive distillation of coal or woodStronger smell, carcinogenic; not fully soluble in CS₂; better adhesive on wet aggregate; pipe coating and wood preservation (creosote)
AsphaltNatural (Trinidad lake) or manufacturedBitumen + inert mineral matter; rock asphalt (natural bitumen + limestone), mastic asphalt (hot-applied waterproofing)

"Asphalt" in American usage simply means bitumen — a classic trap option.

Forms of bitumen

  • Cutback: bitumen + volatile solvent; grades RC / MC / SC (rapid, medium, slow curing). Used for prime and tack coats.
  • Emulsion: bitumen + water + emulsifier; anionic (RS / MS / SS) or cationic (CMS / CRS). Applies cold and works in wet weather — patch repairs, slurry seals.
  • Plastic bitumen: bitumen + inert filler (asbestos powder) — crack filling.
  • Blown bitumen: air-oxidized for special uses.

Grades: penetration grades (IS 73) 30/40 (hardest — hot climate, heavy traffic), 60/70, 80/100 (moderate), 180/200 (softest — cold regions). Viscosity grades (IS 73:2013): VG-10, VG-20, VG-30, VG-40. Tar is graded RT1–RT5 (RT1 has the lowest viscosity).

Tests on bitumen

TestIS codeMethodLimit / result
PenetrationIS 1203100 g needle, 5 s, 25 °CHardness in dmm (0.1 mm units)
DuctilityIS 1208Briquette pulled at 5 cm/min, 27 °CMin 75 cm for paving
Softening pointIS 1205Ring & ball≈ 45–55 °C for 80/100 grade
Flash & fire pointIS 1209Pensky-Martens (closed cup)Min flash point 175 °C
Water content——< 0.2%
Loss on heatingIS 1212—< 1%
Solubility in TCE——> 99% (insoluble impurities < 1%)

Asphalt concrete (AC) is a hot mix of graded aggregate + filler + bitumen, mixed at about 150–160 °C and compacted to 92–97% of lab density — the standard wearing course.

Memory hooks: Ductile = mild steel; brittle = cast iron, concrete, glass. Steel is the most elastic common structural material. Creep matters in concrete, timber and plastics. Fatigue comes from cyclic loading. Malleable = hammered into sheets; ductile = drawn into wires.
Trap alerts: Tar ≠ bitumen — the sources differ. US "asphalt" = bitumen. First-class brick absorption: the course book says < 15% (older references 20%) — prefer 15% with 10.5 N/mm² strength. Gypsum retards setting, never accelerates. C₃A = flash set and high heat; C₂S = ultimate strength and low heat.

1.2 Standards (NS & IS) and Tests for Civil Engineering Materials (ACiE0102)

A. Standards system

NS (Nepal Standards) are issued by the Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology (NBSM), established in 1980 under the NBS Act 2037. NS numbering largely mirrors the IS codes — NS 1/2035 ↔ IS 1077 (bricks), NS 49/2041 ↔ IS 269 (cement), NS 297/2050 ↔ IS 383 (aggregates), NS 305/2050 ↔ IS 2386 Pt-3 (bulking), NS 84/2042 ↔ IS 432 (mild steel bars), NS 191/2046 ↔ IS 1786 (deformed bars), NS 203/2046 ↔ IS 1608 (tensile test). Where NS codes are silent, Nepal practises with IS codes.

IS codeSubject
IS 456Plain and reinforced concrete — the most quoted civil code
IS 383Aggregates for concrete
IS 4031 (Pts 1–11)Cement test methods
IS 3495 (Pts 1–4)Brick tests
IS 1077Common burnt clay bricks
IS 1786 / IS 432HYSD bars / mild steel bars
IS 875 (Pts 1–5)Loads (dead, imposed, wind, snow, combinations)
IS 1893 Pt-1Earthquake loads
IS 8112 / IS 12269OPC 43 / OPC 53
IS 800 / IS 13920 / IS 15988Steel structures / ductile detailing / retrofitting

Other international systems: ASTM (USA), BS (UK), EN (Europe), ACI (American Concrete Institute).

B. Tests on Bricks (IS 3495)

Water absorption (Pt-2): oven-dry the brick at 105–110 °C and weigh (W₁), immerse it in water at 27 ± 2 °C for 24 hours and weigh again (W₂).

Absorption % = (W₂ − W₁) / W₁ × 100

Limits: 1st class < 15% (course value; the classic first-class classification agrees — IS 1077's ≤ 20% applies only up to class 12.5, 15% for higher classes), 2nd ≤ 20%, 3rd ≤ 25%.

Compressive strength (Pt-1): test 5 bricks; fill the frog with 1:1 mortar, cure 7 days, immerse 24 hours, then load at 14 N/mm² per minute. Report the average. If (max − min)/average exceeds 20%, retest with 10 bricks.

Efflorescence (Pt-3): stand the brick in 25 mm of water for 7 days, dry in shade, and rate the deposit: nil, slight, moderate, heavy, serious. Heavy and serious are rejected.

Warpage (Pt-4): maximum 3% of the surface dimension for concave warping, 5% for convex.

Field tests: metallic ringing sound when struck, uniform red colour, scratch test for hardness, drop test, and dimensional tolerance (±3% length, ±2% width and height).

C. Tests on Cement

TestIS codeMethodRequirement (OPC)
Normal consistencyIS 4031 Pt-4Vicat apparatus, 10 mm plungerPlunger stops 5–7 mm above the bottom of the mould (equivalently 33–35 mm below the top); water = P (≈ 25–35%)
Initial setting timeIS 4031 Pt-5Vicat 1 mm² square needle, water 0.85P≥ 30 min — needle fails to pierce to 5 mm above the bottom
Final setting timeIS 4031 Pt-5Vicat needle with annular collar≤ 600 min (10 hr) — collar leaves no impression
SoundnessIS 4031 Pt-3Le Chatelier (free lime), water 0.78P; autoclave (magnesia)Expansion ≤ 10 mm; autoclave ≤ 0.8%
Compressive strengthIS 4031 Pt-670.6 mm cubes of 1:3 cement-sand mortar, w/c = (P/4 + 3)%, vibratedOPC 33: 16/22/33 MPa (3/7/28 d); OPC 43: 23/33/43; OPC 53: 27/37/53
FinenessIS 4031 Pt-1/290-micron sieve / Blaine air permeabilityResidue ≤ 10% OPC, ≤ 5% RHPC; surface ≥ 225 m²/kg OPC, ≈ 325 m²/kg RHPC
Heat of hydrationIS 4031 Pt-8Vacuum flask calorimeterLow-heat cement ≤ 270 kJ/kg at 7 d, ≤ 314 at 28 d
Specific gravityIS 4031 Pt-11Le Chatelier flask with kerosene≈ 3.15

Causes of unsoundness: free lime (detected by Le Chatelier), free magnesia (detected by autoclave). Excess gypsum also causes unsoundness — and neither test catches it.

The course also quotes the older tensile briquette test: 3 days 20 kg/cm², 7 days 25 kg/cm², six specimens; and 1:3 mortar cubes reaching ≈ 115 kg/cm² at 3 days and 175 kg/cm² at 7 days.

D. Bulking of Sand

The phenomenon: surface moisture coats each grain with a water film, pushing grains apart. The volume of moist sand therefore grows above its dry volume. Bulking peaks at 20–30% when moisture is about 4–5%; beyond roughly 10% moisture the films break down and the volume falls back to the dry value.

Fig 1.8 — Bulking of sand: surface moisture films push grains apart → moist volume ↑; add water by bulking correction at batching

Field test (IS 2386 Pt-3): fill a measuring jar with moist sand, tamp it, note the volume V₁. Add water and stir until fully saturated; note the volume V₂.

% Bulking = (V₁ − V₂) / V₂ × 100

Why it matters: in volume batching you must add extra sand (the bulked volume) to get the required solid quantity, or the mix runs lean. Weigh batching needs no correction. Ignoring bulking also upsets the water demand and weakens the concrete.

E. Other Aggregate Tests (IS 2386)

  • Sieve analysis (IS 460 sieves): classifies sand into grading Zones I–IV. Zone I is coarsest (best for M25 and above); Zone IV is finest. Fineness modulus = sum of cumulative % retained on the standard sieves ÷ 100; fine aggregate FM runs 2.2–3.2 (typically 2.6–2.9).
  • Specific gravity & water absorption (Pt-3): pycnometer method; absorption < 2% for coarse aggregate.
  • Crushing value (Pt-4): 40 t applied for 10 minutes through a 25 mm gauge; % crushed < 30 for concrete surface wearing course.
  • Impact value (Pt-4): 15 hammer blows; < 30% for surface course, < 45% for base course.
  • Los Angeles abrasion (Pt-4): wear < 30–35% for concrete roads, < 50% for bituminous roads.
  • Flakiness & elongation indices: a particle is flaky if its thickness < 0.6 × mean sieve size. Flakiness index < 15–25% is desirable (max 35%).
  • Also asked: soundness (sodium/magnesium sulphate cycling), deleterious materials, organic impurities, alkali–aggregate reaction (expansive gel). Ten percent fines value varies inversely with crushing value.

F. Tensile Test of Rebar (IS 1786 / IS 1608)

The Universal Testing Machine (UTM) stretches a bar specimen ≥ 560 mm long over a gauge length of 5d for the elongation measurement (5.65√A for non-circular sections, IS 1608). The test reads the yield stress (0.2% proof stress for HYSD bars, which have no sharp yield point), the ultimate tensile strength (UTS), the % elongation, and the modulus of elasticity.

Fig 1.9 — Mild steel: elastic → yield → plateau → strain hardening → necking → cup–cone fracture (UTS > yield)
GradeMin yield (MPa)Min UTS (MPa)Min elongation
Fe 250 (IS 432, mild steel)25041023%
Fe 41541548514.5%
Fe 500500545 (D: 565)12% (D: 10%)
Fe 550550585 (D: 600)10%

The bend and re-bend test (mandrel 3d–7d, bent 180°) checks ductility and bendability. The "D" suffix means ductile — better for seismic design. Rolling margin on weight per length is ±7%.

High-yield numbers: Vicat plunger stops 5–7 mm above the bottom (consistency); IST ≥ 30 min; FST ≤ 600 min; Le Chatelier ≤ 10 mm; cement cube = 70.6 mm, 1:3 mortar, w/c = P/4 + 3%; bulking peak at 4–5% moisture; brick loading rate 14 N/mm²/min; Fe 415 UTS ≥ 485 MPa, elongation ≥ 14.5%.

1.3 Building Technology (ACiE0103)

A. Brick Masonry

Vocabulary

A brick shows its stretcher (long face) or its header (short face) on the wall. A course is one horizontal row. The bed joint is the horizontal mortar layer; the head (vertical) joint lies between bricks in a course. A wythe is a vertical section one brick thick. Cut bricks: a bat is cut across the width; a closer is cut along the length (king, queen, bevelled, mitred). A quoin is the corner block; a reveal is the jamb face of an opening. Lap is the horizontal offset between vertical joints of successive courses — minimum one-quarter of the brick length.

Bonds

BondPatternUse / remark
StretcherAll stretchers, half-lapHalf-brick partition walls, cavity walls
HeaderAll headersOne-brick-thick and curved walls; weak
EnglishHeader and stretcher courses alternate; queen closer after the first header of each header courseStrongest bond for load-bearing walls
FlemishHeader and stretcher alternate within every coursePrettier, slightly weaker, needs fewer facing bricks
Double FlemishFlemish in each wytheFlemish face on both sides of a 1-brick wall
Garden wallEnglish or Flemish with 3 stretcher courses to 1 header courseDecorative, low walls
Rat-trapBricks on edge with a cavitySaves 20–30% brick and mortar; better insulation; popular in Nepal
OthersDiagonal, Dutch, raking, zig-zag, hoop, monk, silverlock, herring-boneDecorative and patching work

Rules of good brickwork

  • Lay every brick frog up with the frog fully flooded with mortar.
  • Keep joints 10–12 mm (minimum 7 mm, maximum 15 mm); vertical joints must stagger — lap ≥ 1/4 brick.
  • Keep the wall plumb and level using the line and plumb-bob.
  • Build no higher than about 1.0–1.5 m per day (course value for half-brick walls: ≤ 1.0–1.5 m).
  • Soak bricks at least 1 hour before use (course value); cure the finished wall 7–10 days.
  • Strength rises with stronger bricks, thin dense joints and proper bonding; thick joints weaken the wall.

B. Stone Masonry

Rubble masonry uses undressed or roughly dressed stones. Uncoursed random rubble is the cheapest; coursed rubble lays stones in layers about 15–30 cm deep; dry rubble (no mortar) suits low retaining walls.

Ashlar masonry uses finely dressed stones with joints ≤ 3 mm — fine tooled ashlar is the best grade; other forms include rough tooled, chamfered, block-in-course and facing ashlar. Ashlar facing over rubble backing is the common economical composite.

Rules: lay each stone on its natural bed (perpendicular to the pressure it will carry); place headers through the wall about every 0.5 m² of face; never align vertical joints; cure with water for 2–3 days. Ashlar is stronger than rubble, and the joints are the weakest part of any stone wall.

C. Carpentry (Doors, Windows, Joints)

Door parts: the frame (head, jambs, sill, horns, holdfasts) and the shutter (styles/stiles, rails including the lock rail, panels, muntins).

Door types: battened and ledged / braced / braced-and-framed / framed-and-braced (economy, light rooms); framed-and-panelled (the residential standard); flush (plywood faces); glazed; louvered (ventilation); collapsible and rolling shutters (security); sliding; revolving; swing.

Rule-of-thumb sizes (Nepal): door height 2.0–2.1 m, width 0.8–1.0 m; window 1.0 × 1.2 m or 1.2 × 1.5 m; sill height 0.9 m.

Timber joints: lengthening joints (scarf — halved, fished, keyed); widening joints (tongue & groove, matchboarding); angle joints (mortise & tenon, dowel, bridle, halving, dovetail, housing).

Tool families: marking (rule, square, marking gauge), sawing (rip, cross-cut, tenon, compass), planing (jack, smoothing, rebate, plough), boring (brace, auger, gimlet), chiselling (firmer, mortise, paring), driving (hammer, mallet, screwdriver).

D. Painting

Sequence on plaster: putty filling → primer (cement primer or exterior sealer) → first and second top coats, sanding between coats. On timber: knotting → priming → stopping → undercoats → finishing.

Coverage: distemper 1 kg / 8–10 m²; emulsion 1 L / 10–14 m² (2 coats); enamel 1 L / 8–10 m². Nepal practice: 3 coats enamel on wood (1 primer + 1 under + 1 finish); putty + 1 primer + 2 emulsion coats on walls.

E. Plastering

Purpose: smooth and protect the surface, conceal masonry joints, and provide the base for painting.

Thicknesses: internal 12 mm (Nepal 12–15 mm), external 15–20 mm (Nepal 20 mm), ceiling 6 mm (Nepal 6–8 mm).

Mortar ratios: 1:3 for surfaces exposed to moisture (soaked/marine); 1:4 internal sponged finish; 1:5 or 1:6 general internal and external work; lime plaster 1:3 lime-sand.

Types: lime; cement (plain, sponged, sand-faced); rough cast / spatter dash (1:1.5:3 to 1:2:6); pebble dash; depressed; mosaic (marmarite); textone; stucco (3-coat decorative); gypsum plaster (POP); acoustic plaster.

Process: fix ground mortar strips (2–3 m horizontal screeds) → fill between them → float with a wooden float → finish with steel trowel → cure 7 days.

Defects: cracking (fast drying, thick coats, settlement), efflorescence, flaking and peeling, puffing/blistering, hollowness (found by tapping), rust stains, damp patches, out-of-plumb walls.

F. Concrete Roofing and Flooring

RCC slab roofs run 100–125 mm thick. Waterproofing options: brickbat coba (brickbats with lime/cement, slope 1:50–1:100), IPS + screed, bituminous membrane, polyurethane coating, or the inverted roof (XPS above the membrane). Rural Nepal commonly uses GI corrugated sheets (0.45–0.63 mm) or traditional mud, jack-arch and timber-shingle roofs.

Slopes: flat roofs minimum 1:50 to 1:100; pitched roofs 15–20° for tiles, 5–10° for metal sheets.

Flooring build-up: sub-grade → soling/sub-base → base concrete (PCC 1:4:8, 75–100 mm) → finish (IPS 1:2:4 at 20–40 mm, or tiles 8–12 mm on 20–25 mm bedding). Types include mud, brick, stone (kota, marble, granite), cement concrete, mosaic/terrazzo, ceramic and vitrified tiles, timber (plank, strip, parquet), rubber, cork, linoleum, PVC and epoxy. Provide the DPC at plinth level below the floor; slope bathroom floors 1:50–1:100.

G. Damp Proof Course (DPC)

Why dampness enters: rising damp through capillaries, rain penetration, condensation, leaky roofs, defective drainage.

Materials: hot bitumen (1.5–2 kg/m², 2 coats); bituminous felt/membrane; cement concrete 1:2:4, 20 mm thick with waterproofing compound; metal sheets (lead, copper, aluminium); mastic asphalt 25 mm; polythene sheet 0.2–0.5 mm; stone slabs 20 mm; crystalline (PVA-based) compounds.

Placement rules: lay the horizontal DPC at plinth level, 150–450 mm above ground level, full wall thickness, continuous over the whole width, never over openings. Lap joints 100 mm. The vertical DPC sits at the parapet junction on the outer face. Lime-based DPC is not used — it is permeable; cement concrete DPC with about 2% waterproofing compound is standard.

Other damp-control methods: cavity walls, surface paints, integral waterproofing, guniting, pressure grouting, water-repellent plaster, and drainage provisions.

H. Building Byelaws (Nepal — NBC & local rules)

NBC structure (authoritative course catalogue)

Part 1 — Codes (detailed design)Part 2 — Mandatory Rules of Thumb
NBC 101 material specifications · 102 unit weight · 103 imposed loads · 104 wind · 105 seismic design · 106 snow · 107 fire · 108 site considerations · 109 masonry · 110 concrete · 111 steel · 112 timber · 113 aluminium · 114 construction safety · 115 energy efficiencyNBC 201 RC buildings with masonry infill · 202 load-bearing masonry · 203 low-strength masonry · 204 earthen buildings · 205 RC without masonry infill · 206 architectural design · 207 electrical · 208 sanitary & plumbing

Key numeric rules (Kathmandu Valley practice)

  • FAR = total built-up floor area ÷ plot area. NBC 206 leaves FAR to the local byelaws, which fix the permitted FAR — and the height limit that follows — from the plot size, road width and zone, so always read the byelaw of the concerned municipality
  • Ground coverage (Model / Kathmandu Valley Building Byelaws §4.4): residential and mixed-residential buildings may cover up to 70% of plots of 250 m² or less and 60% of larger plots; all other buildings up to 50% of the plot area
  • Setbacks (residential): front 1.5–3 m (varies with road width per local byelaw), side 0.6–1.5 m, rear 1.2–1.5 m.
  • Minimum room sizes: a habitable room (bedroom/living) ≥ 6 m² with a minimum dimension of 2.0 m; kitchen ≥ 5 m² (min 1.8 m); water closet ≥ 1.2 m² (min 0.9 m); bathroom ≥ 1.8 m²; combined WC + bathroom ≥ 2.8 m² (NBC 206:2015 §3.2.2); corridor and stair widths are fixed by the local byelaw
  • Room / ceiling heights (NBC 206:2015 §3.2.1): all habitable rooms ≥ 2.4 m floor-to-ceiling (2.4 m average under a pitched roof); ≥ 2.1 m clear headroom under a beam or false ceiling; bathroom/WC ≥ 2.0 m; office and commercial ≥ 2.9 m; assembly, hospital, educational and industrial ≥ 3.2 m (hills) or 3.6 m (Terai).
  • Staircase (NBC 206:2015 Table 4): residence tread ≥ 250 mm and riser ≤ 190 mm; other buildings tread ≥ 279 mm and riser ≤ 175 mm; maximum 15 risers per flight; headroom under a flight ≥ 2.0 m; handrail 900 mm.
  • Light and ventilation: openings for light and ventilation ≥ 1/10 of the room's floor area (NBC 206:2015 §3.3); door area ≈ 1/20; at least 2 windows per room.
  • Height limits follow FAR and road width; some municipalities make lifts mandatory above 4 storeys.

Purpose of byelaws: orderly growth, structural and fire safety, health (light, ventilation, sanitation), aesthetics, traffic flow, and infrastructure capacity.

Traps: English bond is strongest; Flemish is prettier. DPC sits 150–450 mm above ground, never lime-based. Window = 1/10 of floor area; door = 1/20. Residential minimum room height 2.4 m (NBC 206:2015 §3.2.1). FAR = built-up ÷ plot area.

1.4 Geometric Properties of Sections (ACiE0104)

A. Axes of Symmetry & Centre of Gravity

An axis of symmetry is an imaginary line that divides a figure into two mirror halves — reflect one half across the axis and it exactly overlaps the other. A plane figure can have none, one, two or infinitely many axes; the centroid always lies on every axis of symmetry, so with two axes the centroid sits where they cross. Counting axes is a repeated NEC one-marker:

FigureAxes of symmetryFigureAxes of symmetry
Scalene triangle0Rectangle2
Isosceles triangle1Square4
Equilateral triangle3Rhombus2
Trapezoid (general)0 (isosceles: 1)Parallelogram0
Kite1Regular n-gonn
Ellipse2Circleinfinite
Fig 1.10 — Axes of symmetry (dashed blue) — course-deck catalogue. The centroid lies on every axis of symmetry; two axes intersect at the centroid. A parallelogram and a general trapezoid have none.

The centroid (C) is the geometric centre of the shape — the point where the total area of a plane figure is thought to be concentrated. It coincides with the centre of gravity only when gravity is uniform and the material is homogeneous (for a homogeneous body, CG of mass = centroid; CG may even lie outside the body, e.g. a ring or an L-section).

Centroid of plane figures

FigureCentroidArea
Rectangle b × db/2, d/2 (where diagonals cross)bd
Triangle (base b, height h)h/3 above the base; 2h/3 below the vertex; where medians meetbh/2
Semicircle (radius r)4r/3π ≈ 0.424 r above the diameterπr²/2
Quarter circle4r/3π from both edgesπr²/4
Circlecentreπr²
Parabolic spandrel (vertex at corner, axis along b)3b/4 from the vertex = b/4 from the taller edge (along the base)bh/3
Semi-parabola (vertex above mid-base)3b/8 from each end of the base; 2h/5 above the base2bh/3
Trapezium (parallel sides a, b; height h)h/3 × (b + 2a)/(b + a) from side bh(a + b)/2
Composite sections: x̄ = ΣAᵢxᵢ / ΣAᵢ ; ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ / ΣAᵢ — holes count as negative area.

Centroids of lines and curved boundaries

For thin rods or curved edges the centroid lies on the element itself, not inside an area:

Line figureCentroid from the centre O (along the symmetry axis)
Quarter-circular arc (radius r)2r/π ≈ 0.637 r from O along each radius — i.e. 2√2·r/π from each edge end
Semicircular arc (radius r)2r/π ≈ 0.637 r from the centre O, on the axis of symmetry (from the diameter: 2r/π)
Circular arc of half-angle α (radius r)r·sin α / α from O

General spandrel y = h·(x/a)ⁿ (the deck's general case covering all parabolic shapes): x̄ = (n+1)a/(n+2) from the y-axis; ȳ = (n+1)h / [2(2n+1)] from the base; area A = ah/(n+1). Check it: n = 1 gives a triangle (x̄ = 2a/3); n = 2 gives the parabolic spandrel (x̄ = 3a/4, ȳ = 3h/10) and its complementary semi-parabolic area (x̄ = 3a/8, ȳ = 3h/5) — the same values tabulated above.

Centroids of solids (course values): solid prism z̄ = h/2 with V = Ah; solid pyramid or cone z̄ = h/4 above the base with V = Ah/3; hollow (thin) pyramid or cone z̄ = h/3 above the base; hemisphere z̄ = 3r/8 with V = 2πr³/3. In a right-angle triangle the centroid and the geometric centre do not coincide.

Standard steel sections (IS 808 / IS Handbook No. 1) publish weight per metre, geometric dimensions, I, Z and k — you read them from tables rather than compute them. A single angle is eccentric: its centroidal distances along xx and yy differ. For a T-section the centroid lies on the vertical axis of symmetry.
