B. Moment of Inertia (Second Moment of Area)

SectionIxx (centroidal)IyyOther
Rectangle b (width) × d (depth)bd³/12db³/12About the base: bd³/3
Triangle (base b, height h)bh³/36—About the base: bh³/12
Circle (dia d)πd⁴/64πd⁴/64Polar J = πd⁴/32
Semicircle (radius r)0.11 r⁴—About the base: πr⁴/8 = πD⁴/128
Hollow circleπ(D⁴ − d⁴)/64sameJ = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32
Ellipse (semi-axes a, b)πba³/4πab³/4—
Square (side s)s⁴/12s⁴/12About a diagonal: also s⁴/12

Triangle ratios worth remembering: base : centroidal = 12 : 36 → 1 : 3; centroidal : top axis = 1 : 9. Quarter-circle I ≈ 0.055 R⁴. A cylinder about its own central axis: MR²/2 — but for a circular area the exam form is πd⁴/64.

Theorems

Parallel axis: I = Ig + A·h² — h is the distance between the two parallel axes; Ig is the minimum among all parallel axes.
Perpendicular axis (plane lamina): Iz = Ix + Iy — the polar moment of inertia.
Composite: I = ΣIg,i + ΣAᵢhᵢ² (holes negative). Product of inertia Ixy = ∫xy dA; where Ixy = 0 the axes are principal.
Principal moments: (Ixx + Iyy)/2 ± √[((Ixx − Iyy)/2)² + Ixy²]

Radius of gyration and section modulus

k = √(I/A) — rectangle: d/√12 ≈ 0.289 d; circle: d/4.
Z = I / y_max — rectangle bd²/6; circle πd³/32; hollow circle π(D⁴−d⁴)/(32D); polar Zp = J/r.

Where each is used: the column slenderness ratio = effective length ÷ k, and the minimum k (weak axis) governs buckling. Bending stress σ = M/Z in the elastic range. The plastic modulus Zp > Z, and the shape factor = Zp/Z: rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, I-section 1.1–1.2, diamond 2.0 (the theoretical maximum).

More Depth: 1.4 — Worked Concepts and Standard Steel Sections

Worked example (composite I-section, symmetric). Top and bottom flanges 100 × 10 mm, web 10 × 200 mm, overall depth 220 mm:

A = 2(100×10) + 10×200 = 4000 mm²
ȳ from bottom = [100×10×5 + 10×200×110 + 100×10×215] / 4000 = (5,000 + 220,000 + 215,000)/4000 = 110 mm — the mid-depth, since the section is symmetric
Ixx = 2[100×10³/12 + 1000×(105)²] + 10×200³/12 = 2×(8,333 + 11,025,000) + 6.67×10⁶ ≈ 28.73 × 10⁶ mm⁴
Symmetric-section shortcut: if the flanges are equal, ȳ is simply half the overall depth and the centroid shift terms cancel — compute I of each part about its own centroid (bh³/12) and add A·h² for the parts that sit away from the axis. For this section the web contributes 6.67×10⁶ mm⁴ and each flange ≈ 11.03×10⁶ mm⁴.
  • Product of inertia Ixy = ∫xy dA. For a section symmetric about an axis, Ixy = 0 and the axes of symmetry are principal axes. (For the composite rectangle example: Ixy comes out negative and the principal axes are rotated — solved by tan 2θ = −2Ixy/(Ixx − Iyy) or by Mohr's circle of inertia, exactly analogous to stress.)
  • Principal moments of inertia: I_max,min = (Ixx + Iyy)/2 ± √[((Ixx − Iyy)/2)² + Ixy²] — rotation angle θp = ½·atan(−2Ixy/(Ixx − Iyy)); Ixy = 0 on the principal axes.
  • Why I-sections are efficient: the flanges sit far from the neutral axis (high I for little area) while the web carries shear; Z = I/y_max comes out large, so bending stress stays low.
  • Shape factor (Zp/Z): rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, I-section ~1.1–1.2, diamond 2.0 (theoretical maximum). Used in plastic analysis.

1.5 Surveying and Levelling (ACiE0105)

A. Fundamentals of Surveying

Surveying is the art and science of determining the relative positions of points or stations on (above or below) the earth's surface by measuring distances, directions and elevations. It is the first step of any civil engineering project. Primary aims: measure horizontal distance and vertical elevation between points; find relative and absolute direction of lines (horizontal angles against an arbitrary direction, absolute direction against a fixed/true direction).

Principles of surveying (course deck + book)

  • Work from whole to part — establish high-precision primary control over the whole area first, then fill in minor control and details with less precise methods. Purpose: to localize errors and prevent their accumulation. (The single most-asked principle.)
  • Locate a point from at least two reference points of known position — gives check lines and tie lines (a third measurement gives a check).
  • Independent check — every field measurement must be re-checked by a suitable independent method so no mistake passes unnoticed.
  • Accuracy required — choose method and instrument for the degree of accuracy the work demands.
  • Consistency — keep the same standard in method, instrument, reading and booking throughout.

Plane vs geodetic: plane surveying treats the earth as flat — areas less than 250–260 km², low precision, private agencies; geodetic surveying accounts for curvature — large areas, high precision, national level, done in Nepal by the Survey Department. The earth is an oblate spheroid (equatorial axis 12,756.75 km; polar axis 12,713.80 km). Scale of the effect: an 18.2 km arc is only 1 cm longer than its chord (1 mm at 1.2 km; 0.3 m at 54.3 km; 0.5 m at 91 km), and a spherical triangle's angle sum exceeds a plane triangle's by 1 second per ~195 km² of area.

Classifications (book): by nature of the field — land (topographic, cadastral, city), hydrographic/marine, astronomical; by purpose — engineering (reconnaissance → preliminary → location surveys), mine, geological, archaeological, military; by instrument — chain, compass, plane table, theodolite, tacheometric, photographic/aerial, modern (GPS); by method — triangulation, traverse, trilateration. Cadastral/revenue mapping of field boundaries = cross-staff survey.

Scales & RF: representative fraction = map distance ÷ ground distance (1 cm = 5 m → RF 1:500). Large scale RF > 1/1000; intermediate 1/1000–1/10000; small < 1/10000. Plain scale reads two units (m, dm); diagonal scale reads three (m, dm, cm); vernier scale reads fractional parts — a direct vernier has its smallest division shorter than the main-scale division (the NEC MCQ case), a retrograde vernier longer.

B. Linear Measurement (Chains, Tapes, Ranging)

Three families of methods: direct (pacing, passometer, pedometer, odometer, chain and tape), optical (tacheometry — theodolite fitted with stadia hairs), and EDM/total station (horizontal angle + vertical angle + sloping distance in one shot). Buildings allow ranging but not chaining (walls obstruct the band).

Chain / tapeDetail
Metric chain5/10/20/30 m, galvanized mild steel; 20 m chain accurate to within ±8 mm; tallies every 5 m; handles joined to links by swivel joints
Steel band / band chain20 or 30 m, stainless steel, uniform width
Gunter's chain (surveyor's)66 ft — land surveying
Engineer's chain100 ft — construction
Revenue chain33 ft — cadastral survey
TapesCloth/linen; metallic (varnished waterproof linen interwoven with brass/copper wires); steel (best field accuracy); invar (36% Ni + 64% steel, lowest expansion — highest precision); synthetic

Ranging rods 2 m and 3 m (2 m very common) painted in 20 cm bands; ranging poles 4–6 m for very long lines. Chain surveying works on the principle of triangulation — a network of well-conditioned triangles (every angle 30°–120°, ideally 60°). Survey lines: main (skeleton), base, check lines (proof lines — verify accuracy), and tie lines — provided primarily to avoid long offsets from chain lines (NEC MCQ). Offsets: short < 15 m, long > 15 m; perpendicular when unobstructed, oblique for distant objects.

Optical method — tacheometry (rapid survey)

A tacheometer is a theodolite fitted with stadia hairs in addition to the central cross-hair; the fixed-hair method is the most used (deck note), the tangential method serves telescopes without stadia hairs, and the subtense bar works without a staff intercept. The stadia principle rests on an isosceles-triangle property — the ratio of base distance to base length is constant:

D = K·s + C — K = multiplying constant = f/i (normally 100); s = staff intercept
C = additive constant = f + d ≈ 0.1–0.3 m (zero with an anallatic lens — fitted in external-focusing telescopes only)
Elevation: V = (K·s·sinθ·cosθ)/2 (+ C·sinθ); RL = HI + V − mid-wire reading

Accuracy 1:250 to 1:1000 — quick but coarser than levelling; ideal for contouring rough terrain, river sections and triangulation figures.

C. Tape Corrections (all five + normal tension)

Standardization: correction per tape length C = l′ − l (l′ actual, l nominal); sign follows l′ − l
True length = measured length × (corrected length of tape / nominal length of tape)
Temperature: Ct = α(Tm − To)L — α linear expansion coeff., Tm mean tape temp., To standard temp.
Pull: Cp = (P − Po)L / (A·E) — P applied pull, Po standard pull, A cross-section, E Young's modulus
Sag: Cs = W²L/(24P²) = w²L³/(24P²) — always subtractive (tape hangs in a catenary)
Normal tension: Pn = W·√(A·E) / √(24(Pn − Po)) — the pull that neutralizes sag against pull
Slope: Cs = −h²/2L (first order) — measured slope length > horizontal, so correction always negative; second order h⁴/8L³; with vertical angle θ: Ch = −L·sin²θ (approx.)
MSL: lengths above MSL reduce (earth's level falls away); correction ∝ +L·h/R (sign per convention) — know it exists; MCQ asks only the slope/sag signs

D. Errors in Surveying

  • Mistakes (gross errors / blunders) — carelessness, inexperience (reading a 6 as 9); cannot be calculated, eliminated only by checking.
  • Systematic / cumulative errors — follow a definite physical or mathematical law, so a correction can be applied (imperfect instrument length, temperature, sag). A tape P cm short stretched N times gives PN cm total error.
  • Compensating errors — occur in both directions and tend to cancel (sag one time, excess pull the next); follow the theory of probability.
  • Accidental / random errors — unavoidable (atmospheric variation, limit of human eye); also governed by probability; cannot be corrected, only minimized.
  • Discrepancy = the difference between two measured values of the same quantity (deck MCQ).
  • Accuracy vs precision: accuracy = closeness to the true value; precision = closeness of repeated observations to each other.

E. Compass Survey (Bearings & Traverse)

Meridians: true (astronomical — geographic poles), magnetic (direction a free needle settles), grid (map-sheet central meridian), arbitrary (assumed, e.g. a chimney top). Bearing = horizontal angle of a line measured from a meridian.

  • WCB system (whole circle / azimuthal): 0–360° clockwise from north — prismatic compass.
  • QB system (quadrantal / reduced): 0–90° from N or S (whichever nearer), E or W — surveyor's compass. Both compasses have least count 30′.
  • Conversion: WCB 240° → S 60° W. On a cardinal direction FB and BB are numerically equal with opposite quadrant letters (N 30° E ↔ S 30° W).
  • FB and BB: BB = FB ± 180° (add if FB < 180°, subtract if > 180°). If BB − FB ≠ 180°, suspect local attraction (magnetic material near a station). Correct by interior angles, or start/end on unaffected lines.
  • Traverse adjustment: Bowditch (compass) rule — corrections ∝ length of the line, used when linear and angular measurement are of equal precision; transit rule — corrections ∝ magnitude of latitude/departure, when angular work is more precise. Latitude = L·cos θ (± N/S), departure = L·sin θ (± E/W).

F. Levelling

Definitions: reduced level (RL) — height relative to datum; benchmark (BM) — GTS, permanent, arbitrary, temporary; backsight (BS) — first reading after setup, on a known RL; foresight (FS) — last reading before moving; intermediate sight (IS); change/turning point (CP/TP).

Height of instrument: HI = RL + BS (add BS to known RL)
New RL = HI − IS or HI − FS (subtract any sight from HI)
Rise & fall: reading difference = BS − IS/FS — positive gives a rise, negative gives a fall (each reading compared with the one before it)
Checks: HI method — ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL (no check on IS)
Rise & fall — ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL (complete check — preferred)
  • HI (plane of collimation) method is quicker and less tedious when there are many intermediate sights (PANA one-liner); rise-and-fall gives the full arithmetic check.
  • Curvature & refraction: curvature makes the staff reading too large — error +, correction −0.0785 D² m (D in km); refraction is 1/7 of curvature but opposite in nature, correction +0.0112 D² m; combined correction −0.0673 D² m (always subtractive).
  • Types: differential/spirit (most precise common), fly (quick BM transfer, BS/FS only), check, profile/longitudinal (plus cross-sections), reciprocal (across rivers/valleys — eliminates collimation, curvature and refraction effects), trigonometric (vertical angle + distance for inaccessible heights).
  • Instruments: dumpy (fixed telescope), tilting, automatic (compensator — most used today), digital (barcode staff).
Fig 1.13 — Levelling in one picture: backsight to a benchmark fixes the height of instrument; any later RL = HI − sight. The arithmetic check ties the whole page together (HI method check ignores intermediate sights). FS < BS ⇒ rise ⇒ CP higher than BM (scale 1 m = 100 px).

G. Contouring and Topographic Survey

Topographic survey (deck definition): the survey carried out to depict the topography of mountainous terrain, rivers, water bodies, wooded areas and cultural details (roads, railways, townships). Users: engineers, architects, government agencies, forestry, construction. Main methods: traversing, radiation, offset, triangulation. The deck's working principles: record field boundaries immediately after instrument orientation; record features with coordinates + levels + unique IDs; capture 'topo' points for elevation; use break lines (point sequences along feature edges) so surfaces can be reconstructed in the office; reference all points to a common datum.

Plane table surveying (the map is drawn in the field)

Instruments: board, alidade (plain or telescopic), plumbing fork, spirit level, compass, sheet. Four methods: radiation (sight points from one station), intersection (sight from two stations — ideal for inaccessible points), traversing (progressive, closed by the last line), and resection (locate the station itself — the three-point problem, solved by tracing paper, trial-and-error, Bessel or Lehmann methods; the two-point problem uses two known points). Merits: quick, cheap, no booking errors. Demerits: weather-dependent, low precision, unusable at night or in rain.

  • Contour = imaginary line joining points of equal elevation; contour interval is constant on one map and is chosen inversely proportional to map scale (smaller CI on flat ground).
  • Properties: contours never cross (exception: overhanging cliff) and never merge (exception: vertical cliff); close spacing = steep slope; closed loops rising inward = hill, falling inward = depression; V pointing uphill = valley; U/V pointing downhill = ridge/spur; equally spaced = uniform slope.
  • Uses: site selection, alignment studies, reservoir capacity (Σ contour area × interval), cut-and-fill balancing, drainage/inter-visibility analysis.

H. Simple Circular Curves

A simple circular curve joins two intersecting straights with one constant radius for smooth, safe vehicle movement. Elements (book p. 96 catalogue): back tangent and forward tangent meeting at the point of intersection (PI, apex); PC/TC (point of curve — beginning) and PT/CT (point of tangency — end); intersection angle φ and deflection angle Δ (φ + Δ = 180°).

Fig 1.14 — Elements of a simple circular curve: tangent length T = R·tan(Δ/2); length of curve L = πRΔ/180 (Δ in degrees); long chord C = 2R·sin(Δ/2); external (apex) distance E = R[sec(Δ/2) − 1]; mid-ordinate (versine) M = R[1 − cos(Δ/2)]. Chainage: TC = PI − T; CT = TC + L. φ + Δ = 180°; drawn true to scale for Δ = 60°, R = 200 (T = 115.5, E = 30.9, M = 26.8, C = 200)
T = R tan(Δ/2) ; L = πRΔ/180 ; C = 2R sin(Δ/2) ; E = R[sec(Δ/2) − 1] ; M = R[1 − cos(Δ/2)]
Degree of curve: D = 1720/R for a 30 m chord; D = 1146/R for a 20 m chord (R in m)
Rankine deflection angle for chord c: δ = 1718.9 × c/R minutes (first chord c/2; successive full chords)
Setting out — linear: offsets from the long chord; offsets from tangents (perpendicular / radial); offsets from chord produced; successive bisection of chords. Angular: Rankine's deflection-angle method (most accurate), two-theodolite method.
  • Obstacles in chaining (also an H-topic in the deck): to ranging but not chaining — reciprocal ranging; to chaining but not ranging (river) — similar triangles; to both — go around (random line, 3-4-5 perpendicular, equilateral-triangle constructions).
  • Transition curves (spiral/cubic parabola) introduce super-elevation gradually: length by rate of change of centrifugal acceleration Ls = 0.0215 V³/(C·R) (V in km/h, C in m/s³) or by super-elevation introduction Ls = N·e·W; equilibrium super-elevation e = V²/(gR), maximum 7% (plain terrain, IRC), friction limited to f ≤ 0.15. Vertical curves are parabolic — summit (crest) and sag (valley), length from sight distance with K = L/A.

Instrument quick facts (deck/book): least counts — prismatic compass 30′, surveyor's compass 30′, theodolite 20″. The cross-staff sets 90° offsets; the optical square uses double reflection through 45° mirrors. Theodolite-traverse closure ≈ 5√n to 15√n seconds (by class); linear closure 1:5000–1:20000.

I. GPS and GIS

  • GPS principle: satellite-based navigation using signals to determine position, velocity and time of a receiver — based on trilateration (ranges from satellites). Minimum 4 satellites for a 3D fix (3 coordinates + receiver-clock correction); 3 satellites for 2D. History (deck-confirmed): US DoD launched the project in 1973; first prototype satellite 1978; the full 24-satellite constellation became operational in 1993. Accuracy: SPS ≈ 5–10 m; DGPS 0.5–3 m; RTK 1–2 cm. Uses: surveying and mapping, navigation, agriculture, transportation.
  • GIS principle: a computer-based system to capture, store, manipulate, analyse, retrieve and display data related to the earth's surface. The term was coined by Roger Tomlinson (Canada, 1968); GIS represents a location in three-dimensional coordinates (deck MCQs). Five components: hardware, software, data, people, methods. Applications: urban planning, natural-resource management, environmental management, watershed analysis, transportation planning, disaster mitigation, cadastral information systems, utility planning, EIA.
Too short / too long (error vs correction): error = measured − true. Too short chain/tape (e.g. used length less than nominal): measured distance reads more than true → error positive, correction negative; true length = (actual/nominal) × measured. Too long: measured reads less than true → error negative, correction positive.

1.6 Estimating, Costing, and Valuation (ACiE0106)

A. Estimation Basics

Estimation is the approximate calculation of the quantities of various items of work and the probable cost of construction, done before the actual construction. Actual cost is what the project really costs on completion — a good estimate keeps the deviation between estimated and actual cost to a minimum. Data required (deck): fully dimensioned drawings (plan, elevation, sections), schedule of rates (government-approved), specifications (general and detailed), and the method of measurement.

B. Types of Estimate

TypeWhen / purposeKey numbers (course values)
Preliminary / approximate / roughAdministrative approval, feasibility, taxation, valuation, insurance — prepared by the owner/clientbased on plinth area / cube rate / unit rate
— Plinth-area estimateplinth area × rate per m² of a similar buildingplinth area = floor area + wall area; carpet = livable area; carpet ≈ 50–65% of plinth area (residential, book)
— Cube-rate estimatevolume × rate per m³more accurate than plinth area
— Unit-rate estimateper km of road, per bed (hospital), per student (school), per seat (cinema), per m of bridgeservice-unit method
Detailed / item-rate estimateafter administrative sanction; quantities × unit rate per item; most reliablequantity surveying → BOQ; abstract of cost; contingencies 5–10% + work-charge establishment ≈ 2% (book)
Revised estimateoriginal sanctioned estimate likely to be exceeded by more than 5% (rates found insufficient) or expenditure exceeding / likely to exceed the administrative approval by 10%; or material deviation of designcomparison table of original vs revised required
Supplementary estimateadditional works thought necessary while work is in progress, not provisioned originallyabstract shows original + supplementary amounts
Annual repair & maintenanceyearly upkeep of the property≤ 1.5% of capital cost; annual + special repair ≤ 2.5% (deck)
Extension & improvementchanges/extensions beyond what annual repair can covera detailed estimate of the additional works
Complete estimateall related costs: land, feasibility/survey, design, fee, services, maintenance (book)—

C. Methods of Estimating (quantity take-off)

  • Long wall–short wall (out-to-out / in-to-in) method: long walls measured out-to-out = centre-to-centre length + half breadth at each end; short walls in-to-in = c/c length − half breadth at each end. Most accurate; suits unsymmetrical / complicated buildings; less chance of mistake.
  • Centre-line method: total centre-line length × breadth × depth. Quickest and easiest; suits circular, hexagonal, octagonal buildings; more chance of mistake. Junction deductions (PANA): L-junction — none; T-junction — 0.5 × breadth; cross (+) junction — 1 × breadth.
  • Crossing method: overall perimeter − 4 × wall thickness = total centre-line length.
  • Bay method: cost of one bay × number of bays — garages, factories, railway platforms (identical bays).
  • Service-unit method: cost per service unit (bed, seat, student, km) × number of units — colleges, hospitals, cinemas, prisons.

D. Rate Analysis

Total unit rate = A (materials) + B (labour: skilled + semi-skilled + unskilled) + C (T&P hire = 3% of unskilled labour) + D (contractor's overhead & profit = 15% of (A+B+C) = 10% profit + 5% overhead)
  • VAT is not included in rate analysis (deck note).
  • Overall labour cost of a building ≈ 25% of total construction cost (deck).
  • Purpose (book): fix current local rates, check the viability of a contractor's quoted rate, calculate material and labour quantities, settle contractor–client disputes, insurance compensation, identify resources.
  • Affects the rate: quality/quantity of materials, construction facilities, technology, site location, material availability, overheads.

Worked rate analysis — per m³ brickwork in 1:4 cement mortar

ComponentQuantityNotes
Bricks500 nos (often 520 with 5% wastage)modular count
Cement≈ 1.5 bags (75 kg)dry mortar 0.3 m³; 1:4 → cement ≈ 0.06 m³ ≈ 86 kg (varies by spec)
Sand≈ 0.24–0.27 m³adjusted for bulking
Mason0.8–1.0 dayoutput ≈ 1.25 m³/day
Helper / mazdoor1.5–2.0 daysmixing, carrying, scaffolding
Waterlump summixing + curing

E. Specifications

A specification is the specific description of a particular item of work — nature and class of work, materials, proportions, workmanship — and a part of the contract documentation. Why needed: drawings cannot show quality of materials, proportion, workmanship or execution method; specifications never mention dimensions (dimensions live on the drawings). Purpose (deck): specify the nature of work; estimate quantity and cost; clarify ambiguity; identify quality of materials, material proportions, and type of workmanship.

General (brief) specificationDetailed specification
Brief description of nature and class of work and names of materials for every item — gives the general idea of the whole work; useful for estimating; not part of the contract document (e.g. "1st class brickwork in 1:6 cement mortar")Qualities, quantities and proportions of materials plus method of preparation and execution, item by item; written in the same sequence as the work is carried out; forms part of the contract document

F. Valuation

Valuation is the technique of finding the fair price of a property (building, land, other structures). Purposes: buying/selling, taxation, rent fixation (rent usually 6–10% of valuation, book), security of loans/mortgage (loan ≈ 50–70% of value, book), compulsory acquisition/compensation, insurance and betterment.

Terms you must be able to define

TermMeaning (course values)
Market valueprice obtainable at any time on the open market — fluctuates with demand and supply
Book valueoriginal cost − depreciation to date (what the account book shows)
Distress / forced-sale valuesold below market value under pressure — seller's financial difficulty, war/riot panic, partner quarrels, ignorance of market
Salvage valuevalue at end of utility period without dismantling (sold as-is)
Scrap valuevalue of dismantled materials; book: 7–10% of construction cost (course MCQ ≈ 10%)
Rateable valuevalue ascribed to a building (size, location, etc.) to determine the rent payable
Sentimental valuehigher-than-market price realized through sentiment
Outgoingsexpenses to maintain the property: taxes, periodic repairs, management & collection, sinking fund, loss of rent
Net incomenet income = gross income − outgoings
Capitalized valuethe amount whose interest at the highest prevailing rate equals the net income: capitalized value = net income × year's purchase
Year's purchase (YP)capital sum required to receive an annuity of Re 1: YP = 100/rate% = 1/i; with sinking fund: YP = 1/(i + S), S = sinking-fund coefficient = iₛ/[(1 + iₛ)ⁿ − 1]
Sinking fundperiodic deposit accumulating to replace the property at the end of its useful life (also used to repay loans)
Obsolescencevalue loss from outdated style/design/technology — not physical decay
Depreciationloss of value from structural deterioration, wear & tear, decay, obsolescence
Annuityreturn of capital in annual instalments for a fixed number of years
Mortgageproperty conveyed as loan security; loan usually 50–70% of property cost
Depreciation methods:
Straight line: D = (C − S)/n each year (book value falls linearly)
Constant percentage / declining balance: Dn = C(1 − p)ⁿ⁻¹·p ; p = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n)
Sinking-fund method: depreciation = annual sinking-fund instalment + interest on the fund that year; book value decreases at an increasing rate

Methods of valuation: (1) rental method — value = land + net income × YP; (2) direct comparison of capital value with similar properties; (3) profit-based — cinemas, hotels, commercial complexes (net profit × YP); (4) cost-based — land + present construction cost − depreciation; (5) development method — for land to be plotted/developed (developed value − development cost); (6) depreciation method — land + depreciated value of building.

Worked example (deck): useful life 30 years, interest 5%, sinking-fund rate 3% → S = 0.03/(1.03³⁰ − 1) = 0.021; YP = 1/(0.05 + 0.021) = 14.08 ≈ 14.

Valuation extras (course capsules)

  • Outgoings run 15–25% of gross rent: repairs ≈ 1.5%/yr of building cost, sinking fund 1.5–2%, taxes, insurance 0.3–0.5%, management 3–5% of rent.
  • Sinking-fund deposit: S = (C − Sc) × i / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] — annual deposits that replace the asset at end of life n.
  • Capitalized value worked example: rent 100,000/yr, outgoings 20%, i = 8% → net 80,000, YP = 12.5 → value 1,000,000.

G. Measurement, Units and Out-turns

  • Precision (book/deck): linear measurement to the nearest 0.01 m; areas to 0.01 m²; volumes to 0.01 m³. Order of booking dimensions: length × breadth × height (NEC MCQ).
  • Running metre (r.m.): cornice, coping, expansion/contraction joints, railing, pipe. Quintal: steel reinforcement and ironwork — binding wire 0.9–1.2 kg per quintal of rebar. m²: plastering, pointing, DPC, formwork, painting, whitewashing, flooring, skirting, honeycomb brickwork, brick flat soling, half-brick walls/partitions. m³: earthwork, concrete (PCC/RCC), brick/stone masonry in foundation and superstructure, wood frames. Numbers: wash basin, doors, windows.
  • Expected out-turn: 2.5 cm cement-concrete floor ≈ 7.5 m² per mason per day (deck MCQ).
  • Steel in RCC when not specified: take 0.6–1% of RCC volume (deck MCQ).
  • Nepal land units: 1 ropani = 5476 sq ft = 16 anna; 1 anna = 4 paisa; 1 paisa = 4 dam; 1 bigha = 72,900 sq ft = 20 kattha; 1 kattha = 20 dhur; 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft. Volume: 1 gallon = 4.546 L (UK) = 3.785 L (US); 1 barrel = 164 L (UK) = 159 L (US).
  • Deduction rules (IS 1200 practice): openings up to 0.5 m² are not deducted (some DSRs use 0.1 m² for plaster); larger openings are deducted, the half-deduction convention balancing jamb additions for openings up to 3 m². Concrete is measured net — no deduction for steel volume under 1% or openings under 0.1 m². Plaster includes jambs and soffits. Painting on corrugated sheets takes a flatness coefficient ×1.1–1.25. Earthwork carries a standard lift of 1.5 m and lead of 30 m; extra lift/lead paid separately.
  • Reinforcement basics (bar bending schedule): weight of bar (kg/m) = d²/162 — 16 mm → 1.58 kg/m, 12 mm → 0.89 kg/m; standard bar 12 m. Development length Ld = φσs/(4τbd); laps tension ≈ 50d (Fe 415, M20 — check code), compression ≈ 40d; semi-circular hook 9d; 45° bend +0.5d; 90° bend +1d. Nominal cover (IS 456): footing 50 mm, column 40 mm, beam 25 mm, slab 15–20 mm. Steel wastage 2–3%; rolling margin ±7%.
Plinth-area includes: all floors (excluding offsets), internal shafts < 2 m², non-cantilever porch, machine room, lift. Excludes: cantilever porch, internal shafts > 2 m², courtyard, loft, barsati. (Classic MCQ list — courtyard area is the favourite "not included" answer.)
Memory hooks (1.4–1.6): axes ladder — scalene 0, iso 1, equilateral 3, rectangle 2, square 4, rhombus 2, parallelogram 0, n-gon n. Sag & slope corrections always subtract ("the tape sags and the hill cheats"). Normal tension = pull that makes sag = pull effect. Whole → part: control first, details later. Curvature −0.0785, refraction +0.0112 (1/7th, opposite), combined −0.0673. Curve formulas all hang off Δ/2: tan → T, sin → C, sec − 1 → E, 1 − cos → M. Salvage = saved whole; scrap = stripped. YP = 1/i; with sinking fund YP = 1/(i+S). Detailed estimate = most reliable; cube rate beats plinth area; revised at 10% (5% when rates fail); annual repair 1.5% (+ special → 2.5%).

Extended High-Yield Additions (Exam-Focused Extras)

K. Miscellaneous Building Materials (frequently asked)

Glass

Glass is made by fusing silica sand (60–70%) + soda (15%) + lime (5–10%) at about 1500 °C. Cullet (broken glass) speeds the melt. It is a supercooled liquid — no crystal structure — and ordinary glass refracts at ≈ 1.5.

TypeProperty
Soda-limeGeneral windows — cheap, breaks easily
Lead (crystal)High refractive index
Borosilicate (Pyrex)Low expansion, heat resistant — labware
WiredSteel mesh holds fragments — fire resistant
Safety/laminatedPVB interlayer holds shards
Tempered/toughened4–5× stronger; shatters into small granules

Plastics & polymers

Thermoplastics (PVC, PE, PP, polystyrene, acrylic) soften repeatedly; thermosets (bakelite, urea formaldehyde, epoxy, polyester) set permanently. PVC pipes are light and corrosion-proof but UV-degrade and weaken hot; HDPE carries water supply; CPVC carries hot water. Advantages: light, corrosion-free, mouldable. Disadvantages: toxic fumes in fire, UV degradation, low stiffness, creep.

Asbestos & asbestos cement

Asbestos is a fibrous silicate — chrysotile (white), amosite (brown), crocidolite (blue, most hazardous). AC sheets are cement + 10–15% fibre: light, fireproof, durable, but a serious health hazard (asbestosis, mesothelioma) — cut wet, and is being phased out.

Fly ash, slag & supplementary materials

  • Fly ash is pozzolanic — reacts with Ca(OH)₂, improves later strength, cuts permeability and heat. PPC uses 15–35%. Class F is low-lime; Class C is self-cementing.
  • GGBS (ground granulated blast furnace slag): 30–70% replacement; suits marine works and lowers heat.
  • Silica fume (microsilica): ultrafine pozzolan for high-strength concrete (5–10%).
  • AAC blocks weigh 550–650 kg/m³, fly-ash based, autoclaved, insulate well, cut with a hand saw.

Adhesives & sealants

Epoxy (structural, strongest), PVA (wood), silicone (weatherproof joints), polyurethane (floor and expansion joints), bituminous sealants.

L. Mortar — Types and Properties

MortarMix (by volume)Use
Cement1:3 to 1:6 (cement : sand)Structural masonry, plaster, pointing, work near DPC
Lime1:2 to 1:3 (lime : sand)Historic and restoration masonry, plaster undercoats
Lime-cement (gauged)1:1:6 to 1:2:9 (lime : cement : sand)Workable general-purpose mortar
Mudclay + water (+ straw)Rural and rubble masonry, eco-housing
Surkhilime : burnt-clay powder 1:2Water-resistant lime mortar substitute
Fire clayfire clay + crushed firebrickBoilers, chimneys, furnaces

Mortar binds units, spreads load uniformly, seals joints, and lets you adjust bricks while laying. The water-cement ratio governs its strength (Abrams' law). Traditional practice keeps mortar strength below brick strength; modern high-strength units use richer 1:3–1:4. Lab checks: flow cone, 50 mm cube compression at 7/28 days, air content.

More Depth: 1.3 Building Technology — Stairs, Lintels, Arches, Scaffolding, Formwork

Stairs — design rules (MCQ gold)

Components: tread (going), riser, stringer, nosing, landing, headroom, balustrade/handrail.

Comfort rules: 2R + T = 600–640 mm (the classic check); riser 150–200 mm (residential ≈ 150–175; public buildings max 150 mm); tread 250–300 mm; ≤ 12–16 steps per flight; width 0.9–1.0 m residential, 1.5–2.0 m public; headroom ≥ 2.1–2.2 m; landing length ≥ stair width; handrail 0.85–1.0 m high.

Types: straight; dog-legged (two flights over a half-space landing — the most common); open-well; quarter-turn; half-turn; three-quarter-turn; winder (triangular treads, no landing); spiral/helical; bifurcated.

RCC stairs (waist-slab design) dominate; timber, steel and stone serve specific cases.

Lintels & arches

A lintel is the beam over an opening carrying the wall above. RCC is standard; steel, brick (soldier/arched), stone and timber are alternatives. Bearing at each end ≥ 15–20 cm (min 150 mm); RCC lintel depth typically 100–150 mm. Design load = the load inside the arching (triangular/isosceles) zone plus any superimposed load above that zone.

An arch carries load in compression. Parts: springing, skewback, voussoirs, keystone, extrados, intrados (soffit), spandrel, haunch, crown, span, rise. Flat arch rise ≈ 1/12 of span; semi-circular rise = span/2.

Types: flat (French), segmental, semi-circular, relieving (discharging — built over a lintel to shed load), bull's-eye, elliptical, equilateral, pointed/Gothic, stilted, infirmed. Gauged bricks are rubbed to exact shape. The two exam favourites: the relieving arch transfers load off a lintel; the gauged brick arch is rubbed-brick precision work. (Hammerbeam is a roof form, not an arch.)

Abutments must resist the thrust; arches fail by rotation of a voussoir about its edge, sliding of voussoirs, or crushing.

Scaffolding, shoring, underpinning

Scaffolding is a temporary working platform: single (bricklayer's — putlogs rest in the wall), double (independent of the wall), cantilever/needle, suspended (cradle, bosun's chair), and steel/tubular patented systems. Safety kit: guard rails, toe boards, base plates, ties every 4 m.

Shoring supports unsafe structures: raking (inclined rakers — best for walls), flying (between two buildings when the intermediate one is removed), dead/vertical shores (carry the full load during repair).

Underpinning strengthens an existing foundation — pit method, pile method, needle-beam/jack methods — always in segments to avoid settlement.

Formwork (shuttering)

Materials: timber/plywood, steel (reusable, smooth finish), aluminium, plastic-composite. Requirements: tight joints (no grout loss), rigidity, true line and level, easy release, economic reuse; apply release oil; camber long spans.

Striking times (IS 456, OPC, ≈23 °C):

FormWhen to remove
Vertical forms (columns, walls)16–24 hr
Slab soffits (props left)3 days
Beam soffits (props left)7 days
Props to slabs (span < 4.5 m)7 days
Props to slabs (span > 4.5 m)14 days
Props to beams (span < 6 m)14 days
Props to beams (span > 6 m)21 days

High-early-strength cement shortens these; cold weather lengthens them. Never strike formwork before the concrete can carry its own weight plus the imposed loads.

Rapid-Fire One-Liners (Last-Minute Revision)

  • Most elastic structural material — steel; most ductile common metal — copper; most malleable — gold.
  • Hardness scale for minerals — Mohs (1 talc → 10 diamond).
  • Brick earth harmful constituents — lime lumps, organic matter, pebbles, pyrites.
  • Clay burning minimum temperature for vitrification — ≈ 850 °C; kiln firing range 900–1200 °C.
  • Frog area ≈ 1/10 of brick face; frog depth 10–20 mm.
  • Number of standard modular bricks per m³ of masonry — 500.
  • Efflorescence is caused by — soluble salts (sulphates of Ca, Mg, alkalis).
  • C₃A heat of hydration highest; C₂S lowest; gypsum retards C₃A.
  • OPC specific gravity — 3.15; bulk density — 1440 kg/m³; one bag = 0.0347 m³.
  • Autoclave soundness limit — 0.8% expansion (magnesia); Le Chatelier — 10 mm (lime).
  • Blaine fineness OPC — ≥ 225 m²/kg; RHPC ≈ 325 m²/kg.
  • Standard sand for cement tests — Ennore (IS 650) graded sand; w/c for mortar cubes = P/4 + 3%.
  • Maximum bulking of sand — 20–30% at 4–5% moisture.
  • Sand grading zones — Zone I (coarsest) → Zone IV (finest); FM of sand 2.2–3.2.
  • Flakiness index limit for concrete aggregates — < 25–35% (rounded aggregate preferred).
  • Water absorption limit coarse aggregate — < 2%; building stone < 5%; 1st-class brick ≤ 15% (course value).
  • Ten percent fines value & aggregate crushing value are inversely related; ACV < 30% for surface course.
  • Mild steel E = 2 × 10⁵ MPa; yield 250 MPa; elongation ≥ 23% (Fe 250).
  • Fe 500D: yield 500, UTS ≥ 565, elongation ≥ 10% (D = ductile — better seismic).
  • Timber moisture for furniture — 10–12%; construction 12–15%; fungi attack above 20% MC.
  • Knots — most common timber defect; shakes — cracks between rings (frost action).
  • Bethell (full-cell) process = pressure creosoting; Rueping = empty-cell.
  • Bitumen penetration units — dmm (0.1 mm) at 25 °C, 100 g, 5 s.
  • Cutbacks: RC/MC/SC; emulsions: RS/MS/SS (anionic) and cationic (CMS/CRS) — usable in rain.
  • Flash point minimum for paving bitumen — 175 °C (Pensky-Martens closed cup).
  • Mastic asphalt — hot-applied waterproofing; rock asphalt — natural bitumen + limestone.
  • Carbon ladder: pig iron 3–4%; cast iron 2–4%; wrought iron < 0.15%; mild steel 0.15–0.3%.
  • Galvanizing = zinc coating; sherardizing = zinc dust; Parkerizing = phosphate; anodizing = thickened aluminium oxide layer.
  • Paint driers — litharge, red lead, lead acetate, cobalt naphthenate.
  • French polish = shellac in methylated spirit; lacquer = cellulose nitrate.
  • White cement: Fe₂O₃ < 1%; raw materials — pure limestone + kaolin; oil as fuel to avoid ash.
  • Distemper = chalk + glue (water paint) — interior only; cement paint — exterior, needs damp curing.
  • Window:floor = 1:10; door:floor ≈ 1:20; stair 2R + T = 60–64 cm; headroom ≥ 2.1 m.
  • NBC catalogue: 105 seismic; 103/104 imposed/wind loads; 110 concrete; 201 RC with masonry infill (MRT), 202 load-bearing masonry (MRT), 203/204 low-strength masonry / earthen buildings, 205 RC without masonry infill (MRT).
  • FAR typical residential Kathmandu — 1.5–2.5; ground coverage ≤ ~50–60%.
  • HI = RL + BS; RL_new = HI − FS; check ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL.
  • Curvature −0.0785D², refraction +0.0112D², combined −0.0673D² m (D in km).
  • Prismatic compass reads WCB; surveyor's compass reads QB; least count 30′.
  • Bowditch rule — corrections proportional to line length (compass traverse); transit rule — proportional to lat/dep (theodolite traverse).
  • Contour interval smaller on flat ground; V uphill = valley; closed contours = hill/depression.
  • Tacheometry: D = Ks + C with K = 100, C ≈ 0.1–0.3 (0 with anallatic lens).
  • GPS: began 1973 (US DoD), first prototype 1978, full constellation operational 1993; minimum 4 satellites for a 3D fix; RTK accuracy 1–2 cm.
  • GIS 5 components — hardware, software, data, people, methods.
  • Curves: T = R tan(Δ/2), L = πRΔ/180, C = 2R sin(Δ/2), E = R(sec Δ/2 − 1), M = R(1 − cos Δ/2), D = 1720/R (30 m chord).
  • Rankine deflection angle δ (min) = 1718.9 × C/R.
  • Estimate types: preliminary (±15–20%), detailed (±5%); revised when expenditure exceeds the administrative approval by 10% (course value; some references quote 5% for rate insufficiency); annual repair ≈ 1–1.5% of capital cost (≤ 1.5%).
  • Formwork striking: slab props 7 d (< 4.5 m span), beam props 14 d (< 6 m), vertical forms 16–24 hr (IS 456).
  • Bar weight kg/m = d²/162; development length Ld = φσs/4τbd; cover: footing 50, column 40, beam 25, slab 15–20 mm.
  • YP = 1/i; capitalized value = net annual income × YP; sinking fund deposit = (C − S)i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1].
  • Straight-line depreciation D = (C − S)/n; declining balance p = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n).
  • Scrap ≈ 10% of cost (dismantled); salvage = without dismantling; book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (1.1–1.6)

These are the course-book values, rewritten for readability. Where the course value differs from older textbooks, the course value stands (it is what NEC asks).

Building Stones — Course Values

  • Physical classification: stratified rocks (layered, split along beds — sandstone, limestone); unstratified/massive (granite, marble); foliated (split in one direction — slate, schist, gneiss; all metamorphic except quartzite and marble).
  • Chemical classification: siliceous (silica main — granite, quartzite, sandstone, basalt); calcareous (lime main — limestone, marble, dolomite); argillaceous (clay/alumina main — slate, laterite, kaolin).
  • Good building stone: crushing strength ≥ 100 MPa; specific gravity 2.4–2.8; water absorption < 5% (rejected if > 10%); salt content 0%.
  • Mohs hardness scale: 1 talc, 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite, 6 orthoclase, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum, 10 diamond. Fingernail scratches ≈ 2; knife ≈ 7; marble's minimum hardness = 3.
  • Stone tests: Smith (clay/dirt), Brard's (frost resistance), acid (weather resistance), crushing (strength), absorption, attrition/Deval/Dorry (abrasion), impact (toughness).
  • Key facts: minimum hardness for road-pavement stone = 17 (attrition value); gneiss has the highest crushing strength; pumice (igneous) serves lightweight construction; silica shows no cleavage. Ornamental work wants soft stone; retaining walls want heavy stone; rubble masonry wants hard stone.
  • Rock origin: igneous — cooling of magma (intrusive below surface: granite; extrusive above: basalt); sedimentary/aqueous — water-deposited (limestone, sandstone); metamorphic — altered by heat/pressure (marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone, slate from shale).

Bricks — Course Values

  • Composition of good brick earth: silica 50–60% (retains shape, prevents shrinkage/warping; excess → brittleness), alumina 20–30% (plasticity; excess → cracks on burning), lime ≈ 10% (binds, reduces shrinkage; excess → loss of shape), iron oxide < 7% (red colour; excess → dark blue), magnesia ≈ 1% (prevents warping; excess → yellow tint), alkalis < 1% (excess → efflorescence).
  • Manufacturing sequence: unsoiling → digging → weathering (monsoon) → blending (dry mix) → tempering (wet mix, pug mill) → moulding → drying → burning. Moulds: shisham wood, internal size slightly larger than the brick.
  • Burning: clamp out-turn ≈ 60%; Bull's trench kiln (most common in Nepal) 80–90%.
  • Classification: 1st class — absorption < 15%, strength ≥ 10.5 N/mm²; 2nd — < 20%, ≥ 7 N/mm²; 3rd — < 25%, ≥ 3.5 N/mm²; 4th — over-burnt "jhumb" bricks.
  • Defects: bloating (carbonaceous matter + sulphur), black core (bituminous matter), chuffs (rain on hot bricks), checks/cracks (lime lumps or excess water), lamination (entrapped air).
  • Nepal sizes: NBC 109:1994 (Masonry) standard brick = 240 × 115 × 57 mm (with a 10 mm vertical joint); IS non-modular = 230 × 110 × 70 mm; IS modular = 190 × 90 × 90 mm. Handmade ≈ 560/m³ of masonry; machine-made ≈ 530/m³; modular 500/m³. Soak ≥ 1 hour before use; minimum brick strength per NBC = 3.5 N/mm²; half-brick wall height ≤ 1.0–1.5 m per day.

Tiles

  • Composition for good tiles: sand 40%, silt 30%, clay 30%; max fine sand content ≈ 40%.
  • Glazing gives smoothness, imperviousness and attractive finish; maximum warping along tile sides = 2%.

Cement — Course Values

  • Ingredients: lime 60–65% (strength/soundness; excess → unsoundness), silica 17–25% (strength; excess → slow setting), alumina 3–8% (quick setting; excess → lowers strength), iron oxide 0.5–6% (colour), magnesia 0.5–4% (hardness/colour; excess → unsoundness), SO₃ 1–2%, alkalis 0.5–1% (excess → efflorescence).
  • Bogue compounds: C₃S (alite) — early strength, high heat, less chemical resistance; C₂S (belite) — ultimate strength, low heat, more resistance; C₃A (celite) — first to react, initial set, sulphate-vulnerable; C₄AF (felite) — least functional, gives the grey colour.
  • Manufacture: burning at 1400–1700 °C — choose 1400 °C when the MCQ offers it; limestone + clay are the raw materials.
  • Tests: fineness — 90-micron sieve, residue ≤ 10% OPC / ≤ 5% RHPC; consistency — Vicat 10 mm plunger stopping 5–7 mm above the bottom (the course PDF phrases the same point as 33–35 mm below the top), water = P (≈ 25–35%); soundness — Le Chatelier, water 0.78P, expansion ≤ 10 mm; setting — 1 mm² square needle (initial, water 0.85P), annular collar (final); IST 30 min, FST 600 min; quick-setting cement 5/30 min.
  • Compressive strength: 1:3 mortar, 7.06 cm cubes; 3 days ≈ 115 kg/cm², 7 days ≈ 175 kg/cm². Tensile briquette: 3 days 20, 7 days 25 kg/cm², six specimens.
  • Constants: density 1440 kg/m³; SG 3.15; bag 50 kg = 0.0347 m³; specific surface OPC 2250 cm²/g, RHPC 3250 cm²/g; loss on ignition ≤ 4%; insoluble residue ≤ 2% (NS 572). Good cement is greenish grey, feels cool in the bag, floats briefly on water.
  • Selection: blast-furnace slag → bridge abutments (avoid thin walls); high-alumina → refractory (no steam curing); PPC → seawater; sulphate-resisting → canals/sewage; white → finishes; rapid hardening → precast/road repair; low heat → mass concrete.

Lime — Course Values

  • Lime = calcium carbonate calcined at ≈ 800 °C. Quicklime CaO + water → hydrated lime Ca(OH)₂ (slaking); excess water → milk of lime; lump lime = quicklime straight from the kiln.
  • Hydraulicity comes from clay; source of hydraulic lime = kankar. Feebly hydraulic 5–10% clay; moderately 10–25%; eminently 25–30%.
  • Fat lime (< 5% clay) slakes to 2–3× volume — whitewashing; lean lime > 30% clay — inferior work. Hydraulic lime: initial set 120 min, curing 7 days, ball test after 6 h.

Timber — Course Values

  • Growth: endogenous (inward — palm, bamboo, cane); exogenous (outward — sal, teak, deodar, chir). Hardwoods mostly tropical (sal, teak, oak, shisham); softwoods mostly temperate (pine, kail, deodar, walnut).
  • Seasoning: freshly felled timber may hold up to 100% moisture; well-seasoned = 10–12%. Natural 60–90 days; artificial 4–5 days. Purpose: remove moisture, increase stability, resist shrinkage/warping/decay.
  • Defects: heart shake, star shake (radial from bark), cup/ring shake, rind galls (branch-stub swellings), burls, knots, foxiness (red/yellow decay tint), druxiness (white fungoid spots), wane (conversion), bow/cup/twist/check (seasoning), termites/beetles, rots.
  • Preservation: charring (fire/termites), tarring, painting, creosoting (rot and white ants — sleepers), ASCU (white ants), Wolman salt (all-round), ammonium compounds (fire).
  • Market forms: plank < 5 cm thick; board < 5 cm thick & > 12 cm wide; batten > 5 cm & > 12 cm; baulk > 5 cm & > 20 cm; deal 5–10 cm thick & < 25 cm wide; strip 5 × 10 cm. Sap = viscous salt solution in the tree; teak → boats, willow → cricket bats; strength maximum parallel to grain; radial sawing strongest, tangential weakest.

Metals & Alloys — Course Values

  • Iron family (carbon %): pig iron 3–4% (Bessemer from haematite; foundry/grey — high fuel & temperature; forge/white — low fuel & temperature; mottled — between, ornamental); cast iron 2–4% (columns, struts, sanitary fittings — strong compression, weak tension); steel 0.15–1.5% (mild 0.15–0.3 structural/rebar; medium 0.3–0.8; high 0.8–1.5); wrought iron < 0.15% (electromagnets, roof coverings — most pure, fibrous).
  • Alloys: brass Cu+Zn; bronze Cu+Sn; solder Sn+Pb; stainless Fe+Cr+Ni; invar steel+Ni (low expansion); German silver Ni+Cu+Zn; monel Ni+Cu; gun metal Cu+Zn+Sn+Pb; brazing solder Cu+Zn+Sn.
  • Malleability = hammered into sheets; ductility = drawn into wires. Removing impurities from ore = concentration; iron-manufacture dust = inorganic sludge.

Paints & Varnishes — Course Values

  • Ingredients: base (white lead, red lead, zinc white), vehicle (linseed oil), pigment (colour), solvent/thinner (turpentine, naphtha, petroleum), drier (lead acetate, red lead), filler (barium sulphate).
  • Defects: blistering (moisture swelling), flaking (detachment), crazing (hairline cracks in small areas), cracking (through the full layer), alligatoring (layer slides), chalking (powdering), fading, sagging, blooming.
  • Key facts: PVC = pigment volume concentration; radiator paint = bronze paint; fire-resistant = asbestos paint; corrosion pigment = red lead; Duco = cellulose paint trade name; stucco = for stone and brick masonry; priming coat steel = red lead, wood = white lead; most durable varnish = oil varnish; most brilliant = spirit varnish; enamel's liquid medium = varnish; emulsion coverage ≈ 10–14 m²/L per coat.

Bitumen, Asphalt & Tar — Course Values

  • Bitumen: from petroleum distillation; VG grades 10/20/30/40 (IS 73:2013). Forms: cutback (with solvent), emulsion (in water), plastic bitumen (with inert filler — crack filling), blown (air-oxidized).
  • Tar: from destructive distillation of coal/wood; grades RT1–RT5 (RT1 lowest viscosity); carcinogenic. Asphalt = bitumen + mineral aggregate/filler.
  • Loss on heating of bitumen < 1%; insoluble impurities < 1%; bitumen paint gives a smooth, hard, shining protective surface.

1.2 Standards & Tests — Course Mapping (NBC 101:1994)

  • Nepal Standards are prepared by NBSM; IS codes fill the gaps where NS are insufficient.
  • Bricks: NS 1/2035 ↔ IS 1077; compression IS 3495 Pt-1; water absorption IS 3495 Pt-2.
  • Cement: NS 49/2041 ↔ IS 269; consistency IS 4031 Pt-4; setting time Pt-5; soundness Pt-3; compressive strength Pt-6.
  • Aggregates: NS 297/2050 ↔ IS 383; bulking NS 305/2050 ↔ IS 2386 Pt-3.
  • Rebar: mild steel NS 84/2042 ↔ IS 432; deformed NS 191/2046 ↔ IS 1786; tensile test NS 203/2046 ↔ IS 1608.
  • Master codes: IS 456 (RCC), IS 800 (steel), IS 875 Pts 1–5 (loads), IS 1893 Pt-1 (earthquake), IS 13920 (ductile detailing), IS 15988 (retrofitting).
  • Test essentials: Vicat (consistency + setting), Le Chatelier/autoclave (soundness), bulking of sand (max 20–30% at 4–5% moisture), rebar tensile test (yield, UTS, % elongation over 5d gauge).

1.4 Geometric Properties — Course Formulas

  • Centroid of volumes: ȳ = ΣyᵢVᵢ/ΣVᵢ; solid prism z̄ = h/2, V = Ah; solid pyramid/cone z̄ = h/4, V = Ah/3; hollow (thin) pyramid/cone z̄ = h/3; hemisphere z̄ = 3r/8, V = 2πr³/3.
  • Triangle about base: I = Bh³/12; about CG: Bh³/36 (base:CG = 1:3; CG:top = 1:9).
  • Semicircle: about base I = πD⁴/128; centroidal 0.11R⁴; CG from base = 4r/3π = 2D/3π.
  • Quarter circle I = 0.055R⁴; rectangle about base Bd³/3; circle Z = πd³/32; trapezoid CG from base (parallel sides a, b): h/3 × (b + 2a)/(b + a).
  • Parallel axis I = Icg + Ah²; perpendicular axis Izz = Ixx + Iyy (polar). CG and geometric centre do not coincide for a right-angle triangle. Cylinder about its central axis = MR²/2; for a circular area the asked form is πd⁴/64.

1.5 Surveying — Course One-Liners

Quick-recall one-liners from the course deck — the full treatment lives in the Study Notes pane (fundamentals → GPS/GIS).

  • Surveying = art & science of determining relative positions of points on the earth's surface; the first step of any civil project.
  • Principles: work from whole to part (prevents error accumulation); locate a point from two reference points; independent check; accuracy; consistency.
  • Plane vs geodetic: plane survey ignores curvature (< 250–260 km², low precision); geodetic considers curvature (national Survey Department of Nepal).
  • An 18.2 km earth arc is only 1 cm longer than its chord; spherical-vs-plane triangle angle excess = 1 second per 195 km².
  • Linear measurement methods: direct (chaining, taping, pacing), optical (tacheometry — theodolite with stadia hairs; fixed-hair method most used), EDM (total station: horizontal angle + vertical angle + sloping distance).
  • Linear tools: pacing, passometer, pedometer, odometer, chain/tape, tacheometry, EDM, GPS. Buildings allow ranging but not chaining.
  • Well-conditioned triangle: all angles between 30° and 120°.
  • HI method is quicker with many intermediate sights; rise & fall gives the full arithmetic check. Contours of different elevations unite only at a vertical cliff; closely spaced contours = steep slope; contour interval is inversely proportional to scale.
  • FB = BB ± 180°; GPS started by the US DoD in 1973 with the full 24-satellite constellation operational in 1993; total station = H angle + V angle + sloping distance.

1.6 Estimating & Costing — Course One-Liners

Quick-recall one-liners from the course deck — the full treatment lives in the Study Notes pane (estimate types → measurement & units).

  • Units: cornice, coping, expansion/contraction joints, railing → running metre (r.m.); steel reinforcement & iron works → quintal; binding wire 0.9–1.2 kg per quintal of rebar.
  • Plinth area = floor area + wall area; floor area = circulation + carpet + bath/kitchen; carpet = livable area. Plinth-area estimate includes all floors (excluding offsets), internal shafts < 2 m², non-cantilever porch, machine room, lift; excludes cantilever porch, shafts > 2 m², courtyard, loft, barsati.
  • Cube-rate estimate is more accurate than plinth-area; unit-rate estimate per km of road / per bed / per student.
  • Detailed estimate = most reliable; prepared after administrative sanction; quantity surveying produces the BOQ.
  • Junctions: L-junction — no deduction; T-junction — deduct 0.5b; cross (+) junction — deduct b (b = wall breadth).
  • Revised estimate when the original sanctioned estimate is likely to be exceeded by more than 5% (rates found insufficient), or when expenditure exceeds / is likely to exceed the administrative approval by 10%, or on a material change of design — the course deck states both triggers. Supplementary estimate for additional works; annual repair/maintenance ≤ 1.5% of capital cost (book value; commonly quoted 1–1.5%).
  • Valuation: scrap value = dismantled material value (≈ 10%); salvage = whole structure without dismantling; book value = cost − depreciation; capitalized value = net annual income × year's purchase (YP = 1/i); sinking fund accumulates for replacement; obsolescence reduces value by outdating.
  • Rate analysis — book method (deck): water ≈ 1.5%, T&P = 3% of unskilled labour, overhead & profit = 15% of (materials + labour + T&P) = 10% profit + 5% overhead (generic textbook ranges: T&P 1–3%, overheads 5–10%); straight-line depreciation D = (C − S)/n.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): First-class brick absorption — course value < 15%, which the classic first-class classification agrees with (IS 1077's ≤ 20% applies only up to class 12.5, 15% for higher classes); for NEC exams key 15% (with 10.5 N/mm² strength). The revised-estimate trigger is quoted as both 5% (rates found insufficient) and 10% (expenditure exceeding the administrative approval) — the course deck and the licensing reference book both use 10%, so the MCQ bank keys 10%.
