Chapter 2: Soil Mechanics and Foundation Engineering (ACiE02)

NEC License Exam (1-Mark MCQ Focus) | NEC prep-course edition — v5.5

This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

2.1 Soil Properties and Laboratory Tests (ACiE0201)

A. Soil as a Three-Phase System

Fig 2.1 — Three-phase diagram: the source of every phase relationship (n < 100%, e can exceed 1, S: 0 dry → 100% saturated)

Soil is a three-phase material: solid mineral grains + water + air. All three phases present means the soil is partially saturated. Voids fully filled with water = saturated; voids fully filled with air = dry.

  • Volume relations: total volume V = Vs (solids) + Vv (voids); Vv = Vw (water) + Va (air).
  • Weight relations: total weight W = Ws + Ww (air weighs nothing).

Fundamental definitions (memorize all)

Void ratio e = Vv/Vs (can exceed 1; sands 0.4–0.7, clays 0.5–1.5+)
Porosity n = Vv/V; n = e/(1+e); e = n/(1−n); n is always < 100%
Degree of saturation S = Vw/Vv (0 dry → 100% saturated)
Water content w = Ww/Ws × 100% (oven dry at 105–110 °C, 24 hr)
Air content ac = Va/V ; Percentage air voids na = Va/V × 100
Bulk (moist) unit weight γ = W/V (≈ 15–20 kN/m³)
Dry unit weight γd = Ws/V = γ/(1+w) ; γd = G·γw/(1+e)
Saturated unit weight γsat = (G+e)γw/(1+e)
Submerged (buoyant) γ' = γsat − γw = (G−1)γw/(1+e) ; γw = 9.81 kN/m³
Specific gravity of solids G (sands 2.63–2.67, clays 2.67–2.75, organic soils < 2.4)
  • Relationships to memorize:
    • e·S = w·G (the master relation)
    • γd = G γw (1 − n)
    • γ = γd(1 + w)
    • γsat = γd + n γw
    • γ' = γd (G−1)/G (approximate, S = 1)
  • Density index / relative density Id describes cohesionless soils:
    Id = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100%
    0–15% very loose · 15–35% loose · 35–65% medium · 65–85% dense · 85–100% very dense
    Also Id = (γd − γd,min)/(γd,max − γd,min) × γd,max/γd. The lab measures it by maximum/minimum index density tests; the field correlates it with the SPT N-value.

B. Index Properties and Atterberg Limits (fine-grained soils)

Fig 2.2 — Atterberg limits: consistency states between shrinkage (SL), plastic (PL) and liquid (LL) limits

Atterberg limits (Albert Atterberg, 1911; test procedures by Casagrande) are the water contents at which a clayey soil changes consistency state.

LimitDefinitionTest
Shrinkage Limit (SL)water content below which no further volume decrease occurs (the soil is just fully saturated at its minimum volume)Shrinkage dish (mercury displacement)
Plastic Limit (PL)lowest water content at which the soil can be rolled into 3 mm threads without crumblingHand rolling
Liquid Limit (LL)water content at which the soil starts to flow (groove closes 12 mm at 25 blows)Casagrande cup (25 blows) or fall-cone penetrometer (IS 2720 Pt-5)
Plasticity Index PI = LL − PL (0 = non-plastic; low < 7; medium 7–17; high > 17)
Shrinkage Index SI = PL − SL ; Consistency Index CI = (LL − w)/PI
Flow Index If = slope of the water-content vs log(blows) flow curve
Toughness Index It = PI/If
  • Liquidity Index LI = (w − PL)/PI. LI > 1: the soil is in its liquid state (sensitive or quick clays); LI < 0: dry and hard.
  • Consistency is resistance to deformation, described as very soft / soft / medium / stiff / very stiff / hard and correlated with SPT N and cu.
  • Activity A = PI / (% clay fraction < 2 μm). A < 0.75 inactive (kaolinite ≈ 0.3–0.5); 0.75–1.25 normal (illite ≈ 1); > 1.25 active (montmorillonite ≈ 1.5–7 — the expansive black cotton soil).
  • Sensitivity St = cu(undisturbed)/cu(remoulded): 2–4 normal, 4–8 sensitive, > 8 extra sensitive, > 16 quick clay.
  • Thixotropy is the regain of strength by a remoulded clay with time at constant water content.

C. Particle Size Analysis

Fig 2.3 — Gradation curve: D10, D30, D60 read at 10/30/60% finer; Cu and Cc classify the grading
  • Sieve analysis (coarse fraction): sieves from 80/75 mm down to 75 μm (0.075 mm); dry sieving normally, wet sieving when fines exceed about 5% (the book's rule: wet sieving whenever the fines dominate the sample). D10 is the effective size (10% finer by weight).
  • Sedimentation analysis (hydrometer or pipette, fines < 75 μm): based on Stokes' law — terminal velocity v = (Gs−1)γw d²/(18η).
Coefficient of uniformity Cu = D60/D10 (> 4 gravel, > 6 sand = well graded)
Coefficient of curvature Cc = D30²/(D10×D60) (1–3 for well graded)
Well graded: smooth curve with all sizes · Gap graded: sizes missing · Uniformly graded: one size dominates
ParticleSize range (IS/USCS)
Boulder> 300 mm
Cobble80–300 mm
Gravel4.75–80 mm (coarse 20–80, fine 4.75–20)
Coarse sand2–4.75 mm
Medium sand0.425–2 mm
Fine sand0.075–0.425 mm
Silt0.002–0.075 mm
Clay< 0.002 mm (2 μm)

D. Soil Classification Systems

1. USCS (Unified Soil Classification System — Casagrande)

  • Two-letter symbols. Coarse soils: GW, GP, GM, GC (gravel) and SW, SP, SM, SC (sand) — W = well graded, P = poorly graded, M = silt, C = clay. Fine soils: ML, CL, OL (LL < 50), MH, CH, OH (LL ≥ 50), Pt (peat). Dual symbols like CL-ML exist.
  • The A-line, PI = 0.73(LL − 20), separates CL (above) from ML (below). The U-line is the empirical upper bound.
  • Classification needs gradation (Cu, Cc), LL and PI.

2. IS Classification (IS 1498 — same family as USCS)

  • The fine/coarse boundary is 50% passing the 75 μm sieve; of the coarse fraction, more than 50% larger than 4.75 mm makes it a gravel, otherwise a sand. The plasticity chart is identical, with the A-line.

3. Textural/descriptive (MIT & USDA)

  • MIT size boundaries: gravel > 2 mm, sand 2–0.06 mm, silt 0.06–0.002 mm, clay < 0.002 mm. The textural triangle chart combines % sand/silt/clay into names like clay loam and silty clay loam.
  • USDA: silt–clay boundary at 0.002 mm, sand–silt at 0.05 mm.

4. Plasticity chart (Casagrande)

  • A-line: PI = 0.73(LL−20). Above the A-line = clays (C); below = silts (M). The vertical line LL = 50% divides low from high plasticity. CH, CL, MH, ML, OH, OL are placed by chart.
Fig 2.4 — Casagrande plasticity chart: A-line separates clays (above) from silts (below); U-line bounds natural soils from above

E. Laboratory Tests (IS 2720 parts — high-yield list)

TestIS 2720 PartKey values
Water content (oven dry)Pt-2105–110 °C, 24 hr (to constant mass)
Atterberg limitsPt-5LL at 25 blows; thread 3 mm
Grain sizePt-475 μm boundary; Cu, Cc
Specific gravity (pycnometer)Pt-3G at 27 °C; kerosene or white spirit instead of water when the soil contains soluble salts or organics (prevents dissolution); de-airing essential
Proctor compactionPt-7 (light) / Pt-8 (heavy)see compaction section
Field density (sand replacement / core cutter)Pt-28/29control of field compaction
PermeabilityPt-17 (constant head) / Pt-18 (falling head)k values by soil type
Direct shearPt-13φ, c for sands and undisturbed blocks
Triaxial compressionPt-11/12UU, CU, CD tests
Unconfined compressionPt-10cu = qu/2 (φ = 0)
Vane shearPt-30soft saturated clays; cu = T/(π d²(h/2 + d/6))
Consolidation (oedometer)Pt-15Cc, mv, cv, preconsolidation pressure
CBRPt-16see pavement chapter
Free swell indexPt-40> 100% = expansive soil indicator

F. Boring Log Interpretation

  • Bore log = the vertical record of a borehole: depth scale, strata with SPT N values and consistency/density descriptions, groundwater level (▲ symbol), sampling depths, Atterberg limits, classification symbols, and rock core RQD.
  • SPT N correction: N60 = measured N / energy ratio; overburden correction N' = 350 N/(σv + 70) (σv in kPa), or N1 = Cn·N with Cn = √(95.8/σ'v) capped.
  • N-value interpretation:
    Sand NDensityφ approx
    0–4Very loose26–28°
    4–10Loose28–30°
    10–30Medium30–36°
    30–50Dense36–41°
    > 50Very dense41–48°
    Clay NConsistencycu (kPa)
    < 2Very soft< 12
    2–4Soft12–25
    4–8Medium25–50
    8–15Stiff50–100
    15–30Very stiff100–200
    > 30Hard> 200
  • RQD (Rock Quality Designation) = percentage of intact core pieces longer than 10 cm in the total run: < 25 very poor, 25–50 poor, 50–75 fair, 75–90 good, > 90 excellent.
  • TCR = total core recovery %; SCR = solid core recovery; fractures per metre and rock strength description complete the log.
Fig 2.5 — Annotated bore log: strata, SPT N at 1.5 m intervals, GWL at 1.6 m, RQD grades for the rock core
Quick identification: black cotton soil (expansive, montmorillonite) → CH with high PI; loess → wind-deposited silt (ML); laterite → residual tropical soil rich in Fe/Al oxides; peat → Pt, very compressible.

2.2 Stresses on Soil and Seepage (ACiE0202)

A. Effective Stress Principle (Terzaghi, 1925)

Fig 2.6 — Effective stress with water table and capillary zone; seepage modifies σ′ by izγw
σ = σ' + u → σ' = σ − u
σ' = effective stress (inter-granular — controls strength & compressibility)
σ = total stress ; u = pore water pressure
  • Every measurable engineering behaviour — shear strength, consolidation settlement, bearing capacity — is governed by effective stress, not total stress.
  • Uplift (high water table): a fully submerged — buoyant — soil can reach σ' = 0; capillary suction instead increases σ' (negative u).
  • Capillary rise: water climbs above the water table through small pores. hc = 4T cos α/(γw d) — rise reaches several metres in silts (the maximum at silt-size pores), stays small in sands, and can be huge in clays but very slow. Capillary water is in tension (u negative), so it increases σ' and gives temporary "apparent" strength (apparent cohesion in sands).
  • Quicksand condition: with upward seepage, effective stress falls to zero at the critical gradient.
    Critical hydraulic gradient ic = γ'/γw = (G−1)/(1+e) ≈ 1.0 (typical G = 2.65, e = 0.65 → ic ≈ 1.0)
    At ic the soil loses all strength and behaves like a viscous liquid (boiling) — the danger in excavations below the water table; sheet-pile cut-offs are the cure. Quicksand is a condition, not a soil type.

B. Stress Distribution (Boussinesq & Westergaard)

  • Boussinesq (1885): point load on an elastic, homogeneous, isotropic, semi-infinite half-space without soil weight.
    Δσz = (3P/2π z²) / [1 + (r/z)²]^(5/2)
    Under the centre of a flexible circular footing of radius R: Δσz = q[1 − 1/(1+(R/z)²)^(3/2)] (q = contact pressure). Newmark's influence chart handles irregular loaded areas.
  • Westergaard: layered soil with thin stiff seams (varved clays) — lateral restraint between layers; gives smaller stresses than Boussinesq in layered media.
  • Newmark's influence chart builds up Δσz at a point beneath any irregular loaded plan area (influence value per unit × q).
  • 2:1 (2V:1H) approximate method: Δσz = qBL/[(B+z)(L+z)] — the quick hand method for rectangular footings.
  • Pressure bulb: an isobar of equal vertical stress (commonly drawn at 0.1q) — the zone of significant stress extends to about 2B deep. A narrower footing carrying the same load pushes its bulb deeper and can load weak layers below.
Fig 2.7 — Pressure bulb: Boussinesq isobars (0.5q, 0.2q, 0.1q) under a footing; the 2:1 method approximates the same spread
  • Contact pressure: a rigid footing on sand shows pressure zero at the edges and maximum at the centre; on clay, maximum at the edges and minimum at the centre. A flexible footing keeps contact pressure uniform while settlement stays non-uniform — edges settle more on sand, the centre settles more on clay.

C. Seepage Analysis

Fig 2.8 — Flow net under a sheet-pile wall: quantity q from Nf (flow channels) and Nd (potential drops)
  • Seepage is the flow of water through soil pores under a hydraulic gradient. It governs uplift under dams, piping, drainage quantities, and the stability of slopes and excavations.
  • Darcy's law (1856): v = k·i ; Q = k·i·A. Valid for laminar flow (Reynolds number < 1). In gravels (turbulent), v = k·i^m with m < 1.
Soilk (cm/s)Drainage
Gravel> 1Excellent
Sand1–10⁻³Good
Silt10⁻³–10⁻⁶ (often quoted 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁹ m/s)Poor
Clay< 10⁻⁶ cm/s (down to 10⁻⁹)Practically impervious
  • Factors affecting k: grain size (k ∝ D10² — Hazen's formula k = C·D10², C ≈ 100 (cm/s)·cm⁻²); void ratio (k ∝ e³/(1+e); Casagrande k = 1.4 e² k0.85); degree of saturation; temperature/viscosity (k is standardized at 27 °C); adsorbed water; fabric and stratification (k_horizontal is typically 3–10× k_vertical).
  • Stratified deposits:
    k_eq horizontal = Σ(kᵢ Hᵢ)/ΣHᵢ ; k_eq vertical = ΣHᵢ / Σ(Hᵢ/kᵢ)
  • Flow nets are the graphical solution of the Laplace equation: two orthogonal families of flow lines and equipotential lines forming curvilinear squares in isotropic soil.
    Seepage discharge q = k·H·(Nf/Nd) per unit length
    Nf = number of flow channels ; Nd = number of equipotential drops ; H = total head loss
    Head loss per drop Δh = H/Nd — pore pressure at any point follows from the remaining head
    Uses: uplift under a weir, exit-gradient/piping check, seepage quantity, pore pressures in slopes.
  • Flow net properties: flow lines cross equipotentials at right angles; flow lines never intersect each other; each channel carries the same quantity; cells are curvilinear squares in homogeneous isotropic soil.
  • Piping / exit gradient: Khosla's theory gives the exit gradient GE = (H/d)·1/(π√λ) (see 7.3). Safety against piping requires GE below the critical gradient ic with a factor of safety of about 4–5 (permissible exit gradient ≈ ic/4 to ic/5).
  • Seepage force: per unit volume j = i·γw, acting in the flow direction — it drives piping in upward flow and adds to the driving stress in slopes.
  • Falling head test suits fine soils (k < 10⁻⁴ cm/s); constant head suits coarse soils; in the field use the pumping test (Thiem) and piezometers.

D. Soil Compressibility Indices

  • One-dimensional consolidation (oedometer): the e–log p curve; the slope of the virgin compression line is:
    Compression Index Cc = (e1 − e2)/log(p2/p1) (slope of the e–log σ' virgin line)
    Cc ≈ 0.009(LL−10) (Skempton, undisturbed normally consolidated clay)
    Modified (strained) compression index Ccε = Cc/(1+e0)
    Recompression index Cr (swelling Cs) ≈ (1/5 to 1/10) Cc
  • Preconsolidation pressure (σ'p) is the maximum past effective stress, read from the Casagrande construction (point of minimum radius + bisectors). Overconsolidation ratio OCR = σ'p/σ'v0: OCR = 1 normally consolidated; > 1 overconsolidated; < 1 underconsolidated (still consolidating).
  • Coefficient of compressibility av = −de/dp; coefficient of volume compressibility mv = av/(1+e0) (m²/kN).
  • Rate of consolidation: cv = k/(mv·γw) (m²/yr) — the coefficient of consolidation governs how fast settlement happens.
  • Secondary compression (creep) continues after primary consolidation; its index Cα = Δe/Δlog t is large for organic soils and peat.

E. Compaction

Fig 2.9 — Compaction curve: peak at OMC/MDD; field spec 95% relative compaction; ZAV line bounds the curve from above
  • Definition: mechanical densification by expelling air — no water leaves the soil; particles are rearranged; the process is instantaneous. (Consolidation is the slow expulsion of water under sustained load.)
  • Proctor tests (mould 1000 cc in both):
Standard Proctor (IS 2720 Pt-7)Modified Proctor (Pt-8)
Mould volume1000 cc1000 cc
Layers × blows3 × 255 × 25
Rammer2.6 kg, 310 mm drop4.9 kg, 450 mm drop
Energy≈ 592–600 kJ/m³ (modified is ≈ 4.5× this)≈ 2700 kJ/m³
  • Compaction curve: γd vs w. The zero-air-voids (ZAV, S = 100%) line is the theoretical upper bound:
    ZAV: γd = G γw/(1 + wG) — the compaction curve can never cross the ZAV line
    The curve's peak is the Maximum Dry Density (MDD) at the Optimum Moisture Content (OMC).
  • Increasing compactive effort raises MDD and lowers OMC, flattening the curve; the air voids at the peak stay ≈ 4–5%.
  • Factors affecting compaction: water content (water lubricates grains for rearrangement; too much water is incompressible and blocks densification), compactive effort and method (kneading vs static vs dynamic/vibratory), soil type (well-graded gravelly soils respond best; CH clay gives low MDD and high OMC), gradation, and rock-fragment content.
  • Roller selection: vibratory rollers for sands and gravels; pneumatic-tyred for granular soils with some fines; sheepsfoot/padfoot for clays (kneading); smooth-wheel for finishing passes.
  • Field control: relative compaction = γd(field)/γd(lab max) × 100% — ≥ 95% is typical for fills (98% for road sub-base). Measured by sand replacement, core cutter or nuclear density gauge; the Proctor needle estimates in-situ water content.
  • Moisture side matters for special soils: expansive (black cotton) fills are compacted dry of optimum to limit later swelling; clay liners that need low permeability are compacted wet of optimum. (Bulking of damp sand is a batching issue, not a compaction issue.)

2.3 Shear Strength of Soil and Stability of Slopes (ACiE0203)

A. Concepts

  • Shear strength is the resistance to sliding between particles along a failure plane — the single most important soil property for bearing capacity, lateral earth pressure and slope stability.
  • Principal planes carry zero shear stress; only normal (principal) stresses σ1 (major), σ2, σ3 act on them. In the triaxial test σ2 = σ3 (the cell pressure) and the deviator stress (σ1 − σ3) is applied axially.
  • On any plane at angle θ from the major principal plane:
    σn = (σ1 + σ3)/2 + (σ1 − σ3)/2 · cos 2θ
    τ = (σ1 − σ3)/2 · sin 2θ
    Maximum shear τmax = (σ1 − σ3)/2 at θ = 45°
  • The Mohr circle represents the stresses on all planes graphically; the pole method reads the stress on any plane.

B. Mohr–Coulomb Failure Theory

Fig 2.10 — Mohr circle and c–φ envelope: failure when the circle touches τf = c + σtanφ (tangent, not secant)
τf = c + σ' tan φ (effective stress form)
τf = c + σ tan φ (total stress form)
c = cohesion ; φ = angle of internal friction ; σ' = effective normal stress on the failure plane
  • The failure envelope is tangent to the Mohr circle at failure:
    σ1f = σ3 tan²(45 + φ/2) + 2c tan(45 + φ/2)
    or σ1f = σ3·Nφ + 2c√Nφ with Nφ = tan²(45+φ/2) = (1+sin φ)/(1−sin φ)
    Failure plane inclination θ = 45° + φ/2 from the major principal plane
  • Typical parameter values:
Soilc (kPa)φ
Gravel/sand032–45° (dense higher)
Silt0–1526–32°
NC clay≈ 0 (small c')20–30°
OC clay10–50+22–30°
Undrained clay (total stress)cuφu = 0
  • Sands: φ 28–40°. Dense sand shows a peak φ then dilatancy; loose sand contracts to its constant-volume φcv. Dense sand fails in general shear; loose sand in local shear.
  • Clays: strength comes from cohesion plus friction; drained c' can be zero for NC clay. Undrained strength cu governs short-term stability (the φu = 0 analysis).
  • Skempton's pore pressure parameters A and B connect total and effective stress in undrained tests. The critical state framework (Roscoe) shows ultimate strength is independent of the initial state.

C. Types of Shear Tests

TestDrainage conditionMeasuresUse
Direct shear (box)Drained (slow) — drainage through porous stonesc', φ' (predominantly drained)Sands, long-term stability; simple, but the failure plane is forced and stress is non-uniform
Triaxial UU (unconsolidated undrained)No drainage at any stagecu, φu ≈ 0Short-term (immediate) stability — total stress analysis
Triaxial CU (consolidated undrained)Consolidate drained, shear undrained (measure u)cu, and with pore pressure measurement c', φ'Most common — both total and effective parameters
Triaxial CD (consolidated drained)Drainage throughoutc', φ' directlyLong-term stability, slow loading
Unconfined compressionUndrained, σ3 = 0qu; cu = qu/2Saturated clays (φ = 0)
Vane shearField/labcu = T/[πd²(h/2 + d/6)] (rectangular vane)Soft sensitive clays (no sampling disturbance)
Ring shearDrained, unlimited rotationResidual strength: c'r ≈ 0, φ'r 8–15°Slip surfaces of old landslides
Field tests: SPT, CPT, plate load, pressuremeter, field vane—N, qc, cu, EIn-situ strength/stiffness

D. Stability of Slopes

Fig 2.11 — Rotational slip in cohesive soil: FOS = resisting / disturbing moments along the trial circle
  • Failure modes: rotational slip (finite slopes in homogeneous cohesive soil), translational/planar slide (long natural slopes moving along a weak layer), flow slides (liquefaction), and compound/wedge failures.
  • Infinite slope, cohesionless (c = 0): FOS = tan φ/tan β — independent of height; failure comes when β reaches φ (the angle of repose).
  • Infinite slope with seepage (fully saturated, flow parallel to the slope): FOS = (γ'/γsat)·(tan φ/tan β) ≈ ½ tan φ/tan β — a water table at the surface halves the FOS.
  • Infinite slope with cohesion (c, dry or no seepage):
    FOS = c/(γ z cos²β tan β) + tan φ/tan β (z = depth to the failure surface)
  • Swedish slip circle methods:
    • φu = 0 analysis (total stress, saturated clay): FOS = (cu·L̄·R̄)/(W·x̄) — resisting moment over disturbing moment; the critical circle centre is found by trial (Fellenius lines).
    • Swedish slip circle for c–φ soil: friction-circle method or Taylor's stability number.
    • Method of slices (Ordinary/Fellenius): FOS = Σ[c·l + (W cos α − u·l) tan φ'] / Σ[W sin α]; Bishop's simplified method is more accurate and iterative.
  • Taylor's stability number Sn:
    Sn = c/(FOS·γ·H) → H_critical = c/(Sn·γ)
    Sn comes from charts against slope angle β and φ. For φ = 0 and β = 90° (a vertical cut): Sn ≈ 0.261, giving Hc = c/(0.261γ) ≈ 3.85c/γ — consistent with the theoretical 4c/γ (which corresponds to FOS 1.0 before tension cracks form)
    Theoretical maximum height of an unsupported vertical cut in clay: Hc = 4c/γ (Rankine); Taylor with a tension crack gives 3.85c/γ.
  • Factors affecting slope stability: seepage/rainfall (pore pressure ↑ → FOS ↓), surcharge, excavation or erosion at the toe, earthquakes (pseudo-static kh), tension cracks, progressive failure, vegetation and roots.
  • Bio-engineering (Nepal context): vetiver grass, bamboo, napier planting, brush layering and live check dams stabilize rural road slopes.
Exam traps: Direct shear can neither control drainage nor measure pore pressure. In a UU test the water content never changes, so all three specimens share the same cu — the Mohr circles have equal diameters and the envelope is horizontal (φu = 0). The CD test is the slowest (days to weeks for clay). The φu = 0 concept is valid only for saturated clays.

2.4 Soil Exploration, Earth Pressure and Retaining Structures (ACiE0204)

A. Soil Exploration

Stages: reconnaissance (walkover, existing data) → preliminary (geophysical) → detailed (borings, sampling, testing) → report.

Methods

  • Open excavation / test pits: to 3–4 m; direct visual inspection and block sampling; cheap but shallow.
  • Auger boring: hand augers (2–5 m) or power augers; cohesive soils without stones; disturbed samples only.
  • Wash boring: casing plus water jetting; progress by churning; the SPT is done here; cheap, no undisturbed sample.
  • Rotary drilling: for rock and strong strata; core drilling with single/double-tube core barrels; RQD measured here.
  • Percussion drilling: for boulders and gravels (Nepal river beds!); heavy chisel.
  • Geophysical: seismic refraction (velocity contrast finds depth to bedrock; it fails when a low-velocity layer hides beneath a high-velocity one) and electrical resistivity (Wenner array — moisture/mineral contrast; does not directly identify soil type).

Sampling

  • Disturbed samples — for classification tests (bag samples from SPT split-spoons and augers).
  • Undisturbed samples — for strength/compressibility: thin-walled tube samplers; Shelby tube (50–75 mm, area ratio < 10%, inside clearance 1–3%); piston sampler (Osterberg — better quality); block sampling gives the best quality.
    • Area ratio Ar = (De² − Di²)/Di² × 100 (< 10% for undisturbed work; < 20% acceptable in stiff soils)
    Inside clearance Ci = (Ds − Dc)/Dc × 100 (Ds = tube inside dia, Dc = cutting-edge inside dia; 1–3%, to reduce friction)
  • Sample disturbance grows with high area ratio, no inside clearance, over-driving, and poor sealing/transport.

Field tests

  • SPT: 63.5 kg hammer, 750 mm fall, split spoon 50.8 mm; N = blows per 300 mm of penetration after a 150 mm seating drive; corrections as in 2.1F.
  • SCPT/CPT (static cone): 60° cone, 10 cm² area; qc; friction ratio Fr = fs/qc identifies soil type; pore pressure version (CPTU); gives no sample.
  • Plate load test: 300–750 mm plate; load–settlement curve; gives the modulus of subgrade reaction k and allowable bearing pressure — but only for the shallow influence zone (≈ 2B) and immediate settlement (scale effect).
  • Also: pressuremeter, dilatometer (DMT), field vane, pumping test (k), borehole permeability tests.

Planning & reports

  • Boring spacing 15–45 m for buildings; depth to significant strata or 1.5B below footing level; rock coring 3 m into sound rock. Minimum exploration depth for foundations: 1.5×B below base or to a competent stratum; for piles, 5× pile diameter beyond the tip (20–30 m in Nepal's deep fills).
  • Report contents: introduction, site description, geology, exploration methods, logs, lab results, groundwater, analysis (bearing capacity, settlement, slopes), recommendations (foundation type and levels, dewatering, protection), limitations.

B. Earth Pressure Theories

Fig 2.12 — Rankine states: active, at-rest and passive pressure wedges on a wall (triangles drawn to relative magnitude)

Rankine (1857) — soil in plastic equilibrium, smooth wall (δ = 0), semi-infinite homogeneous backfill

Active: Ka = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45 − φ/2) ; Pa = ½ Ka γ H² (triangular)
Passive: Kp = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = tan²(45 + φ/2) ; Pp = ½ Kp γ H²
At rest: K0 = 1 − sin φ (Jaky, NC soils) ; OC: K0 = √(OCR)·(1 − sin φ)
With cohesion c: σa = Ka γ z − 2c√Ka → tension crack depth zc = 2c/(γ√Ka)
Total active force with c: Pa = ½Ka γH² − 2cH√Ka + 2c²/γ
  • The wall moving away from the backfill mobilizes active (minimum) pressure; pushed into the soil it mobilizes passive (maximum); no movement gives at-rest (intermediate). Required wall movement: rotation about the base of ~0.2–0.5% H for active in dense sand; passive needs much more (2–5% H).

Coulomb (1776) — wedge theory with wall friction δ, sloping wall/backfill, planar failure

  • P acts at angle δ to the wall normal; the trial wedge of critical inclination gives maximum Pa / minimum Pp. With δ > 0, Coulomb gives a slightly smaller active and a larger passive value than Rankine. For passive resistance, keep δ small (≤ φ/3) — the real failure surface is curved, so the planar assumption overestimates passive resistance at high δ.
  • Culmann's graphical method — general wedge analysis for irregular backfill and surcharge.
  • Rebhann's theorem — the analytical solution of Coulomb for simple cases.

Applicability

  • Rankine assumes a vertical smooth wall without wall friction — it suits cantilever and lightly frictional walls. Coulomb handles rough walls and sloping backfill — retaining walls and bridge abutments.
  • Surcharge: a uniform surcharge q adds a rectangular Pa = Ka·q·H; line and point loads are superposed elastically.
  • Water in the backfill: use submerged unit weight plus full water pressure (the worst case); weep holes and filters drain it away.

C. Retaining Walls — Types and Stability

Fig 2.13 — Gravity retaining wall: Pa (overturning + sliding) vs W (stabilising); check all four modes

Types

  • Gravity (masonry/rock-filled): resist by self-weight; 3–6 m typical; Nepal uses stone masonry retaining walls extensively on rural roads.
  • Cantilever RC (inverted-T/L): economical to ~6–8 m; the heel slab carries backfill weight; the stem resists bending.
  • Counterfort (buttressed) walls: for > 6–10 m; counterforts at the back (buttresses at the front) tie the stem to the base.
  • Also: crib, gabion, anchored, sheet pile, diaphragm/slurry wall, soil nailing, reinforced earth (MSE — geosynthetics or metal strips).

Stability checks (typical FOS)

ModeCheckRequired FOS
Overturning (about toe)ΣM_resisting/ΣM_overturning≥ 1.5–2.0
Sliding (along base)(μ ΣV + passive if considered)/Pa≥ 1.5 (1.2 under extreme loading)
Bearing (eccentric loading)q_max = ΣV/(B·1)·(1+6e/B) ≤ q_a ; no tension requires e ≤ B/6 (middle third rule)≥ 2.5–3.0
Deep-seated (global) stabilityslip circle below the wall (Swedish)≥ 1.5
  • Base width B ≈ (1/2 to 2/3) H for gravity walls; B ≈ 0.5–0.7H for cantilever walls.
  • Drainage is critical: weep holes (75–100 mm dia at 1.5–3 m spacing), granular filter or geo-drain behind the stem, drainage pipe at the heel. Full hydrostatic pressure destroys walls — most failures trace back to water.
  • Ways to increase stability: widen the base or add a toe projection, provide a shear key below the base, drain the backfill, terrace or batter to reduce effective height, add tie rods with anchors, use MSE reinforcement or deadman tie-backs, lower the water table, roughen the base for friction, pitch the toe with stone.
  • Failures seen in Nepal: monsoon clogging of weep holes, poorly compacted backfill, foundations on loose scree — which is why gabion walls are widely adopted on rural roads.

2.5 Fundamentals of Foundation (ACiE0205)

A. Definitions and Functions

  • Foundation (substructure): the part of the structure in contact with the ground that transmits loads safely. The footing is the widened base element.
  • Functions: spread the load to the soil at a safe stress, prevent settlement and differential movement, resist lateral and uplift forces, anchor the structure, provide a level surface.
  • A good foundation: stable against overturning and sliding, adequate bearing (FOS ≥ 2.5–3), settlement within limits (total ≈ 40–65 mm for isolated footings; differential ≈ 1/500 of the span), deep enough to be below scour, frost and plinth level, built of durable materials.

B. Types of Foundations

Shallow (Df/B ≤ 1 — load spread near the surface)Deep (load transferred to deeper strata)
Spread/isolated footing (square, rectangular, circular)Pile foundations (end bearing / friction / compaction; bored or driven)
Strip (continuous) footing — wallsPier foundations (caissons, drilled piers — large-diameter, ~0.7 m and above)
Combined footing (rectangular/trapezoidal — two columns)Well foundations (caissons — bridges across Nepal's rivers)
Strap (cantilever) footing — eccentric columns connected by a beamPile groups & pile-raft
Mat/raft foundation (whole footprint — differential settlement control; floating concept)Compaction/stone columns, sand drains (ground improvement)
Grillage foundation (steel — heavy column loads on low bearing)Under-reamed piles (expansive soils)
  • Shallow vs deep criterion: Df/B ≤ 1 is shallow (a few codes allow 2–3); behaviour differs too — shallow foundations spread load by Boussinesq-type pressure bulbs, piles transfer by tip and shaft resistance.
  • Spread footing concept: the column load spreads through the footing to reduce pressure to qa; thickness is set by one-way and punching shear; reinforcement goes at the bottom (tension on the cantilever face of the column).
  • Mat/raft: chosen when column loads are heavy, soil weak, or columns closely spaced (footing coverage > 50% of the footprint). It cuts differential settlement; a buoyant (floating) raft balances the excavation weight. Types: flat plate, plate with beams, cellular, pile-raft.
Fig 2.14 — The foundation family: isolated, strip, combined and raft footings spread load near the surface (Df/B ≤ 1); piles carry it to deeper strata

C. Factors Affecting Foundation Selection

  • Nature and depth of the bearing strata (SPT N, soil profile); groundwater level (dewatering, buoyancy); loads (magnitude, eccentricity, moment, cyclic/dynamic); structural type (frames are sensitive to differential settlement); adjacent structures; scour depth at bridges (Lacey); frost depth in cold regions; expansive or collapsible soils; seismic zone; construction feasibility and cost; environment (contamination, noise from driven piles).

D. Site Investigation for Foundations

  • Desk study (geology, old maps, previous reports) → walkover → geophysics → borings at about 1 per 200–400 m² (at least 2 per structure) with SPT every 1.5 m → undisturbed sampling in clays → lab tests → groundwater monitoring (standpipes/piezometers) → geotechnical report with recommendations.
  • Nepal practice: required for building permits above G+2 in municipalities; DOA/DoR standards govern bridges.

2.6 Bearing Capacity and Foundation Settlements (ACiE0206)

A. Bearing Capacity Concepts

  • Ultimate bearing capacity (qu): the gross pressure at which the soil fails in shear.
  • Net ultimate (qnu): qu minus the overburden at foundation level, γDf.
  • Net safe (qns): qnu/FOS with FOS 2.5–3.
  • Safe bearing capacity (gross): qns + γDf.
  • Allowable bearing pressure: the lesser of the safe bearing capacity (shear) and the pressure producing the permissible settlement — on sands, settlement usually governs.
  • Presumptive safe bearing capacity comes from code tables (NBC 105 / IS 1904). Common values: rocks 1650–3300 kPa; gravel 250; coarse sand 250; medium sand 150; fine sand/silt 100; soft clay 100; black cotton soil 50–100 kPa — approximations; codes govern.

B. Modes of Shear Failure

ModeSoilBehaviour
General shearDense sand, stiff clay (low compressibility)Well-defined peak, sudden failure, surface heave, failure surfaces reach the ground
Local shearLoose sand, soft clayLarge settlement before peak, slight heave; strength mobilized at reduced values (φ and c reduced by ~2/3 in Terzaghi's local formula)
Punching shearVery compressible soil / deep foundations / thin crust over a soft layerVertical shearing, no surface heave

C. Terzaghi's Bearing Capacity Theory (1943)

Strip footing (general shear): qu = c·Nc + γDf·Nq + 0.5·γ·B·Nγ
Square: qu = 1.3 c Nc + γDf Nq + 0.4 γ B Nγ
Circular: qu = 1.3 c Nc + γDf Nq + 0.3 γ B Nγ
Local shear: use c' = 2c/3 and tanφ' = (2/3)tanφ → qu = (2/3)c Nc' + γDf Nq' + 0.5 γB Nγ'
  • Bearing capacity factors depend on φ only: Nq = e^(π tanφ)·tan²(45+φ/2) — the tables are computed from it. Landmarks: φ = 0 → Nc = 5.7, Nq = 1, Nγ = 0; φ = 30° → Nc ≈ 37, Nq ≈ 22, Nγ ≈ 19 (Terzaghi values).
  • Assumptions: shallow strip footing (Df ≤ B), general shear, rough base, homogeneous isotropic soil; failure zones I (elastic wedge under the base), II (radial shear — log spiral), III (Rankine passive zones).
Fig 2.15 — Terzaghi's bearing-capacity failure zones: elastic wedge I under the base, radial-shear zones II, Rankine passive zones III with surface heave
  • Shape/depth/inclination corrections (IS 6403):
    qu(net) = c Nc sc dc ic + q(Nq−1) sq dq iq + 0.5 γ B Nγ sγ dγ iγ
    Shape factors: sc = 1+0.2B/L (φ = 0); sq = sγ = 1+0.1B/L (φ > 10° approximations)
    Depth factors: dc = 1+0.2 Df/B (φ = 0); dq = dγ = 1+0.1 Df/B
    Water table: WT at base level → use γ' in the Nγ term; WT at surface → γ' throughout; WT deeper than B below the base → no change. The Nq term always uses the actual (wet or dry) surcharge weight above base level; the 0.5 reduction factor in course notes applies to the Nγ term when the WT sits at base level
  • Other theories: Meyerhof (inclined/eccentric loading, shape+depth factors, effective width B' = B−2e), Hansen, Vesic — remember the names and the hierarchy (Terzaghi → Meyerhof/Hansen/Vesic refinements).
  • Eccentric loading: Meyerhof's effective-area method — L' = L − 2e and B' = B − 2e (e = eccentricity); check q_max at the edge ≤ qa; keep the resultant within the middle third to avoid tension.

D. Bearing Capacity from Field Tests

  • SPT (Teng's formula): qa ≈ 33.4·N̄·((B+0.3)/B)²·Kd in kN/m² (kPa), with B in metres, N̄ the corrected average N, and Kd = 1+0.33Df/B ≤ 1.33 — settlement limited to 25 mm.
  • Plate load test: extrapolate settlement to the real footing by S_f = S_p[(B_f)/(B_p)]² for clay (same pressure) or S_f = S_p[(B_f(B_p+0.3))/(B_p(B_f+0.3))]² for sand. Take the load intensity at 25 mm settlement or breaking load/2.5–3.
  • Presumptive values — NBC/IS tables (see above).

E. Consolidation Settlement

Primary consolidation (1-D, Terzaghi), NC clay: S = (Cc H)/(1+e0) · log[(σ'0 + Δσ)/σ'0]
OC clay crossing σ'p: S = (Cr H)/(1+e0) · log(σ'p/σ'0) + (Cc H)/(1+e0) · log[(σ'0 + Δσ)/σ'p]
Time rate: Tv = cv t/d² ; d = drainage path (H/2 for double drainage, H for single)
U ≤ 60%: Tv = (π/4)U² ; U > 60%: Tv = 1.781 − 0.933 log(100−U%)
  • Terzaghi's 1-D consolidation assumptions: homogeneous saturated clay, small strains, Darcy flow, incompressible water and grains, k and av constant, vertical flow only.
  • Time factor Tv: U = 50% → Tv = 0.197 (memorize); U = 90% → 0.848.
  • Settlement types: immediate (elastic, undrained in clays; plastic in sands), primary consolidation (excess pore pressure dissipation — clays), secondary compression (creep — peats/organics). Total = the sum.
  • Permissible settlements (IS 1904 practice): isolated footing on sand ≈ 40 mm, on clay ≈ 65 mm; raft 75–100 mm; differential settlement limited to about 1/500 for frames. Wall cracking starts around an angular distortion of 1/150–1/300.
  • Settlement reduction: deep foundations, preloading with sand drains (vertical drains + surcharge), stone columns, densification, larger footing area (reduces Δσ but deepens the pressure bulb), balanced raft/floating foundation.
  • Rate: t = Tv d²/cv — doubling the drainage path quadruples the time; sand drains shorten the path.

F. Pile Foundations (basics — deep)

  • Types by material/installation: timber, steel (H, pipe), precast and cast-in-situ RCC (bored; under-reamed for expansive soils); driven (displacement) vs bored (replacement).
  • Load transfer: end bearing Qb plus skin friction Qs; negative skin friction (downdrag) comes from settling fill.
  • Group efficiency: Converse–Labarre equation η = 1 − θ[(n−1)m + (m−1)n]/90mn (θ = arctan(d/s), d pile dia, s spacing, degrees); Feld's rule — reduce each pile's capacity by 1/16 per adjacent pile; check block failure; group settlement exceeds single-pile settlement.
  • Verification: load tests (kentledge); dynamic formulas (Hiley) are indicative only; integrity tests (PIT/PDA) check the shaft.
Vesic's classification refines these with transition zones — for NEC, remember the three modes and their soil examples. Settlement at failure: general < local < punching.

Worked Numericals (MCQ Patterns You Will Meet)

Phase relationships

  • Soil: w = 15%, G = 2.70, e = 0.75. Then S = wG/e = (0.15×2.70)/0.75 = 54%; γd = Gγw/(1+e) = 2.70×9.81/1.75 = 15.12 kN/m³; γ = γd(1+w) = 17.39 kN/m³; γsat (S = 100%) = (G+e)γw/(1+e) = 3.45×9.81/1.75 = 19.34 kN/m³.
  • Wet soil 1.9 kg in a 1-litre mould; oven-dry 1.6 kg → γ = 1.9 kg/0.001 m³ = 1900 kg/m³ = 18.64 kN/m³; w = 0.3/1.6 = 18.75%; γd = 18.64/1.1875 = 15.7 kN/m³.
  • Relative density: emax = 0.9, emin = 0.5, field e = 0.6 → Id = (0.9−0.6)/(0.9−0.5) = 75% → dense.

Effective stress with seepage

  • 3 m sand layer (γsat = 20 kN/m³), water table at the surface, downward seepage with 3 m head loss (i = 1): σ at 3 m = 3×20 = 60 kPa; u = 3×9.81 − 3×9.81 = 0; σ' = 60 kPa — downward seepage increases effective stress.
  • Upward seepage at i = 0.8: u = 29.43 + 3×9.81×0.8 = 52.97 kPa; σ' = 60 − 52.97 = 7 kPa — nearly quick; at i ≥ ic ≈ 1.04 the layer becomes quick.

Stress increase beneath footings

  • Square footing 2×2 m, q = 100 kPa; 2:1 method at z = 2 m: Δσ = 100×4/(4×4) = 25 kPa.
  • Point load P = 500 kN at the surface; Δσz at 3 m directly below (Boussinesq, r = 0): 3×500/(2π×9) = 26.5 kPa.
  • Flexible circular raft R = 5 m, q = 100 kPa, at z = 5 m below centre: R/z = 1 → Δσ = 100×[1 − (1/2)^1.5] = 64.6 kPa.

Flow nets

  • Weir: H = 8 m, Nf = 5, Nd = 16, k = 4×10⁻⁵ m/s → q = 4×10⁻⁵×8×(5/16) = 1×10⁻⁴ m³/s per m; uplift at the mid-floor point (12 drops remaining): u = γw(H − 4×H/16) = 9.81×6 = 58.9 kPa.
  • Unit check for a smaller case: k = 10⁻⁴ cm/s = 10⁻⁶ m/s, H = 5 m, Nf/Nd = 4/10 = 0.4 → q = 10⁻⁶×5×0.4 = 2×10⁻⁶ m³/s per m — always convert k to m/s first.
  • Exit gradient (Khosla): GE = (H/d)·1/(π√λ) with λ from geometry; keep ic/GE ≥ 4–5 in sands.

Consolidation settlement & time

  • NC clay 4 m thick (double drainage), e0 = 1.0, Cc = 0.3, σ'0 = 80 kPa, Δσ = 80 kPa: S = (0.3×4/2)×log(160/80) = 0.6×0.301 = 0.18 m = 180 mm.
  • cv = 4 m²/yr, d = 2 m (double drainage): t50 = 0.197×4/4 = 0.197 yr ≈ 72 days; t90 = 0.848 yr ≈ 310 days (0.848 yr × 365).
  • Same layer with single drainage (d = 4 m): all times ×4 (t50 ≈ 288 days) — the classic exam trap.
  • OCR: σ'p = 150 kPa, σ'0 = 75 kPa → OCR = 2 (overconsolidated; settlement uses Cr until σ'p is crossed).

Shear strength numericals

  • Triaxial CD on sand: σ3 = 100, failure at σ1 = 400 kPa → sinφ = (σ1−σ3)/(σ1+σ3) = 300/500 = 0.6 → φ = 37°; failure plane at 45+18.5 = 63.5°.
  • Clay with c = 20 kPa, φ = 0: σ1f = σ3 + 2c = 100 + 40 = 140 kPa (cu = 20).
  • c = 10 kPa, φ = 30°, σn' = 100 kPa → τf = 10 + 100×tan30° = 67.7 kPa.
  • Direct shear, normal stress 50 kPa, failure shear 40 kPa → with c = 0: tanφ = 0.8 → φ = 38.7°.

Earth pressure numericals

  • Wall H = 6 m, φ = 30°, γ = 18 kN/m³, no surcharge: Pa = ½×(1/3)×18×36 = 108 kN/m acting at H/3 = 2 m above the base.
  • Add surcharge q = 20 kPa: extra Pa = Ka·q·H = (1/3)×20×6 = 40 kN/m (uniform, acting at H/2 = 3 m).
  • c–φ soil, c = 10 kPa, φ = 20°, γ = 17, H = 5 m: Ka = 0.49; Pa = ½×0.49×17×25 − 2×10×5×√0.49 + 2c²/γ = 104.1 − 70 + 11.8 = 45.9 kN/m; tension crack depth zc = 2c/(γ√Ka) = 20/(17×0.7) = 1.68 m.
  • Passive wedge in sand: H = 3 m, φ = 30°, γ = 18: Pp = ½×3×18×9 = 243 kN/m.

Bearing capacity numericals

  • Strip footing B = 2 m, Df = 1 m, c = 10 kPa, φ = 30° (Nc = 37, Nq = 22, Nγ = 19), γ = 18: qu = 10×37 + 18×1×22 + 0.5×18×2×19 = 370 + 396 + 342 = 1108 kPa; qnu = 1108 − 18 = 1090; qns = 1090/3 ≈ 363 kPa; safe gross = 363 + 18 ≈ 381 kPa.
  • Square footing in the same soil: qu = 1.3×10×37 + 396 + 0.4×18×2×19 = 481+396+274 = 1151 kPa.
  • Clay, φ = 0 (Nc = 5.7): strip B = 1.5 m, Df = 1.5 m, cu = 50 kPa, γ = 18: qu = 5.7×50 + 18×1.5 = 285+27 = 312 kPa; qns = (312−27)/3 = 95 kPa; gross 113 kPa.
  • Water table at base level: use γ' = 18−9.81 = 8.19 in place of γ in the Nγ term.

Settlement limit checks

  • Angular distortion = Δs/L: cracking becomes likely beyond 1/150–1/300; frames are limited to about 1/500. Adjacent columns 6 m apart settling differentially by 15 mm give 1/400 — worse than the 1/500 frame limit, so the design must be tightened.

Extended High-Yield Additions (Exam-Focused Extras)

Soil structure & mineralogy

  • Clay minerals: kaolinite (1:1 lattice, thick packets, low activity), illite (2:1 with potassium ions bonded — medium activity), montmorillonite (2:1 expanding lattice with isomorphous substitution — huge swelling, the black cotton soil of the Terai).
  • Soil structures: flocculated (edge-to-face — loose marine clays), dispersed (face-to-face), single-grained (sands), honeycomb (silts).
  • Diffuse double layer — the attracted water layer around clay particles. High-valence cations shrink the layer and promote flocculation. Lime stabilization works by cation exchange plus pozzolanic reaction.

Soil stabilization & ground improvement (rural roads relevance)

  • Mechanical: compaction, grading, reinforcement (geogrid/geotextile).
  • Chemical: lime 2–8% for clays (reduces PI, increases strength; lime column piles), cement 3–10% for granular soils, fly ash, bitumen for sands.
  • Drainage-based: sand drains, prefabricated vertical drains (PVD), electro-osmosis (clays, expensive).
  • Others: vibro-flotation (sands), stone columns (soft clay — Nepal bridge-approach fills), grouting (permeation/jet), preloading.

Machine foundations & dynamic soil (one-liners)

  • Keep the natural frequency of the foundation-soil system below the machine frequency (avoid resonance); respect amplitude limits; the coefficient of elastic uniform compression comes from the plate vibration test; Barkan's method.
  • Liquefaction: saturated loose sands under cyclic (earthquake) loading lose effective stress (u → σ). Assessed by the SPT-N-based simplified procedure (Seed); remedied by densification, stone columns and drainage.

Numerical one-liners for MCQ

  • e = n/(1−n): n = 40% → e = 0.667; e = 1 → n = 50%.
  • γd = γ/(1+w): γ = 18 kN/m³, w = 10% → γd = 16.36 kN/m³.
  • eS = wG: G = 2.7, e = 0.81, S = 60% → w = 18%.
  • γ' = γsat − 9.81: γsat = 20 → γ' = 10.2 kN/m³; ic = γ'/γw ≈ 1.0 (≈ 1.04 at the exact value).
  • Ka = 1/3 → φ = 30°; Kp = 1/Ka = 3; K0 = 1 − sinφ = 0.5 (for NC soil).
  • Failure plane at 45+φ/2: φ = 30 → 60° from the major principal plane.
  • cu = qu/2: qu = 100 kPa → cu = 50 kPa.
  • τmax = (σ1−σ3)/2, acting at 45° from the principal planes.
  • q = kH·Nf/Nd: k = 10⁻⁴ cm/s = 10⁻⁶ m/s, H = 5 m, Nf/Nd = 4/10 → q = 2×10⁻⁶ m³/s per m (convert k to m/s first).
  • Cc ≈ 0.009(LL−10): LL = 60 → Cc = 0.45.
  • S = (Cc H/(1+e0))·log((σ'0+Δσ)/σ'0): doubling the stress on an NC layer (H = 4 m, e0 = 1, Cc = 0.3) → S = 0.3×4/2×log2 = 0.18 m.
  • Tv = 0.197 at U = 50%; t50 = 0.197 d²/cv.
  • Relative compaction = γd,field/γd,max × 100; ≥ 95% is the typical acceptance.
  • Standard Proctor energy ≈ 600 kJ/m³; Modified ≈ 2700 kJ/m³ (4.5× more).
  • FOS (infinite slope, c–φ, no seepage) = c/(γz cos²β tanβ) + tanφ/tanβ.
  • FOS (c = 0, seepage parallel) = (γ'/γsat)·tanφ/tanβ ≈ ½ tanφ/tanβ.
  • Taylor Sn = c/(FOS·γ·H); vertical cut Hc ≈ 4c/γ (Rankine theoretical).
  • Rankine tension crack depth zc = 2c/(γ√Ka); support pressure is zero above the crack in c-soils.
  • Overturning FOS ≥ 1.5–2, sliding ≥ 1.5, bearing ≥ 2.5–3; middle third rule e ≤ B/6.
  • Terzaghi: strip qu = cNc + qNq + 0.5γBNγ; φ = 0 → Nc = 5.7, Nq = 1, Nγ = 0.
  • Shape factors: square footing uses 1.3 on the Nc term; circular uses 0.3 on the Nγ term.
  • Eccentricity: effective width B' = B − 2e (Meyerhof).
  • Water table at footing base level → the Nγ term uses γ' (submerged).
  • SPT: 63.5 kg hammer, 750 mm fall, N = blows/300 mm; drive shoe 50.8 mm OD.
  • Shelby tube area ratio < 10%; inside clearance 1–3%.
  • RQD: % of core pieces ≥ 10 cm; > 90% excellent, < 25% very poor.
  • Sand N = 10–30 medium dense; clay N = 4–8 medium consistency (cu 25–50 kPa).
  • Permeability: clay < 10⁻⁶ cm/s; gravel > 1 cm/s; Hazen k = C·D10².
  • kx > kz (stratification); kh/kv typically 3–10.
  • Quicksand: ic = (G−1)/(1+e) ≈ 1; a condition, not a soil type.
  • Boussinesq Δσz = 3P/2πz² at r = 0; Westergaard for layered soils (lower stress).
  • Pressure bulb: the 0.1q isobar reaches ~2B deep; stress at depth z under a circular raft centre ≈ q[1 − (1/(1+(R/z)²))^1.5].
  • Flocculated structure = honeycomb, edge-to-face; dispersed = face-to-face parallel.
  • Activity: montmorillonite > 1.25 (expansive); kaolinite < 0.75.
  • Sensitivity: quick clay > 16; thixotropy = strength regain with time.
  • A-line PI = 0.73(LL−20); LL 50 divides low/high plasticity (USCS/IS).
  • Cu = D60/D10; Cc = D30²/(D10·D60); well-graded sand: Cu > 6 and 1 < Cc < 3.
  • D10 = effective size (10% finer); Hazen's formula uses D10.
  • Atterberg: LL at 25 blows (Casagrande cup); PL thread 3 mm; PI = LL−PL.
  • LI = (w−PL)/PI; LI > 1 liquid state; CI = (LL−w)/PI.
  • Oven drying at 105–110 °C; specific gravity by pycnometer — use kerosene or white spirit (not water) when the soil holds soluble salts, gypsum or organics, so the solids do not dissolve.

Field Identification & Descriptive Classification

  • Dry strength test: crushing resistance of a dry lump — none (silt), low–medium (clayey silt), high (CL), very high (CH).
  • Dilatancy (shake) test: a shiny film appearing when shaken = fine sand/rock flour (silt), not clay.
  • Toughness test: kneading a 3 mm thread — weak crumbs = ML, medium = CL, tough putty = CH.
  • Odour & colour: organic musty odour (OL/OH); dark grey/black = organics; red/yellow = iron oxides (laterite); white salts = efflorescence.
  • Field descriptions: boulders, cobbles, gravel, sand and fines fractions with percentages describe coarse soils; consistency terms describe clays; density terms describe sands.

Closing Bank — Chapter 2 (Extra High-Yield Facts)

A. More Phase-Relationship & Index-Property Numericals

  • Wet soil 1.8 kg, oven-dry 1.5 kg → w = 0.3/1.5 = 20%; with G = 2.70 and e = 0.65: γd = 2.7×9.81/1.65 ≈ 16.05 kN/m³; γsat = (2.7+0.65)×9.81/1.65 ≈ 19.92 kN/m³; γ' = (G−1)γw/(1+e) = 1.7×9.81/1.65 ≈ 10.11 kN/m³ (at e = 1 it would be exactly 9.81 — the classic (G−1) shortcut).
  • Volume–mass check: e = 0.54 → n = 0.54/1.54 = 35.1%; S = wG/e with w = 15%, G = 2.68 → S = 0.15×2.68/0.54 = 74.4% — partially saturated (an air phase exists below 100%).
  • Relative density: emax = 0.9, emin = 0.5, e = 0.6 → Id = 0.3/0.4 = 75% — dense sand (good bearing, low SPT-correlated settlement).
  • Atterberg trio: LL = 42, PL = 21 → PI = 21; LI at w = 30%: (30−21)/21 = 0.43 (plastic state); activity with 35% clay fraction = 21/35 = 0.6 → inactive–normal (kaolinitic).
  • USCS call: LL = 48 (< 50), PI = 19. The A-line at LL 48 gives PI = 0.73×(48−20) = 20.4; since 19 < 20.4 the point plots below the A-line → ML (silt of low plasticity). The A-line check always decides clay vs silt.

B. Compaction & Field Control Extras

  • Proctor mould 1000 cm³, wet mass 2.05 kg, w = 12% → γwet = 20.5 kN/m³; γd = 20.5/1.12 = 18.3 kN/m³ — repeat over w; the peak gives MDD at the matching OMC.
  • Standard vs Modified: Modified energy ≈ 4.5× standard (heavier hammer, more layers, higher drop) → MDD up ~5–8%, OMC down ~2–4%. Modified suits airfields and heavy-duty fills.
  • Field specs: earth-dam core relative compaction ≥ 95–98% Standard Proctor; road subgrade 95–100% (the top 500 mm the highest). Measured by sand cone, core cutter or nuclear density gauge; degree of compaction = field γd / lab MDD × 100.
  • OMC–soil trend: clay > silt > sand OMC (the finest soil holds the most water). Uniform sand compacts by vibration (dry or flooded); clays need kneading (sheepsfoot/padfoot); granular soils take smooth vibratory rollers.
  • Lift thickness rule: 150–200 mm compacted layers are typical; over-thick lifts leave uncompacted cores — a favourite "reason of failure" MCQ.

C. Consolidation & Settlement — Extra Drills

  • Cv from t50: Cv = 0.197 Hd²/t50 (time factor 0.197 at 50%; Hd = half the thickness for double drainage). A 5 m layer with t50 = 2 yr → Cv = 0.197×2.5²/2 = 0.616 m²/yr.
  • Time to 90%: t90 = 0.848×Hd²/Cv = 0.848×6.25/0.616 ≈ 8.6 yr — same layer, same load.
  • mv and settlement: S = mv·Δσ'·H; mv = 0.5 m²/MN, Δσ' = 100 kPa, H = 4 m → S = 0.5×10⁻⁶×100×10³×4 = 0.2 m — 200 mm under a wide fill, plausible.
  • Compression index estimate: Cc ≈ 0.009(LL−10) (Skempton, NC undisturbed clay); on the e–log p plot each load doubling moves one log cycle. OCR = σ'p/σ'0: 200/100 = 2 → overconsolidated (lightly), settlement small; σ'p comes from Casagrande's graphical construction (point of maximum curvature).
  • Immediate vs consolidation: immediate = undrained elastic distortion (saturated clay changes shape, not volume); primary = drainage of excess pore pressure (time–log curve); secondary = creep after u = 0 (organic soils worst). The three-part settlement classification is a guaranteed MCQ.

D. Shear Strength & Slopes — Final Facts

  • τ = c' + σ' tanφ' (effective) vs τ = cu (total, undrained φ = 0 analysis): short-term (end of construction) uses undrained; long-term uses drained — the "which analysis when" MCQ.
  • Direct shear vs triaxial: direct — simple, drainage uncontrolled, failure plane forced; triaxial — drainage controlled (UU, CU, CD), pore pressure measurable, failure plane free — three separate one-mark comparisons.
  • Vane shear for soft clays: cu = T/(πD²(H/2 + D/6)); a quick field test, not valid for fissured or stiff clays.
  • Infinite slope (seepage to surface): Fs = (γ'/γsat)·tanφ/tanβ (c = 0); with cohesion: Fs = (c' + γ'z cos²β tanφ')/(γsat z cosβ sinβ) — the two formulas cover most slope MCQs.
  • Swedish slip circle (Fellenius): Fs = resisting moments/driving moments. Taylor's stability number Sn = c/(Fs·γ·H); toe vs base circle chosen by β and φm; the friction-circle method handles c–φ soils.

E. Ten-Second Tally (Chapter 2 final flash)

  • e·S = w·G — the master phase key; γ' = (G−1)γw/(1+e).
  • Cu ≥ 4 gravel, ≥ 6 sand for well-graded; Cc = 1–3.
  • A-line: PI = 0.73(LL−20); above = clays (C), below = silts (M).
  • SPT 63.5 kg / 750 mm; corrected N = Cn·N; N60 = N×(Em/60).
  • ic ≈ 1 (boiling); σ' = σ − u; flow net Q = kH(Nf/Nd).
  • Cc ≈ 0.009(LL−10); Tv = 0.197 at 50%, 0.848 at 90%.
  • Mohr: σ1 = (σx+σy)/2 + R; sinφ = (σ1−σ3)/(σ1+σ3) at failure.
  • Tv for U ≤ 60%: Tv = (π/4)U²; U > 60%: Tv = 1.781 − 0.933 log₁₀(100 − U%).
  • Ka ≈ 1/3 (φ = 30°); Kp = 3; Ka·Kp = 1.
  • Terzaghi: strip qu = cNc + qNq + 0.5γBNγ; square 1.3cNc + qNq + 0.4γBNγ; circular 1.3cNc + qNq + 0.3γBNγ — memorize the 0.5 / 0.4 / 0.3 set.
  • Consistency N: 4–8 medium, 15–30 stiff, > 30 hard.
  • γd = Gγw/(1+e) = γ/(1+w); γsat = (G+e)γw/(1+e); γ' = (G−1)γw/(1+e).
  • Id = (emax − e)/(emax − emin)×100; 65–85% dense.
  • Atterberg: LL at 25 blows; PL thread 3 mm; PI = LL − PL; LI = (w−PL)/PI.
  • Activity = PI/clay%; montmorillonite > 1.25 — expansive; kaolinite < 0.75.
  • Cu = D60/D10; Cc = D30²/(D10·D60); well-graded sand: Cu > 6, 1 < Cc < 3.
  • Hydrometer/pipette use Stokes' law for particles < 75 μm.
  • A-line PI = 0.73(LL−20); above = clay, below = silt; LL 50 = low/high boundary.
  • SPT: 63.5 kg hammer, 750 mm fall, N = blows per 300 mm after 150 mm seating.
  • Shelby tube: area ratio < 10%, inside clearance 1–3%.
  • RQD counts pieces ≥ 10 cm: > 90% excellent; < 25% very poor.
  • Clay consistency: N 4–8 medium (cu 25–50 kPa); N > 30 hard (> 200 kPa).
  • Sand density: N 10–30 medium; N > 50 very dense.
  • Seismic refraction fails over a hidden low-velocity layer; resistivity is ambiguous with multiple layers.
  • σ' = σ − u; capillary water in tension raises σ' (apparent cohesion); full uplift (submergence) can drive σ' to zero.
  • ic = (G−1)/(1+e) ≈ 1.0; quicksand = a condition, not a soil type.
  • Boussinesq: Δσz = 3P/2πz² (r = 0); Westergaard for layered soils (smaller stress).
  • 2:1 method: Δσ = qBL/[(B+z)(L+z)].
  • Rigid footing on sand: contact pressure minimum at the edges; on clay: maximum at the edges.
  • Darcy v = ki (laminar, Re < 1); Hazen k = C·D10²; kx > kz.
  • keq,h = ΣkiHi/ΣHi; keq,v = ΣHi/Σ(Hi/ki).
  • q = kH·Nf/Nd; equipotential drop Δh = H/Nd; flow lines ⊥ equipotentials.
  • Cc = 0.009(LL−10); Cr ≈ Cc/5–10; OCR = σ'p/σ'0; mv = av/(1+e0); cv = k/(mvγw).
  • Compaction expels air; consolidation expels water.
  • Standard Proctor 3×25, 2.6 kg, 310 mm (≈ 600 kJ/m³); Modified 5×25, 4.9 kg, 450 mm (≈ 2700 kJ/m³).
  • More energy: MDD ↑, OMC ↓; the ZAV line γd = Gγw/(1+wG) is the ceiling.
  • Sheepsfoot for clay; vibratory for sand; relative compaction ≥ 95% typical.
  • Failure plane 45° + φ/2 from the major principal plane; τmax = (σ1−σ3)/2 at 45°.
  • Mohr–Coulomb τf = c' + σ'tanφ; Nφ = tan²(45+φ/2); σ1f = σ3Nφ + 2c√Nφ.
  • UU: φu = 0 with cu; CU with u measurement gives c', φ'; CD gives drained parameters directly.
  • cu = qu/2; vane cu = T/[πd²(h/2+d/6)]; ring shear → residual φr 8–15°.
  • Infinite slope: FOS = tanφ/tanβ (c = 0); with seepage ≈ ½ tanφ/tanβ; vertical cut Hc = 4c/γ.
  • Taylor Sn = c/(F·γ·H); Fellenius/Bishop method of slices — Bishop's iterative method is more accurate.
  • Ka = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ) = 1/Kp; K0 = 1 − sinφ (Jaky).
  • Pa acts at H/3 above the base (triangular); surcharge adds Ka·q·H at H/2.
  • Tension crack depth zc = 2c/(γ√Ka); submerged backfill: use γ' plus full water pressure.
  • Wall stability: overturning ≥ 1.5–2; sliding ≥ 1.5; bearing ≥ 2.5–3; e ≤ B/6 (middle third).
  • Weep holes 75–100 mm; most failures come from clogged drainage.
  • Shallow vs deep: Df/B ≤ 1 (some codes 2); the well foundation (caisson) serves bridge piers in Nepal's rivers.
  • Mat for weak soils/heavy loads; strap for eccentric boundary columns; under-reamed piles for expansive soil.
  • General shear — dense sand/stiff clay; local — loose sand/soft clay; punching — very compressible soils.
  • Terzaghi: strip qu = cNc + γDfNq + 0.5γBNγ; square 1.3/0.4; circular 1.3/0.3; φ = 0: Nc 5.7, Nq 1, Nγ 0.
  • Meyerhof effective width B' = B − 2e; water table at base → Nγ term with γ'.
  • FOS on net ultimate 2.5–3; sands are governed by settlement, clays by shear.
  • Tv = 0.197 (U = 50%); 0.848 (U = 90%); t = Tv d²/cv; halving the drainage path cuts time to ¼.
  • S = (Cc H/(1+e0))·log[(σ'0+Δσ)/σ'0] for NC clay; immediate + primary + secondary = total.
  • Negative skin friction — downdrag from settling fill; group efficiency < 1 typically (Converse–Labarre equation).
  • Liquefaction — saturated loose sand + cyclic loading; remedies: stone columns, vibro, densification.
  • Lime stabilizes clays (cation exchange, 2–8%); cement suits granular soils (3–10%).
  • Black cotton soil of the Terai = montmorillonitic CH; free swell index > 100% is the indicator.

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (2.1–2.6)

Soil Formation & Origin (2.1)

  • Karl von Terzaghi (1925) is the father of soil mechanics. Modern-era contributors: Proctor (compaction), Taylor (consolidation, shear strength, slope stability), Casagrande (seepage through earth dams), Skempton (pore pressure, effective stress, bearing capacity), Meyerhof (bearing capacity of shallow/deep foundations). Early period: Coulomb (earth pressure), Rankine, Darcy, Mohr, Boussinesq (stress distribution), Atterberg (1911, limits), Fellenius (slope stability).
  • Residual (sedentary) soil stays at its place of formation; transported soil is moved elsewhere — most deposits engineers deal with are transported.
  • Physical disintegration (thermal changes, ice wedging, root spreading, abrasion) keeps the parent-rock chemistry → coarse soils (gravel, sand). Chemical decomposition (hydration, carbonation, oxidation, solution, hydrolysis) creates new minerals → clay soils.
  • Transported deposits: alluvial (rivers/streams), lacustrine (lake beds), marine (sea), aeolian (wind — dunes; loess = wind-blown silt), glacial (drift; till = direct ice deposit; moraine = ground from till; outwash = meltwater-borne), colluvial/talus (gravity).
  • Nomenclature: bentonite = high-montmorillonite clay; black cotton soil = residual high-clay soil (best stabilizer = hydrated lime); boulders > 300 mm; cobbles 80–300 mm; loam = sand+silt+clay; tuff = volcanic ejecta; varved clays = alternating silt/clay layers each < 1 cm; dispersive clays deflocculate in still water; rock flour = cohesionless.
  • Nepal seismic zones: NBC 105:1994 divided the country into three zones (A1–A3, zone factor Z ≈ 1.0–1.1); NBC 105:2020 replaced the discrete zones with a continuous seismic-zonation map (Z ≈ 0.84–1.12). Don't confuse Nepal's zoning with India's four seismic zones (II–V) — a favourite distractor.

Phase Relationships & Index Properties

  • n = e/(1+e); γt = Gγw(1+w)/(1+e); γsat = γw(G+e)/(1+e); γd = Gγw/(1+e); γsub = γsat − γw; S = Vw/Vv.
  • Sieve analysis serves particles > 75 μm (coarse); the smallest IS sieve = 45 μm; sedimentation analysis (Stokes' law, hydrometer/pipette) serves fines < 75 μm. Wet sieve analysis is required when fines exceed 5%.
  • Coarse sieves: 80, 40, 20, 10, 4.75 mm; fine sieves: 2 mm, 1 mm, 600, 425, 212, 150, 75 μm.
  • Hydrometer corrections: meniscus (+ve), temperature (±, zero at 27 °C), dispersing agent (always −ve). The standard dispersant is sodium hexametaphosphate at 33 g/L (IS 2720 Part 4).
  • Cu = D60/D10; Cc = D30²/(D60·D10). Well graded: gravel Cu > 4, sand Cu > 6, 1 < Cc < 3; Cu < 2 → uniform. D10 is the "effective size".
  • Specific gravity by density-bottle (pycnometer) method; quick field water content = calcium-carbide (speedy) method.
  • Maximum grain size of silt ≈ 0.06 mm (the 0.075 mm boundary in IS).

Atterberg Limits & Consistency (course definitions)

  • LL — water content at the plastic→liquid boundary; Casagrande cup (120 g air-dried sample on the 425 μm fraction, 2 rev/s; flow curve with water content on the arithmetic ordinate and blows on the log abscissa) or fall-cone (20 mm penetration at 5 s). PL — plastic→semi-solid; 3 mm thread crumbling (30 g sample, ~10 g rolled). SL — semi-solid→solid; the lowest water content at which the soil is still saturated.
  • PI = LL − PL; LI = (w − PL)/PI; CI = (LL − w)/PI; SI = PL − SL; Activity A = PI/% clay fraction (< 0.75 inactive, 0.75–1.25 normal, > 1.25 active — montmorillonite); flow index If = slope of the flow curve; toughness index It = PI/If.
  • At LL, all soils share the same small shear strength; plasticity comes from adsorbed (dipolar) water around the negatively charged clay minerals — rock flour is non-plastic.
  • Classification: USCS divides fine from coarse at 50% passing the 75 μm sieve; fines are classified on the plasticity chart (A-line: PI = 0.73(LL−20)); above A-line = clays (C), below = silts (M); USCS fines: LL < 50 low (L), LL ≥ 50 high (H) plasticity — the LL 50 boundary the doc's own notes and Fig 2.4 use; ISSCS (IS 1498) uses the low/intermediate/high 35/50 boundaries; textural, MIT and descriptive systems are also asked.

Effective Stress, Seepage & Compressibility (2.2)

  • Terzaghi's effective stress: σ′ = σ − u (u = pore water pressure). Effective stress — not total stress — controls shear strength and volume change.
  • Capillary rise h = 4Tcosα/(γw·d) — decreases as particle size increases; capillary water sits above the water table but adds to effective stress (its pore pressure is negative).
  • Quicksand condition occurs when the upward seepage gradient reaches the critical value icr = (G−1)/(1+e) ≈ 1.0 for sands — effective stress becomes zero and the soil loses strength (not a soil type!).
  • Flow nets: seepage discharge q = k·H·Nf/Nd; seepage pressure acts in the flow direction; flow lines and equipotential lines are orthogonal — flow crosses equipotentials at right angles.
  • Compressibility: av = −Δe/Δp; mv = av/(1+e₀); Cc = (e₀−e)/log(p/p₀) — the e–log p slope; Cs ≈ Cc/5 (recompression); time factor Tv = Cv·t/d², with Tv = (π/4)U² for U ≤ 60% and Tv = 1.781 − 0.933 log₁₀(100−U) for U > 60%. Cv = k/(mv·γw).
  • Compaction: degree of compaction = field dry density / maximum dry density (Proctor). Sheepsfoot rollers suit clayey soils; smooth-wheel rollers granular; vibratory rollers sandy; pneumatic-tyred rollers all types. More compactive effort lowers OMC and raises MDD. The zero-air-voids line is the theoretical upper limit (never attained).
  • Relative density Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) — the density index of sands; the course defines "degree of compaction" as the ratio of the dry unit weight in the natural state to that in the densest state.

Shear Strength & Slopes (2.3)

  • Mohr-Coulomb: τf = c + σ′ tanφ (c = cohesion, φ = angle of internal friction). The failure plane makes 45° + φ/2 with the major principal plane; τmax = (σ1 − σ3)/2 at 45°.
  • Shear tests: direct shear (simplest, for cohesionless soils; drainage uncontrolled), triaxial (most reliable — pore pressure measurable; UU for short-term saturated clays, CU with pore measurement, CD for long-term stability of excavated clay slopes), unconfined compression (saturated clays; qu; cu = qu/2), vane shear (soft sensitive clays, field/lab).
  • Sensitivity = qu(undisturbed)/qu(remoulded); > 8 = quick clay. Thixotropy = strength regain at constant water content.
  • Slope stability: Taylor's stability number Sn = c/(Fc·γ·H); the largest Taylor stability number = 0.261 (φ = 0, toe failure); Swedish slip-circle (Fellenius) method; Culmann's construction belongs to the wedge method. Infinite sand slopes fail at the φ angle; drainage and flattening raise stability.

Earth Pressure & Retaining Structures (2.4)

  • Rankine active: Pa = Ka·σz − 2c√Ka with Ka = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ); passive Kp = (1+sinφ)/(1−sinφ); at-rest K₀ = 1 − sinφ (Jaky). Ka·Kp = 1. Active pressure for cohesive soil: Pa = Kaσz − 2c√Ka.
  • Coulomb's wedge theory assumes a planar failure wedge with wall friction; Culmann's graphical construction solves it. Ka(Coulomb) < Ka(Rankine); Kp(Coulomb) > Kp(Rankine) when wall friction acts.
  • Retaining wall stability: check overturning (FS ≥ 1.5–2 about the toe), sliding (FS ≥ 1.5; base friction + shear key), bearing (resultant inside the middle third to avoid tension). Stability improves with a wider base, heel/toe projections, shear keys, counterforts, backfill drainage (weep holes), reduced surcharge, a battered front face, and tie-backs or soil reinforcement.
  • Soil exploration: open excavation (pits/trenches), auger boring (hand/power), wash boring, rotary drilling, percussion; geophysical — seismic refraction and electrical resistivity. Samplers: thin-walled Shelby tube (undisturbed clays), split-spoon (SPT, disturbed). SPT: 63.5 kg hammer; refusal at 100 blows per 300 mm. Rock coring gives RQD (pieces ≥ 10 cm over total core run); sampler area ratio < 10% for undisturbed sampling.
  • Site investigation report: borehole logs (strata, SPT N, groundwater table), plan of locations, recommendations. The number of borings increases with the irregularity of the strata.

Foundations & Bearing Capacity (2.5–2.6)

  • Shallow foundations (Df ≤ B): spread/isolated footing, wall footing, combined footing (two columns close together), strap (cantilever) footing — for columns far apart, raft/mat foundation (weak soils, heavy loads, equalizes settlement). Deep: pile (end-bearing/friction), pier, caisson, well foundation.
  • Selection factors: soil type and bearing capacity, load magnitude/type, groundwater, settlement limits, adjacent structures, cost.
  • Terzaghi's ultimate bearing capacity (general shear): qu = cNc + γDf·Nq + 0.5γB·Nγ (strip); circular: qu = 1.3cNc + γDfNq + 0.3γBNγ; square: 1.3cNc + γDfNq + 0.4γBNγ. Net ultimate = cNc + γDf(Nq−1) + 0.5γBNγ; net safe = qnu/F; safe = net safe + γDf.
  • Terzaghi assumptions: soil homogeneous, isotropic, saturated; rough base; Darcy's law valid; the tabulated factors assume general shear failure.
  • Failure modes: general shear — dense sand/stiff clay (clear peak, bulging heave); local shear — medium dense sand/soft clay; punching shear — loose sand/weak clay (vertical compression, little heave).
  • Water table at base reduces bearing capacity (the Nγ term uses γ'; correction factor 0.5 when the WT sits at base level). Footing width ↑ → qu ↑ (width term); Df ↑ → qu ↑ (surcharge term).
  • Consolidation = time-dependent volume decrease by pore-water expulsion (no limiting moisture content); compaction = instantaneous air expulsion. Normally consolidated clay: present stress = maximum past stress; overconsolidated: past > present (OCR > 1); underconsolidated: still consolidating under new load.
  • Oedometer height comes from the Md/γw·GA relation (course one-liner); consolidation settlement Sc = mv·Δσ′·H = Cc·H/(1+e₀)·log[(σ′0+Δσ)/σ′0].
  • Settlement: immediate (elastic, all soils), primary consolidation (clays, pore water), secondary consolidation/creep (organic soils). Permissible values (IS 1904/IS 8009 practice): isolated footing on sand ≈ 40 mm, on clay ≈ 65 mm; raft on sand 75–100 mm. Differential settlement should stay within ~1/500 (frames); wall cracking appears near 1/150 angular distortion.
  • Bearing capacity from field tests: SPT (corrected N → qa), plate load test (settlement grows with plate size; short duration), static cone penetrometer (CPT). Plate load limitations: size effect and short duration — it gives immediate settlement only.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): "Degree of compaction" is defined in the course as the ratio of natural-state dry unit weight to densest-state dry unit weight (relative compaction in disguise). IS permissible settlement for an isolated footing: 40 mm on sand / 65 mm on clay; raft 75–100 mm — remember the pairs.
