This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

3.1 Fluids and Their Properties (ACiE0301)

A. Fluids — Definitions and Types

  • A fluid deforms continuously under any applied shear stress, however small — it cannot resist shear at rest (unlike a solid, which springs back). Liquids and gases are both fluids.
  • Types of fluids: the table below classifies them by how shear stress grows with the rate of deformation:
TypeBehaviourExamples
Ideal (perfect)Inviscid (μ = 0) and incompressible — imaginary; simplifies analysis—
Real fluidHas viscosity — every actual fluidWater, air, oil
Newtonianτ = μ(du/dy) — linear with velocity gradient; μ constant at a given temperatureWater, air, kerosene, thin oils
Bingham plastic (ideal plastic)τ = τy + μ(du/dy) — needs a yield stress first, then linearToothpaste, drilling mud, sewage sludge
PseudoplasticApparent μ decreases with shear rateBlood, milk, polymer solutions
DilatantApparent μ increases with shear rateQuicksand, sugar-in-water suspension
Thixotropicμ changes with time of shearingGels, printer ink, paints
  • Liquid vs gas: liquids are incompressible, keep a fixed volume and have a free surface; gases are compressible, fill the container and have no free surface.
Fig 3.1 — Rheograms: Newtonian straight through the origin; Bingham straight from τy; pseudoplastic thins (concave), dilatant thickens (convex)

B. Fluid Properties (values to memorize)

PropertyDefinition / formulaUnitWater value (20 °C)
Mass density ρmass/volumekg/m³998 (≈ 1000)
Specific weight w (γ)weight/volume = ρgN/m³ (kN/m³)9810 N/m³ = 9.81 kN/m³
Specific gravity Sρ(fluid)/ρ(water at 4 °C)dimensionless1.0; mercury 13.6
Specific volume1/ρm³/kg0.001
Viscosity μ (dynamic)τ/(du/dy); Newton's lawPa·s = N·s/m²; 1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s1.0×10⁻³ Pa·s (1 cP)
Kinematic viscosity νμ/ρm²/s; 1 stoke = 10⁻⁴ m²/s1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s (1 cSt)
Compressibility β−(dV/V)/dp; inverse of bulk modulus KPa⁻¹K ≈ 2.1×10⁹ Pa
Surface tension σforce per length at the surface; causes droplets and capillarityN/m0.0728 N/m
Vapour pressure pvpressure at which the liquid boils at a given TkPa absolute2.34 kPa (101.3 at 100 °C)
  • Viscosity causes: cohesion between molecules (in liquids) and molecular momentum transfer (in gases). Temperature effect: in liquids μ decreases with T (cohesion weakens); in gases μ increases with T (momentum transfer grows). Pressure effect: negligible.
  • Newton's law of viscosity: τ = μ du/dy — the velocity gradient is the rate of shear deformation.
  • Surface tension is work per unit increase of surface area (N/m = J/m²); it decreases with temperature. Excess pressure inside a droplet p = 4σ/d; inside a soap bubble p = 8σ/d; inside a jet/cylinder p = 2σ/d. Raindrops stay spherical because of surface tension.
  • Capillarity — rise or fall in small tubes from adhesion–cohesion plus surface tension:
    h = 4σ cos α/(γ d) (α = contact angle; water α ≈ 0° → rise; mercury α ≈ 130–140° → depression)
    Water: h ≈ 30/d mm (d in mm) ; mercury: h ≈ −10.15/d mm
    Capillary rise decreases as temperature rises.
  • Cavitation: when local pressure falls below vapour pressure, vapour bubbles form and collapse violently in high-pressure zones — pitting, erosion, noise, efficiency loss (pump suctions, propellers, venturi throats). Prevention: keep an NPSH margin (net positive suction head — the suction-side pressure cushion that stops the water boiling off), avoid sharp bends, limit suction lift (~7–8 m theoretical, 6–7 m practical).
  • Compressibility: liquids are practically incompressible (K large); gases compressible (pV = mRT). Mach number M = V/C separates the regimes — incompressible for M < 0.3. Bulk modulus B = ΔP/(−ΔV/V); B = ∞ for a truly incompressible fluid.
  • Ideal fluid: inviscid + incompressible + no surface tension.
  • Mercury density 13,600 kg/m³ (SG 13.6); sea water 1025 kg/m³; ice SG ≈ 0.917 — it floats with 91.7% of its volume submerged (8.3% above water).
  • Viscosity is measured by rotating-drum, capillary (Saybolt/Ostwald) and falling-sphere (Stokes) instruments; surface tension by capillary rise, du Noüy ring or drop-weight.
3.1 must-knows: fluid cannot resist shear at rest; water ρ ≈ 1000, γ = 9.81 kN/m³, μ = 1 cP, ν = 1 cSt; mercury SG 13.6; μ of liquids falls with T, gases rises; droplet p = 4σ/d, soap bubble 8σ/d, jet 2σ/d; water capillary rise ≈ 30/d mm; Mach < 0.3 incompressible; Bingham needs yield stress (toothpaste).

3.2 Hydrostatics (ACiE0302)

A. Pressure and Head

Fig 3.2 — Pressure prism on a vertical wall: triangular distribution p = γh; resultant F = γ·h̄·A acts at H/3 above the base; surcharge adds a rectangle at H/2
p = γh (gauge pressure at depth h below the free surface)
Absolute pressure = atmospheric + gauge ; atmospheric ≈ 101.3 kPa = 10.33 m of water = 760 mm Hg
p/γ = pressure head h (m of fluid)
  • Pascal's law: pressure at a point in a fluid at rest is equal in all directions (isotropic) and acts normal (perpendicular) to surfaces; it is transmitted undiminished — the basis of the hydraulic press/jack/lift: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ (force multiplication by piston-area ratio). In a viscous moving fluid the equality does not hold.
  • Gauge vs absolute: gauge pressure may be negative (vacuum/suction); absolute zero is perfect vacuum. p_abs = p_atm − p_vacuum.
  • Manometers:
DeviceMeasuresNote
PiezometerGauge pressure of liquids onlyNo gases, no negative pressures
U-tube manometerLiquid or gas pressure with a heavy fluid (mercury)Differential version measures the difference between two points
Inverted U-tube (two-liquid)Pressure difference between two liquid pointsTop fluid is air or a lighter liquid
Inclined micro-manometerVery small differencesReading multiplied by 1/sinθ (θ = 10° gives ≈ 5.76×)
Bourdon gaugeGauge pressure (elastic tube deflection)Calibrated against a dead-weight tester
  • Manometer equation: equate pressures at the same level in a continuous homogeneous fluid (the datum line). For a mercury differential U-tube between same-level pipes: pA − pB = h(γm − γ).
Fig 3.3 — Real-life example: a mercury U-tube manometer pressure-tests a new water service pipe. With h = 200 mm and a = 0.4 m, equating pressures at the datum gives p = γm·h − γ·a = 26.7 − 3.9 ≈ 22.8 kPa (≈ 2.3 m of water head)

B. Forces on Submerged Surfaces (plane)

Total pressure force on a plane surface: F = γ·h̄·A (h̄ = vertical depth of the centroid)
Centre of pressure (point of action): h* = h̄ + Ig/(h̄·A) — measured vertically from the surface
Inclined plane: F = γ·h̄·A with h̄ the VERTICAL centroid depth; along the incline the centre of pressure sits at ȳ + Ig/(A·ȳ) from the water line
  • Key facts: F depends only on the centroid depth (the total magnitude does not change with inclination); the centre of pressure is always below the centroid for non-horizontal surfaces (pressure grows with depth, so the average push sits low); on a horizontal surface h* = h̄.
  • Standard results:
SurfaceFh* − h̄
Rectangle (b×d) vertical, top edge at surfaceγ·b·d·(d/2)d/6
Triangle vertical (base at top)γ·A·(2d/3)—
Circle verticalγ·A·h̄Ig/(h̄A) = d²/16h̄
  • Curved surfaces: resolve into two components — horizontal Fx = γ·h̄v·Av (the force on the vertical projection of the curve) and vertical Fy = weight of water (real or virtual) above the surface up to the free surface (or buoyancy if the water is below). The resultant passes through the point where the components meet, and acts radially (normal to the surface) — through the centre for cylindrical surfaces.
  • Pressure diagrams: triangle (wall with water to the top), trapezoid (surcharge + water); the area = total force and the centroid of the diagram = point of action. On a vertical rectangular wall of height H with water to the top: F = γH²/2 acting at H/3 from the bottom. With a uniform surcharge, add a rectangle of intensity q acting at H/2.
Fig 3.4 — Forces on submerged surfaces: (1) vertical plane — F = γ·h̄·A with h* = 2d/3, centre of pressure d/6 below the centroid; (2) inclined plane — h̄ is the vertical centroid depth, y* = ȳ + Ig/(A·ȳ) along the incline; (3) pressure diagrams — triangle (F = γH²/2 at H/3) plus surcharge trapezoid (rectangle q at H/2); (4) curved surface — Fx = γ·h̄v·Av on the vertical projection, Fy = water weight above, resultant radial through O

C. Buoyancy and Flotation

  • Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid and acts upward through the centre of buoyancy (the centroid of the displaced volume). B < W → sinks; B = W → floats at any depth. A floating body displaces its own weight; a submerged body displaces its own volume. Buoyant force on a fully submerged body is independent of depth — go deeper and nothing changes.
  • Metacentre (M): the intersection of the tilted buoyant line of action with the body's original vertical axis — think of it as the pivot point the ship leans about. Metacentric height GM = BM − BG, where BM = I/V (I = second moment of the waterplane area, V = displaced volume).
  • Stability:
ConditionFloating bodySubmerged body
StableM above G (GM > 0)B above G
UnstableM below G (GM < 0)B below G
NeutralM coincides with GB coincides with G
  • A submerged body is stable only when the centre of buoyancy is above the centre of gravity (like a balloon held underwater — it wants to flip upright); a floating body is stable when GM > 0 (G may sit above B because M then sits above both).
  • Experimental GM (inclining experiment): tanθ = w·d/(W·GM), so GM = w·d/(W·tanθ).
  • Roll period T = 2π√(k²/(g·GM)) — T grows as 1/√GM, so halving GM multiplies the roll period by √2 (small GM = tender ship, large GM = stiff ship).
  • Relative equilibrium (accelerating container): the free surface inclines opposite to horizontal acceleration, tanθ = a/g; vertical acceleration changes the apparent gravity — p = γh(1 ± a/g); rotation about a vertical axis lifts the surface into a paraboloid h = ω²r²/2g.
Fig 3.5 — Metacentric stability: the buoyancy force through the shifted centre B′ cuts the centreline at M; M above G → righting couple, M below G → overturning couple
3.2 must-knows: p = γh; atm ≈ 101.3 kPa = 10.33 m water = 760 mm Hg; F = γh̄A on the centroid; centre of pressure h* = h̄ + Ig/(h̄A) — always below the centroid; curved surface: Fx on vertical projection, Fy = weight above; float displaces own weight, submerged displaces own volume; stable floating when GM > 0; GM = w·d/(W·tanθ); tanθ = a/g for accelerating containers.

3.3 Hydro-kinematics and Hydro-dynamics (ACiE0303)

A. Flow Classification

  • Steady vs unsteady — conditions at a point do not change with time when steady (∂/∂t = 0).
  • Uniform vs non-uniform — conditions do not change along the length when uniform (∂V/∂s = 0).
  • Laminar vs turbulent: Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν. Pipe: Re < 2000 laminar, > 4000 turbulent (2000–4000 transition). Open channel: Re < 500 laminar, > 2000 turbulent. Stokes' law regime: Re < 1.
  • Compressible vs incompressible (Mach M < 0.3 → incompressible).
  • Rotational vs irrotational — irrotational means a tiny paddle wheel carried along by the flow would not spin (vorticity zero).
  • 1-D/2-D/3-D by spatial description; streamline (a curve tangent to the velocity everywhere — no flow crosses it), pathline (the actual trace of one particle), streakline (the trace of dye injected at a point), stream tube (a bundle of streamlines).
  • Continuity:
    ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρV) = 0 (general); incompressible: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ (Q = AV constant)
    Q (discharge) in m³/s; mass flow ρQ in kg/s.
  • Material derivative carries convective + local acceleration; Euler's equation along a streamline: dp/ρ + g dz + V dV = 0.
  • Stream function ψ (2-D incompressible): ψ is constant along streamlines and the difference Δψ between two lines equals the discharge Q flowing between them. Velocity potential φ exists only for irrotational flow; both satisfy Laplace's equation, and the ψ and φ families cross at right angles — the basis of the flow-net.
  • Free vortex (v·r = const, irrotational — water draining a bathtub) vs forced vortex (v = ωr, rigid-body rotation — a stirred tea cup).
  • Correction factors: real velocity profiles are not uniform, so the kinetic-energy term needs α (2 for laminar pipe flow, ≈ 1.05 turbulent) and the momentum term needs β (≈ 1.33 laminar, 1.01–1.05 turbulent).

B. Bernoulli's Equation

Fig 3.6 — Venturimeter: the convergent cone accelerates flow to the throat, so the pressure falls there; the mercury U-tube reads that drop as Δh (h = 12.6·Δh for water), giving Q = Cd·a1a2·√(2gΔh)/√(a1²−a2²) with Cd ≈ 0.95–0.98
p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant (along a streamline, ideal steady incompressible flow)
Head terms: pressure head + velocity head + datum head (all in metres)
  • Assumptions: steady, incompressible, inviscid (frictionless), along a streamline, no shaft work, no heat transfer. Real systems add: + pump head − turbine head − losses.
  • Applications:
DeviceBasisDischarge relation
VenturimeterPressure drop between inlet and throatQ = Cd·(a₁a₂/√(a₁²−a₂²))·√(2gh) ; Cd ≈ 0.95–0.98
Orifice meterOrifice-plate pressure dropSame form; Cd ≈ 0.60–0.65 (higher loss)
Pitot (static) tubeStagnation − static pressure = velocity headV = Cv√(2gh); Cv ≈ 0.98 — measures velocity at a point
Nozzle meter, weirs, flumes—see below
Fig 3.7 — (A) The pitot-static tube subtracts static from stagnation pressure; the manometer difference h is the velocity head, giving V = Cv√(2gh) at that point. (B) A sharp-edged orifice contracts the jet to a vena contracta (ac ≈ 0.61–0.64 a); with Cd = Cc·Cv ≈ 0.60–0.65 the orifice meters discharge
  • Momentum equation: ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁) — thrust blocks on bends, jet impact (flat plate normal: F = ρAV²; inclined: ρAV²sinθ; moving plate: ρAV(V−u)), Pelton bucket force, forces on reducers, and the sudden-expansion loss hL = (V₁−V₂)²/2g (Borda–Carnot).
  • Vena contracta: the minimum jet area after an orifice; Cc ≈ 0.61–0.64; Cd = Cc × Cv. Cc = 1 only for a perfectly rounded mouthpiece (then Cd = Cv ≈ 0.98).
  • Venturimeter parts: convergent cone (21° ±), throat (d/D 0.25–0.75), divergent cone (5–7° — prevents separation); the least head loss of all meters; works horizontal, inclined or vertical.
  • Jet on a series of plates (Pelton principle): F = ρAV(V−u); hydraulic efficiency peaks near u = V/2; Pelton cup deflection ≈ 165–170° gives theoretical efficiency up to ~90%.
3.3 must-knows: steady = no change in time, uniform = none along length; pipe Re 2000/4000; open-channel Re 500/2000; A₁V₁ = A₂V₂; Bernoulli = pressure + velocity + datum head, needs steady, incompressible, frictionless, streamline; venturi Cd 0.95–0.98, orifice 0.60–0.65, pitot 0.98; Cc ≈ 0.61–0.64; momentum ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁); sudden-expansion loss (V₁−V₂)²/2g.

3.4 Pipe Flow (ACiE0304)

A. Head Losses

Major (friction) loss — Darcy–Weisbach: hf = f·L·V²/(2gD) = f·L·Q²/(12.1 D⁵)
f (Darcy) = 64/Re in laminar flow; turbulent f(ε/D, Re) from Colebrook–White or the Moody chart
Chezy: V = C√(RS) → hf = (V²/C²)(L/R) ; Manning: V = (1/n)R^(2/3)S^(1/2)
Hazen–Williams (water supply): V = 0.85 C_H R^0.63 S^0.54
Minor losses (as multiples of V²/2g):
Sudden enlargement: (V₁−V₂)²/2g ; Sudden contraction: 0.5 V₂²/2g (Cc factor; 0.33–0.5 typical)
Entrance: 0.5 V²/2g ; Exit: 1.0 V²/2g (full loss)
90° bend ≈ 0.5–0.9 ; mitre elbow 1.1 ; 45° elbow 0.4 ; open gate valve 0.15–0.2 ; globe valve 8–10 ; tee branch 1.8, tee run 0.6 ; foot valve with strainer 1.5–2.5
  • Moody diagram: a chart of f against Reynolds number, one curve per relative roughness ε/D; the laminar line ignores roughness; in the fully rough region f is independent of Re (roughness, not viscosity, controls). Colebrook–White is implicit (f appears on both sides): 1/√f = −2log₁₀(ε/3.7D + 2.51/Re√f); Swamee–Jain is the explicit approximation. Blasius (smooth pipes): f = 0.316/Re^0.25. Darcy f = 4 × Fanning f — the classic factor-of-4 trap; NEC uses Darcy.
  • Hagen–Poiseuille (laminar): hf = 32μLV/(γD²); flow rate ∝ D⁴ — doubling D gives 16× the discharge at the same loss, which is why small pipes choke so fast.
  • Equivalent length replaces a fitting by the straight pipe with the same loss; an equivalent pipe replaces a whole combination by one pipe of the same total loss. Pipes in series: Q the same through all, hf = Σhf,i; pipes in parallel: hf the same across each, Q = ΣQi. For network resistance written hf = rQ²: series r = Σri; parallel 1/√r_eq = Σ1/√ri.

B. HGL and TEL (Energy Grade Line)

Fig 3.8 — Energy grade lines along a pipe with a constriction: both lines start at the reservoir surface and fall with friction; the TEL always stands V²/2g above the HGL. Where the throat raises velocity the gap widens and the HGL dips — below the pipe centreline the gauge pressure is negative (siphon/cavitation zone). At a free exit p = 0, so the HGL meets the outlet, TEL stays V²/2g above
  • HGL = piezometric head line (z + p/γ); TEL = total energy line (z + p/γ + V²/2g). TEL is always above HGL by exactly V²/2g; both fall in the flow direction by the losses (horizontal for ideal flow).
  • HGL slope = hydraulic gradient i = hf/L. At reservoirs and pipe outlets the HGL coincides with the free surface; at a free exit the TEL stands V²/2g above the surface.
  • Pipes not flowing full: when the pipe rises above the HGL the gauge pressure goes negative (below atmosphere) — a siphon; cavitation threatens if p < pv. Siphon summit height ≈ 7.6 m max (barometric 10.3 m minus velocity head and vapour margin); the siphon must be primed.

C. Pipe Design & Networks

  • Design velocity: water mains 0.6–3 m/s (economical ≈ 1–1.5 m/s); self-cleansing > 0.6 m/s; scouring limit 3–3.5 m/s.
  • Economic diameter (Lea's): D ≈ 1.22√Q (SI, Q in m³/s; Garg's range 0.97–1.22√Q) — it minimizes lifetime cost (capital + pumping energy).
  • Water hammer (unsteady): sudden valve closure sends a pressure wave:
    Pressure rise: Δp = ρcV (rigid pipe, instant closure — Joukowsky; ≈ 1400V kPa per m/s in water pipes)
    Wave speed: c = √(K/ρ)/√(1 + KD/(Et)) (elastic pipe; c ≈ 1200–1400 m/s in water pipes)
    Critical closure time tc = 2L/c — shorter closure = sudden (maximum rise); longer = gradual (rigid-column analysis)
    Relief devices: surge tanks (simple, restricted-orifice, differential), air vessels, pressure relief valves, slow-closing valves, standpipes. The closest relief to the valve is the most effective; on pumping mains beware column separation — fit air chambers at the pump discharge.
  • Network analysis: Hardy Cross method (successive correction of assumed flows; ΣQ = 0 at nodes, Σhf = 0 around loops); equivalent pipe method; electrical analogy (Q ↔ current, hf ↔ voltage, r ↔ resistance); modern gradient method / EPANET.
  • Three-reservoir problem: assume a common junction head H_J; apply continuity Q1 = Q2 + Q3 with signs set by the relative heads; solve by trial.
  • Dupuit assumption: for long pipes (L > 500–1000 D) neglect velocity head and minor losses.
  • Pipe materials: CI/DI (spun), MS/steel (welded large mains), GI (small old supply), PVC/HDPE, RCC (gravity mains) — chosen by pressure, corrosion and cost. Ageing: tuberculation raises ε — Hazen–Williams C falls from 130 (new CI) to ≈ 100 over decades; PVC stays ≈ 150.
  • Air valves sit at the summits of long mains (release trapped air that would otherwise throttle the flow); washouts at the valleys (remove sediment).
Fig 3.9 — Moody-chart anatomy: laminar line, critical zone, roughness family and the fully-rough zone (log–log)
3.4 must-knows: hf = fLV²/2gD; laminar f = 64/Re; Darcy = 4 × Fanning; sudden enlargement (V₁−V₂)²/2g; exit loss 1.0 V²/2g; entrance 0.5; globe valve ≈ 8–10; HGL = z + p/γ, TEL = HGL + V²/2g; water hammer Δp = ρcV, c ≈ 1200–1400 m/s, sudden if closure < 2L/c; series: same Q; parallel: same hf; Lea D ≈ 1.22√Q; air valves at summits, washouts at valleys.

3.5 Open Channel Flow (ACiE0305)

A. Geometric Properties & Flow Types

Fig 3.10 — Trapezoidal channel: bed width b, depth y, side slope 1V:zH; shaded area A = (b+zy)y, highlighted wetted perimeter P = b + 2y√(1+z²), R = A/P
Rectangular: A = by ; P = b+2y ; R = A/P = by/(b+2y)
Trapezoidal (side slope zH:1V or 1:m): A = (b+zy)y ; P = b + 2y√(1+z²) ; R = A/P ; top width T = b+2zy
Triangular: A = zy² ; P = 2y√(1+z²) ; T = 2zy ; R = zy/(2√(1+z²))
Hydraulic depth D = A/T ; section factor Z = A√D (critical flow) and A√R (uniform flow)
ClassificationTypes
TimeSteady / unsteady
SpaceUniform / gradually varied / rapidly varied
Re (ν = VR)Laminar (< 500) / transition / turbulent (> 2000)
Froude F = V/√(gD)Subcritical (F < 1, tranquil) / critical (= 1) / supercritical (F > 1, rapid/shooting)
  • Most economical (best hydraulic) sections: rectangle — b = 2y; trapezoid — the half-hexagon (side slope 60°, z = 1/√3), R = y/2, and top width = 2× the side length; circle — maximum velocity at y = 0.81D, maximum discharge at y = 0.95D.
  • Uniform-flow resistance: Chezy C = √(8g/f) = (1/n)R^(1/6) (Manning relation); Manning n: concrete 0.012–0.015, earth canal 0.0225–0.03, natural river 0.03–0.06. Conveyance K = (1/n)A R^(2/3). Manning's n from Strickler: n = d^(1/6)/21.1 (d in m). Large channels are hydraulically "smoother" because C ∝ R^(1/6).
  • Specific energy — the energy head measured above the channel bed:
    E = y + V²/2g = y + Q²/(2gA²)
    Critical flow: F = 1; E minimum; rectangular: yc = (q²/g)^(1/3); E_min = (3/2)yc ; Vc = √(g·yc)
    Alternate depths: same E (sub- and supercritical pair); critical depth separates them
    Sequent (conjugate) depths: same momentum (hydraulic jump)
    For one value of E above the minimum, the curve gives two possible depths — the alternate depths — one subcritical (deep, slow) and one supercritical (shallow, fast).
  • Specific force F = Q²/(gA) + z̄A stays constant through the jump (z̄ = centroid depth).
  • Hydraulic exponents: wide rectangle N = 3, triangle N = 4, circular ≈ 5.1 — used in direct-integration GVF (Bresse for wide rectangles).
Fig 3.11 — Specific-energy curve: the left (supercritical) limb climbs to infinity as y→0, the right (subcritical) limb follows the 45° line E = y; the minimum at (yc, Emin) separates them, and any E above Emin gives two alternate depths y1, y2 on the horizontal line

B. Gradually Varied Flow (GVF) Profiles

Fig 3.12 — Mild-slope GVF profiles: bed, yc and yn create three zones; M1 backwater above yn (dam), M2 drawdown between yn and yc (free overfall), M3 supercritical below yc (sluice gate) ending in a hydraulic jump
dy/dx = (S0 − Sf)/(1 − F²) (wide-rectangular form)
Profiles are named by zone (1, 2, 3 — where y sits relative to yn and yc) and slope letter:
M (mild: yn > yc) · S (steep: yn < yc) · C (critical: yn = yc) · H (horizontal: S0 = 0) · A (adverse: S0 < 0)
ProfileConditionShape / example
M1y > yn > ycBackwater — upstream of a dam (the most common)
M2yn > y > ycDrawdown — canal to a free overfall
M3yn > yc > ySupercritical — below a sluice gate on a mild slope, ends in a jump
S1, S2, S3—S1 before a jump on a steep slope; S2 drawdown from reservoir to steep channel; S3 below a gate
C1, C3—Rare, nearly horizontal water surface
H2, H3; A2, A3—Horizontal/adverse slopes (drawdown and brink profiles)
  • Direct step method (prismatic channels — constant shape — computes the length between two depths); standard step method (non-prismatic — needs cross-section data at each step); both integrate dy/dx stepwise.
  • GVF curves asymptote to yn on one side and to yc (or horizontal) on the other; control sections (where critical depth is known) — spillway crest, sluice gate, free overfall, break in grade — anchor the computation, because the profile is computed outward from them.

C. Hydraulic Jump

Fig 3.13 — Hydraulic jump: supercritical inflow (y1 < yc) rises abruptly through a turbulent roller to the subcritical sequent depth (y2 > yc); the energy line falls by ΔE = (y2−y1)³/(4 y1 y2), the power a stilling basin dissipates. Sequent depths: y2/y1 = ½[√(1+8F1²) − 1]

A hydraulic jump is the rapidly varied transition from supercritical to subcritical flow with energy dissipation (a standing wave). It occurs where a steep slope meets a mild one, below gates, and downstream of weirs.

Sequent depth relation (rectangular, horizontal bed): y2/y1 = ½[√(1+8F1²) − 1]
Energy loss: ΔE = (y2 − y1)³/(4 y1 y2)
Froude before jump F1 = V1/√(g y1); power dissipated P = γQΔE
F1Jump typeNote
1–1.7UndularSmall ripple — not used for dissipation
1.7–2.5WeakLow efficiency
2.5–4.5OscillatingWave trouble — avoid for stilling basins
4.5–9SteadyBest for stilling basins (efficient, stable)
> 9StrongRough, high dissipation
  • Jump length ≈ 5–7 y2; stilling basins (USBR Types II, III, IV) use chute blocks, baffle piers and end sills; efficiency = E2/E1.
  • Jump location follows the tailwater: at the toe, drowned (submerged), or swept out downstream depending on tailwater level.
  • Applications: energy dissipation below spillways, chemical mixing, aeration, raising downstream water levels, shortening the uplift length on floors.
  • Energy loss grows fast with F1: at F1 = 2, ΔE ≈ 0.27 y1; at F1 = 5, ΔE ≈ 6.6 y1 — which justifies stilling basins.

D. Mobile Boundary Channels (Sediment)

  • Inception of motion (Shields): the bed grains start moving when the drag of the flow exceeds a critical shear stress τc = (γs − γ)d·θc; the Shields diagram gives θc = τc/((γs−γ)d) ≈ 0.03–0.06 (≈ 0.06 for coarse grains, boundary Reynolds > 400).
    • Tractive force (du Boys): τ0 = γ R S ; the design check is τ0 < τc
    Competent velocity: Kennedy v0 = 0.55·m·y^0.64 (m = critical velocity ratio) ; Lacey regime equations — see Ch 7
    Shields parameter θ = τ0/((γs−γ)d) > θc → motion begins
  • Design approaches: threshold (critical tractive force) method, regime method (Kennedy/Lacey — India/Nepal practice), permissible velocity method (USBR).
  • Sediment transport: bed load (Einstein, Meyer-Peter–Müller), suspended load (Rouse), total load; bedforms run ripple → dune → antidune as F increases.
3.5 must-knows: rectangle best section b = 2y; trapezoid half-hexagon z = 1/√3; F = V/√(gD); F < 1 subcritical, > 1 supercritical; yc = (q²/g)^⅓ for rectangles; E_min = 1.5yc; jump: y2/y1 = ½[√(1+8F1²) − 1]; ΔE = (y2−y1)³/4y1y2; F1 = 4.5–9 steady jump = best basin; jump length 5–7 y2; τ0 = γRS vs τc (Shields); Manning n: concrete 0.012–0.015, earth 0.0225–0.03.

3.6 Hydrology (ACiE0306)

A. Hydrologic Cycle & Water Balance

P = R + E + T + I + ΔS (precipitation = runoff + evaporation + transpiration + infiltration + storage change)
Basin water budget: P − Q − E = ΔS ; evapotranspiration ET, potential PET (Thornthwaite, Penman)
  • Components: precipitation, interception (rain caught by leaves), infiltration, percolation (downward movement to groundwater), groundwater flow, baseflow (the dry-weather groundwater contribution), surface runoff, evaporation, transpiration, sublimation.
  • Infiltration: Horton's equation f = fc + (f0 − fc)e^(−kt) — capacity starts high (f0) and decays to a final constant fc; the φ-index is the constant loss rate that yields the observed runoff; the W-index also includes initial losses; measured with infiltrometers. Actual infiltration = min(capacity, rainfall intensity).
  • Evaporation measurement: US Class A pan — pan coefficient ≈ 0.7 (Colorado pan ≈ 0.8); lake evaporation = pan evaporation × coefficient; Piche atmometer; Meyer's and Penman estimation formulas.

B. Precipitation & Measurement

Fig 3.14 — Rain gauges: the non-recording Symons gauge (127 cm² brass rim, funnel, collecting bottle) is read by hand once a day at 8:30; the tipping-bucket gauge records itself — every 0.2–0.5 mm tip closes a reed switch counted by a logger, giving intensity in mm/h. Weighing and float/siphon types are the other recording family members
  • Rain gauges: non-recording (Symons — 127 cm² / 5-inch, read daily at 8:30) and recording (tipping bucket, weighing bucket, float/siphon); radar now supplements gauges. Siting: open ground, obstacle distance ≥ 2× (ideally 4×) the obstacle height, rim 30 cm above ground, level.
  • Mean areal precipitation: arithmetic mean, Thiessen polygons (weights by area), isohyetal method (the most accurate), inverse distance.
    • Fig 3.15 — Thiessen polygons: each gauge owns the area nearer to it than to any other gauge; its weight = polygon area share
  • Missing data: arithmetic mean or normal-ratio method; record consistency is checked by the double-mass curve (a slope break = a change in exposure or setting).
  • Intensity-duration-frequency (IDF): i = KT^a/(t+b)^n — design storms for drainage (Nepal practice: culverts 25–50 yr, bridges 50–100 yr).
  • Rainfall excess = rainfall − infiltration/abstractions — this drives the runoff.
  • Precipitation types: convective (thunderstorms), orographic (windward heavy — the Nepal monsoon), cyclonic/frontal. Nepal monsoon: ~80% of annual rain falls June–September, with a strong orographic gradient (Pokhara > 4000 mm; Mustang rain shadow < 300 mm). Gauge density norms ≈ 1 per 520 km² (plains), with at least 10% recording gauges.

C. Flow Measurement & Rating Curves

  • Velocity: current meters (cup/propeller), floats (surface float × 0.85 = mean velocity), ADCP; discharge by mid-section/mean-section methods using the 0.2d & 0.8d two-point or 0.6d single-point rule.
  • Weirs and flumes:
DeviceFormula (SI)Note
Rectangular weirQ = (2/3)Cd√(2g)·L·H^1.5 (Cd ≈ 0.62)Francis: suppressed 1.84LH^1.5; with n end contractions 1.84(L−0.1nH)H^1.5
90° V-notchQ = (8/15)Cd√(2g)tan(θ/2)·H^2.5 ≈ 1.38H^2.5For small flows
Cipolletti (trapezoidal, 1H:4V sides)Q ≈ 1.86LH^1.5Side correction built in
Broad-crested weirQ ≈ 1.705·Cd·b·H^1.5 (Cd ≈ 0.85–1.0)Critical depth on the crest — robust for sediment-laden flow
Ogee spillwayQ = C·L·H^1.5, C ≈ 2.1–2.3Profile follows the sharp-crested nappe
Parshall flumeFree-flow rating tableFixed geometry
Fig 3.16 — Weirs & notches: rectangular and broad-crested in SIDE view, V-notch and Cipolletti in FRONT view (opening shape in the plate). Q ∝ H^1.5 for weirs, H^2.5 for the V-notch (best for small flows); the broad-crested weir passes flow at critical depth on its crest
  • Rating curve: Q vs stage — Q = C(G−a)^n on log-log (a = gauge height of zero flow); unsteady flow loops the curve; extrapolate high stages with caution; permanent vs shifting control.
  • Dilution gauging (constant-rate injection) suits turbulent mountain streams.

D. Hydrographs & Unit Hydrograph

Fig 3.17 — Flood hydrograph with straight-line baseflow separation: the shaded DRH is what remains after removing base flow; its volume equals ER depth × area. Dividing DRH ordinates by the ER depth (cm) gives the D-hr unit hydrograph; lag time runs from the ER centroid to the peak
Components: rising limb, crest/peak, recession; baseflow separation; effective rainfall (ER)
Unit Hydrograph (Sherman 1932): a D-hr UH = the direct runoff hydrograph from 1 cm of effective rainfall applied uniformly over the catchment in D hours
Assumptions: linearity (proportionality & superposition), time-invariance, uniform distribution
Synthetic UH (ungauged basins): Snyder's method (tp = Ct(L·Lca)^0.3, qp, coefficients Ct & Cp); S-curve converts durations
  • Derivation: separate baseflow → divide the DRH ordinates by the ER depth in cm.
  • S-curve: the hydrograph of continuous 1 cm/D-hr rainfall; lag a copy by D; the difference ×D/D' gives the D'-hr UH. Never rescale time directly.
  • Instantaneous UH, Nash cascade (n gamma), Clark (time-area) — recognize the names.
  • Design flood: PMP-based (probable maximum precipitation → probable maximum flood — the physical upper limit, used for high dams) or frequency-based (return period T: annual probability 1/T; risk in n years = 1 − (1−1/T)ⁿ).

E. Flood Frequency Analysis

Return period T; exceedance probability p = 1/T
Weibull plotting position: m/(n+1)
Gumbel (EV-I) reduced variate: yT = −ln[ln(T/(T−1))] ; frequency factor K = (yT − ȳn)/Sn
Q_T = Q̄ + K·σ
Log-Pearson III (US federal standard), log-normal — recognized names
  • Risk in n years: R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ; e.g., the 100-yr flood within 30 years: 26%. Use (1−1/T)ⁿ for "no occurrence" — never multiply 1/T by n.
  • Design return periods (DoR Nepal practice): culverts 25–50 yr, bridges 50–100 yr, aqueducts/irrigation structures 25–50 yr; spillway by dam class (up to PMF); urban drainage 2–10 yr.
  • Flood routing: hydrologic — Muskingum (storage = K[xI + (1−x)O]) and level-pool (Puls) for reservoirs — and hydraulic (Saint-Venant). Reservoir routing damps and delays the peak; Muskingum translates and attenuates.
  • Ungauged flood estimation in Nepal: regional empirical formulas — WECS/DHM methods — and the rational formula Q = CiA/360 (SI: C runoff coefficient, i mm/hr, A ha) for small catchments; Kirpich time of concentration Tc = 0.01947 L^0.77 S^-0.385 (minutes). Annual maximum series vs partial duration series — PDS gives slightly higher estimates for T < 10 yr.

F. Groundwater Hydrology

FormationDescription
AquiferStores and transmits water (sand, gravel, sandstone, karst)
AquitardStores but transmits poorly (sandy clay) — leaky
AquicludeStores but does not transmit (clay)
AquifugeNeither stores nor transmits (solid granite)
  • Types: unconfined (open to the water table), confined (artesian — squeezed between two clay layers, its piezometric surface stands above the layer, so a well can rise on its own), perched (a local lens sitting on a small clay bed above the true water table).
  • Well hydraulics (Thiem/Theis):
    Steady confined: Q = 2πT(s1−s2)/ln(r2/r1) ; T = k·b (transmissivity)
    Steady unconfined: Q = πk(h2²−h1²)/ln(r2/r1) — the equivalent-confined trick substitutes T = k(h1+h2)/2
    Storativity S: volume of water released per unit area per unit head decline — confined 10⁻⁵–10⁻³ (elastic release only); unconfined = specific yield 0.05–0.3 (gravity drainage)
    Specific capacity = Q/drawdown at a standard time; well losses split into laminar formation loss + turbulent well loss; step-drawdown tests separate them; constant-rate tests fit the Theis curve.
  • Well types: dug/open wells (shallow), tube wells (shallow/deep), artesian (flowing confined); infiltration galleries (horizontal riverbed collectors — used in Nepal rural water supply).
  • Recharge & safe yield: abstraction must balance replenishment; over-pumping → declining water table, land subsidence, sea-water intrusion. Transmissivity T = k·b; hydraulic conductivity depends on the medium AND the fluid (k_intrinsic × ρg/μ).
  • Groundwater provinces of Nepal: Terai alluvial aquifers (the main resource), inner Terai valleys, Kathmandu Valley (semi-confined, over-extracted); the hills rely on springs (depression, contact, artesian types) with recession Q = Q0·e^(−t/k) sizing the dry-season storage. Spring protection = spring box + recharge-zone conservation.
Fig 3.18 — Groundwater formations in one cross-section: perched lens on a clay lens above the water table; unconfined aquifer below it; confined aquifer sandwiched between aquiclude and aquifuge, with the piezometric surface above ground → flowing artesian well
Fig 3.19 — Cone of depression: pumping lowers the water table into a drawdown cone; at steady radial flow the Thiem equations relate Q to the drawdowns (s1, s2) measured in two observation wells at radii (r1, r2)
3.6 must-knows: P = R + E + T + I + ΔS; Horton f = fc + (f0 − fc)e^(−kt); Class A pan coefficient ≈ 0.7; Symons gauge 127 cm², read 8:30; Thiessen by area, isohyetal most accurate; double-mass curve checks consistency; 90° V-notch Q ≈ 1.38H^2.5; UHG = 1 cm effective rain in D hr; S-curve changes duration; risk = 1 − (1−1/T)ⁿ; rational Q = CiA/360; aquifer stores + transmits; confined storativity 10⁻⁵–10⁻³.

Worked Numericals (MCQ Patterns You Will Meet)

Fluid properties

  • 1 litre of oil weighs 8.5 N → γ = 8.5/0.001 = 8500 N/m³ = 8.5 kN/m³; ρ = 8500/9.81 = 866 kg/m³; SG = 0.866.
  • Plate 0.5 m² pulled at 0.3 m/s over a 1 mm oil film, force 5 N: τ = 5/0.5 = 10 N/m²; μ = τ/(V/y) = 10/(0.3/0.001) = 0.0333 Pa·s.
  • Capillary rise in a 0.5 mm tube: h = 30/d = 60 mm (water).

Manometers

  • U-tube mercury manometer reads a 20 cm difference with water flowing: p = 0.20×13.6×9810 = 26.7 kPa gauge.
  • Convert 500 mm Hg vacuum to absolute: 101.3 − 0.5×13.6×9.81 = 101.3 − 66.7 = 34.6 kPa abs.
  • Mercury differential with water in the other limb uses ×12.6 (γm − γw = 13.6−1), not 13.6.

Forces on surfaces

  • Vertical square gate 1×1 m with its top edge 2 m below water: F = 9.81×2.5×1 = 24.5 kN; h* = 2.5 + (1³/12)/(2.5×1) = 2.533 m.
  • Circular gate 1 m dia with centre 3 m deep: F = 9.81×3×(π/4) = 23.1 kN; h* − h̄ = d²/16h̄ = 1/48 ≈ 0.021 m.
  • Semicircular gate (r = 1 m), diameter at the surface, vertical: F = γ·(4r/3π)·(πr²/2) = 9.81×0.4244×1.571 = 6.54 kN.
  • Quadrant cylinder r = 2 m, water to the top, 2 m wide: Fx = 9.81×1×(2×2) = 39.2 kN (projection 2 m deep × 2 m wide = 4 m², centroid at r/2 = 1 m — don't multiply the width twice); Fy = γ×(πr²/4)×2 = 61.6 kN.

Buoyancy

  • Wood block SG 0.6 floating: 60% submerged, 40% above the surface.
  • Ice SG 0.917: 91.7% submerged, 8.3% above.
  • Block 2×1×1 m weighing 15 kN in water: displaced volume = 15/9.81 = 1.53 m³; draft = 1.53/2 = 0.76 m; GM = I/V − BG = (2×1³/12)/1.53 − (0.5−0.38) ≈ −0.01 → unstable unless ballasted low.

Bernoulli applications

  • Venturi: D1 = 200 mm, d = 100 mm, mercury differential 200 mm, Cd = 0.98: a1 = 0.0314, a2 = 0.00785 m²; h = 0.2×12.6 = 2.52 m; Q = 0.98×(0.0314×0.00785/√(0.0314²−0.00785²))×√(2×9.81×2.52) ≈ 0.0558 m³/s = 55.8 L/s.
  • Pitot in a river reads 0.6 m of water: V = 0.98√(2×9.81×0.6) = 3.36 m/s.
  • Tank discharging through a 50 mm orifice, Cd = 0.62, head 4 m: V = Cv√(2gH) ≈ 0.98×8.86 = 8.68 m/s (0.62 is Cd — it scales Q, not V); Q = 0.62×(π/4×0.0025)×8.86 = 0.0108 m³/s.
  • Time to empty: t = (2A/(Cd·a·√2g))(√H1 − √H2) — tank 4 m², orifice 0.01 m², 9 m down to 4 m: t = (2×4/(0.62×0.01×4.43))×(3−2) = 291 s.

Pipe friction

  • 300 mm pipe, 2 km, f = 0.02, V = 1.5 m/s: hf = 0.02×2000×2.25/(19.62×0.3) = 15.3 m; power lost = γQhf = 9810×0.106×15.3 = 15.9 kW.
  • Reynolds check: Re = 1.5×0.3/10⁻⁶ = 4.5×10⁵ — turbulent.
  • Equivalent pipe: three series pipes with hf1+hf2+hf3 replaced by one pipe of the same hf at the same Q.
  • Parallel pipes 1 & 2 of equal length and dia but f2 = 4f1: Q1/Q2 = √(f2/f1) = 2 (Q ∝ 1/√f at equal hf).

Open channel

  • Rectangular channel b = 3 m, y = 1.5 m, S = 0.001, n = 0.014: A = 4.5, P = 6, R = 0.75; V = (1/0.014)×0.75^(2/3)×0.0316 = 1.86 m/s; Q = 8.38 m³/s.
  • Critical depth with q = 8.38/3 = 2.79: yc = (2.79²/9.81)^(1/3) = 0.91 m < y → subcritical (F = 0.49).
  • Trapezoid b = 2, z = 1, y = 1: A = 3, P = 4.83, R = 0.62, T = 4, D = A/T = 0.75.
  • Jump: y1 = 0.5, V1 = 8 m/s → F1 = 3.61; y2 = 0.5×½(√(1+8×13.05)−1) = 2.32 m; ΔE = (1.82)³/(4×0.5×2.32) = 1.30 m; power for Q = 12 m³/s: 9.81×12×1.30 = 153 kW.

Hydrology

  • Thiessen: station A covers 20 of 100 km² with P_A = 40 mm → contribution 8 mm; sum weights × areas.
  • Rational: C = 0.5, i = 40 mm/hr, A = 20 ha → Q = 0.5×40×20/360 = 1.11 m³/s.
  • SCS-CN: CN = 80 → S = 25400/80 − 254 = 63.5 mm; P = 100 mm → Ia = 0.2S; Q = (100−12.7)²/(100−12.7+63.5) = 50.5 mm.
  • UH scaling: 3 cm effective rain triples the unit ordinates; two consecutive 2 cm pulses superpose, lagged 4 hr apart.
  • Gumbel: Q̄ = 500, σ = 200; y(100) = −ln[ln(100/99)] = 4.60; with sample ȳ = 0.55, S = 1.1 → K = 3.68 → Q100 = 500 + 3.68×200 = 1236 m³/s.
  • Well (confined): T = 0.01 m²/s, drawdown 2 m at 10 m and 1 m at 100 m: Q = 2π×0.01×1/ln(10) = 0.0273 m³/s ≈ 2357 m³/day.

Numerical Traps Checklist (avoid losing easy marks)

  • Units: γw = 9.81 kN/m³; keep units consistent; Q in m³/s = 1000 L/s; 1 cusec = 28.32 L/s.
  • Manometer factor: mercury difference ×12.6 (not 13.6) when water occupies the other limb (13.6 − 1).
  • Centre of pressure: use the vertical depth h̄ (not the slant distance) in F = γh̄A; Ig about the centroid, not the top edge.
  • Hinged gates: take moments about the hinge and use the force position h*; on a gate submerged from both sides the net force = γ·Δh̄·A.
  • Critical depth: the rectangular formula works per unit width q; trapezoids need iteration or the exponent method.
  • Jump sequent: the y2 formula uses F1 (the upstream supercritical Froude), not F2.
  • Manning S: bed slope is dimensionless; "1 in 1000" → S = 0.001; n carries units s/m^(1/3) — never "convert" n.
  • Darcy vs Fanning: f_Darcy = 4×f_Fanning; NEC uses Darcy.
  • Open-channel Reynolds: laminar threshold 500 with the R-form convention.
  • UH scaling: divide by the effective rainfall depth in cm (not mm).
  • Return-period risk: use 1 − (1−1/T)ⁿ; don't multiply 1/T by n.
  • Model scales: state which scale you use; distorted models apply Lr² horizontal × Lr^1.5 vertical carefully.
  • Confined vs unconfined well: h² appears in the unconfined Thiem; substituting T = k(h1+h2)/2 converts it.

Extended High-Yield Additions (Exam-Focused Extras)

Dimensional analysis & model similitude

  • Dimensional homogeneity; Buckingham π theorem (n − m π terms).
  • Model laws: Froude (gravity — open channels, spillways, ships): Fr_m = Fr_p; Reynolds (viscous — pipes, low-speed aircraft); Mach (compressible); Weber (surface tension); Euler (pressure). Undistorted and distorted models; Froude scale ratios: velocity √Lr, time √Lr, discharge Lr^2.5, force Lr³, power Lr^3.5, pressure Lr.

Boundary layer & drag (brief)

  • Boundary-layer growth δ ~ √(νx/V) (laminar); separation follows an adverse pressure gradient around bluff bodies; drag = Cd·½ρV²A; Stokes' law F = 3πμVd (Re < 1) — the basis of the hydrometer analysis of soils.

Turbines & pumps (intro — detailed in Ch 7)

  • Turbines: impulse (Pelton) / reaction (Francis, Kaplan, propeller); specific speed Ns = N√P/H^1.25 (P in hp): Pelton < 35, Francis 60–300, Kaplan > 300 — with P in kW: < 30, 51–225, > 225 (1 hp = 736 W); the draft tube of reaction types recovers head.
  • Pumps: centrifugal (radial/mixed/axial); head = manometric; NPSH available vs required (cavitation); affinity laws (Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³); series/parallel operation; cavitation follows low suction head.

Rainfall–runoff methods for Nepal hills

  • SCS-CN (curve number): S = 25400/CN − 254 (mm); Ia = 0.2S; Q = (P−Ia)²/(P−Ia+S) — widely used for ungauged catchments.
  • Rational method Q = CiA/360 (SI) for small urban catchments; WECS/DHM regional flood formulas for Nepal rural roads and bridges.
  • GLOF (glacier lake outburst flood) — the Nepal-specific hazard for hydropower intakes (Tsho Rolpa, Imja).

Rapid-Fire One-Liners (Last-Minute Revision)

  • Ideal fluid: inviscid + incompressible; real fluids have viscosity.
  • Bingham plastic τ = τy + μdu/dy; pseudoplastic μ↓ with rate; dilatant μ↑.
  • μ(liquid) ↓ with T; μ(gas) ↑ with T; 1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s; 1 stoke = 10⁻⁴ m²/s.
  • Water: ρ 1000, γ 9.81 kN/m³, μ 1 cP, ν 1 cSt, σ 0.0728 N/m (20 °C), pv 2.34 kPa.
  • Mercury SG 13.6; seawater 1.025; atmosphere 101.3 kPa = 10.33 m water = 760 mm Hg.
  • Drop p = 4σ/d; soap bubble 8σ/d; jet 2σ/d; capillary h = 4σcosα/γd (≈ 30/d mm for water).
  • Cavitation: p < pv; suction lift ≤ 7 m; NPSHa > NPSHr.
  • Pascal: equal in all directions; jack F2 = F1·A2/A1.
  • F = γh̄A; h* = h̄ + Ig/(h̄A) — the centre of pressure sits below the centroid; on a horizontal surface h* = h̄.
  • Wall with water to the top: F = γH²/2 at H/3; with surcharge: rectangle at H/2 + triangle at H/3.
  • Curved surfaces: Fx on the vertical projection; Fy = weight of (real/virtual) water above.
  • Floating stable when GM > 0; BM = I/V; inclining test tanθ = wd/(W·GM).
  • Submerged stable only when B is above G; relative equilibrium tanθ = a/g; paraboloid ω²r²/2g.
  • Re pipe: < 2000 laminar, > 4000 turbulent; channel laminar < 500.
  • Continuity A1V1 = A2V2 (incompressible).
  • Bernoulli: steady, incompressible, frictionless, along a streamline, no work.
  • Cd: venturi 0.95–0.98; orifice 0.60–0.65 (Cc 0.61–0.64, Cv 0.97–0.98); pitot Cv 0.98.
  • Venturi cone 21°/5–7°; throat d/D 0.25–0.75; jet force ρAV²; moving plate ρAV(V−u).
  • Expansion (V1−V2)²/2g; exit 1.0; entrance 0.5; gate valve 0.2; globe 8–10.
  • Darcy hf = fLV²/2gD; laminar f = 64/Re; Blasius 0.316/Re^0.25; Chezy C = √(8g/f).
  • Manning V = (1/n)R^(2/3)S^(1/2); concrete n 0.012–0.015; earth 0.0225–0.03.
  • TEL − HGL = V²/2g; TEL falls by the losses; siphon summit ≤ 7–7.6 m.
  • Water hammer Δp = ρcV; tc = 2L/c; surge tank/air vessel/relief valve.
  • Hardy Cross: node ΣQ = 0, loop Σhf = 0; series same Q; parallel same hf.
  • Economical sections: rectangle b = 2y; trapezoid half-hexagon (60°); circle max Q at 0.95D, max V at 0.81D.
  • F = V/√(gD); F = 1 critical; yc = (q²/g)^(1/3); Emin = 1.5yc.
  • Alternate depths — same E; sequent depths — same momentum; jump y2/y1 = ½(√(1+8F1²)−1).
  • ΔE jump = (y2−y1)³/(4y1y2); steady jump F1 4.5–9; length 5–7y2.
  • GVF dy/dx = (S0−Sf)/(1−F²); M1 dam backwater; M2 overfall drawdown; M3 below gate.
  • Shields θc 0.03–0.06; τ0 = γRS; Kennedy v0 = 0.55·m·y^0.64 (m = critical velocity ratio); Lacey regime equations.
  • Water balance P = R + E + T + I + ΔS; Horton f = fc+(f0−fc)e^(−kt); φ-index = constant loss.
  • Thiessen polygons — weighted mean rainfall; isohyetal the most accurate; double-mass checks consistency.
  • Rectangular weir Q = 1.84LH^1.5; 90° V-notch ≈ 1.38H^2.5; Cipolletti (1H:4V sides) 1.86LH^1.5.
  • Rating Q = C(G−a)^n; loop for unsteady flow; dilution gauging for torrents.
  • UH: 1 cm effective rain, uniform, D hours; linear + time-invariant; S-curve changes duration; Snyder synthetic.
  • Weibull m/(n+1); Gumbel for floods; risk = 1−(1−1/T)ⁿ (the 100-yr flood within 30 yrs ≈ 26%).
  • Muskingum S = K[xI+(1−x)O]; reservoir routing level-pool (Puls).
  • Rational Q = CiA/360 (SI); SCS-CN S = 25400/CN − 254, Ia = 0.2S.
  • Aquifuge (neither stores nor transmits); aquiclude (stores, no transmit); aquitard (leaky); aquifer (good at both).
  • Artesian = confined; perched = local lens; Thiem confined Q = 2πTΔs/ln(r2/r1).
  • Specific capacity = Q/drawdown; over-pumping → decline, subsidence, intrusion.
  • Froude law for spillways; Qr = Lr^2.5; Mach for compressible flow.
  • Ns (metric hp): Pelton < 35, Francis 60–300, Kaplan > 300; kW: < 30, 51–225, > 225; affinity P ∝ N³.
  • Class A pan coefficient ≈ 0.7; Nepal monsoon ≈ 80% of the annual rain.

Extra Depth: Pressure Measurement Details

  • Single-column/micro-manometer: reservoir type for small gauge changes; inclined-tube sensitivity = 1/sinθ (θ = 10° gives ≈ 5.76× magnification).
  • Differential U-tube: pA − pB = h(γm − γ) for same-level pipes with a mercury reading h.
  • Inverted U-tube (two-liquid) — for heavy measured liquids with air or a lighter fluid on top.
  • Bourdon gauge — elastic tube deflection; dead-weight tester — the calibration standard; Fortin barometer for atmospheric pressure.
  • Vacuum terms: p_abs = p_atm − p_vacuum; gauge zero at atmosphere.

Extra Depth: Orifices, Mouthpieces, Weirs

  • Coefficients: Cc ≈ 0.64, Cv ≈ 0.97–0.98, Cd = Cc×Cv ≈ 0.61–0.62 (sharp-edged small orifice).
  • Large rectangular orifice — integrate across the varying head; partially submerged — split into free + drowned parts.
  • Drowned orifice: Q = Cd·a·√(2gH_diff) — depends on the differential head only.
  • Borda mouthpiece (re-entrant): running full Cc = 0.5, Cd = 0.5; external mouthpiece Cd ≈ 0.855 (recovers some head).
  • Francis weir corrections: suppressed (no end contraction) Q = 1.84LH^1.5; with n end contractions Q = 1.84(L−0.1nH)H^1.5 (SI).
  • Broad-crested weir: Q = 1.705·Cd·b·H^1.5; critical depth on the crest makes it robust for sediment-laden flows.
  • Ogee spillway: profile follows the sharp-crested nappe; Q = C·L·H^1.5 with C ≈ 2.1–2.3 (SI).

Extra Depth: Pipes — Compound, Branching, and Design

  • Three-reservoir problem: assume the common junction head H_J; apply continuity Q1 = Q2 + Q3 (signs by relative heads); solve by trial or head equations.
  • Dupuit: neglect velocity head and minor losses when L > 500–1000 D.
  • Pipe materials: CI/DI (spun), MS/steel (welded large mains), GI (small old supply), PVC/HDPE, DI, RCC (gravity mains); select by pressure, corrosion, cost.
  • Ageing: roughness ε grows (tuberculation) → f rises, capacity drops; Hazen–Williams C falls from 130 to ≈ 100 over decades.
  • Air vessels near the pump dampen pulsations and cut the acceleration head in long suction lines.
  • Surge tank functions: on sudden load rejection the flow diverts up the tank; it reduces water hammer on tunnel and penstock and improves governor stability. Types: simple, restricted-orifice (throttled), differential (internal riser + outer tank).

Extra Depth: Open Channel — Rapidly Varied Flow Devices

  • Spillway ogee + chute + stilling basin: USBR Type II (F1 > 9), Type III (F1 4.5–9), Type IV (F1 2.5–4.5); chute blocks, baffle piers, end sill.
  • Bucket dissipators: ski-jump/flip bucket (plunge pool) and roller bucket — alternatives to the jump basin on high dams.
  • Free overfall: brink depth ≈ 0.715 yc — the end-depth method measures discharge.
  • Venturi/standing-wave flume: the narrowed throat forces critical flow, so the discharge becomes independent of the downstream level when modular (free-flow); the Parshall flume is the fixed-geometry version.
  • Transitions: expansions ≈ 4:1 (horizontal), contractions steeper; bridge contractions analyzed by momentum (afflux).

Extra Depth: Hydrology — Extra Standard Facts

  • Rain gauge density (IS/WMO): ≈ 1 per 520 km² (plains); minimum 10% recording gauges.
  • Precipitation types: convective (thunderstorms), orographic (windward heavy — Nepal monsoon), cyclonic/frontal.
  • Nepal monsoon: ~80% of annual rain in June–September; strong orographic gradient (Pokhara > 4000 mm; Mustang rain shadow < 300 mm).
  • Evaporation pans: Class A coefficient 0.7; Colorado pan 0.8; lake evaporation = pan × coefficient.
  • Infiltration capacity vs actual infiltration — actual = min(capacity, intensity).
  • Baseflow separation: straight-line, fixed-% (N-day recession), master-recession methods.
  • UH derivation pitfalls: storms must be uniform and single-peaked; adjust for non-uniform ER; average several events.
  • Flood frequency: annual maximum series vs partial duration series — PDS gives slightly higher estimates for T < 10 yr.
  • Design return periods (DoR Nepal): culverts 25–50 yr, bridges 50–100 yr, aqueducts/irrigation structures 25–50 yr; spillway per dam class (up to PMF).
  • Groundwater provinces of Nepal: Terai (thick alluvium, high potential), inner Terai valleys, Kathmandu Valley (semi-confined, over-extracted); hill storage is limited.
  • Springs — the main rural hill source; types: depression, contact, artesian; protection = spring box + recharge-zone conservation.

Section-by-Section Exam Focus Summary

3.1 Fluids — property quick reference

  • Density vs weight density vs SG vs specific volume — four ways to state "how heavy" a fluid is; SG uses water at 4 °C (maximum density 1000 kg/m³).
  • Viscosity devices: rotating drum, capillary (Saybolt/Ostwald), falling sphere (Stokes) — name–device pairs are common questions.
  • Surface tension devices: capillary rise, du Noüy ring, drop-weight; σ falls with temperature and with detergent (surfactants).
  • Vapour pressure grows with temperature; water boils when pv = local pressure — high altitude lowers the boiling point (Kathmandu ≈ 95 °C); hot water cavitates sooner.
  • Compressibility: K water ≈ 2.1 GPa; air K = γp (≈ 142 kPa adiabatic); oil K ≈ 1.5–2 GPa; hydraulics treats liquids as incompressible except in water hammer.

3.2 Hydrostatics — extra worked facts

  • Pressure diagrams: rectangle (uniform surcharge), triangle (hydrostatic), trapezoid (both); total force = area of the diagram; acts through the diagram's centroid.
  • Two-liquid layering: pressures add across interfaces; same-level points in the same continuous fluid share pressure; the interface shifts with the SG ratio — the classic manometer trap.
  • Buoyant force on a fully submerged body = γ·V (independent of depth); apparent weight = W − γV; this is the hydrometer principle.
  • Floating stability: GM = (I/V) − BG; small GM = tender (slow roll), large GM = stiff (quick roll); ships ballast to tune GM; inclining with weight w moved distance d: GM = w·d/(W·tanθ).
  • Roll period T = 2π√(k²/(g·GM)) — halve GM and T grows by √2 (not ×2).
  • Rotation about a vertical axis: paraboloid h = ω²r²/2g; in a closed tank with no spillover the vertex position follows volume conservation — the MCQ usually asks for the shape.

3.3 Kinematics & Dynamics — details

  • Stream function ψ (2-D incompressible): constant along streamlines, Δψ = Q between lines; velocity potential φ (irrotational); both satisfy Laplace; the ψ and φ families are orthogonal — the flow-net link.
  • Free vortex (v·r = const, irrotational) vs forced vortex (v = ωr, rigid-body rotation).
  • Euler and Bernoulli come from F = ma along a streamline; the extended Bernoulli with machine/loss terms: p1/γ + V1²/2g + z1 + Hp = p2/γ + V2²/2g + z2 + HT + hL.
  • Venturi–scour–cavitation coupling: the throat pressure is minimum — check pv in meter runs and pump suctions.
  • Correction factors: kinetic-energy α = 2 laminar, ≈ 1.05 turbulent; momentum β ≈ 1.33 laminar, 1.01–1.05 turbulent.
  • Jet on a series of plates: F = ρAV(V−u); efficiency η = 4u(V−u)/V² peaks near u = V/2; Pelton cup deflection ≈ 165–170° gives theoretical efficiency ≈ 90%.

3.4 Pipes — extra facts

  • Colebrook–White (implicit): 1/√f = −2log₁₀(ε/3.7D + 2.51/Re√f); Swamee–Jain is the explicit form — recognize the names.
  • Hagen–Poiseuille: hf = 32μLV/(γD²) — laminar; equivalent f = 64/Re; Q ∝ D⁴ (double D → 16× Q at the same loss).
  • Water-hammer wave speed in a thin-walled pipe: c ≈ 1440/√(1 + KD/(Et)) m/s; rigid-pipe algebra gives Δp ≈ 1400V kPa per m/s — a 1 m/s instant closure ≈ 14 bar; hence slow-closing valves and surge tanks.
  • Network resistance: hf = rQ² with r = fL/(12.1D⁵); series r = Σri; parallel 1/√r_eq = Σ1/√ri.
  • Distribution residuals: Hazen–Williams C — new CI 130, old ≈ 100, PVC 150; economical diameter D ≈ 1.22 √Q (SI, Q m³/s).

3.5 Open channel — extra facts

  • Hydraulic depth D = A/T; hydraulic radius R = A/P; section factor for uniform flow A√R; for critical flow Z = A√D.
  • Hydraulic exponent N: wide rectangle 3, parabola 3.5, triangle 4, circular ≈ 5.1 — used in direct-integration GVF (Bresse for wide rectangles).
  • Chezy C = (1/n)R^(1/6) (Manning relation); C ∝ R^(1/6) is why large channels behave as hydraulically "smoother".
  • Specific energy at the critical section: Emin = 1.5yc (rectangle); flow passes critical over a broad-crested weir — a measuring device.
  • Jump energy loss grows rapidly with F1: F1 = 2 → ΔE ≈ 0.27 y1; F1 = 5 → y2/y1 = 6.59 and ΔE ≈ 6.6 y1 — strong dissipation justifies stilling basins.
  • Slope classes M/S/C/H/A; control sections (critical depth) — spillway crest, sluice gate, free overfall, break in grade — anchor the GVF computation.
  • Standard step method needs cross-section data (non-prismatic); direct step suits prismatic channels; both integrate dy/dx stepwise.

3.6 Hydrology — extra facts

  • Rain gauge siting: open ground, obstacle distance ≥ 2× (ideally 4×) the obstacle height, rim 30 cm above ground, level.
  • Design storms from IDF curves; Nepal DoR culverts 25–50 yr; Kirpich Tc = 0.01947 L^0.77 S^-0.385 (minutes, SI).
  • UH ordinates scale linearly with ER depth; base width constant; storms superpose; the S-curve ordinate difference gives the UH of a new duration.
  • Gumbel yT = −ln ln(T/(T−1)); frequency factor Q_T = Q̄ + Kσ; Log-Pearson III is the US federal standard.
  • Reservoir routing (level-pool): dS/dt = I − O with storage-elevation and outflow-elevation curves — attenuates and delays the peak; Muskingum translates + attenuates.
  • Well testing: step-drawdown separates well loss; constant-rate tests fit Theis; safe yield < recharge; Kathmandu valley aquifer depletion is a policy question.
  • Springs: gravity (depression/contact) vs artesian; recession Q = Q0·e^(−t/k) sizes the dry-season storage.
  • Nepal floods: glacier-fed rivers (Koshi, Gandaki, Karnali) — GLOF risk; monsoon flash floods on gravel-bed rivers; WECS/DHM empirical formulas where gauges are absent.

Quick Concept Cards (read the morning of the exam)

Card 1 — Statics chain

Fluid at rest → pressure only normal → p = γh → Pascal (equal in all directions) → F = γh̄A on planes (CP below centroid) → curved surfaces resolved (Fx projection, Fy water weight) → buoyancy = displaced weight → stability via metacentre (GM = I/V − BG) → accelerating containers tilt the free surface (tanθ = a/g) or rotate it (paraboloid).

Card 2 — Dynamics chain

Continuity (AV = const) → Bernoulli (energy heads) → venturi/orifice/pitot as energy meters → momentum for forces (jets, bends, jump) → real flow adds losses: major (friction, Darcy/Manning) + minor (fittings) → TEL/HGL picture → water hammer for unsteady → Hardy Cross for networks.

Card 3 — Channel chain

Geometry (A, P, R, T) → resistance (Manning) → uniform flow (yn) → critical flow (yc, F = 1, Emin) → compare yn & yc → slope class (M/S/C/H/A) → GVF profiles (dy/dx = (S0−Sf)/(1−F²)) → controls anchor profiles → jump where supercritical meets subcritical (sequent depths, ΔE, stilling basin) → sediment: Shields threshold, tractive-force design.

Card 4 — Hydrology chain

Rain (gauges, Thiessen/isohyetal, IDF) → losses (Horton, φ-index, SCS-CN) → excess rain → UH (1 cm, D-hr, linear) → S-curve & synthetic (Snyder) → design flood (Weibull/Gumbel, risk formula, or PMP/PMF) → routing (Muskingum/level-pool) → channels: rating curves, weirs/flumes, dilution → groundwater: aquifer types, Thiem/Theis wells, safe yield.

Additional One-Mark Facts (potpourri)

  • Buoyant force on a submerged body is independent of depth (depends only on the displaced volume).
  • A floating body displaces its own weight; a submerged body displaces its own volume.
  • Piezometric head = p/γ + z; the HGL is the piezometric head line.
  • Hydraulic gradient i = hf/L — the slope of the HGL; groundwater Darcy uses the same idea.
  • Cd = Cc × Cv; Cc is unity only for a perfectly rounded mouthpiece (then Cd = Cv ≈ 0.98).
  • Impulse–momentum handles flows with unknown losses (jump, sudden expansion) where the energy equation fails.
  • Chronology trap: Chezy (1775) predates Manning (1889); Darcy (1856) precedes Hazen (1905); Rankine (1857) first treated earth pressure.
  • Manning's n from Strickler: n = d^(1/6)/21.1 (d in m) for rough channels — the Strickler–Manning name pair.
  • Water-hammer relief closest to the valve is most effective; the surge tank protects the tunnel and penstock of hydro plants (and improves governor stability).
  • Air valves at the summits of long mains (release trapped air); washouts at the valleys (remove sediment).
  • Free overfall end depth ≈ 0.715 yc — the "end-depth method".
  • Venturi flume modular flow: discharge depends only on the upstream head when the throat is critical; drowned when the tailwater is high.
  • Runoff coefficient C: paved 0.7–0.95, residential 0.3–0.5, forest 0.05–0.25.
  • Time of concentration (Kirpich): Tc = 0.01947 L^0.77 S^-0.385 (min, SI) — the rational-method intensity uses Tc as its duration.
  • UH duration must match the ER duration; changing duration uses the S-curve — never rescale time directly.
  • Gumbel is the Type-I extreme-value distribution; Weibull m/(n+1) is a plotting position (not a distribution) — don't confuse the names.
  • Storativity of confined aquifers 10⁻⁵–10⁻³; unconfined specific yield 0.05–0.3.
  • Transmissivity T = k·b; conductivity k depends on the medium AND the fluid (k_intrinsic × ρg/μ).
  • Flow nets: equipotential drop Δh = H/Nd; pore pressure at any point = γw × the remaining head above it.
  • Laminar sublayer: a pipe is hydraulically smooth when k < δ′.

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (3.1–3.6)

Fluid Properties (3.1) — Course Values

  • Specific volume v = 1/ρ. Water density is maximum at 4 °C (1000 kg/m³).
  • Newton's law of viscosity: τ = μ·du/dy — dynamic viscosity μ in N·s/m² (Pa·s); kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ in m²/s.
  • Surface tension effects: in a capillary tube the liquid's weight is balanced by the vertical component of surface tension; h = 2T·cosθ/(ρ·g·R). Wetting liquids: contact angle 0°; non-wetting > 90°; partial wetting 0–90°. Capillary rise decreases as temperature rises.
  • Excess pressure: inside a drop or air bubble ΔP = 2T/R; inside a soap bubble ΔP = 4T/R (two surfaces). Raindrops are spherical because of surface tension.
  • Cavitation forms when local pressure falls below vapour pressure and the bubbles collapse under high pressure — pitting on turbine runners and pump impellers.
  • Compressibility: bulk modulus B = ΔP/(−ΔV/V); for an incompressible fluid B = ∞.
  • Rheology classes: Newtonian — strain rate proportional to shear stress (water, air); dilatant — viscosity increases under shear (quicksand, corn-flour paste, putty); thixotropic — viscosity decreases with shear and time (paints, cosmetics); pseudoplastic — viscosity decreases with shear rate (blood, milk).

Hydrostatics (3.2)

  • The area of the pressure diagram gives the total pressure force on a submerged plane surface; the force acts through the diagram's centroid (below the area's centroid).
  • Pressure at a point is equal in all directions only in a fluid at rest; not in a viscous moving fluid.
  • Bourdon gauge measures gauge pressure; U-tube manometers measure gas/liquid pressures; micromanometers for very small differences.
  • Total head = piezometric head + velocity head. In a static fluid the piezometric head is constant everywhere; the piezometric line is horizontal.
  • Buoyancy: the buoyant force equals the displaced weight and opposes weight (Archimedes). B < W → sinks; B = W → floats at any depth. Stability: GM = BM − BG; GM > 0 stable, GM = 0 neutral, GM < 0 unstable; for an inclined body the buoyancy-weight resultant acts below the CG when stable.

Kinematics & Dynamics (3.3)

  • Flow classification: steady/unsteady (with time at a point), uniform/non-uniform (with space along the flow). A constant cross-section pipe carrying changing discharge is unsteady uniform flow.
  • Conservation principles: continuity = mass; momentum = Newton's second law; Bernoulli = energy (valid along a streamline for steady, incompressible, inviscid flow).
  • In a venturimeter the throat velocity exceeds the inlet velocity (pressure energy converts to kinetic); the discharge relates to √(manometer deflection). The Pitot-static tube measures velocity at a point (stagnation − static head). The U-tube manometer is preferred for gas pressure.
  • Reynolds number Re = inertia/viscous force. Pipe: laminar < 2000, transition 2000–4000, turbulent > 4000. Open channel: laminar < 500, transition 500–2000, turbulent > 2000.
  • Froude number Fr = V/√(gy): < 1 subcritical (tranquil), = 1 critical, > 1 supercritical (rapid). The hydraulic jump converts supercritical → subcritical.
  • Momentum applications: a jet on a stationary flat plate exerts F = ρQV; on a moving plate F = ρQ(V − u).
  • In open channels the mean velocity sits at 0.2 d and 0.8 d depth from the surface — their average gives the section mean.

Pipe & Open Channel Flow (3.4–3.5)

  • Major loss = friction (Darcy-Weisbach hf = fLV²/2gD; Chezy/Manning for channels); minor losses at entries, bends, valves and expansions scale with V²/2g. The HGL sits above the pipe by the pressure head; the TEL adds the velocity head; both slope in the flow direction.
  • Pipe networks: Hardy-Cross (ΔQ iterations balancing loop head losses); water hammer relief by surge tanks, slow valve closure and relief valves — critical closure time Tc = 2L/c.
  • Specific energy E = y + V²/2g; minimum at critical depth yc = (q²/g)^⅓ (rectangular); Froude = 1 at critical state.
  • GVF profiles: M1, M2, M3 (mild); S2, S3 (steep); C1, C3 (critical); H2, H3 (horizontal); A2, A3 (adverse). M1 backs water up behind dams; M2 draws down to a free overfall.
  • Hydraulic jump types by pre-jump Froude — undular (1–1.7), weak (1.7–2.5), oscillating (2.5–4.5), steady (4.5–9, the most efficient dissipation), strong (> 9). Conjugate depths satisfy momentum; ΔE = (y2−y1)³/(4y1y2).
  • Mobile boundary channels: inception of motion from Shields' diagram (critical shear stress vs grain Reynolds number); design by tractive force (permissible shear) or regime theory (Lacey/Kennedy — India-Nepal practice).

Hydrology (3.6)

  • Water balance: P = R + E + T + I + ΔS (precipitation = runoff + evaporation + transpiration + infiltration + storage change).
  • A rating curve is the discharge-stage relation at a gauging section (log-log linear extrapolation for high stages).
  • The double-mass curve checks arithmetic/homogeneity errors in rainfall records (accumulated station rain vs accumulated regional mean; a slope break marks a data change).
  • Unit hydrograph ordinates = direct runoff ordinates ÷ direct runoff depth (cm); assumes linearity, time-invariance, constant duration. The S-curve from consecutive UHs gives any-duration UH. Synthetic UH (Snyder): basin lag tp = Ct(L·Lca)^0.3.
  • Rainfall-runoff: the runoff coefficient depends on soil, slope, vegetation; infiltration indices W (initial losses) and φ (constant loss).
  • Flood frequency: return period T = 1/probability; Gumbel/Weibull plotting positions; design flood = the flood adopted for design (probable maximum flood for high dams, standard project flood for major works). Frequency factor: Q_T = μ + K·σ.
  • Groundwater: water table (unconfined), piezometric surface (confined); Darcy's law v = ki for laminar flow; well hydraulics — steady radial flow (Theis/Thiem); specific capacity = yield per unit drawdown.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): "Which instrument measures velocity at a point?" → the Pitot-static tube (not the venturimeter). "Pressure at a point is equal in all directions" — only for a fluid at rest. Pipe vs channel Reynolds thresholds (2000/4000 vs 500/2000) are a favourite one-mark trap; so are the soap-bubble (4T/R) vs drop (2T/R) pressure formulas.
