This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

4.1 Shear Forces and Bending Moments (ACiE0401)

A. Internal Actions

Fig 4.1 — Beam cut at a section: N (⊥), V (∥) and M (about the NA) appear on the exposed face; positive V = left-up/right-down, positive M = sagging (tension at bottom)
  • Cut a beam anywhere and three internal resultants appear at the cut: the axial force N (perpendicular to the section), the shear force V (parallel to it) and the bending moment M (moment about the neutral axis).
  • Sign conventions (exam standard): shear is positive when the left portion tends to slide up relative to the right ("left-up, right-down"); bending moment is positive when it sags (concave up, tension at the bottom) and negative when it hogs (tension at the top).
  • Differential relationships (Euler–Bernoulli):
    w = dV/dx (load intensity is the slope of the shear diagram)
    V = dM/dx (shear is the slope of the moment diagram)
    w = d²M/dx²
    Consequences: the moment is maximum or minimum where the shear is zero; a concentrated load steps the shear diagram and kinks the moment diagram; an applied couple steps the moment diagram but leaves the shear unchanged; a uniform load gives a linear shear diagram and a parabolic moment diagram. For a simply supported beam with UDL over the full span: M_max = wL²/8 at midspan and V_max = wL/2 at the supports.
  • Point of contraflexure: where the bending moment changes sign — the curvature reverses there. It occurs in overhanging, continuous and fixed beams.
  • Overhang effect: equal overhangs of length a reduce the midspan moment: M_mid = wL²/8 − wa²/2. When a = L/√8 ≈ 0.354L the midspan and support moments are equal in magnitude (wL²/16 each); when a = L/2 the midspan moment becomes zero.

B. Standard Cases (memorize table)

Beam caseV_maxM_maxPosition
Simply supported — central point load WW/2WL/4midspan
SS — point load W at a from leftWb/LWab/Lunder the load
SS — UDL w over spanwL/2wL²/8midspan
SS — triangular load, peak w at centrewL/4wL²/12midspan
Cantilever — end point load WWWLfixed end
Cantilever — UDL wwLwL²/2fixed end
Fixed beam — central WW/2WL/8 at support and midspan—
Fixed beam — UDLwL/2wL²/12 (support); wL²/24 (span)—
Propped cantilever — UDLprop 3wL/8; fixed end 5wL/8wL²/8 (fixed end); 9wL²/128 (span)span max at x = 3L/8 from the prop

C. Loading and Superposition

  • Principle of superposition — the effects of separate loads simply add — is valid only for linear elastic systems (Hookean material, small deflections); a cracked or buckling structure breaks this rule.
  • Load types: concentrated (point), distributed (uniform, varying) and applied couples; diagrams for complex loading are built piecewise by superposition.
  • Moving loads are handled with influence lines (section 4.5) to find the worst positions.
Fig 4.2 — The three diagram sets every NEC paper draws: correct shapes are rectangle+step (SS point load), linear+parabola (SS UDL) and triangle+parabola (cantilever UDL, worst at the fixed end)
Memorize: Propped cantilever UDL — prop reaction 3wL/8, fixed-end moment wL²/8, maximum span moment 9wL²/128 at x = 3L/8 from the prop. Fixed beam UDL — support moment wL²/12, midspan wL²/24 (span/support ratio 1/2), points of contraflexure at x = L/2 ± L/(2√3) ≈ 0.211L from the ends.
4.1 must-knows: w = dV/dx, V = dM/dx; M max/min where V = 0; couple steps M, not V; SS central load WL/4, SS UDL wL²/8, cantilever UDL wL²/2 at the fixed end; propped cantilever: prop 3wL/8, fixed-end wL²/8, span 9wL²/128 at 3L/8; contraflexure = M changes sign; overhang a = L/√8 balances mid and support moments.

4.2 Stress and Strain Analysis (ACiE0402)

A. Simple Stress and Strain

σ = P/A ; ε = ΔL/L ; E = σ/ε (Hooke's law, linear elastic)
Elongation of a prismatic bar: Δ = PL/AE
Bar under its own weight: Δ = γL²/2E = WL/2AE (W = total weight)
Bar of varying section: Δ = Σ PᵢLᵢ/(AᵢE)
  • Units: stress in N/mm² (MPa). Moduli: steel E = 2×10⁵ MPa, concrete ≈ 5000√fck, aluminium ≈ 0.7×10⁵ MPa.
  • Poisson's ratio μ (ν) = lateral strain / longitudinal strain (within the elastic limit). Values: steel 0.25–0.33, concrete 0.10–0.20, cork ≈ 0, rubber ≈ 0.5. Theoretical limits −1 to 0.5; practical range 0 to 0.5; in the plastic range μ ≈ 0.5 (volume stays constant).
  • Volumetric strain: εv = εx + εy + εz. The bulk modulus connects mean stress to volumetric strain:
    K = σm/εv = E/3(1−2μ)
  • Elastic-constant relations:
    G = E/2(1+μ) ; K = E/3(1−2μ) ; E = 9KG/(3K+G) = 2G(1+μ) = 3K(1−2μ)
    0 ≤ μ ≤ 0.5 for isotropic materials
    Independent elastic constants: isotropic 2, orthotropic (wood, plywood) 9, anisotropic 21.
  • Temperature stress: a fully restrained bar develops σ = αΔT·E (steel α = 12×10⁻⁶/°C, ΔT = 40 °C → σ = 96 MPa); partial restraint reduces it; free thermal strain = αΔT. If a gap g exists and free expansion exceeds it, the force developed is P = (αΔT·L − g)AE/L.
  • Composite bars: load is shared by stiffness (AE/L); bonded bars share a common strain: σ₁/E₁ = σ₂/E₂.
  • Strain energy: U = σ²V/2E = P²L/2E A (gradual load). A suddenly applied load doubles the stress; a drop of height h gives an impact factor (1 + √(1+2h/δst)). A bar stretched by its own weight both stores energy and extends only half as much as under the same weight applied at the end.
  • Resilience = energy per unit volume within the elastic limit = σ²/2E; proof resilience uses the yield stress; toughness = total area under the stress–strain curve up to fracture.
Fig 4.3 — Simple stress and strain: (1) prismatic & stepped bars — σ = P/A, ε = ΔL/L, E = σ/ε, Δ = PL/AE (varying section: Σ PᵢL/AᵢE), own weight Δ = γL²/2E; (2) stress–strain curve — E = slope, resilience = σ²/2E, toughness = total area to fracture; sudden load doubles the stress; (3) Poisson's ratio μ = εlat/εlong (steel 0.25–0.33, rubber ≈ 0.5), εv = εx+εy+εz, E = 2G(1+μ) = 3K(1−2μ) = 9KG/(3K+G); (4) temperature stress σ = αΔT·E fully restrained (gap g: P = (αΔT·L − g)AE/L) and composite bars sharing strain σ₁/E₁ = σ₂/E₂, load shared by stiffness

B. Plane Stress Transformation & Principal Stresses

σθ = (σx+σy)/2 + (σx−σy)/2·cos2θ + τxy·sin2θ
τθ = −(σx−σy)/2·sin2θ + τxy·cos2θ
Principal stresses: σ1,2 = (σx+σy)/2 ± √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²]
Principal planes: tan2θp = 2τxy/(σx−σy) — shear is zero on them
Maximum shear: τmax = √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²] = (σ1−σ2)/2, on planes at 45° to the principal planes
Uniaxial case (σx only): σ1 = σx, σ2 = 0, τmax = σx/2 at 45°
  • Mohr's circle: centre on the σ-axis at (σx+σy)/2, radius = in-plane τmax; angles on the circle are twice the physical angles; the pole method locates the planes.
  • 3-D state: the absolute maximum shear is (σ1 − σ3)/2 — the largest of the three Mohr circles. Thin cylinder: hoop pr/t, longitudinal pr/2t, radial ≈ 0 → in-plane τmax = pr/4t, absolute τmax = pr/2t on an out-of-plane 45° plane (the classic trick — see the watch-outs).
  • Theories of failure — each predicts when a material yields or breaks: maximum principal stress (Rankine — brittle materials), maximum shear (Guest/Tresca — ductile), maximum distortion energy (von Mises — ductile, most accurate), maximum principal strain (St. Venant), total strain energy (Haigh), Mohr's theory (brittle with unequal tensile/compressive strengths).
Fig 4.4 — Mohr's circle: the two face-points X and Y lie on a diameter; the circle cuts the σ-axis at the principal stresses (τ = 0) and tops out at τmax = R; every angle on the circle is double the physical angle

C. Torsion

Fig 4.5 — Shaft in torsion: shear stress varies linearly from zero at the axis to τmax at the surface (τ = T·r/J); twist θ = TL/GJ
T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L (circular shafts, elastic)
J solid = πd⁴/32 ; J hollow = π(D⁴−d⁴)/32
τmax = 16T/πd³ (solid) ; hollow: 16TD/π(D⁴−d⁴)
Power: P = 2πNT/60 (W; N in rpm, T in N·m) ; T = 9550·P(kW)/N
Shafts in series: same T, θ = Σθi ; in parallel: same θ, T shared
  • Assumptions: circular section, homogeneous and elastic, plane sections remain plane, no warping. Non-circular sections warp — St. Venant's theory applies instead.
  • Torsional shear is linear: zero at the axis, maximum at the surface. Hollow shafts are more efficient because the material sits far from the axis.
  • Torsional rigidity = GJ; stiffness = GJ/L; torsional strain energy U = T²L/2GJ.
  • Combined bending + torsion (max-shear theory): equivalent bending moment Me = ½(M + √(M²+T²)); equivalent torque Te = √(M²+T²).
4.2 must-knows: E = 2×10⁵ MPa steel; Poisson: steel 0.25–0.33, cork ≈ 0, rubber ≈ 0.5; E = 2G(1+μ) = 3K(1−2μ); temperature stress αΔT·E (steel 96 MPa for 40 °C); sudden load doubles stress; resilience σ²/2E, toughness = full area; σ1,2 = (σx+σy)/2 ± √[((σx−σy)/2)²+τxy²]; τmax = (σ1−σ2)/2 at 45°; thin cylinder absolute τmax = pr/2t (out-of-plane); torsion τ = Tr/J, J = πd⁴/32; P = 2πNT/60; Te = √(M²+T²).

4.3 Theory of Flexure and Columns (ACiE0403)

A. Pure (Simple) Bending

Fig 4.6 — Bending stress is linear across the depth (zero at the NA, max at the fibres) and constant along a pure-bending span.
Bending equation: M/I = σ/y = E/R
σ = M·y/I — maximum at the extreme fibre: σ = M/Z with Z = I/y_max (elastic section modulus)
Bending stiffness = EI ; curvature 1/R = M/EI

Assumptions of simple bending theory

  • Homogeneous, isotropic, linear-elastic material (E equal in tension and compression); plane sections remain plane and normal to the neutral axis; initially straight beam of constant EI in pure bending (no shear); small deflection, large radius of curvature.
  • Neutral axis: passes through the centroid of the section in pure bending (net axial force zero); stress is zero along it — compression above, tension below for sagging. (In fully plastic bending the plastic NA balances the areas instead and can shift.)
  • Elastic curve: the deflected shape of the neutral axis:
    EI d²y/dx² = M(x) ; EI d³y/dx³ = V ; EI d⁴y/dx⁴ = −w

Standard deflection/slope results (memorize)

CaseMax deflectionEnd slope
SS beam, central load WWL³/48EIWL²/16EI
SS beam, UDL w5wL⁴/384EIwL³/24EI
SS beam, moment M₀ at one endML²/(9√3 EI) at x = L/√3ML/3EI (near end), ML/6EI (far)
Cantilever, end load WWL³/3EI (free end)WL²/2EI
Cantilever, UDLwL⁴/8EIwL³/6EI
Cantilever, moment M₀ at free endML²/2EIML/EI
Fixed beam, central WWL³/192EI0 at ends
Fixed beam, UDLwL⁴/384EI0
Propped cantilever, UDLwL⁴/185EI (= 0.0054wL⁴/EI)δ_max at x ≈ 0.42L from the fixed end

Deflection methods

  • Double integration (basic) and Macaulay's method (singularity brackets ⟨x−a⟩ handle point loads/moments in one integration).
  • Moment-area (Mohr's) theorems: (1) the change of slope between two points equals the area of the M/EI diagram between them; (2) the deviation of B from the tangent at A equals the moment of that M/EI area about B.
  • Conjugate beam method: load the conjugate beam with the M/EI diagram; supports transform (simple→simple, fixed→free, free→fixed); conjugate shear = slope, conjugate moment = deflection.
  • Castigliano's theorem and unit load — see 4.4.

B. Columns and Struts — Euler's Theory

Fig 4.7 — Euler buckling shapes: each dashed curve is the buckled mode; the shorter the effective length kL, the higher the load.
Euler buckling load: Pcr = π²EI/Le² (Le = effective length)
Effective lengths: pinned–pinned Le = L ; fixed–fixed Le = 0.5L ; fixed–free Le = 2L ; fixed–pinned Le = L/√2 ≈ 0.7L
Buckling stress: σcr = π²E/λ² with slenderness λ = Le/k ; k = √(I/A) (minimum axis governs)
End conditionLePcr (× π²EI/L²)
Both ends hingedL1
Both ends fixed0.5L4
One fixed, one free2L0.25
One fixed, one hingedL/√2 ≈ 0.7L2
  • Euler's assumptions: homogeneous isotropic elastic material, initially straight column, axial load through the centroid, no initial stress, self-weight neglected, frictionless pins, failure by buckling.
  • Validity: long columns only (λ ≳ 100–120 for steel); short columns (λ < 30–50) fail by crushing, which Euler cannot predict. Doubling the length quarters the Euler load.
  • Intermediate columns — empirical formulas: Rankine–Gordon 1/Pr = 1/Pc + 1/Pe (crushing Pc = σc·A, Euler Pe; Rankine constant a = σc/π²E — steel ≈ 1/7500, cast iron 1/1600, timber 1/750); Johnson's parabolic Pcr = σyA[1 − σyλ²/4π²E]; secant formula for eccentric loading; Perry–Robertson in codes.
  • Slenderness classification (steel practice): very short λ < 30, short 30–60, medium 60–100, long > 100 — codes vary; the concept (below/above Euler) is what NEC tests.
  • Eccentric loading: the secant formula amplifies stress by 1/(1−P/Pe); the middle-third rule keeps masonry columns in compression.
    • Fig 4.8 — Middle-third rule: with the load resultant inside the kern (e ≤ B/6) the bearing diagram stays compressive (trapezoid → triangle); outside it, the diagram demands tension the material cannot supply.
  • Euler load is independent of strength: it depends only on E, I and Le — high-strength steel does not help a long column (a favourite concept question).
  • Efficient column sections place material far from the axis (hollow tubes, I/H shapes); the minimum-I axis buckles first. Built-up columns use lacing (40–70°) or battens.
4.3 must-knows: M/I = σ/y = E/R; NA through the centroid; Z = I/ymax; SS central WL³/48EI, SS UDL 5wL⁴/384EI, cantilever end WL³/3EI, cantilever UDL wL⁴/8EI, fixed UDL wL⁴/384EI; moment-area: slope = M/EI area, deviation = its moment; conjugate: fixed→free, free→fixed; Euler Pcr = π²EI/Le², Le: hinged L, fixed–fixed 0.5L, fixed–free 2L, fixed–hinged 0.7L; doubling length quarters Pcr; Rankine 1/Pr = 1/Pc + 1/Pe; Euler ignores strength.

4.4 Determinate Structures-1 (ACiE0404)

A. Degree of Static Determinacy

Plane truss (pin-jointed): m + r = 2j determinate ; degree Ds = m + r − 2j
Plane frame (rigid-jointed): Ds = 3m + r − 3j − (releases) ; Dse = r − 3 ; Dsi = 3 × closed loops
Beams: Ds = r − 3 (simply supported r = 3 → Ds = 0; propped cantilever r = 4 → Ds = 1; fixed + hinged r = 5 → Ds = 2; fixed at both ends r = 6 → Ds = 3)
Kinematic indeterminacy: plane truss Dk = 2j − r ; plane frame (axial neglected) Dk = 2j − r for beams
Space frame: Ds = 6m + r − 6j − releases ; space truss: Ds = m + r − 3j
  • Stability check: reactions must be neither all parallel nor all concurrent — a structure can satisfy the counting formula and still be geometrically unstable (critical form).
  • Statically determinate structures: internal forces follow from equilibrium alone — they are independent of material and section, and temperature, settlement and fabrication errors create no stress (a favourite MCQ).
  • Indeterminate structures: need compatibility; temperature/settlement/fabrication errors create internal forces proportional to stiffness; loads distribute according to relative stiffness; redundancy gives reserve safety but sensitivity to support movement.

B. Energy Methods

Strain energy: axial U = P²L/2AE ; bending U = ∫M²dx/2EI ; torsion U = T²L/2GJ ; shear U = ∫kV²dx/2AG (k = 1.2 rectangle, 10/9 circle)
Castigliano's 2nd theorem: δ = ∂U/∂P (deflection at the load point, in the load direction)
Truss: δ = Σ(S ∂S/∂P)L/AE ; rotation: θ = ∂U/∂M ; dummy loads serve points with no real load
Least work (Menabrea): redundants minimize U → ∂U/∂R = 0 (equivalent to compatibility)
Clapeyron: U = ½ΣPδ for linear systems
  • Virtual work (unit load method) — apply a dummy unit load where the deflection is wanted; the internal "virtual" forces do no real work, but their product with the real displacements gives the deflection:
    Truss: δ = Σ u·P·L/AE ; beam/frame: δ = ∫ m·M/EI dx
    u, m = internal forces due to a unit load placed at the point/direction wanted
    Temperature: δ = Σ u·αΔT·L ; lack of fit: δ = Σ u·e ; unit couple gives rotations
  • Reciprocal theorems: Betti's theorem (work of system 1 acting through displacements of system 2 equals the reverse); Maxwell's reciprocal δ12 = δ21 — the deflection at 1 due to a unit load at 2 equals the deflection at 2 from a unit load at 1, so flexibility matrices are symmetric.
  • Clapeyron's three-moment equation for continuous beams:
    M_A·L1 + 2M_B(L1+L2) + M_C·L2 = −6(A1x̄1/L1 + A2x̄2/L2)
    UDL on both spans: M_A L1 + 2M_B(L1+L2) + M_C L2 = −(w1L1³ + w2L2³)/4
  • Portal-frame deflections: apply the unit load at the point of interest and integrate ∫mM/EI over every member; sway frames add a horizontal unit-load case.
4.4 must-knows: truss Ds = m + r − 2j; determinate ⇒ temperature/settlement/fabrication create NO stress; U axial = P²L/2AE, bending = ∫M²dx/2EI; Castigliano δ = ∂U/∂P; least work ∂U/∂R = 0; δ = ΣuPL/AE; Maxwell δ12 = δ21; three-moment UDL: MAL1 + 2MB(L1+L2) + MCL2 = −(w1L1³+w2L2³)/4.

4.5 Determinate Structures-2 (ACiE0405)

A. Influence Lines

  • Definition: the graph of a function (reaction, shear, moment, deflection) at a fixed section as a unit load moves across the structure.
  • Müller-Breslau principle: the influence line for a force/moment is the deflected shape of the structure when that constraint is released and given a unit displacement/rotation — qualitative IL construction.
  • Simple-beam IL shapes:
FunctionIL shape (unit load at x from A)Peak value
Reaction R_Atriangle from 1 at A to 0 at B1
Shear at Ctwo parallel lines: −a/L (left of C), +b/L (right)±a/L, b/L
Moment at Ctriangle peaking at Cab/L
  • Load effects:
    Point load W at a position: effect = W × IL ordinate under it
    UDL w over a length: effect = w × IL area covered by the load
    Train of loads: ΣWᵢ·yᵢ ; max moment under a wheel when the section and the wheel satisfy the equal-average-loads criterion
  • UDL of length l < L: place it where the IL has maximum area — for midspan moment, centre the load: M = w·l(2L − l)/8, reducing to wL²/8 when l = L.
  • ILs for cantilevers are straight; for continuous beams and arches they are curved (Müller-Breslau deflected shapes).
Fig 4.9 — Influence lines of a simple beam: reaction is a 1→0 triangle; moment at C peaks at ab/L under C.

B. Two-Hinged Arches

Horizontal thrust: H = ∫(M·y/EI)dx / ∫(y²/EI)dx (M = simple-beam moment at the section, y = rise)
Parabolic arch, UDL over the full span: H = wL²/(8h) — the parabola is the funicular shape, so bending is zero everywhere
At a section θ: normal thrust N = V·sinθ + H·cosθ ; radial shear R = V·cosθ − H·sinθ (V = simple-beam shear)
  • Arch types: three-hinged (statically determinate; immune to temperature and settlement), two-hinged (1× indeterminate; common in steel arch bridges), fixed (3× indeterminate; stiffest, temperature stresses).
  • Parabolic arch with full UDL: pure compression — zero bending moment everywhere; partial loads introduce bending.
  • Temperature rise in a two-hinged arch: H = E·α·ΔT·L·I/∫y²dx (uniform I) — the thrust develops and the arch rises. Two-hinged arches do carry temperature thrust; three-hinged arches do not.
  • Rib shortening reduces H; it is neglected in a first analysis. Both effects matter only for two-hinged and fixed arches — a three-hinged arch is immune (determinate).
  • Line of thrust (pressure line): the locus of the resultant compression; when it coincides with the arch axis there is no bending (funicular polygon).
  • Eddy's theorem: bending moment at a section = H × (ordinate between the arch axis and the pressure line).
Fig 4.10 — Two-hinged arches: (1) parabolic arch under full-span UDL — H = wL²/(8h), funicular so M = 0 everywhere, y = 4h·x(L−x)/L²; (2) section at θ — normal thrust N = V·sinθ + H·cosθ, radial shear R = V·cosθ − H·sinθ (V = simple-beam shear); (3) line of thrust & Eddy's theorem — M = H × ordinate between arch axis and pressure line; (4) arch types — three-hinged determinate (immune to temp/settlement), two-hinged 1° indeterminate, fixed 3° — with temperature thrust H = E·α·ΔT·L·I/∫y²dx (rib shortening reduces H; both effects only for two-hinged & fixed arches)
4.5 must-knows: IL = effect at a fixed section from a moving unit load; Müller-Breslau = remove the constraint and deflect it; point load × ordinate, UDL × area; midspan-moment UDL of length l: w·l(2L−l)/8; parabolic arch full UDL: H = wL²/8h, no bending anywhere; two-hinged arch carries temperature thrust, three-hinged does not; Eddy: M = H × ordinate between axis and pressure line.

4.6 Indeterminate Structures (ACiE0406)

A. Flexibility (Force) Method

  • Concept: release the redundants to get a primary determinate structure, then enforce compatibility of displacements through flexibility coefficients (f = displacement due to a unit force).
    • [f]{R} = −{Δ0} (matrix form) ; f11 = displacement due to unit R1 ; f12 = f21 (Maxwell)
  • Examples: fixed beam (release the end moments), two-hinged arch (release H), propped cantilever (release the prop), continuous beams (three-moment is a flexibility method in disguise).
  • Suits structures with few redundants; the column-analogy method handles fixed arches/frames.
Fig 4.11 — Determinacy & energy methods: (1) counting Ds — truss Ds = m + r − 2j (frame Ds = 3m + r − 3j − releases = Dse + Dsi, closed loop adds 3), Dk = 2j − r; (2) beams Ds = r − 3, and the critical forms — parallel or concurrent reactions → unstable; (3) strain energy U = P²L/2AE, ∫M²dx/2EI, T²L/2GJ with Castigliano δ = ∂U/∂P and unit-load virtual work δ = ∫mM/EI dx (truss ΣuSL/AE, temperature Σu·αΔT·L, lack of fit Σu·e); (4) Maxwell δ12 = δ21 / Betti reciprocity and the three-moment equation

B. Slope Deflection Method

Fixed-end moments: UDL wL²/12 (both ends) ; central point load WL/8
Member-end moment: M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θA + θB − 3ψ) + FEM_AB (ψ = chord rotation, clockwise +)
Equilibrium: ΣM at each joint = 0 ; sway frames: Σ horizontal forces = 0
  • Classical displacement method — the unknowns are joint rotations θ and translations (sway) ψ; it suits frames with few kinematic unknowns and is the parent of the stiffness method.
  • FEM values to memorize: UDL wL²/12 both ends; central point load WL/8; point load W at a from A: −Wab²/L² at A and +Wa²b/L² at B (each end carries the square of the distance to the OTHER end); triangular load 0 at A → w at B: −wL²/30 at A, +wL²/20 at B; symmetric triangular load (peak w at midspan): ±5wL²/96; support settlement δ: 6EIδ/L² at both ends.
  • No distribution factors are needed — simultaneous equations solve it directly.

C. Moment Distribution (Hardy Cross, 1930)

Relative stiffness: far end fixed k = 4EI/L ; far end pinned k = 3EI/L
Distribution factor DF = k/Σk at the joint
Carry-over factor: 1/2 to a fixed far end ; 0 to a pinned far end
Procedure: lock all joints → FEMs → release each joint (distribute the unbalanced moment by DF) → carry over ½ → repeat until negligible → sum
  • No-sway frames follow the standard cycle; sway frames add a unit-sway analysis (FEMs of the 6EIΔ/L² pattern) scaled to cancel the out-of-balance horizontal force. Column shears come from (M_AB + M_BA)/h.
  • Advantages: iterative, no simultaneous equations. For shear walls and very large frames the computer stiffness method wins.
  • Symmetry tricks: symmetric loading → use modified stiffness 2EI/L at the axis (joint rotation zero); antisymmetric → 6EI/L.
  • Taller columns attract less moment (translational stiffness 12EI/h³). Kani's method is an alternative iterative rotation-contribution scheme (name recognition).

D. Stiffness (Displacement) Method — Matrix

[K]{D} = {F} ; truss member element: k = AE/L [1 −1; −1 1]
Beam element (4 DOF): the standard 12-6L/6L-4L² matrix in EI/L³ units
Reactions recovered from K·D after solving
  • The stiffness method suits computers (direct stiffness assembly); its unknowns are displacements — the opposite philosophy to the force method (unknowns = forces). DOF count: 3 per rigid joint minus restraints; 2 per truss joint.
  • Member stiffness: axial AE/L; translational 12EI/L³; rotational 4EI/L and 2EI/L; the carry-over ½ reflects the 2EI/L term.

E. Influence Lines for Continuous Beams

  • Curved ILs from Müller-Breslau (release the constraint, impose unit displacement); span moments are positive under loads in that span and negative elsewhere.
  • Worst position of train loads on continuous beams is found by trial (shift the train and watch the IL slope) — qualitative understanding is enough for one-mark questions.

F. Elementary Plastic Analysis

Plastic moment Mp = σy·Zp ; shape factor = Mp/My = Zp/Z — rectangle 1.5, I-section ≈ 1.12, circle 1.7, diamond 2.0
Collapse by virtual work: external work P·δ = internal work ΣMp·θ
Hinges to form a mechanism: Ds + 1 (Ds = static indeterminacy)
Collapse loads — SS beam UDL: w = 8Mp/L² ; fixed beam UDL: w = 16Mp/L² (hinges at both ends + midspan)
SS central point load: P = 4Mp/L ; fixed central: P = 8Mp/L
Propped cantilever UDL: w = 11.66Mp/L² (hinges at the fixed end and at (√2−1)L ≈ 0.414L from the prop, i.e. (2−√2)L ≈ 0.586L from the fixed end)
  • Plastic hinge: a zone of rotation at the full plastic moment; the structure becomes a mechanism when Ds + 1 hinges form.
  • Theorems: upper bound (kinematic — every mechanism gives a collapse load ≥ true), lower bound (static — every equilibrium moment field with M ≤ Mp gives ≤ true), uniqueness (when both hold).
  • Shape-factor order: I-section (≈1.1) < rectangle 1.5 < circle 1.7 < diamond 2.0 — I-sections use material most efficiently.
  • Load factor = collapse load / working load (≈ 1.7–1.75 steel; 1.5–2.0 RCC per codes). Plastic design requires compact sections (buckling check first).
4.6 must-knows: flexibility = force unknowns + compatibility; slope-deflection MAB = (2EI/L)(2θA+θB−3ψ) + FEM; FEMs: UDL wL²/12, central load WL/8, settlement 6EIδ/L²; moment distribution: DF = k/Σk, carry-over ½ (fixed) / 0 (pinned), far pinned k = 3EI/L; sway frames add unit-sway case; stiffness method suits computers; hinges to collapse = Ds + 1; shape factor rectangle 1.5, I ≈ 1.12; collapse: fixed UDL 16Mp/L², SS 8Mp/L²; upper bound ≥ true ≥ lower bound.

Numerical Traps Checklist (Chapter 4)

  • Deflection formula swaps: WL³/48 (SS central) vs WL³/192 (fixed central) — factor 4; 5wL⁴/384 (SS UDL) vs wL⁴/384 (fixed UDL) — factor 5; cantilever end load WL³/3. Write the support type first.
  • Euler Le: fixed–fixed gives Pcr = 4π²EI/L² — don't simplify (0.5L)² twice.
  • λ uses k_min: rectangle k_min = d/√12 about the minor axis — never the major-axis value.
  • Units in P = 2πNT/60: T in N·m gives watts; use T = 9550·P(kW)/N when kW is given.
  • τ = VQ/Ib: Q is the first moment of the area on ONE side of the fibre; b is the LOCAL width — the flange–web jump is the classic error.
  • Principal angle: tan2θp gives 2θ — halve it; the two solutions are 90° apart; choose the one aligning with the larger normal stress for σ1.
  • Sudden vs impact: sudden (h = 0) doubles the stress; a drop h gives 1 + √(1+2h/δst) — read the wording.
  • Shape factor ≠ load factor: shape factor is a section property (Zp/Z); load factor is the design multiplier.
  • IL ordinate vs area: ordinate × point load; AREA × UDL — IL ordinates carry units of length for moments and are dimensionless for reactions/shear.
  • Parabolic arch thrust: H = wL²/8h uses the crown rise h — don't plug a quarter-point rise.
  • Thin cylinder shear: in-plane τmax = pr/4t but ABSOLUTE τmax = pr/2t (σ3 = 0 out of plane) — read which is asked.

Worked Diagram Walkthroughs (narrated for exam intuition)

Walkthrough A — Overhanging beam

Beam ABC: supports at A and B (span 6 m), overhang BC = 2 m, UDL 10 kN/m everywhere. Moments about A: the total load 80 kN acts at 4 m, so R_B = 10×8×4/6 = 53.33 kN and R_A = 26.67 kN. The shear starts at +26.67, falls 10 kN per metre and crosses zero at 2.67 m; the hogging moment at B is −10×2²/2 = −20 kN·m; the maximum sagging moment (at the zero-shear point) is 26.67×2.67 − 10×2.67²/2 = 35.6 kN·m. Two moment extrema and one contraflexure between them — the exact exam-style reasoning.

Walkthrough B — Two-span continuous beam (three-moment)

Spans AB = BC = 6 m, UDL 10 kN/m, simple ends. Three-moment: 0 + 2M_B(12) + 0 = −(10×216 + 10×216)/4 = −1080 → M_B = −wL²/8 = −45 kN·m (hogging). End shear: R_A = R_C = wL/2 − |M_B|/L = 30 − 7.5 = 22.5 kN; R_B = 120 − 45 = 75 kN. Maximum span moment 0.0703wL² = 25.3 kN·m at x = 3L/8 from each end — sagging in both spans, hogging at B.

Walkthrough C — Moment distribution on a 2-span joint (no sway)

Joint B with BA (6 m, far end pinned) and BC (6 m, far end fixed): k_BA = 3EI/6, k_BC = 4EI/6 → DF_BA = 3/7, DF_BC = 4/7. FEMs: BA carries −wL²/8 (pinned-end beam, full UDL), BC carries ±wL²/12. Balance, carry over to C only — a three-line calculation.

Walkthrough D — Virtual work on a frame

Horizontal deflection of a portal knee: apply a unit horizontal load at the knee, draw the m-diagram on every member, then integrate mM/EI with the real M from the loads. Columns usually dominate (large M over the full height); beams add little for lateral load — that is where the flexibility lives.

Extended High-Yield Additions (Exam-Focused Extras)

Shear stress distribution in beams

τ = VQ/(Ib) (Q = first moment of the area on one side of the level, about the NA; b = width at that level)
Rectangle: τmax = 1.5·τavg (parabolic) ; Circle: τmax = (4/3)·τavg ; I-section: the web carries most of the shear
  • At the neutral axis of a rectangular beam τ = 3V/2A; the flange–web junction shows a sudden jump because b changes.
  • Shear centre: the point through which a transverse load must pass to produce bending without twist. For channels it lies outside the web; for equal-leg angles at the corner intersection; for a T-section on the web axis; for doubly symmetric sections it coincides with the centroid.

Fixed beams & intermediate results

  • Fixed beam UDL: M_support = wL²/12, M_mid = wL²/24; contraflexure at 0.211L from the ends.
  • Fixed beam central load: M_sup = M_mid = WL/8; contraflexure at L/4 from the ends.
  • Sinking of one support by δ: end moments ±6EIδ/L².
  • Axial temperature rise with both ends fixed: axial force = αΔT·EA.
  • Propped cantilever with the prop sinking δ: R_prop = 3wL/8 − 3EIδ/L³ (a sinking prop sheds load — the sign matters).

Trusses

  • Methods: method of joints (two equations per joint), method of sections (three equations — cut no more than three unknown members), graphical Maxwell–Cremona.
    • Fig 4.12 — Truss analysis: method of joints, method of sections (≤3 cut members) and zero-force members (marked ⭘)
  • Zero-force members: two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint are both zero; at a three-member joint with two collinear, the third is zero — spotting them saves work.
  • Truss families: Pratt (tension diagonals toward centre), Howe (compression diagonals), Warren (equilateral), K-truss, Fink, bowstring; a perfect truss has m = 2j − 3 (with r = 3).
  • Truss deflection by unit load: δ = ΣSuL/AE.
  • Assumptions: pin joints, loads at joints only, members two-force (axial). Deviations cause secondary (bending) stresses.

Worked numericals (MCQ style)

  • SS 6 m, central 20 kN: R = 10 kN each, M = 30 kN·m; δ = 20×6³/(48×2×10⁵×10⁶·I).
  • SS 8 m UDL 10 kN/m: V = 40 kN, M = 80 kN·m; fixed version: M_sup = wL²/12 = 53.3, M_mid = wL²/24 = 26.7 kN·m.
  • Rectangular beam 200×400: Z = 5.33×10⁶ mm³; M at σ = 20 MPa: 106.7 kN·m; τmax = 1.5V/A.
  • Bar 20 mm dia, 2 m, P = 100 kN: σ = 318 MPa; δ = 3.18 mm; U = Pδ/2 = 159 J.
  • Steel bar fixed both ends, ΔT = 30 °C: σ = 12×10⁻⁶×30×2×10⁵ = 72 MPa (compression).
  • Shaft: 50 kW at 200 rpm: T = 2387 N·m; solid d for τ = 60 MPa: d³ = 16T/πτ → d ≈ 58.8 mm.
  • Euler: 3 m pinned column, I = 2×10⁶ mm⁴: Pcr = π²×2×10⁵×2×10⁶/9×10⁶ = 438.6 kN; with A = 4×10³ mm², k = 22.4 mm → λ = 134 (long).
  • Two-hinged parabolic arch L = 30, h = 6, UDL 20: H = wL²/8h = 375 kN; at the crown the force is pure horizontal thrust, bending zero (funicular).
  • Plastic: SS 6 m UDL with Mp = 100 kN·m: w = 8×100/36 = 22.2 kN/m; fixed: 44.4 kN/m (collapse load doubles).
  • Two-span continuous beam, equal spans UDL: M_B = −wL²/8; end moments zero — the three-moment equation gives the same result directly.
  • Castigliano on a truss: δ = ΣS(∂S/∂P)L/AE — the standard three-member example.

Rapid-Fire One-Liners (Last-Minute Revision)

  • w = dV/dx, V = dM/dx; zero shear = max/min M; contraflexure = M changes sign.
  • SS UDL wL²/8; central W: WL/4; cantilever UDL wL²/2; fixed UDL wL²/12 (support), wL²/24 (span).
  • Propped cantilever UDL: prop 3wL/8, fixed M wL²/8, max span 9wL²/128.
  • Superposition: linear elastic only.
  • E = 9KG/(3K+G); G = E/2(1+μ); μ: steel 0.3, cork 0, rubber 0.5.
  • Principal planes: zero shear; τmax = (σ1−σ3)/2 at 45°; Mohr radius = τmax.
  • Failure theories: Rankine (brittle), Tresca (ductile), von Mises (best for ductile).
  • Torsion: T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L; J = πd⁴/32; τmax = 16T/πd³; P = 2πNT/60.
  • Non-circular shafts warp — St. Venant; equivalent Me = ½(M+√(M²+T²)), Te = √(M²+T²).
  • Flexure: M/I = σ/y = E/R; NA through centroid; Z = I/y_max.
  • Deflections: WL³/48 (SS central), 5wL⁴/384 (SS UDL), WL³/3 (cant end), wL⁴/8 (cant UDL), wL⁴/384 (fixed UDL).
  • Moment-area: slope change = M/EI area; deviation = its moment about the point.
  • Conjugate beam: M/EI as load; shear→slope, moment→deflection; fixed↔free swap.
  • Euler: Pcr = π²EI/Le²; Le = L, 0.5L, 2L, 0.7L; valid for long columns; Rankine 1/P = 1/Pc + 1/Pe.
  • Truss determinacy: m + r = 2j; perfect truss m = 2j − 3 (r = 3).
  • Determinate structures: no temperature/settlement stress; forces independent of material.
  • Castigliano δ = ∂U/∂P; virtual work δ = ∫mM/EI dx (beams), ΣSuL/AE (trusses); Maxwell f12 = f21.
  • Three-moment: M_A·L1 + 2M_B(L1+L2) + M_C·L2 = −6(A₁x̄₁/L1 + A2x̄2/L2), where A is the area of each span's free bending-moment diagram and x̄ the distance of its centroid from the end nearer the joint; for UDL it reduces to −(w1L1³ + w2L2³)/4.
  • IL = effect per unit moving load; Müller-Breslau = deflected shape with the constraint released; use area × w, ordinate × W.
  • Two-hinged arch H = ∫My/EI ÷ ∫y²/EI; parabola + full UDL: H = wL²/8h, zero bending.
  • Three-hinged: determinate, settlement- and temperature-immune; two-hinged: 1× indeterminate; fixed: 3×.
  • Eddy's theorem: M = H × offset between pressure line and arch axis.
  • Slope-deflection: M_AB = 2EI/L(2θA + θB − 3ψ) + FEM; FEM UDL = wL²/12; settlement 6EIδ/L².
  • Moment distribution: DF = k/Σk; COF ½ (fixed far end), 0 (pinned); k = 4EI/L or 3EI/L.
  • Stiffness method: [K]{D} = {F}; suits computers; DOK = kinematic unknowns.
  • Plastic: Mp = σyZp; shape factor rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, I ≈ 1.12; SS UDL collapse 8Mp/L², fixed 16Mp/L²; SS central 4Mp/L, fixed 8Mp/L.
  • Upper bound ≥ true ≥ lower bound; uniqueness when both met.
  • τ = VQ/Ib; rectangle τmax = 1.5τavg; circle 4/3; I-section web carries the shear; shear centre stops twist.
  • Suddenly applied load doubles stress; impact factor 1+√(1+2h/δst); resilience σ²/2E; axial U = P²L/2AE.
  • Hoop stress = 2 × longitudinal (cylinder); both pr/2t (sphere).
  • Moment distribution — Hardy Cross (1930); slope-deflection — Bendixen (1914).
  • Euler critical stress π²E/λ² — independent of yield strength.
  • Cable sag d, UDL w: H = wL²/8d — the arch-thrust formula mirrored in tension; catenary = self-weight, parabola = UDL/span.
  • Supports: roller 1 reaction, hinge 2, fixed 3; Ds = r − 3 for beams.

Deeper Concept Discussions (why the formulas work — helps you guess right)

Why bending stress is zero at NA and maximum at the extreme fibre

  • Plane sections stay plane → strain varies linearly with y → stress = Eε is linear → zero at the NA, maximum at the extreme fibre. Above the NA the material compresses; below it stretches (sagging).
  • The NA sits at the centroid because the net axial force must vanish (∫σ dA = 0) for pure bending of a linear-elastic section.
  • Moment of resistance = σ_max × Z; the I-section places area far from the NA — that is why rolled joists beat rectangles.
  • Unsymmetric bending: load off the principal axis → inclined neutral axis; resolve: σ = Mu·yu/Iu + Mv·yv/Iv. Channel purlins: load through the centroid but not the shear centre → twist plus unsymmetric bending (an NEC favourite).

Why zero shear locates the maximum moment

  • dM/dx = V, so a local moment extremum needs V = 0. In overhanging and continuous beams, find where the SF diagram crosses zero — the max hogging/sagging sits there.
  • Two zero-shear crossings (trapezoidal SF) → one local max and one local min — compute both.
  • The area under the SF diagram between two points = the change in M — quick diagram construction.

Energy viewpoint (the unifying idea)

  • Virtual work, Castigliano and unit-load methods all express compatibility through strain energy U.
  • Clapeyron: U = ½ΣPδ for linear systems.
  • Reciprocity: symmetric flexibility and stiffness matrices (Maxwell–Betti).
  • Virtual work logic: an equilibrium force set × a compatible displacement set → external work = internal work; a unit virtual force reads the displacement directly.
  • Least work: among admissible redundants, nature picks the set that minimizes U — the force method's foundation.

Deeper: influence-line numerics

  • SS beam, UDL 10 kN/m over 4 m on a 10 m span, moment at midspan: the IL is a triangle peaking at L/4 = 2.5 m; ordinates at ±2 m from midspan: 1.5 m; the covered area is a trapezoid: ½(2.5+1.5)×2 ×2 = 8 m² → M = 80 kN·m. Statics check: resultant 2 m left of centre, R_A = 20 kN → M = 80 kN·m ✓.
  • Wheel trains: shift the train 1 m and recompute — the IL slope's sign tells whether the effect grows; the "criterion of the maximum" formalizes this.
  • Absolute maximum BM in an SS beam under a train: near midspan, under the heaviest wheel, with midspan bisecting the distance between that wheel and the train's centre of gravity.

Deeper: fixed-end moments table

Load caseFEM_ABFEM_BA
UDL w−wL²/12+wL²/12
Central point load W−WL/8+WL/8
Point load W at a from A−Wab²/L²+Wa²b/L²
Triangular load (0 at A → w at B)−wL²/30+wL²/20
Symmetric triangular (peak w at midspan)−5wL²/96+5wL²/96
Moment M₀ at midspanM₀/4 at each end(both ends react the applied moment)
Support settlement δ (B below A)+6EIδ/L²+6EIδ/L²
  • Settlement FEM: 6EIδ/L² at both ends — a frequent MCQ value.
  • Sign conventions differ between textbooks; NEC follows clockwise-positive. Keep one convention per problem.

Deeper: sway frames in moment distribution

  • Procedure: (1) non-sway analysis with joints locked; (2) compute the out-of-balance horizontal force; (3) run a unit-sway analysis (FEMs of the 6EIΔ/L² pattern); (4) superpose the scaled sway solution to cancel that force.
  • Column shear from member end moments: V = (M_AB + M_BA)/h; the shear condition is Σ column shears = external load.

Deeper: plastic analysis extended

  • Mechanism types: beam, panel (sway), combined (joint) — check all, plus combinations; the lowest load factor governs (upper-bound minimization).
  • Plastic hinge length ≈ section depth; the moment–rotation idealization is elastic–perfectly plastic.
  • Reserve strength = shape factor × load factor; compact sections only (buckling first).

Deeper: columns — additional exam facts

  • Euler load is independent of σy — only E, I and Le matter; high-strength steel does not help long columns.
  • Secant formula: σmax = (P/A)[1 + (ec/k²)sec(Le/2k·√(P/EA))] — stress grows nonlinearly, no sharp bifurcation.
  • Rankine constant a = σc/π²E: steel ≈ 1/7500, wrought iron 1/9000, cast iron 1/1600, timber 1/750.
  • Laced built-up columns: lacing angle 40–70°; component slenderness ≤ 50 or 0.7× overall.

Deeper: strain energy & impact extended

  • Drop W from h: δmax = δst[1 + √(1+2h/δst)]; h = 0 → factor 2.
  • Same energy, stiffer structure → higher force: flexible barriers absorb impact better (concept MCQ).
  • Bending strain energy: SS central load U = W²L³/96EI; cantilever end load U = W²L³/6EI.

Deeper: trusses and cables

  • Funicular shapes carry load in pure axial force — parabola (UDL per horizontal span) and catenary (self-weight) in cables; the same geometry inverted works in compression as an arch.
  • Cable sag T = wL²/8d for UDL — the same form as arch thrust. Suspension bridges: cable carries load, the stiffening girder distributes it; the tower force is the vertical component of cable tension.

Deeper: stress transformation extras

  • In-plane vs absolute τmax: when σ1 and σ2 have the same sign, the absolute maximum uses the zero-stress third direction — thin cylinder: hoop pr/t, longitudinal pr/2t → absolute τmax = pr/2t (not pr/4t).
  • Hoop failure splits a cylinder longitudinally (hoop = 2 × longitudinal).
  • Strain rosettes (0–45–90 rectangular) convert measured strains to principal stresses.
  • Mohr's circle for pure shear is centred at the origin: principal stresses ±τ at 45° — chalk fractures at 45° in torsion (brittle, max principal stress) while mild steel in tension fails on the 45° max-shear planes (cup-and-cone).

More worked one-mark patterns

  • Fixed beam 6 m, UDL 10 kN/m: M_sup = 30 kN·m; M_mid = 15 kN·m; contraflexure at 1.27 m from each end.
  • SS 4 m, 15 kN at 1 m from A: R_A = 11.25, R_B = 3.75; M_max = 11.25 kN·m under the load.
  • Steel bar 20 mm dia, 2 m, 80 kN: σ = 254.6 MPa; δ = 2.55 mm; U = 102 J.
  • Compound bar (steel + aluminium, common strain): σa = σs·Ea/Es — aluminium carries less stress.
  • Hollow shaft D = 100, d = 60, τ = 50 MPa: T = τπ(D⁴−d⁴)/(16D) ≈ 8.54 kN·m.
  • Combined bending + torsion: Te = √(M²+T²), then d³ = 16Te/(πτ_allow).
  • Euler 4 m fixed–pinned, E = 200 GPa, I = 5×10⁶ mm⁴: Le = 0.7 × 4000 = 2800 mm; Pcr = π²×2×10⁵×5×10⁶/2800² = 1259 kN.
  • Propped cantilever UDL collapse: hinges at the fixed end and at (√2−1)L ≈ 0.414L from the prop, i.e. (2−√2)L ≈ 0.586L from the fixed end; w = 11.66Mp/L².

Final Rapid-Fire Additions

  • Fixed-end moment for settlement: 6EIδ/L² at both ends.
  • Unit-load method = Castigliano with a dummy load (Part I/II distinction).
  • Portal sway mechanism: P·h = 2Mp·θ type combos — the combined mechanism usually governs.
  • Stiffness-method DOF: 3 per rigid joint (2 translations + 1 rotation) minus restraints; 2 per truss joint.
  • Flexibility = force method (unknowns: forces); stiffness = displacement method (unknowns: displacements).
  • Geometric stability: reactions non-parallel and non-concurrent.
  • IL ordinate units: dimensionless for reaction/shear; length for moment.
  • IL for deflection at a point of an SS beam = the deflection curve itself (Maxwell) — peak at that point.

Section 4.1 Extended — More Diagram-Reading Rules

  • SF construction: start from the left reaction, step up/down at each concentrated load, slope −w under UDL; where SF crosses zero, the moment is extreme.
  • BM by parts: draw each load's diagram separately and add — fastest route for complex loading.
  • Equal overhangs a, span L: M_mid = wL²/8 − wa²/2; a = L/√8 ≈ 0.354L equalizes midspan and support moments; a = L/2 zeroes the midspan moment.
  • Triangular load (zero at A, peak w0 at B): R_A = w0L/6, R_B = w0L/3; M_max = w0L²/(9√3) ≈ 0.064w0L² at x = L/√3 from A.
  • Couple M₀ on an SS beam at x = a: reactions = M₀/L pair; the BM diagram jumps by M₀ at the point; the adjacent peaks are M₀a/L and M₀b/L.
  • Shape memory: w constant → V linear → M parabolic; w zero → V constant → M linear; w linear → V parabolic → M cubic.

Section 4.2 Extended — Miscellaneous Stress Facts

  • Bars in series vs parallel: series — same force, deflections add (compliance adds); parallel — same deflection, forces add (stiffness adds) — the pipe-circuit analogy of Ch 3.
  • Temperature with a gap: if free expansion exceeds the gap g: P = (αΔT·L − g)AE/L.
  • Self-weight vs end load: hanging bar δ = WL/2AE — half the end-load result for the same W.
  • Principal strains: ε1 = (σ1 − μσ2)/E etc.; max shear strain γmax = ε1 − ε2.
  • Cylinder under axial load: εv = εz(1−2μ).
  • Why sudden load doubles stress: the full load acts from zero deformation, so the external work W·δ equals the stored U = σ²V/2E with twice the gradual-load strain energy per unit stress.
  • Proof resilience = σy²/2E; modulus of toughness needs the plastic region (area to fracture).

Section 4.3 Extended — Bending Beyond Basics

  • Flanged sections: τ jumps at flange–web junctions; the web carries most of V, the flanges most of M — the division of labour between τ = VQ/Ib and σ = My/I.
  • Shear centre locations: equal-leg angle — corner; T-section — web axis; circle — centre; load through the shear centre → bending without twist.
  • Curved beams (Winkler–Bach): hyperbolic stress distribution (not linear); the NA shifts toward the centre of curvature — hooks and chain links.
  • Beams of uniform strength: Z varies with M — linearly tapered or parabolic profiles (leaf springs) keep the maximum stress constant.
  • Elastic-curve sketching: slope continuous at rigid joints; inflection at contraflexure; zero slope at fixed ends; zero deflection at supports; symmetry for symmetric load.
  • Macaulay's method: singularity brackets ⟨x−a⟩ keep one integration valid across discontinuities.

Section 4.4 Extended — Determinacy & Energy Extras

  • Kinematic indeterminacy (DOK): the unknown joint displacements. SS beam: 2 rotations (axial neglected); fixed beam: 0; basic portal frame: 3 (2 joint rotations + 1 sway).
  • Trade-off: the two counts are complementary — with all three DOF counted at each joint DOK = 3j − r, so Ds + DOK = 3m for a plane frame (= m for a plane truss): adding a redundancy removes a joint displacement.
  • Temperature deflection by virtual work: beams δ = ∫m(αΔT)dx (curvature from thermal gradient); trusses δ = Σu·αΔT·L (axial).
  • Lack of fit: determinate trusses — rigid-body movement only (no force); indeterminate — internal forces ∝ stiffness.
  • Rotation at a point: apply a unit couple and use the m-diagram.
  • Standard assumptions: axial and shear deformations neglected in Euler–Bernoulli analysis unless asked.

Section 4.5 Extended — Arch & IL Extras

  • Three-hinged arch thrust: H = M_c(simple beam)/rise; UDL: H = wL²/8h; central point load: H = WL/4h. For a semicircular three-hinged arch with central load W (h = R = L/2): H = W/2.
  • At a section θ: N = H cosθ + V sinθ (thrust), R = V cosθ − H sinθ (radial shear) — know the combination idea; sign conventions vary.
  • IL for two-hinged arch thrust is curved; Eddy's theorem enables graphic analysis once H is known.
  • Rib shortening lowers H; temperature raises it — second-order effects for two-hinged and fixed arches only.
  • Spandrel-braced / open-spandrel arches: the deck carries load to the arch through posts — terminology only.

Section 4.6 Extended — Method Selection Cheat Table

Propped cantileverForce method (compatibility at the prop)1
Fixed beam (both ends fixed)Force method / superposition formulas3

Portal frame with swayMoment distribution + sway correction / slope deflectionrotations + sway

  • Balancing a joint: distribute the unbalanced moment by DF with a sign reversal; carry over ½; 2–3 cycles suffice in exams.
  • Symmetry: symmetric load → modified stiffness 2EI/L at the axis; antisymmetric → 6EI/L — halves the work.
  • Kani's rotation-contribution method — alternative iterative scheme (name recognition).

Concept Cards (exam morning)

Card 1 — Beam internal forces

Load → shear → moment chain (w = dV/dx, V = dM/dx). Jumps at point loads/couples, extrema at zero shear, contraflexure at sign change. Values: wL²/8 (SS UDL), wL²/12 & wL²/24 (fixed), 9wL²/128 & wL²/8 (propped).

Card 2 — Stress states

Axial → biaxial transformation → principal stresses (zero shear) → max shear at 45° → Mohr circle → failure theories (Rankine brittle / Tresca–von Mises ductile) → torsion as pure shear (τmax = 16T/πd³) → vessels (hoop = 2 × longitudinal).

Card 3 — Flexure & columns

M/I = σ/y = E/R; NA at centroid; Z = I/y_max; the five standard deflections. Columns: Euler π²EI/Le² with Le = 1L/0.5L/2L/0.7L, λ = Le/k, Rankine for all ranges, Euler independent of strength.

Card 4 — Analysis methods

Determinacy (m+r = 2j trusses; r−3 beams) → energy (U = ∫M²/2EI; δ = ∂U/∂P; unit load) → ILs (Müller-Breslau) → arches (flexibility; parabola+UDL zero bending; Eddy) → indeterminate toolkits (three-moment, slope-deflection, moment distribution, stiffness matrix) → plastic (Mp = σyZp, mechanisms, bounds, shape factors).
