Interleaved Revision Quiz Points (self-check before exam)

  • Can you write the 6 standard M-values (SS/fixed × UDL/central load) without notes?
  • Can you state the 4 Euler effective lengths and Pcr multiples (1, 4, 0.25, 2)?
  • Can you recall the 5 standard deflection maxima (WL³/48, 5wL⁴/384, WL³/3, wL⁴/8, wL⁴/384)?
  • Can you write the principal-stress formula, τmax, and their planes?
  • Can you reproduce the FEM table (UDL wL²/12, PL/8) with carry-over ½ and DF = k/Σk?
  • Can you give plastic collapse loads: SS UDL 8Mp/L², fixed UDL 16Mp/L², SS central 4Mp/L, fixed central 8Mp/L?
  • Do you know why determinate structures have no thermal/settlement stresses (equilibrium suffices)?
  • Ductile vs brittle failure theory pairing (von Mises vs Rankine)?

Topic-wise MCQ Frequency Map (what NEC tends to ask)

  • Very frequent: SFD/BMD values (wL²/8, WL/4…), Euler loads & effective lengths, deflection formulas, plastic shape factors & collapse loads, determinacy counting, FEM values, Müller-Breslau statements, arch H for UDL, failure-theory pairing.
  • Frequent: principal stresses/τmax, Mohr radius, torsion power/shaft design, Castigliano/unit-load identification, shear-stress ratios (1.5, 4/3), reciprocal theorems, contraflexure locations, SS-beam IL constructions.
  • Occasional: conjugate-beam support swaps, Kani, Winkler–Bach, shear-centre locations, secant formula, strain rosettes, catenary vs parabola.

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (4.1–4.6)

Elastic Constants & Stress-Strain (4.2) — Course Values

  • Poisson's ratio μ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain (within the elastic limit); theoretical limits −1 to 0.5, practical 0 to 0.5. Course values: cork 0.0, glass 0.18–0.30, steel 0.25–0.33, concrete 0.10–0.20, copper 0.33, rubber 0.5. In the plastic range μ ≈ 0.5 (volume constant).
  • Relations: G = E/2(1+μ); K = E/3(1−2μ); E = 9KG/(3K+G) = 2G(1+μ) = 3K(1−2μ); μ = (3K−2G)/(6K+2G).
  • Independent elastic constants: isotropic 2 (steel, aluminium, copper, gold); orthotropic (wood, plywood) 9; anisotropic 21.
  • Mild-steel tensile curve: limit of proportionality → elastic limit → upper yield → lower yield (yield stress initiates plastic flow) → ultimate stress → necking → breaking stress. Hooke's law holds up to the limit of proportionality; a "more elastic" material has a higher E (steel > rubber).
  • Sudden load: σ = 2W/A (double the gradual); U = σ²V/2E; proof resilience at the elastic limit; modulus of resilience = σ²/2E per unit volume.
  • Vertical bar under its own weight: δ = WL/2AE.

Shear Stress, Bending & Torsion — Course Formulas

  • Bending: σ = My/I; M/I = σ/y = E/R. Shear: τ = VQ/(Ib); rectangular τmax = 1.5V/A at the NA; circular 4V/3A; parabolic distribution.
  • Torsion: T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L; J = πD⁴/32 (solid), π(D⁴−d⁴)/32 (hollow); τmax = 16T/πD³.
  • Load–SFD–BMD shapes: point load → SFD constant, BMD linear; UDL → SFD linear, BMD parabolic; UVL → SFD parabolic, BMD cubic. Zero-BM point = point of contraflexure.

Deflection Formulas (Moment-Area table from the capsule)

CaseMax BMSlope θDeflection δ
Cantilever, moment M at free endMML/EIML²/2EI
Cantilever, point load W at free endWLWL²/2EIWL³/3EI
Cantilever, UDL wwL²/2wL³/6EIwL⁴/8EI
Cantilever, UVL (zero at free end)wL²/6wL³/24EIwL⁴/30EI
SS beam, central load WWL/4—WL³/48EI
SS beam, UDL wwL²/8wL³/24EI (end)5wL⁴/384EI

Euler buckling: Pcr = π²EI/Le² with Le = 0.5L (both fixed), 0.7L (fixed–pinned), L (both pinned), 2L (fixed–free). Slenderness ratio = Le/r with r = √(I/A); long columns fail by buckling, short by crushing.

Principal Stresses & Mohr's Circle — Course Formulas

  • σ1,2 = (σx+σy)/2 ± √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²]; τmax = (σ1−σ2)/2 = circle radius; tan2θp = 2τxy/(σx−σy); principal planes carry zero shear; planes of max shear sit at 45° to them.
  • Transformation: σx′ = (σx+σy)/2 + (σx−σy)/2·cos2θ + τxy·sin2θ; τx′y′ = −(σx−σy)/2·sin2θ + τxy·cos2θ.

Determinacy & Energy Methods (4.4) — Course Formulas

  • Ds = Dse + Dsi. Plane frame: Ds = 3m + r − 3j − a (a = released, m′−1); Dse = r − 3; Dsi = 3 × loops. Space frame: Ds = 6m + r − 6j − a, Dse = r − 6. Plane truss: Ds = m + r − 2j; Dk = 2j − r. Space truss: Ds = m + r − 3j; Dk = 3j − r. Beams (axial neglected): Dk = 2j − r.
  • Strain energy: U = ∫P²dx/2EA, ∫M²dx/2EI, ∫T²dx/2GJ, ∫kV²dx/2AG (k = 1.2 rectangle, 10/9 circle).
  • Unit-load deflection: Δ = Σ∫(Mm/EI)dx (beams), ΣPuL/AE (trusses). Castigliano: δ = ∂U/∂P at the load point.

Influence Lines & Arches (4.5–4.6) — Course Facts

  • ILD use: point-load effect = load × ILD ordinate under it; UDL effect = intensity × ILD area covered.
  • Three-hinged parabolic arch: y = 4h·x(l−x)/l²; H = wl²/8h (full UDL); point load P: H = M_c/h = P·min(a,b)/(2h), i.e. Pa/(2h) for a ≤ l/2 (central P: H = Pl/4h). Radial shear Q = V cosθ − H sinθ; normal thrust N = V sinθ + H cosθ.
  • Supports at different levels (equal-tension parabolic cables/arches): l₁/√h₁ = l₂/√h₂; l₂ = L√h₂/(√h₁+√h₂).
  • Two-hinged arch: indeterminate to degree 1 (H is the redundant); temperature rise increases the thrust.
  • Indeterminate analysis: flexibility (force) method for low indeterminacy; slope-deflection (unknowns = joint rotations/displacements, modified for sway); moment distribution (COF = 0.5 prismatic; FEMs wL²/12 UDL, PL/8 central load); stiffness (displacement) method for high indeterminacy (matrix).
  • Plastic analysis: shape factors — rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, I-section ≈ 1.12–1.15; propped cantilever UDL: Mp = 0.0858wL² (w = 11.655Mp/L²); fixed beam UDL: Mp = wL²/16; fixed central point load: Mp = PL/8. Load factor = collapse ÷ working load (≥ 1.75 steel; 1.5–2.0 RCC).
  • ILD for continuous beams (Müller-Breslau): the ILD of any reaction/internal force is the deflected shape with that constraint removed and a unit displacement applied.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): Poisson's ratio limits (−1 to 0.5) vs practical (0–0.5); "more elastic" = higher E (steel), not stretchier rubber; upper vs lower yield point; shape factor rectangle 1.5 vs circle 1.7; fixed-beam plastic moments (wL²/16 UDL vs PL/8 point load) — the classic one-mark swaps.

Chapter 5: Design of Structures (ACiE05)

NEC License Exam — High-Yield Notes (v5.5 edition)

Chapter 5: Design of Structures (ACiE05)

NEC License Exam (1-Mark MCQ Focus) | NEC prep-course edition — v5.5

This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

5.1 Loads and Load Combinations (ACiE0501)

A. Dead Loads (IS 875 Part-1 / NBC 102)

  • Dead loads are permanent, constant and position-fixed: self-weight of the structure, finishes, walls and fixed equipment.
  • Unit weights (IS 875-1): RCC 25 kN/m³, PCC 24, brick masonry 19–20 (commonly 19.2), stone masonry 20.4–26.5, steel 77–78.5 (design value 7850 kg/m³ ≈ 77 kN/m³), timber 5–8, cement plaster ≈ 20 kN/m³ (12 mm ≈ 0.24 kN/m² per side).
  • Slab dead load = thickness × 25; floor finish ≈ 1–1.5 kN/m²; brick wall load per metre run = thickness(m) × height × 19.2 + plaster.

B. Imposed (Live) Loads (IS 875 Part-2 / NBC 103)

OccupancyLive load (kN/m²)
Residential rooms2.0
Offices2.5–3.0 (with partition allowance)
Classrooms, reading rooms3.0
Assembly halls, cinemas (fixed seats)4.0 (movable seats 5.0)
Stairs, corridors, balconies3.0–5.0
Warehouses/storage5.0–7.5 (heavy storage 10)
Roofs (access provided / not)1.5 / 0.75
  • Live load may be reduced for large supported floor areas and for multi-storey columns (probability of simultaneous full loading is low) — never for storage or assembly occupancies.
  • Live load is movable and variable; moving loads (lifts, machines) carry an impact/dynamic allowance.
  • Roof imposed-load reduction: for slopes above 10°, reduce by 0.02 kN/m² per degree of slope, but never below 0.4 kN/m².

C. Wind Load (IS 875 Part-3 / NBC 104)

Fig 5.1 — Wind on a building: windward face takes pressure (+Cpe), leeward face and both roof slopes take suction (−Cpe), and openings set the internal pressure Cpi = ±0.2 (±0.7 with large openings); net force F = (Cpe − Cpi)·A·pz with pz = 0.6·Vz²
Design wind speed: Vz = Vb·k1·k2·k3·k4
Vb = basic wind speed (Nepal: 47 m/s below 3000 m altitude, 55 m/s above — 3-sec gust, 50-yr return; Kathmandu ≈ 39–47 m/s band in older maps)
k1 = risk/importance factor; k2 = terrain/height factor; k3 = topography factor; k4 = importance for cyclonic regions (1.0 inland)
Design wind pressure: pz = 0.6 Vz² (N/m², Vz in m/s)
Force: F = (Cpe − Cpi)·A·pz (external minus internal pressure coefficient)
  • Wind pressure acts perpendicular to surfaces; the leeward face and roof see suction (negative coefficients); internal pressure Cpi = ±0.2 (large openings ±0.7).
  • Terrain categories 1–4: open sea/flat ground (1) to dense city (4); k2 grows with height and shrinks with surface roughness.
  • Flexible (tall/slender) structures need dynamic-response checks (along-wind, cross-wind).
  • Light roofs (GI sheet) are governed by uplift — design the anchorage for suction reversal.

D. Snow Load (IS 875 Part-4 / NBC 106)

  • Relevant only in Nepal's high hills. Design load S = μ·So (roof shape coefficient × ground snow load); snow density ranges ≈ 0.5–2.5 kN/m³ by zone.
  • The load reduces as the roof steepens; roofs steeper than 60° (course value; some older references say 50°) shed snow and need no snow load.
  • Ice loads matter on cables and overhead lines in cold regions; snow load is treated as a transient (imposed-type) load.

E. Earthquake Load (IS 1893 / NBC 105)

Fig 5.2 — Equivalent static method: base shear VB = Ah·W is distributed as storey forces Qi ∝ Wi·hi (largest at the roof); the dashed line is the deflected shape. Dashed profile exaggerates the drift used in the lateral-displacement check.
Seismic base shear: VB = Ah·W
Ah = (Z/2)·(I/R)·(Sa/g) (IS 1893); NBC 105:2020: C(T) = Ch(T)·Z·I (spectral shape Ch(T) by soil type, Z = PGA for the 475-yr return, I = importance), divided by R
Z = zone factor (IS: II 0.10, III 0.16, IV 0.24, V 0.36; NBC 105:2020 Z = PGA, ≈ 0.25/0.35/0.40 by zone, Kathmandu ≈ 0.35)
I = importance factor — IS 1893:2016 Table 8: 1.0 all other buildings, 1.2 residential/commercial occupied by more than 200 persons, 1.5 important service/community buildings (schools, hospitals, emergency, warehouses, large assembly halls); NBC 105:2020 Table 4-4: 1.0 ordinary, 1.25 schools/colleges/cinemas/assembly and other Class-II structures, 1.5 essential (hospitals, fire stations, power stations)
R = response reduction factor: RC OMRF 3, ductile shear wall 4, RC SMRF 5, steel SMRF 5 (IS 1893:2016 Table 9 — steel ordinary MRF 3, special concentrically-braced frame 4.5; NBC 105:2020 Table 5-2 takes R = 4 for both steel and RC moment frames and 3 for RC shear walls)
Sa/g from the response spectrum vs fundamental period (Ta = 0.075 h^0.75 for RC moment frames)
  • Nepal seismicity: the whole country is zoned; NBC 105:2020 gives Z ≈ 0.25/0.35/0.40 by zone (Kathmandu ≈ 0.35). Soil classes A (stiff/hard) to D (very soft) amplify the spectrum for soft soils.
  • Historical earthquakes: 1934 Nepal–Bihar (M 8.0), 1988 Udayapur (M 6.6), 2015 Gorkha (M 7.8).
  • Seismic weight W: full dead load above the level + the appropriate live-load fraction — IS 1893:2016 Table 10: 25% where the imposed load is ≤ 3 kN/m², 50% where it is above; NBC 105:2020 Table 5-1: 30% for other purposes, 60% for storage, nil for roofs.
  • Load combinations (limit state, IS 1893-5 / NBC):
    • 1.5 (DL + LL)
    • 1.2 (DL + LL + EL)
    • 1.5 (DL + EL)
    • 0.9 DL + 1.5 EL (stability/uplift)
  • The earthquake force acts in any horizontal direction; watch for soft storeys and mass irregularity; ductile detailing per IS 13920 / NBC 105.
5.1 must-knows: RCC 25, brick masonry 19.2, steel 78.5 kN/m³; live load: residential 2, office 2.5–3, stairs 3–5, roofs 1.5/0.75; roof reduction 0.02 kN/m²/° above 10°, floor 0.4; Vz = Vb·k1k2k3k4, pz = 0.6Vz²; Nepal Vb 47 m/s (55 above 3000 m); snow: none steeper than 60°; VB = Ah·W, Ah = (Z/2)(I/R)(Sa/g); Nepal Z ≈ 0.25/0.35/0.40; I = 1.0/1.25/1.5; combos 1.5(DL+LL), 1.2(DL+LL+EL), 1.5(DL+EL), 0.9DL+1.5EL.

5.2 Concrete Technology (ACiE0502)

A. Ingredients & Properties

  • Concrete = cement + aggregate (60–80% of volume) + water + admixtures (+ entrained air). The water-cement ratio governs strength and durability (Abrams' law); typical w/c 0.40–0.55.
  • Grades: M10–M80 — Mxx means the characteristic 150-mm cube strength at 28 days (fck) with 5% of results below it. Ordinary M10–M20, standard M25–M60, high-strength M65+. IS 456 requires M20 minimum for RCC; M25+ for aggressive exposure.
  • Workability tests: slump (25–125 mm; true slump only), compaction factor, Vee-Bee seconds, flow table. Slump bands: very low 0–25, low 25–50, medium 50–100, high 100–125 mm; pumping needs 75–100 mm.
    • Fig 5.3 — Slump test: the frustum cone is lifted and the subsidence of the mound measured against the cone-top reference line; only a true slump is valid.
  • Compaction-factor bands (course values): very low 0.78–0.80, low 0.80–0.85, medium 0.85–0.95, high 0.95–1.0.
  • Admixtures: plasticizers (cut w/c 5–15%), superplasticizers (15–30%, flowing/self-compacting), accelerators (CaCl₂ — avoid in RC for corrosion reasons), retarders (sugar, lignosulphonate — hot weather), air-entrainers (3–6% air, frost resistance), pozzolanic, corrosion inhibitors, waterproofers.
  • Segregation & bleeding: aggregate separates / water rises to the surface; controlled by grading, w/c and handling; honeycombing is the visible result.
  • Curing: keep moisture and temperature — minimum 7 days for OPC, 10–14 days for blended cements (IS 456). Methods: ponding, wet hessian, membrane compounds, steam (precast), curing compounds.
  • Strength gain: 7 days ≈ 65–70% of the 28-day strength; 1 year ≈ 1.2 × fck.

B. Mix Design

  • Nominal mixes (M5–M25): 1:5:10 (M5), 1:4:8 (M7.5), 1:3:6 (M10), 1:2:4 (M15), 1:1.5:3 (M20), 1:1:2 (M25) — by volume.
  • Design mix (IS 10262): target mean strength f'ck = fck + 1.65σ (σ = 3.5 for M10–M15, 4.0 for M20–M25, 5.0 for M30–M50 when not established). Steps: fix free w/c (durability + strength) → water content (workability, aggregate size) → cement = water ÷ w/c → aggregate fractions (SSD basis) → trials and adjust.
  • Exposure conditions (IS 456): each sets a minimum grade, cover and maximum w/c — see the table in the extras (mild M20/20 mm/0.55 up to extreme M40/75 mm/0.40).

C. Testing & Quality Control

  • Cube test: 150 mm cubes, loading 14 N/mm²/min; fck from the average of 3 cubes within a ±15% band. Cylinder strength ≈ 0.8 × cube (fc' ≈ 0.8 fck).
  • Split tensile (IS 5816): fct = 2P/(πLD), typically ≈ 0.66√fck. Flexural: modulus of rupture fr = 0.7√fck (third-point loading, 150×150×700 beam).
  • NDT: rebound (Schmidt) hammer — surface hardness; UPV (PUNDIT) — quality/voids/cracks (> 4.5 km/s excellent); cores — in-situ strength (accept ≥ 85% of fck); pull-out; cover meter; carbonation depth (phenolphthalein — depassivation below pH ≈ 9).
  • Acceptance (IS 456 cl 16): the mean of a group of four non-overlapping results ≥ fck + 0.825·S (σ established) or fck + 4 MPa (σ not established); each individual cube ≥ fck − 3 MPa (M15–M30) or fck − 4 MPa (M35+).
  • Durability: permeability (RCPT), chloride/sulphate attack, alkali-aggregate reaction, carbonation; the cover is the first line of defence. Chloride limit in RC ≈ 0.6 kg/m³ of concrete (acid-soluble; IS 456:2000 states 0.6 kg/m³ for reinforced and 0.4 kg/m³ for prestressed concrete).
  • Crack-width limits: 0.3 mm general, 0.2 mm for aggressive/marine exposure and for water-retaining structures (IS 3370).
Fig 5.4 — Stress–strain: mild steel yields and flows (ductile); concrete rises parabolically to 0.002, holds to 0.0035, then crushes (brittle).
5.2 must-knows: M20 min for RCC; fck = cube 150 mm, 28 d, 5% below; cylinder ≈ 0.8 cube; slump 25–125 mm, pumping 75–100; w/c 0.40–0.55 (Abrams); nominal 1:2:4 = M15, 1:1.5:3 = M20; target f'ck = fck + 1.65σ; curing 7 d OPC / 10–14 blended; 7-day ≈ 65–70% of 28-day; acceptance mean ≥ fck + 0.825S (or +4), individual ≥ fck − 3 (M15–M30); UPV > 4.5 km/s excellent; crack 0.3/0.2 mm.

5.3 RCC Structures-1 (ACiE0503)

A. Working Stress vs Limit State Methods

AspectWorking Stress (WSM)Limit State (LSM)
BasisPermissible stresses under service loads (elastic)Ultimate (strength) + serviceability (deflection, cracking) limit states
Load factorsNone (safety lives in material stresses)Partial factors: 1.5 DL, 1.5 LL, 1.2 combos
Material partial safety—Concrete 1.5; steel 1.15
Stress blockLinear (triangular) concreteRectangular-parabolic (IS equivalent rectangle 0.45fck over 3xu/7)
ResultConservative, heavier; realistic service behaviourEconomical, rational; the IS 456 standard
  • WSM survives for crack-sensitive designs: water tanks (IS 3370), machine foundations, historically bridges.
  • LSM design strengths: concrete in flexural compression fcd = 0.67fck/1.5 = 0.45fck; steel 0.87fy. Stress block: total compression 0.36fck·b·xu acting at 0.42xu from the extreme fibre; steel yields when its strain reaches 0.002 + 0.87fy/Es; xu,max/d: Fe250 0.53, Fe415 0.48, Fe500 0.46.

B. Beams — Flexural Design (LSM)

Fig 5.5 — Limit-state stress block: compression C = 0.36fck·b·xu acts at 0.42xu from the top fibre, tension T = 0.87fy·Ast at the steel; the pair forms the couple Mu = T·(d − 0.42xu). Compression is above the NA — the block never sits at the bottom.
Singly reinforced: Mu = 0.36 fck b xu (d − 0.42 xu) = 0.87 fy Ast (d − 0.42 xu)
Under-reinforced (xu < xu,max): steel yields first — ductile ✓ ; over-reinforced: brittle, avoid
Moment of resistance at balance: Mu,lim = 0.36 fck b xu,max (d − 0.42 xu,max)
≈ 0.148 fck bd² (Fe250) · 0.138 fck bd² (Fe415) · 0.133 fck bd² (Fe500)
Doubly reinforced: compression steel Asc adds capacity when Mu > Mu,lim
Flanged (T/L) beams: bf = lo/6 + bw + 6Df
  • Steel limits (beam): minimum Ast = 0.85bd/fy; maximum 4% of bD (tension or compression).
  • Deflection limits (IS 456): total deflection ≤ span/250; deflection after partitions/finishes ≤ span/350 or 20 mm. Basic span/depth: cantilever 7, simply supported 20, continuous 26 (modified by the M/bd² service-stress factor).
  • Side-face reinforcement: beams deeper than 750 mm need 0.1% of the web area on each side face.
  • Shear design:
    Nominal shear τv = Vu/(bd) ≤ τc,max (M15 2.5, M20 2.8, M25 3.1, M30 3.5 N/mm²)
    Design shear resistance τc from the code table (fck, pt) — where τv > τc, provide stirrups
    Stirrup contribution: Vus = 0.87 fy Asv d / sv
    Minimum shear reinforcement: Asv/(b·sv) ≥ 0.4/(0.87fy); sv ≤ 0.75d (vertical stirrups) or d (inclined), and ≤ 300 mm
  • Bond & anchorage:
    Development length: Ld = φ σs/(4 τbd)
    τbd (M20): plain 1.2, deformed 1.92 N/mm² (deformed = 1.6 × plain); increase 25% for bars in compression (lap design)
    Standard U-hook (mild steel) ≈ 16φ equivalent development; stirrup-hook anchorage ≥ 8φ
    Bars continue ≥ d or 12φ beyond the theoretical cut point (whichever greater)

C. Slabs

  • One-way (Ly/Lx > 2): spans the short direction; main steel short way, distribution long way. Minimum slab steel: 0.15% of gross area (mild) / 0.12% (HYSD) each way.
  • Two-way (Ly/Lx ≤ 2): bends both ways — IS 456 Annex D moment coefficients; span/depth 35 (simply supported), 40 (continuous). Corner torsion steel at discontinuous corners: top & bottom mesh, each direction, area ≥ ¾ of the max midspan steel per unit width.
  • Flat slabs: column heads/drops; punching shear checked on a perimeter 0.5d from the column face; middle-strip vs column-strip moments; drops width ≥ L/3 each way.
  • Thickness: slabs 100–125 mm minimum; span/depth one-way 7/20/26 (cant/SS/cont), two-way 35/40, flat slab ≈ 32 with drops.
  • Staircases: waist-slab design spanning landings/stringers; step loads converted onto the horizontal span; dog-legged is the standard layout.
  • Distribution (temperature/shrinkage) steel: 0.12% (HYSD) / 0.15% (mild) of gross area, both directions regardless of the main steel.
    • Fig 5.6 — One-way vs two-way slabs: Ly/Lx = 2 is the boundary; one-way carries main steel across the short span with distribution steel along the long one; two-way is designed in both directions, with corner torsion mesh at discontinuous corners.
5.3 must-knows: LSM design: 0.45fck concrete, 0.87fy steel; stress block 0.36fck·b·xu at 0.42xu; xu,max/d: 0.53/0.48/0.46 (Fe250/415/500); Mu,lim = 0.138fck·bd² (Fe415); under-reinforced = ductile; Ast,min = 0.85bd/fy, Ast,max 4%; Ld = φσs/4τbd (deformed 1.92 M20); τv = Vu/bd; stirrups Vus = 0.87fy·Asv·d/sv, sv ≤ 0.75d & 300 mm; one-way Ly/Lx > 2; two-way span/depth 35/40; slab steel 0.12/0.15%; corner torsion steel at discontinuous corners.

5.4 RCC Structures-2 (ACiE0504)

A. Columns (LSM)

Short column (lex/D ≤ 12 both axes), axially loaded, tied:
Pu = 0.4 fck Ac + 0.67 fy Asc
Minimum eccentricity: emin = Le/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm (the formula above applies when emin is not exceeded)
Slender column: additional (amplified) moments per IS 456 cl 39.7–39.8
Longitudinal steel: min 0.8%, max 6% (4% practical — congestion at laps)
Ties: dia ≥ max(φ_largest/4, 6 mm); pitch ≤ min(least lateral dim, 16φ_smallest, 300 mm)
  • Spiral columns: Pu = 1.05 × (tied formula) — 5% more capacity plus much better ductility; spiral pitch ≤ min(75 mm, core dia/6) and ≥ 25 mm.
    • Fig 5.7 — Column detailing: tied columns use discrete ties at a pitch limit; spiral columns use a continuous helix that confines the core (Pu × 1.05 and far more ductile). Plans show bar + tie geometry, elevations show the pitch rules.
  • Minimum size: IS 456 allows 200 mm; NBC 201 (MRT) requires columns ≥ 300 mm — the seismic practice in Nepal.
  • Nominal cover 40 mm (mild/moderate), 50 mm severe; every corner bar and alternate bar tied; no more than 50% of bars lapped at one section; laps staggered away from maximum-moment zones.

B. Footings

  • Isolated (spread): designed for the net upward soil pressure; one-way shear at d from the column face, punching (two-way) shear at d/2; bending designed at the column face.
  • Combined: rectangular (equal settlement) or trapezoidal (unequal column loads) — one footing for two columns; strap (cantilever) footing for boundary columns — the strap never touches the soil.
  • Mat/raft: rigid (conventional) vs flexible (subgrade-reaction) analysis; controls differential settlement on weak soils.
  • Cover in footings: 50 mm minimum, on a 75–100 mm PCC blinding layer.
  • Pile caps: check punching of pile heads and the column; strut-and-tie thinking; edge projection ≥ 300 mm by practice.

C. Prestressed Concrete

Tendon force after losses: P = Apt·σpt
Stress at an extreme fibre: ± P/A ± P·e/Z ± M/Z (combined)
Losses: elastic shortening, creep of concrete, shrinkage, relaxation of steel; post-tensioned adds anchorage slip + friction (wobble & curvature) — total typically 15–20%
A parabolic (draped) tendon balances a UDL: w_bal = 8Pe/L²
AspectPre-tensionedPost-tensioned
TensioningBefore casting (long bed)After casting (ducts + jacks)
BondNatural bondGrouted (bonded) or unbonded tendons
Unique losses—Friction + anchorage slip
UseSleepers, small precastBridges, tanks, large/segmental spans
  • Advantages: longer spans, less deflection and cracking, efficient use of high-strength materials; the section stays uncracked at service → better durability.
  • Classification: full/partial/limited prestress; internal/external tendons; bonded/unbonded. IS 1343 governs; Grade 1 allows no tensile stress at service.
  • Materials: high-tensile strands (fpu 1570–1860 MPa), concrete M30–M60; end blocks need bursting reinforcement.
  • Elastic-shortening loss = m·fcs (m = Es/Ec ≈ 6) — computed at the steel level.
Fig 5.8 — Prestressed beam: the draped tendon, eccentric e below the centroidal axis, applies P at both anchorages; the resulting ± P/A ± Pe/Z ± M/Z stresses keep the section uncracked at service. A parabolic profile balances a UDL (w_bal = 8Pe/L²).
5.4 must-knows: tied column Pu = 0.4fck·Ac + 0.67fy·Asc; spiral × 1.05; emin = Le/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm; steel 0.8–6% (4% practical); ties dia ≥ φ/4 & 6 mm, pitch ≤ min(side, 16φ, 300); NBC 201 columns ≥ 300 mm; footing punching at d/2, one-way shear at d; strap footing never touches soil; cover 50 mm on 75–100 PCC; prestress losses 15–20%; draped tendon balances w = 8Pe/L²; post-tension unique losses: friction + anchorage slip.

5.5 Steel Structures (ACiE0505)

A. Sections & Connections Overview

  • Rolled sections: ISMB beams, ISMC channels, ISA angles, ISNT tees, plates, pipes/CHS, SHS; built-up: plate girders, laced/battened columns, box girders. IS 808 lists hot-rolled; IS 811 cold-formed.
  • Grades: E250 (Fe410 — fy 250, fu 410), E350 (Fe490 — fu 490), E450 (Fe570 — fu 570). Design strength fd = fy/γm0 with γm0 = 1.10 (IS 800:2007 LSM; γm1 = 1.25 for rupture).

B. Bolted Connections

Fig 5.9 — Bolted lap joint: bolt shear, plate bearing, and edge shear-out failures (IS 800 limit states)
Bolt types: black (unturned) — clearance holes 1.5–2 mm; turned/close-tolerance; HSFG — friction grip, no slip at service
Shear (LSM): Vdsb = fu·nn·Anb/(√3 γmb), with Anb = 0.78·Asb when threads are in the shear plane
Bearing: Vdpb = 2.5 kb·d·t·fu/γmb
Tension: Tdnb = 0.9 fu Anb/γmb
Prying force adds tension in T/angle connections; joint efficiency η = joint strength / solid-plate strength
  • Pitch: minimum 2.5d (uniform — the rolled/sheared distinction applies only to edge distances); maximum 32t or 300 mm (tension), 16t or 200 mm (compression). Edge distance: minimum 1.5×hole dia (rolled) / 1.7× (sheared); maximum 12tε with ε = √(250/fy).
  • Staggered bolting: net area along the critical path An = (b − n·dh + Σs²/4g)·t — the zig-zag deductions/credits matter.
  • Bolt grades 4.6 and 8.8 (fu = 400/800 MPa; fyb = 0.6fu); HSFG 8.8/10.9; slip factor μ ≈ 0.3–0.5. Hole dia: M16 → 18 mm.
  • Failure modes: bolt shear, bearing (bolt or plate), plate net-section rupture, block shear — IS 800 checks all; bolt value = the least.
  • Bolts vs welding: bolts — fast field erection, no heat effects, replaceable, easy inspection; welds — no holes (full section), rigid moment connections, silent — but QC-dependent.

C. Welded Connections

Fillet weld: strength = fu/(√3 γmw) × (0.7s × L_eff)
Effective throat = 0.7 × size s (90° fillet); min size 3 mm (1.5√t table); max = thinner plate − 1.5 mm
Lap joints: min lap = 4t or 40 mm; end returns 2s recommended
Butt (groove) welds: full penetration = parent-metal strength
γmw = 1.25 (shop), 1.5 (site)
  • Types: fillet (cheapest, common), butt/groove (full strength), plug/slot (shear), spot (sheet metal). Weldability is best at low carbon; high carbon needs preheat/postheat.
  • Defects: undercut, overlap, porosity, slag inclusion, hot/cold cracks, lack of fusion/penetration, spatter. Inspection: visual + NDT (radiography for butt welds, ultrasonic, dye penetrant, magnetic particle).
  • Residual stresses and distortion come from uneven heating — controlled by weld sequence, clamps, preheat.
  • Welded joints can exceed 100% efficiency (no holes); design shear acts on the throat area.

D. Tension Members

Gross yielding: Tdg = fy Ag/γm0
Net rupture: Tdn = 0.9 fu An/γm1 (γm1 = 1.25)
Block shear: Tdb per IS 800 cl 6.4
Design strength = least of the three; slenderness limit for tension members λ ≤ 400
  • An follows the critical failure path with stagger credits; single angles bolted through one leg carry shear lag — the gauge/eccentricity reduces the effective area; gusset-plate checks complete the design.

E. Compression Members (Struts/Columns)

Buckling class a/b/c/d curves; imperfection factors α: a 0.21, b 0.34, c 0.49, d 0.76
Non-dimensional slenderness λ̄ = √(fy/fcc) → reduction factor χ
Pd = Ae·fy·χ/γm0
Slenderness λ = KL/r ≤ 180 (compression members); bracing 250; tension 400
  • Section classification: plastic (full Mp) → compact (My) → semi-compact (extreme-fibre yield) → slender (local buckling reduces capacity); governed by flange/web outstand ratios with ε = √(250/fy).
  • Column bases: slab base (axial loads — grout + anchor bolts) vs gusseted base (moment/heavy loads); base-plate thickness from cantilever bending of the projections; concrete bearing strength 0.45fck.
  • Connections: splices for alignment/continuity; joint classification by moment transfer — simple ≤ 20%, semi-rigid 20–90%, rigid ≥ 90% of the fixed-end moment.
5.5 must-knows: fd = fy/1.10; bolt shear fu·Anb/(√3·1.25), bearing 2.5kb·d·t·fu/1.25; pitch ≥ 2.5d, max 32t/300; edge ≥ 1.5d0; An = (b − n·dh + Σs²/4g)t; HSFG = friction, no slip; fillet throat 0.7s, γmw 1.25 shop/1.5 site; lap ≥ 4t/40 mm; tension: min of yielding fy·Ag/1.10, rupture 0.9fu·An/1.25, block shear; λ ≤ 400 tension, 180 compression; buckling curves a–d; section: plastic→compact→semi-compact→slender; simple joint ≤ 20% FEM.

5.6 Timber and Masonry Structures (ACiE0506)

A. Timber Beams & Columns

  • Design (WSM tradition, IS 883 / NBC 112): bending σ = M/Z with the grade's allowable stress; shear parallel to grain (τ = VQ/Ib — horizontal shear governs notched beams); bearing perpendicular to grain at supports; deflection span/240–360.
  • Notches and holes cut the net section — keep holes near the NA (low bending stress) and notches away from high-shear zones; bolted joints add perpendicular-to-grain bearing checks.
  • Timber columns: slenderness λ = Le/least side; capacity drops as λ rises; wet exposure reduces strength (moisture factor).
  • Species: sal, teak, chir — strength classes; preservative treatment for durability.

B. Masonry Design (NBC 109, IS 1905)

  • Compressive strength: unit strength × mortar grade — but prism strength (1st-class brick + 1:4 mortar ≈ 1.5–2.2 MPa) is far below the unit's own strength (slenderness, slaking, workmanship). Eccentricity and slenderness reduction factors (Ks) apply.
  • Stress reduction (slenderness): SR = heff/t with a maximum of 27 (IS 1905); Ks falls from ≈ 1.0 at SR 6 to ≈ 0.35 at SR 27. Small piers (< 0.2 m²) take an area-reduction factor.
  • Failure modes of masonry walls:
ModeCause / appearance
Vertical compressionCrushing — vertical cracks split the units
Bed-joint slidingLow friction / weak mortar, in-plane shear
Flexural tensile crackingVertically spanning wall → horizontal cracks; horizontally spanning (cross-wall action) → vertical cracks
Diagonal shearIn-plane lateral (seismic) load — stair-step/X-cracking through joints
Overturning/rockingToe lift of unreinforced walls under out-of-plane shaking
  • Mortars:
MortarStrength (28 d)Use
Cement 1:3~10+ MPaHigh-strength, marine
Cement 1:6~3 MPaGeneral load-bearing
Lime-cement 1:1:6 (gauged)2–3 MPaWorkable general masonry
Lime 1:30.5–1 MPaHistoric, flexible, breathable
Mud< 0.5 MPaRural non-engineered
  • The strongest mortar is not the best — a stiff mortar cracks the joints instead of distributing stress; compatibility matters.
  • NBC 201/202 Mandatory Rules of Thumb (low-rise seismic): NBC 201 covers RC buildings with masonry infill (MRT scope: low-rise up to 3 storeys, and not for irregular or soft-storey buildings); NBC 202 covers load-bearing masonry; NBC 205 covers RC buildings without masonry infill. Rules: load-bearing walls ≥ 230 mm (115 mm only for internal non-loadbearing); openings limited (≈⅓ of wall length) with piers ≥ 610 mm between them; RC or timber seismic bands (sill, lintel, gable, roof); vertical reinforcement at corners/jambs for 2–3 storeys; light roofs preferred.
  • Confined masonry: RC tie-columns and bond beams framing masonry panels — much better seismic performance; Nepal's preferred new-build and retrofit system.
  • Buttresses, piers, pilasters strengthen walls — the buttress resists lateral thrust through its self-weight (thrust line kept inside the section).
  • Effective height (IS 1905): top & bottom laterally restrained: heff = 0.75H (when L ≥ 2H) up to 1.0H depending on L/t; free top: 1.5H; use effective thickness for piers/deeper walls.
Fig 5.10 — Timber members (bending, horizontal shear at notches, bearing ⊥ grain, holes at NA, column slenderness) and masonry walls (prism strength, Ks–slenderness, failure modes, NBC seismic rules & confined masonry)
5.6 must-knows: timber: horizontal shear governs notched beams, λ = Le/least side; masonry prism 1.5–2.2 MPa ≪ unit strength; SR = heff/t max 27, Ks 1.0→0.35; failures: crushing, bed-joint sliding, flexural cracking, diagonal stair-step (seismic), overturning; stiffest mortar is not best; NBC 201 walls ≥ 230 mm, piers ≥ 610 mm, openings ≤ ⅓; seismic bands (sill/lintel/gable/roof); confined masonry = tie-columns + bond beams; heff = 0.75H (L ≥ 2H) to 1.5H free top.

Worked Numericals (MCQ Patterns You Will Meet)

Loads

  • Slab 150 mm + finish 1 kN/m² + live 2 kN/m²: DL = 0.15×25 = 3.75 + 1 = 4.75; factored 1.5(4.75+2) = 10.1 kN/m².
  • 230 mm brick wall, 3 m high: 0.23×3×19.2 = 13.2 kN/m + plaster ≈ 0.5 → 13.7 kN/m.
  • Wind: Vz = 39×1.0×1.05×1.0 = 41 m/s → pz = 0.6×41² = 1008 N/m² ≈ 1.0 kN/m².
  • Seismic: W = 5000 kN, Z = 0.35, I = 1.0, R = 5, Sa/g = 2.5: Ah = (0.35/2)(1/5)(2.5) = 0.0875 → VB = 0.0875×5000 = 437.5 kN.

Beam flexure (LSM)

  • Mu = 120 kN·m, b = 230, d = 450, M20-Fe415: Mu,lim = 0.138×20×230×450²/10⁶ = 129 kN·m > 120 → singly reinforced. Solving 0.36×20×230·xu(450−0.42xu) = 120×10⁶ gives xu ≈ 197 mm (< 0.48d ✓); Ast = 120×10⁶/(0.87×415×(450−0.42×197)) ≈ 905 mm² → 3-20φ (942 mm²).
  • Mu = 200 kN·m, same section: Mu,lim = 129 < 200 → doubly reinforced. Mu2 = 71 kN·m; with fsc ≈ 352 MPa, d′ = 50: Asc = 71×10⁶/(352×400) ≈ 504 mm²; extra tension steel Ast2 = Asc·fsc/(0.87fy) ≈ 490 mm².
  • Shear: Vu = 150 kN, b = 230, d = 450: τv = 1.45 MPa; τc (M20, pt ≈ 0.8%) ≈ 0.6 → Vus ≈ 88 kN → 2L-8φ (Asv = 100 mm²): sv = 0.87×415×100×450/88000 ≈ 184 mm → provide 8φ @ 175 c/c.

Slab & column

  • One-way slab 3.5 m span, DL 3.5, LL 3: Mu = 1.5×6.5×3.5²/8 = 14.93 kN·m/m; d = √(14.93×10⁶/(0.138×20×1000)) = 73.5 mm → use 125 mm slab (d ≈ 100); minimum steel 0.12%×1000×125 = 150 mm²/m → 8φ@330 (≈152) — provide 8φ @ 250 (spacing cap).
  • Column 300×300, M20-Fe415, 4-20φ (Asc = 1257): Pu = 0.4×20×(90000−1257)/1000 + 0.67×415×1257/1000 = 710 + 350 = 1060 kN.
  • emin check, L = 3 m: 3000/500 + 300/30 = 6 + 10 = 16 mm < 20 → use 20 mm minimum ✓ (axial formula valid).
  • Punching: 400 mm column, Vu = 800 kN, d = 400: bo = 4(400+400) = 3200 mm; vu = 800000/(3200×400) = 0.625 MPa < τc → OK.

Steel connections & members

  • Bolt 8.8, M20 (fu = 800), single shear, threads excluded: Vdsb = 800×314/(√3×1.25) = 116.1 kN (Anb = Asb = π/4×20² = 314 mm² — the 0.78×245 mm² reduction applies only when threads are included).
  • Fillet weld 6 mm × 150 mm, E250 (fu = 410): P = 410×0.7×6×150/(√3×1.25) = 119.3 kN.
  • Tension ISA 100×100×10, one leg bolted with a 20φ hole: An = Ag − d0·t = 1900 − 220 = 1680 mm² → Tdn = 0.9×410×1680/1.25 = 497 kN; Tdg = 250×1900/1.1 = 432 kN (gross governs).
  • Column buckling: ISMB 300, Le = 3.5 m pinned-pinned (A = 5626 mm²; rzz ≈ 123.7 mm, ryy ≈ 28.4 mm): strong axis λ ≈ 28 (χ ≈ 0.97); weak axis λ ≈ 123 (curve c for h/bf > 1.2, χ ≈ 0.35) → weak axis governs; Pd ≈ 0.35×5626×250/1.1 ≈ 450 kN.

Prestress

  • Beam 300×600, P = 800 kN at e = 100 mm below NA: bottom stress = P/A + Pe/Z = 4.44 + 4.44 = 8.89 MPa compression; under M = 100 kN·m the bottom sees 5.56 MPa tension → net 3.33 MPa compression ✓ uncracked.
  • Elastic-shortening loss: m ≈ 6, fcs = 5 MPa → 30 MPa (≈ 2% of a 1570 strand).

Numerical Traps Checklist (Chapter 5)

  • 0.45 vs 0.446 vs 0.36 fck: 0.446fck = max parabolic-rectangle stress (= 0.67fck/1.5); the IS block puts 0.446fck over depth 3xu/7, giving a total force of 0.36fck·b·xu at 0.42xu. Force uses 0.36; stress level uses 0.446.
  • 0.87fy vs 0.58fy: 0.87 = LSM tension design strength; 0.58fy = shear yield of webs (fyw/√3) — different contexts.
  • xu,max/d by grade: Fe500 = 0.46, not 0.48 — write the grade first.
  • emin floor: Le/500 + D/30 comes out below 20 mm for stocky columns → use the 20 mm minimum.
  • Punching at d/2, one-way at d — footings, slabs and flat slabs share the convention.
  • Cover vs effective cover: nominal (clear) cover to the outermost steel; effective cover = clear + link + φ/2 — read which is asked.
  • Wind and earthquake are never simultaneous — combination-list trap.
  • Live-load reduction — never for storage/public assembly.
  • Friction loss is post-tensioned only — pre-tensioned beds have no ducts.
  • γmw: shop 1.25, site 1.5 — the same weld loses 20% capacity on site.

More Worked Examples (with narrated logic)

Example — T-beam effective flange

Simply supported T-beam L = 6 m, slab 120 mm, web 300 mm, beams 3.5 m c/c: bf = lo/6 + bw + 6Df = (0.7×6000)/6 + 300 + 720 = 1720 mm (lo = 0.7L for SS). Most of the flange participates — big capacity; main steel needs Ld into the web through the flange (hooks).

Example — Deflection control

SS beam 6 m, Fe415, service Mu/(bd²) = 1.2: basic span/depth 20 modified by the fs & pt charts — pt = 0.6%, fs = 200 → factor ≈ 1.3 → allowable L/d ≈ 26 → d_min = 6000/26 ≈ 231 mm. Walk the modification-factor logic once; after that it is mechanical.

Example — Wind on a GI roof

Sloped roof Cpe = −1.2, Cpi = ±0.2: net −1.4pz; with pz = 1.0 kN/m² → 1.4 kN/m² suction. Sheet fasteners and purlin anchorage are designed for this uplift reversal — why light roofs blow off in storms.

Example — Seismic storey-force distribution

Vb = 1000 kN, 3 storeys of equal mass and height: F_i = Vb·(Wi·hi²)/Σ(Wj·hj²) → forces grow as hi² (ratio 1:4:9): bottom 71, middle 286, top 643 kN — the inverted triangle with the squared weighting, a standard exam computation.

Extended High-Yield Additions (Exam-Focused Extras)

Load combinations summary (IS 456 / IS 875-5 / NBC)

  • ULS: 1.5(DL+LL); 1.2(DL+LL+EL/WL); 1.5(DL+EL); 1.5(DL+WL); 0.9DL+1.5EL (uplift). SLS: DL+LL (factors 1.0); with WL/EL present the LL factor drops to 0.8.
  • Wind and earthquake are never combined (different return periods).
  • The 1.5 factor bundles load variability and strength uncertainty — memorize the combinations rather than re-deriving them.

Concrete extras

  • Modulus: Ec = 5000√fck (short-term, IS 456); long-term modular ratio m = 280/3σcbc (WSM).
  • Shrinkage strain ≈ 0.0003 (design); creep coefficient 1.6–2.2 at 5 years (IS 456 Annex) — both grow deflection and prestress loss.
  • Creep rises with stress ratio, lower humidity and younger age at loading.
  • Self-compacting concrete: slump-flow/J-ring tests, no vibration — congested reinforcement.
  • Fibre-reinforced concrete: steel/polypropylene/glass fibres for impact and shrinkage crack control — not primary reinforcement.
  • Batching: weigh batching (±1–2%); transit mixers; pumped concrete needs 75–100 mm slump and 35–40% fine aggregate.
  • Cold/hot weather: below 5 °C strength gain stalls and freezing destroys the mix; above 35–40 °C slump loss, plastic shrinkage, fast set — retarders, cool ingredients, evaporation control.
  • Underwater: tremie pipe (150–200 mm dia, continuous pour, sealed start) or pumped; anti-washout admixtures.
  • Joints: construction (stoppage), expansion/isolation (fillers + sealants), contraction/control (shrinkage spacing); water stops in water-retaining work.

RCC extras

  • Effective cover = clear cover + link dia + bar dia/2; nominal cover also serves fire rating (1 hr ≈ 20 mm beams).
  • Span/depth basics (IS 456 cl 23.2.1): cantilever 7, SS 20, continuous 26; two-way slabs 35/40 (per the course table).
  • Bar spacing: minimum clear gap = max(φ, aggregate size + 5 mm); distribution steel ≤ 5d or 300 mm.
  • Columns: axial plus uniaxial/biaxial interaction (Pu–Mu charts, Bresler reciprocal); minimum eccentricity guarantees the minimum-moment design; slender columns amplify moments.
  • Detailing: 135° seismic hooks with 10φ extension (IS 13920); confinement zones get hoop spacing ≤ min(6db, 150 mm); column laps alternate bars.
  • Water tanks (IS 3370): WSM with 0.2 mm crack control; minimum reinforcement 0.3% of the cross-section; shrinkage joints; membrane vs integral waterproofing.
  • Retaining walls: cantilever (≤ ~6 m), counterfort (> 6 m), gravity; stem/heel/toe with tension faces placed correctly; drainage via weep holes + filter.
  • Flat-slab punching: vu = Vu/(bo·d) on the 0.5d perimeter; enhanced shear near supports; drops increase d and cut vu.

Steel extras

  • Plate girders: tension-field action in shear panels; bearing/intermediate/horizontal stiffeners; flanges carry M, web carries V — the choice for long spans.
  • Rolled beams: laterally restrained → bend-buckling check Md = βb·Zp·fy/γm0 ≤ 1.2Ze·fy/γm0; unrestrained → lateral-torsional buckling curves; plastic shear resistance Av·fyw/(√3 γm0).
  • HSFG bolts: designed by slip (proof load × μ × friction surfaces); no service bearing; fatigue-friendly — bridges prefer them.
  • Trusses: gusset plates, centroidal member lines; roof trusses span 6–30 m; GI-sheet slope 1-in-6 minimum to 1-in-3 typical (tiles steeper); purlins on nodes; uplift reversal needs hold-downs.
  • Fatigue (IS 800 cl 13): stress range × cycles; welded detail categories; bolted beats welded under fatigue.
  • Corrosion protection: galvanizing, zinc-rich primers, weathering steel, cathodic protection (marine).

Masonry/timber extras

  • Units: burnt clay, fly-ash lime-gypsum, AAC, concrete blocks, stone — block masonry is faster and lighter.
  • Bed-joint reinforcement (GFRP/metal mesh every 3rd–4th course) for seismic crack control.
  • Post-Gorkha retrofit: mesh-reinforced plaster, splints at corners, tie bands, corner stitching, wall-to-wall and wall-to-roof anchors.
  • Timber joints: mortise-tenon, bolted steel plates, split-ring connectors (higher efficiency), glulam for long spans — connections govern timber design.
  • Bamboo (NBC 109): tensile ≈ 150–350 MPa along grain — high strength-to-weight; needs borer treatment; weak in connections and fire; Nepal rural staple.
  • Load path: roof → walls → bands → foundation; roof diaphragm action (band + bracing) is critical in seismic; openings weaken piers — centre and limit them.

Nepal-specific design facts

  • NBC 105:2020: site spectra with soil classes; Z = PGA (475-yr) ≈ 0.25/0.35/0.40 by zone, Kathmandu ≈ 0.35; importance I = 1.0 general, 1.25 schools/assembly, 1.5 essential.
  • NBC 201 (MRT): RC with masonry infill, low-rise (up to 3 storeys, and not for irregular/soft-storey buildings); columns ≥ 300 mm.
  • Materials of Nepal practice: RCC with Fe415/500 TMT, OPC/PPC; brick-cement masonry in the Terai and valleys; stone masonry in hills; bamboo/timber rural; GI-sheet roofs everywhere (uplift design).
  • Typical Kathmandu residential: RCC frame + brick infill, 230 mm walls, M20–M25, Fe500, DPC at plinth, 2.75 m storey height.

Rapid-Fire One-Liners (Last-Minute Revision)

  • Load factors: 1.5(DL+LL); 1.2(DL+LL+EQ); 0.9DL+1.5EQ (uplift).
  • Partial safety: concrete 1.5, steel 1.15 (RCC); γm0 1.10, γm1 1.25 (steel).
  • Wind pz = 0.6Vz²; Vz = Vb·k1k2k3k4; Nepal Vb = 47 m/s (< 3000 m), 55 above.
  • Roof live load: −0.02 kN/m² per degree above 10°, floor 0.4 kN/m² minimum.
  • Snow: S = μ·So; no snow load beyond 60° slope (course value).
  • Ah = (Z/2)(I/R)(Sa/g); I = 1.0/1.25/1.5; R: OMRF 3, wall 4, SMRF 5.
  • Live loads: residential 2, office 2.5–3, classroom 3, stairs 3–5, roofs 0.75–1.5 kN/m².
  • Unit weights: RCC 25, PCC 24, brick masonry 19.2, steel ≈ 77–78.5 kN/m³.
  • fck = 150-mm cube @ 28 d; cylinder ≈ 0.8 cube; fr = 0.7√fck; split ≈ 0.66√fck.
  • Ec = 5000√fck; shrinkage 0.0003; creep coefficient ≈ 2.
  • Design strengths 0.45fck & 0.87fy; block force 0.36fck·xu at 0.42xu.
  • Mu,lim: 0.148/0.138/0.133 fckbd² (Fe250/415/500); xu,max/d 0.53/0.48/0.46.
  • Beam steel: min 0.85bd/fy, max 4%bD; slabs 0.12/0.15%.
  • Deflection: total span/250, post-partition span/350 or 20 mm; span/depth 7/20/26 (one-way), 35/40 (two-way).
  • τc,max: M20 2.8, M25 3.1; min stirrups 0.4/(0.87fy); sv ≤ 0.75d or 300 mm.
  • Ld = φσs/4τbd; M20 deformed τbd = 1.92 (×1.6 plain; +25% compression); Fe415-M20 ≈ 47φ.
  • Two-way when Ly/Lx ≤ 2; corner torsion steel at discontinuous corners; punching at 0.5d.
  • Column Pu = 0.4fckAc + 0.67fyAsc; emin = Le/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm; steel 0.8–6% (4% practical).
  • Ties: dia ≥ φ/4 (6 mm); pitch ≤ min(least dim, 16φ, 300); spiral: +5%, pitch ≤ min(75, core/6).
  • lex/D ≤ 12 short; slender amplifies moments.
  • Footing: one-way shear at d, punching at d/2; cover 50 mm; strap footings stay off the soil.
  • Prestress losses 15–20% (friction + slip only in PT); w_bal = 8Pe/L²; strands 1570–1860 MPa, M30+.
  • Steel: fd = fy/1.10; E250 fu 410, E350 fu 490, E450 fu 570.
  • Bolts: min pitch 2.5d; max 32t/300 (T), 16t/200 (C); edge 1.5d0/1.7d0; HSFG no-slip.
  • Fillet throat 0.7s; lap 4t/40; NDT: UT/RT/MT/PT; γmw 1.25 shop / 1.5 site.
  • Tension: min(gross yield, 0.9fuAn/1.25, block shear); λ ≤ 400.
  • Compression λ ≤ 180 (bracing 250); curves a–d (α 0.21–0.76); laced members +5–10% effective slenderness.
  • Classes: plastic/compact/semi-compact/slender; ε = √(250/fy).
  • Base bearing 0.45fck; slab base axial, gusseted for moment; joint rigidity 20/90% rule.
  • Timber: horizontal shear governs; NBC 112/IS 883; moisture cuts strength.
  • Masonry: SR ≤ 27 (IS 1905); prism ≪ unit strength; five failure modes.
  • Mortars: cement 1:6 general; lime flexible; mud rural; stronger mortar ≠ better masonry.
  • NBC 201/202 MRT: bands at sill/lintel/roof, walls ≥ 230 mm, piers ≥ 610 mm, light roofs.
  • Confined masonry: tie-columns + bond beams — the best UD-masonry upgrade.
  • Earthquakes: 1934 M8.0, 1988 M6.6, 2015 Gorkha M7.8.

Steel design strengths & slenderness

  • Bending fd = fy/1.10; tension rupture 0.9fu/1.25; welds fu/√3γmw (shop 1.25, site 1.5).

Deeper Explanations (why values are what they are)

  • Why 0.87fy at ultimate? At the maximum concrete strain 0.0035 the steel strain is well past yield, but the measured average stress sits slightly below fy; the 1.15 material factor gives 0.87.
  • Why the rectangular stress block? The real parabolic-rectangle curve peaks at 0.446fck (strain 0.002); IS idealizes it as a rectangle of 0.446fck over the top 3xu/7 with a parabolic tail below, which integrates to the same force and centroid — 0.36fck·b·xu at 0.42xu from the extreme fibre — with simpler algebra.
  • Why xu limits? At xu,max the concrete (0.0035) and the steel (yield strain) reach their limits together — below it the steel yields first (ductile, desirable); above it failure is brittle compression.
  • Why 0.4fck in columns? The flexural design stress 0.45fck reduced ≈ 10% for long-term (sustained) loading and accidental eccentricity.
  • Why γm differs (1.5 vs 1.15)? Site-cast concrete varies more than factory-controlled steel.
  • Why load factor 1.5? Calibrated to a target reliability index β ≈ 3.8 over 50 years, matching historical safety levels.
  • Why HSFG in bridges? No slip → no alternating bearing wear → longer fatigue life.
  • Why throat 0.7s? The 45° fillet triangle's minimum throat = s·cos45° = 0.707s.
  • Why SR ≤ 27 for masonry? Wall buckling-type instability plus workmanship scatter — the Ks charts are test-calibrated (IS 1905).

Design Flowcharts (how engineers think — and how MCQs are built)

Flowchart 1 — RC beam design (LSM)

Loads → factored Mu → section (span/depth 20/26) → Mu vs Mu,lim → singly (Ast = Mu/0.87fy(d−0.42xu)) or doubly → min/max steel → shear (τv vs τc → stirrups) → deflection (modification factor) → bond/Ld, cover, curtailment → crack/serviceability check.

Flowchart 2 — Column design

Pu & Mu → slenderness (lex/D ≤ 12?) → short: axial/interaction formula → emin check → steel 0.8–4% → ties (dia/pitch) → slender: amplified moments → biaxial interaction (Bresler reciprocal) → detailing: staggered laps, joint confinement.

Flowchart 3 — Steel bolted joint

Loads → grade/dia → bolt count (Vdsb) → pitch/edge/gauge → plate net section → block shear → efficiency → HSFG slip check if needed → detailing.

Flowchart 4 — Slab selection

Ly/Lx > 2 one-way; ≤ 2 two-way coefficients; wall-supported vs flat slab (punching) → thickness (span/depth + minimums) → main/distribution steel → corner torsion (two-way, discontinuous) → deflection check.

Additional One-Mark Facts (potpourri)

  • Impact/dynamic allowance for lifts and machine loads per IS 875-2 occupancies.
  • Live-load reduction: multi-storey columns only (probability of simultaneous full loading is low); never storage/assembly.
  • Wind k2 peaks at the top of tall structures in open terrain; city terrain (cat 4) reduces low-level speeds.
  • Seismic weight = mass above the base: full DL + fractional LL — IS 1893:2016 Table 10: 25% (LL ≤ 3 kN/m²), 50% (LL above 3); NBC 105:2020 Table 5-1: 30% other purpose, 60% storage, nil roof.
  • Soft storey: open ground floors create a stiffness discontinuity — the 2015 Nepal apartment collapse pattern; avoid or strengthen.
  • Ductile detailing (IS 13920): hoop spacing ≤ min(6db, 150 mm) in hinge zones; 135° hooks with 10db extension.
  • Development length: +25% τbd for bars in compression (lap design); excess-reinforcement and epoxy factors exist for special cases.
  • Curtailment: extend ≥ d or 12φ beyond the theoretical cut point.
  • Two-way corner torsion steel: ¾ of the max midspan steel per unit width, top & bottom, each direction, at discontinuous corners.
  • Flat-slab drops: width ≥ L/3 each way; drops/thickened zones cut punching stress.
  • Stairs: waist slab span/25–30; effective span is the horizontal going; loads = self + steps + finishes + LL.
  • Retaining walls: stem cantilevers (max BM near base); heel takes downward soil+surcharge, toe upward pressure — tension faces set the steel.
  • Water tanks (IS 3370): WSM, 0.2 mm crack width, min steel 0.3% of the section.
  • Steel web shear: Av·fyw/√3 (plastic shear); stiffened panels gain tension-field reserve.
  • Base-plate thickness: cantilever bending of the projections under bearing pressure; anchors handle uplift.
  • Battens carry 2.5% of the axial load as transverse shear (IS); lacing angle 40–70°.
  • Gantry girders: vertical + lateral crane bending, fatigue, local wheel loads — the hardest rolled-steel design.
  • Timber: split-ring connectors beat bolts (timber is weak at bolt holes); column capacity × slenderness factor.
  • Brick classes (IS 1077): class 35 → 3.5 MPa up to class 350 → 35 MPa; prism masonry strength ≈ ⅓–½ of the unit.
  • Rat-trap (cavity) bond: lighter, better insulation, 20–30% less material.
  • Retrofit: through-wall anchors, corner splints, mesh plaster (ferrocement) — post-earthquake Nepal standard.

Exam-Morning Concept Cards

Card 1 — Loads & combos

DL 25 kN/m³ RCC; LL 2–5 kN/m²; wind pz = 0.6Vz²; EQ Ah = (Z/2)(I/R)(Sa/g); combos 1.5(DL+LL), 1.2(DL+LL+EQ), 1.5(DL+EQ), 0.9DL+1.5EQ; wind & EQ never together.

Card 2 — RCC LSM numbers

0.45fck & 0.87fy; block 0.36fckxu @ 0.42xu; xu,max/d 0.53/0.48/0.46; Mu,lim 0.148/0.138/0.133; Ast,min 0.85bd/fy; span/depth 7/20/26 (35/40 two-way); τc,max 2.8 (M20); sv ≤ 0.75d/300; Ld ≈ 47φ (Fe415-M20); column 0.4fckAc+0.67fyAsc, emin ≥ 20; ties min(least dim, 16φ, 300); punching d/2.

Card 3 — Steel LSM numbers

fd = fy/1.10; bolts min pitch 2.5d, Vdsb = fu·Anb/(√3·γmb); HSFG friction; fillet throat 0.7s, fu/√3; lap 4t/40; tension min(gross, 0.9fuAn/1.25, block); λ ≤ 180 comp / 400 tension; curves a–d; bearing 0.45fck; classes plastic→slender.

Card 4 — Prestress, timber, masonry

PT losses 15–20% (friction+slip PT only); w_bal = 8Pe/L²; strands 1570–1860 MPa, M30+; timber: horizontal shear critical; masonry: SR ≤ 27, prism ≪ unit, 5 failure modes, NBC 201 bands, confined masonry best.

Rational Comprehension Questions (guess smart when unsure)

  • "Which failure is ductile?" — under-reinforced (steel yields before concrete crushes); pick the under-reinforced answer in safety questions.
  • "What improves ductility?" — more confinement (tighter stirrups) and under-reinforcing.
  • "What reduces creep?" — lower sustained stress ratio, stiffer aggregate, steam curing.
  • "Why 135° stirrup hooks?" — they stay closed when cover spalls (seismic anchorage).
  • "Why laps away from max moment?" — laps are weak points; place near inflection/low-stress zones and stagger.
  • "Why grout PT ducts?" — bond + strand corrosion protection.
  • "Why camber?" — precamber offsets dead-load deflection and creep.
  • "Why temperature steel both ways?" — shrinkage/thermal cracking is biaxial; main steel handles flexure only.
  • "Why 0.8% minimum column steel?" — carries load released by creeping/cracking concrete; guards against sudden brittle failure.
  • "Why λ ≤ 180?" — limits imperfection sensitivity and corrosion section loss.

Terminology Glossary (direct one-markers)

TermMeaning
Characteristic loadValue with ≤5% exceedance probability in the design life
Partial safety factorDivides characteristic strength / multiplies load (γm, γf)
Balanced sectionConcrete & steel reach their limits simultaneously (xu = xu,max)
Under-reinforcedSteel yields first — ductile warning (required practice)
Over-reinforcedConcrete crushes first — brittle (avoid)
Anchorage lengthLd — embedment that develops bar strength without pullout
Effective depth dExtreme compression fibre → centroid of tension steel
Neutral axisZero-stress fibre; shifts as cracking develops
Punching shearTwo-way shear cone around a concentrated load/column
Modular ratioEs/Ec (WSM cracked-section transform)
Shape factorZp/Z (plastic vs elastic modulus)
Slenderness ratioLe/r (steel) or heff/t (masonry)
HSFGHigh-strength friction-grip bolt — slip-critical, pre-tensioned
Confined masonryPanels framed by RC tie-columns & bond beams
Soft storeyStorey much less stiff than those above — seismic collapse pattern
Response reduction factor RDivides the elastic seismic force for inelastic capacity & ductility

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (5.1–5.6)

Loads & Load Combinations (5.1) — Course Code Map

LoadIS CodeNBC
Dead Load (unit weights of materials)IS 875 (Part 1): 2015NBC 102
Imposed (Live) LoadIS 875 (Part 2): 2015NBC 103
Wind LoadIS 875 (Part 3)NBC 104
Snow LoadIS 875 (Part 4)NBC 106
Earthquake LoadIS 1893: 2016NBC 105
  • Imposed load on roofs: for slopes > 10°, reduce by 0.02 kN/m² for every degree rise in slope, but never less than 0.4 kN/m².
  • Wind: basic wind speed 47 m/s (below 3000 m altitude) and 55 m/s (above) — peak 3-second gust, 50-year return. Vz = Vb·k1·k2·k3 (k1 risk, k2 height-terrain, k3 topography); course example: k1 = k3 = 1, k2 ≈ 1.05.
  • Snow load: S = μ·So; minimum roof slope for snow shedding 2:1 (V:H); roofs steeper than 60° (course value; some older refs 50°) need no snow load. Scaling example: μ = 0.75 → 1.5 kN/m², so μ = 0.6 → 1.2 kN/m².
  • Earthquake: soil types A (stiff/hard), B (medium), C (soft), D (very soft). Seismic coefficient method: Ah = (Z·I/2R)·(Sa/g); VB = Ah·W. Design philosophy: minor frequent shaking — no damage to main members; moderate occasional — repairable; strong rare — no collapse.
  • Load combinations (IS 456): Strength — 1.5(DL+LL); 1.5(DL+WL); 1.2(DL+LL+WL); 1.5(DL+EL); 1.2(DL+LL+EL). Serviceability — DL+LL (1.0/1.0); with WL/EL: LL factor 0.8, DL 1.0. Overturning/stability: 0.9DL + 1.5WL (or 1.5EL).
  • Course numerical: DL = 100, LL = 60, WL = 80, EL = 200 kN → 1.5(DL+LL) = 240; 1.5(DL+EL) = 450; 1.2(DL+LL+EL) = 432; 1.2(DL+LL+WL) = 288 → 450 kN governs.

Concrete Technology (5.2) — Course Values

  • Grades: ordinary M10–M20, standard M25–M60, high strength M65+. Mean target strength ft = fck + 1.65S (5% defectives).
  • Moduli: E = 5000√fck; flexural fcr = 0.7√fck; splitting tensile T = 2P/(πLD); flexural test fb = Pl/bd².
  • Workability by compaction factor: very low 0.78–0.80, low 0.80–0.85, medium 0.85–0.95, high 0.95–1.0.
  • Mix design: w/c governs strength (Abrams); nominal mixes M5–M25; designed mixes M20+; σ = 3.5 (M10–M15), 4.0 (M20–M25), 5.0 (M30–M50) when not established.
  • Quality control: cube 150 mm, 28 days at 27 ± 2 °C; acceptance — mean of group ≥ fck + 0.825·S; individual ≥ fck − 3 MPa (M15–M30) / − 4 MPa (M35+).

RCC Design (5.3–5.4) — Course Facts

  • Limit-state moment of resistance (balanced): Mu = 0.36 fck·b·xu(d − 0.42xu); xu,max/d = 0.53 (Fe250), 0.48 (Fe415), 0.46 (Fe500).
  • Span/depth ratios (deflection control): one-way slab — SS 20, continuous 26, cantilever 7; two-way slab — SS 35, continuous 40.
  • Columns: short le/D < 12, slender ≥ 12; minimum eccentricity e = Le/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm.
  • Effective lengths: both fixed 0.5L; fixed–hinged 0.7L; both hinged 1.0L; fixed–free 2.0L.
  • Prestressed: losses — elastic shortening, creep, shrinkage, relaxation, anchorage slip, friction (wobble + curvature); Grade 1 = no tensile stress at service; post-tensioning cuts losses by staged stressing.
  • Footings: isolated, combined, raft/mat; one-way shear at d from the face, two-way (punching) at d/2.

Steel Structures (5.5) — Course Facts

  • Section codes: IS 808:1989 hot-rolled; IS 811:1987 cold-formed; IS 800:2007 general (limit state).
  • Bolts: ordinary (black) — bearing type; HSFG — friction grip, no slip, better fatigue. Bolt value = least of shear, bearing, tension. Pitch ≤ 32t or 300 mm; edge ≥ 1.5×hole dia.
  • Welds: fillet ≥ 3 mm; throat 0.7×size; design shear 110 MPa (shop); length = force/(0.7s·fw).
  • Ties: yield (Tdg = Ag·fy/γm0) vs rupture; struts: buckling curves a/b/c/d; column bases distribute load to concrete (bearing 0.45fck).
  • Built-up: lacing/battens; lacing angle 40–70°; lacing slenderness ≤ 145.

Timber & Masonry (5.6) — Course Facts

  • Timber beams: σb = M/Z with moisture/duration/size factors; columns: λ = Le/least side, permissible stress falls as λ rises.
  • Masonry per IS 1905 / NBC 109 — mortar grades (H1, H2, M1, M2, L1, L2 — H strongest); stress reduction for slenderness and eccentricity.
  • Failure modes: flexural tensile cracking, diagonal shear (in-plane), bed-joint sliding, corner/toe crushing, vertical compression cracking; out-of-plane overturning in earthquakes — bands and tie-columns mitigate.
  • Mortar: mud (lowest, rural), lime (slow, self-healing), cement 1:6 (strong, stiff), composite lime-cement; masonry density ≈ 19–20 kN/m³.
  • NBC 205:2024 (MRT, latest): brick 230 × 115 × 57 mm for a 10 mm joint — NBC 109:1994 Table 3.1 gives 240 × 115 × 57 mm; minimum RC bands at plinth, sill, lintel, roof; load-bearing walls ≥ 230 mm (NBC 202 MRT); opening limits within bands.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): the roof imposed-load reduction is 0.02 kN/m² per degree above 10° with a 0.4 kN/m² floor; snow-exempt slope 60° (course) vs 50° (older refs); soil-type lettering (A = stiff/hard, D = very soft); effective-length pairs (0.5L/0.7L/1.0L/2.0L); span/depth 35 vs 40 for two-way slabs; M-grade boundary at M25 between ordinary and standard.
