NEC License Exam (1-Mark MCQ Focus) | NEC prep-course edition — v5.5

This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

6.1 Water Sources, Water Quality and Water Demand (ACiE0601)

A. Sources of Water

SurfaceGroundwaterRain
Rivers/streams, lakes/ponds, reservoirs, canals, sea (desalination)Wells (dug/tube), springs, infiltration galleries, artesian aquifersRainwater harvesting (roof/catchment + tanks)
Advantages: large quantity, easy access. Disadvantages: turbidity, pathogens, seasonal variation, needs full treatmentAdvantages: good quality (naturally filtered), steady temperature. Disadvantages: hardness/minerals, arsenic/iron risk, over-pumpingSoft, low TDS; storage needed; first-flush contamination
  • Selection factors: quantity (demand vs yield), quality (treatment needed), distance/elevation (pumping vs gravity), reliability (drought), cost, pollution risk (upstream sewage, industry), legal/environmental clearance.
  • Nepal context: hills — spring sources (gravity schemes); Terai — groundwater (tube wells; arsenic in the Terai alluvium); Kathmandu — surface reservoirs plus deep wells (over-extracted).

B. Water Quality — Impurities

TypeExamplesRemoval
SuspendedSilt, clay, algae (turbidity, colour)Sedimentation + filtration
ColloidalFine clay, organic colourCoagulation-flocculation then settling
DissolvedSalts (Ca, Mg, Fe, Mn, F, As, NO₃), gases (CO₂, H₂S, O₂)Softening, aeration, adsorption, RO
BiologicalBacteria, viruses, protozoa (Giardia, Cryptosporidium), wormsDisinfection, filtration

Key quality parameters & units

  • Turbidity: NTU (nephelometric); drinking standard < 5 NTU (1 NTU ideal for effective chlorination).
  • pH: 6.5–8.5 acceptable (neutral 7); corrosion below 6.5; incrustation above 8.5.
  • Hardness: as mg/L CaCO₃ — soft < 75, moderately hard 75–150, hard 150–300, very hard > 300; acceptable 200, permissible 600 (IS 10500); causes scale and soap waste but no health effect.
  • Alkalinity: capacity to neutralize acid — bicarbonate, carbonate, hydroxide (mg/L CaCO₃); measured by phenolphthalein (P) and methyl orange (total T) titrations. Relations: P = 0 → all bicarbonate; P < T/2 → carbonate + bicarbonate; P = T/2 → carbonate only; P > T/2 → hydroxide + carbonate; P = T → hydroxide only.
  • Iron > 0.3 mg/L (taste, staining); manganese > 0.1; fluoride 1.0 mg/L ideal, max 1.5 (dental fluorosis above 1.5; skeletal above 10; deficiency below 0.6 → dental caries); arsenic 0.05 (Nepal NS) / 0.01 WHO (skin lesions, cancer — Terai tube wells); nitrate < 45–50 mg/L (blue-baby syndrome — methemoglobinemia); TDS ≈ 500 mg/L acceptable, 1000–1500 max (WHO palatability: excellent < 300, good 300–600, fair 600–900, poor 900–1200).
  • DO: clean water 6–8 mg/L; saturation ≈ 9 mg/L at 20 °C; fish stress below 4; measured by the Winkler (iodometric) test or membrane electrode.
  • BOD (5-day at 20 °C): oxygen consumed by bacteria decomposing organics; strong sewage 300+ mg/L; Nepal treated-effluent standard < 30 mg/L. For k = 0.1/day (base 10): BOD₅ ≈ 68% of the ultimate BOD L₀.
  • COD: dichromate chemical oxidation (hours vs 5 days); COD > BOD always; COD/BOD < 3 indicates easily biodegradable waste.
  • Coliform — MPN test (most probable number, statistical tubes) or membrane filtration; E. coli = fecal indicator; drinking water 0 cfu/100 mL.
  • Waterborne diseases: cholera, typhoid, bacillary dysentery (bacteria); hepatitis A, polio (viruses); amoebic dysentery, giardiasis (protozoa); roundworm, guinea worm (helminths). Malaria and dengue are water-related vector diseases, not ingested.

C. Drinking Water Standards (NS / WHO)

  • Essential: fecal coliform 0, turbidity < 5 NTU (goal 1), pH 6.5–8.5, residual chlorine ≥ 0.2 mg/L free residual after 30 min contact (Nepal RWSS minimum 0.1–0.2 mg/L; design commonly 0.2–0.5 mg/L at the tap).
  • WHO categories: no health-based guideline (TDS, hardness, iron — aesthetic), health-based (arsenic, nitrate, fluoride, lead), aesthetic.

D. Water Demand

Fig 6.1 — Water demand components: domestic dominates; losses 15–20%; peak factors 1.8 / 2.7
ComponentLPCD (litres/person/day)
Nepal rural (basic access, Level 1)45 (public standpost within 15 min walk)
Nepal intermediate (Level 2)65 (private/yard connections)
Nepal urban design (NWSC practice)70–100; production target ≈ 100–135 incl. all uses
WHO basic requirement20 (minimum access); 50 (low health concern)
India CPHEEO (design)135 with sewerage; 70 without flushing
Total demand Q = Population × per-capita rate (LPCD)
Fire demand (Q in L/min, P in thousands): Kuichling Q = 3182√P ; Buston Q = 5663√P ; Freeman Q = 1136(P/10 + 10) ; National Board of Fire Underwriters Q = 4637√P(1 − 0.01√P)
Design population: Pn = P0(1 + r/100)^n (compound/geometric growth)
Peak factors: maximum daily = 1.8 × average ; maximum hourly = 2.7 × average (= 1.5 × max daily)
  • Components: domestic (~50%, the largest), industrial, commercial/institutional, public (fire, street washing, fountains), losses & wastage (15–20% leakage), fire reserve.
  • Design period: overall 20–30 years; by component — distribution mains 30, source works 30, treatment units 15, pumps 15, reservoirs 30 years.
  • Population forecasting methods: arithmetic (constant increment — old, saturated cities), geometric (constant % growth — young, fast-growing cities), decreasing rate of increase, logistic, master-plan, ratio/correlation with regional cities, density-based. Choose by city age/type — a standard method-matching MCQ.
  • Estimation of water demand
    • 1. Domestic demand: Accounts for 55–60% of total demand. Rates: Rural (45 lpcd), Semi-urban (65 lpcd), Urban (112 lpcd).
    • 2. Livestock demand: Applicable to rural areas only; estimated at ≤ 20% of domestic demand. Rates: Big animals (45 L/day), Medium animals (20 L/day), Birds (0.2 L/day).
    • 3. Industrial demand: Applicable to urban areas only; accounts for 20–25% of total demand.
    • 4. Public or municipal demand: Accounts for 5–10% of total demand (includes street washing, watering parks/gardens, public fountains, and fire hydrants).
    • 5. Institutional and commercial demand: Day scholars (10 lpcd), Boarders (65 lpcd), Offices (500–1000 L/day), Hospitals with beds (500 L/bed/day), Hospitals without beds (2500 L/day), Hotels with beds (200 L/bed/day), Hotels/restaurants without beds (500–1000 L/day).
    • 6. Fire demand: Estimated using empirical formulas (where P = population in thousands, Q = demand in L/min):
      • Kuichling: Q = 3182√P
      • Buston: Q = 5663√P
      • Freeman: Q = 1136(P/10 + 10)
      • NBFU: Q = 4637√P(1 − 0.01√P)
    • 7. Losses and wastage: Accounts for 15–20% of total demand (leakage from mains, service connections, reservoirs, and overflows). This is added on top of all other calculated demands.
Water-related disease classification: Waterborne (ingested — cholera, typhoid); Water-washed (hygiene lack — trachoma, scabies, diarrhoea); Water-based (host in water — schistosomiasis, guinea worm); Water-related insect vector (breeding — malaria, dengue, filariasis). Classic one-mark question!
6.1 must-knows: rural 45 lpcd, urban design ≈ 100–135; max daily = 1.8× avg, max hourly = 2.7× avg; losses 15–20%; fire demand (P in thousands): Kuichling 3182√P, Buston 5663√P; Pn = P0(1 + r/100)^n; essential standards: fecal coliform 0, turbidity < 5 NTU, pH 6.5–8.5, free Cl₂ residual ≥ 0.2 mg/L after 30 min; fluoride ideal 1.0 max 1.5, arsenic 0.05 (NS)/0.01 (WHO), nitrate < 45; BOD₅ ≈ 68% of L₀ (k = 0.1/d, base 10); COD > BOD always; design periods — treatment units & pumps 15 yr, mains & reservoirs 30 yr.

6.2 Intake and Distribution Systems (ACiE0602)

A. Intakes

  • Types: river/lake/reservoir/canal intakes; submerged (simple bell-mouth on a pipe), wet intake (well full of water), dry intake (water in the pipe only), tower (reservoir multi-level gates for quality), spring boxes, infiltration galleries (river-bed laterals), jack wells with causeways.
  • Location factors: best-quality water (upstream of sewage outfalls), adequate depth (avoid ice/silt), current (scour vs deposition), navigation clearance, flood immunity, power/pump access, sound foundation (rock best), low approach velocity 0.1–0.3 m/s (avoids drawing in fish and debris).
  • Components: coarse rack screens (bar spacing ~50–100 mm), fine screens (20–40 mm), sluice valves, bell-mouth entry.

B. Pipes, Joints, Valves, Fittings

Pipe materialUse / note
Cast/ductile iron (CI/DI)Strong, life ≈ 100 yr (DI > 100); corrodes (tuberculation) — cement-mortar lined; DI for high-pressure mains
SteelHigh pressure, large dia; corrodes — needs coating; flexible (settlement areas)
GI (galvanized iron)Small service connections (15–50 mm); rusts over time — replaced by PE/PVC
PVC/UPVCLight, corrosion-free, smooth (C = 150); UV degradation; solvent-weld/ring joints — distribution
HDPEFlexible, fused (leak-free) joints; rural supply, trenchless
RCC/PCCPLarge gravity/transmission mains; heads up to ~100 m (prestressed); rigid, heavy; life ≈ 75 yr
Asbestos cement (AC)Legacy (health concern — phased out)
JointUse
Socket & spigot (caulked lead/cement)CI — old, nearly rigid, slight deflection
FlangedHigh pressure, exposed plant (valves/pumps) — rigid, not usually buried
Mechanical (gland) / push-on rubber gasketModern DI — quick, flexible
Solvent weld / fusionPVC / HDPE (electrofusion is leak-free)
Expansion jointsThermal movement (exposed steel)
ValveFunction
Sluice (gate) valveIsolate sections — full bore, low loss
Butterfly valveCompact isolation/regulation — quarter turn
Globe valveRegulation (high loss) — throttling
Check (reflux/NRV)One-way flow — pump discharge, prevents backflow
Air relief valveAt summits — releases trapped air (prevents air lock)
Scour/blow-off (washout) valveAt valleys — drains sediment, flushes
Pressure reducing valve (PRV)Reduces excess pressure in downhill zones
Pressure sustaining/relief/surge valvesProtect mains from over-pressure/transients
Ball/float valveReservoir/tank level control (automatic shutoff)
  • Hydrants: fire — spacing 100–150 m, fed by pipes ≥ 100–150 mm dia; public/private, wet/dry barrel.
  • Water meters: velocity (turbine/propeller), positive displacement (piston/rotary — domestic standard), electromagnetic/ultrasonic (bulk, no obstruction); class B/C accuracy.

C. Break Pressure Tanks & Service Reservoirs

  • Break pressure tank (BPT): in gravity systems with large elevation drop — Nepal RWSS limits static pressure to ≈ 60 m, so a BPT goes wherever the static head would exceed the limit. Operates by float valve/overflow; no storage intent (small tank).
  • Service reservoirs: balance hourly demand fluctuation, hold emergency/fire storage, maintain pressure; located high (elevated tanks/towers) or on ground at a hill.
    • Storage capacity ≈ ⅓ to ½ (33–50%) of the maximum daily demand (24-hr supply schemes)
    Balancing storage by mass curve (cumulative supply vs demand — the maximum vertical gap)
    Make-up: balancing 30–40% + emergency 10–15% + fire storage per code (1–4 hr fire flow)
  • Types: underground (easy cleaning, saves land), semi-underground, elevated (steel/RC — costlier, pressure assured), standpipes; roof tanks for buildings.
  • Design details: inlet with float/altitude valve, bottom outlet, overflow & scour, screened vent, manholes, water-tightness (IS 3370 crack width 0.2 mm), floor sloped 1:100 to the outlet.

D. Distribution Systems

SystemDescription
Dead-end (branch/tree)Simple, cheap, low pressure at ends; stagnation at dead ends — needs washouts; one break cuts all downstream
Grid-iron (reticulation)Loops everywhere — no dead ends, multiple paths; more pipes/valves; best service (grid-street cities)
Ring (peripheral/loop)Main ring around the area + branches inside — reliable, medium cost (small towns)
RadialDistribution from a central elevated reservoir in spokes — good pressure, shortest mains (planned sectors)
Fig 6.2 — Distribution-network layouts: dead-end, grid-iron, ring and radial systems at a glance
Pressure schemePros/cons
Direct pumping (little storage)Power-dependent; pumps sized for peaks; costly energy; fails on outage
Gravity (source/reservoir high)No energy, reliable, needs elevation — ideal in Nepal hills
Combined (pump to reservoir, gravity down)Standard — pumps run steady (efficient), reservoir balances peaks
  • Design pressures: minimum residual at the farthest consumer ≈ 8–10 m; Nepal guideline residual heads: ≥ 10 m at peak-hourly-of-average-day, ≥ 5 m at peak-hourly-of-max-day (0 m at hydrants while fire engines pump); add ≈ 3 m per additional floor; maximum static at fixtures ≈ 60 m; average network design pressure 15–25 m.
  • Hydraulic design: Hazen-Williams/Hardy Cross (Ch 3); velocities 0.3–3 m/s (0.6 m/s minimum only for untreated water); pipe sizes — mains ≥ 100 mm (fire requirement), branches 50–80 mm, practical minimum tertiary 50–63 mm PVC.
  • Analysis: EPANET (gradient method) or hand Hardy-Cross; nodal demands at peak hourly + fire at the critical point; check residual pressures ≥ minimum.
  • Glossary: Hardy Cross = hand loop-balancing iteration; EPANET = the standard network solver (gradient method) — the "computer answer" in MCQs.
  • Leakage & NRW (non-revenue water): NRW = production − billed; Nepal NWSC historically 30–40%, now ≈ 25%; target < 20%; components are physical leakage + commercial losses (metering, theft).
  • Water-hammer protection on mains: slow-closing valves, surge vessels (Ch 3).
6.2 must-knows: BPT wherever static head would exceed ≈ 60 m; service reservoir ⅓–½ of max daily demand (balancing 30–40% + emergency 10–15%); residuals ≥ 10 m (peak-hourly-of-avg-day), ≥ 5 m (of max-day), + 3 m per extra floor; mains ≥ 100 mm, branches 50–80 mm; velocities 0.3–3 m/s (0.6 for untreated water); layouts — dead end cheap/stagnates, grid-iron no dead ends, ring medium, radial good pressure from a central reservoir; air valves at summits, scour at valleys; NRW ≈ 25% (NWSC), target < 20%.

6.3 Water Treatment Process and Technologies (ACiE0603)

A. Treatment Train (conventional surface water)

Fig 6.3 — Conventional surface-water treatment train with design values

Raw water → screening → plain sedimentation (if very turbid) → aeration (if Fe/Mn/gases) → coagulation-flocculation → sedimentation (clarifier) → filtration (rapid sand) → disinfection (chlorination) → storage/distribution. Groundwater often needs only aeration + disinfection (iron removal) or softening.

B. Individual Processes

Screening

  • Coarse (bar) screens with spacing > 50 mm remove large debris at the intake; fine screens/micro-strainers (< 20 mm mesh) catch algae; self-cleaning rakes.

Plain sedimentation

Stokes (laminar, Re < 1): vs = g(G−1)d²/(18ν)
Transition region: Newton/transition laws; overflow rate vo = Q/A (m³/m²·day) — particles with vs ≥ vo are fully removed
Detention time t = V/Q ; weir loading rate = Q/weir length
  • Settling classes: discrete (Type I — Stokes), flocculent (Type II), hindered/zone (Type III — high concentration), compression (Type IV).
  • Design (plain sedimentation): detention 4–8 hr, surface overflow rate ≈ 15–30 m³/m²·d.
  • Ideal-basin removal: a particle with vs ≥ vo is completely removed; for vs < vo the removed fraction ∝ vs/vo.

Sedimentation with coagulation (clarifiers)

Optimum coagulant dose by jar test (4–6 beakers, varying dose, identical mixing)
Common coagulants: alum Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O (optimum pH 6.5–8.5), ferrous sulfate + lime, ferric chloride/sulfate (wide pH range), PACl (pre-polymerized, pH-insensitive)
Coagulant aids: bentonite (turbidity), polyelectrolytes (floc strengthening)
Rapid mix 30–60 s (G ≈ 700–1000 s⁻¹) ; flocculation 20–30 min (G ≈ 20–80 s⁻¹, Gt ≈ 2–7×10⁴)
  • Clariflocculator: combined paddle flocculation + circular clarification with scraper; hopper-bottom (upflow) clarifiers and solids-contact (sludge-blanket pulsator) types exist.
  • Clarifier design: detention 2–2.5 hr, surface overflow 30–40 m³/m²·d, weir loading ≤ 300 m³/m·d.
  • Alum reacts with alkalinity: Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Ca(HCO₃)₂ → 2Al(OH)₃↓ + 3CaSO₄ + 6CO₂. Each mg/L of alum consumes ≈ 0.5 mg/L alkalinity as CaCO₃ and drops the pH — if natural alkalinity is insufficient, add lime or soda ash.
  • Sludge handling: scraper → sump → drying beds/lagoons; ≈ 0.5–1% solids.

Flocculation

  • Gentle agitation grows the floc: paddle flocculators G = 20–80 s⁻¹ (tapering), t = 20–30 min; hydraulic baffle channels t = 15–30 min, Gt = 2–7×10⁴; visible floc grows to ≈ 0.1–3 mm.
  • G & Gt: G = velocity gradient (mixing intensity, s⁻¹); Gt = G × detention time — rapid mixing wants a big G for seconds, flocculation a gentle G for minutes.

Filtration

FilterRate / mediaNotes
Slow sand0.1–0.2 m³/m²/hr (100–200 L/m²/hr)Biological layer (schmutzdecke) removes bacteria too; rural small schemes; cleaning = scraping the top 1–2 cm; feed turbidity < 50 NTU; large land area
Rapid sand (gravity)3–6 m³/m²/hr (3000–6000 L/m²/hr)Needs coagulated water; sand effective size 0.45–0.7 mm, uniformity coefficient 1.3–1.7; bed 60–90 cm over 45–60 cm gravel; backwash 30–60 m/hr (about 4% of filtered water), air scour + water; run 24–48 hr to terminal head loss 1.8–2.5 m
Pressure filterRapid media in a steel shellSmall plants/pumping direct; no gravity clear well
Dual / multimediaAnthracite+sand / +garnetHigher rates (10–20 m/hr), longer runs, coarse-to-fine top
Activated carbon (GAC/PAC)AdsorptionOdour/taste, organics, chlorine residuals, pesticides
Membrane (UF/NF/RO)Pressure-driven sievingTurbidity/bacteria (UF), hardness/ions (NF/RO); chemical-free; fouling management
Fig 6.4 — Slow vs rapid sand filter: layer build-ups, depths, loading rates (30× apart) and cleaning methods
  • Filter parts: underdrains (perforated pipe manifold or false floor/Wheeler), graded gravel support (45–60 cm), media, backwash troughs, rate controllers (constant-rate or declining-rate). Negative head develops if operation continues past the terminal loss (air binding from released DO — prevent by timely backwash and deeper water cover).
  • Backwash design: bed expansion 30–50%; backwash rate 30–60 m/hr ≈ 8–17 L/s/m² (commonly 10–15 — about 5–20× the filtration rate, typically ~6×); wash water ≈ 4% of production.

Disinfection

Chlorine chemistry: Cl₂ + H₂O → HOCl + HCl ; HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻
HOCl (hypochlorous acid) is the stronger biocide — dominant at pH < 7 (lower pH = better kill)
Breakpoint chlorination: dose ↑ → combined residuals (chloramines) rise, fall to a minimum, then free residual appears past the "breakpoint"
Chick's law: N = N₀e^(−kt) ; Watson: Ct concept (residual × contact time)
  • Agents: chlorine gas (100% Cl₂, cheap, hazardous), bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl (≈ 30–35% available chlorine), calcium hypochlorite (65–70%), chloramines (long-lasting residual, weaker — distribution networks), chlorine dioxide, ozone (powerful, no residual — follow with chlorine), UV (no residual, needs clear water), boiling (household).
  • Types: plain, pre-, post-, super-/breakpoint, double, dechlorination (sulfur dioxide/SMBS); ammonia + chlorine = chloramine (combined residual).
  • Contact: 30 min with ≥ 0.2 mg/L free residual (design 0.2–0.5 mg/L); CT values per organism (Giardia needs high CT, viruses moderate).
  • Chlorine demand = dose − residual; THMs (chloroform family) form from chlorine + organics — regulated byproducts; minimize by precursor removal (coagulation/GAC) or alternative disinfectants.
  • Dechlorination: sodium thiosulfate or sulfur dioxide; superchlorination-dechlorination for badly polluted water.

Softening

  • Lime-soda: lime removes carbonate hardness of Ca and Mg (Mg precipitates as Mg(OH)₂ near pH 10.5); soda ash removes non-carbonate calcium hardness; excess lime is stabilized by recarbonation (CO₂). Removes both hardness classes; large plants; much sludge.
  • Zeolite (ion exchange, base exchange): Na₂Z resin exchanges Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺; regenerated with brine (NaCl); near-zero residual hardness (blend with raw water); compact; brine disposal issue; H⁺-form demineralizers serve boilers.
  • Miscellaneous: aeration (strips CO₂/H₂S; oxidizes Fe²⁺→Fe³⁺ and Mn²⁺ — then filter; cascade/tray/diffused-air), Fe/Mn removal (aeration + settling/filter; greensand; pH adjustment), colour/odour/taste removal (GAC, ozonation, aeration; CuSO₄ ≈ 0.3 mg/L as reservoir algaecide), fluoridation/defluoridation (Nalgonda technique — alum + lime; activated alumina also takes arsenic), arsenic removal (oxidation + coagulation/activated alumina/iron nails — the Nepal Kanchan filter), iron removal plants (Nepal rural standard), household biosand filters.
6.3 must-knows: train = screen → aeration → rapid mix 30–60 s (G 700–1000) → flocculation 20–30 min (G 20–80) → sedimentation 2–2.5 h (30–40 m³/m²·d) → rapid sand 3000–6000 L/m²/hr (ES 0.45–0.7, UC 1.3–1.7, backwash 30–60 m/hr ≈ 4% of production) → chlorination 30 min, free residual ≥ 0.2 mg/L; 1 mg/L alum consumes 0.5 mg/L alkalinity as CaCO₃; slow sand = biological, scraped, feed < 50 NTU; HOCl (stronger biocide) dominates at pH < 7; breakpoint = dose where free residual first appears; THMs = chlorine + organics byproducts; lime-soda removes both hardness classes, zeolite = ion exchange regenerated by brine.

6.4 Design and Construction of Sewers (ACiE0604)

A. Wastewater Quantities

  • Sewage quantity ≈ 80% of the water supply (return factor 0.8) + infiltration/inflow; commercial/industrial flows add; storm is excluded in separate systems.
  • Dry weather flow (DWF) = domestic + industrial + institutional + infiltration; wet weather adds storm (combined system).
  • Peak factor: sewage peaks are higher than water peaks (smaller networks): PF = 1.5–3 (CPHEEO allows up to 3.0 for small populations; Harmon formula PF = (18 + √P)/(4 + √P), P in thousands). Use 2–3 typically — Nepal practice 2–4, higher for small areas.

B. Sewerage Systems

SystemDescription / when
SeparateTwo networks — sanitary + storm drains; treatment efficient (smaller, concentrated flow); duplicate pipes cost more; modern standard
CombinedOne pipe carries all flows — economical piping but a large dilute treatment plant; CSO (combined sewer overflow) pollutes in storms; old cities
Partially separateSanitary + roof/street-wash storm; a compromise mix

C. Sewer Design Criteria

Manning: Q = (1/n)A R^(2/3) S^(1/2) — gravity sewers; n = 0.013 (concrete sewer)
Self-cleansing velocity: ≥ 0.6 m/s — checked at the minimum/nominated flow (a low-flow criterion), not peak — prevents deposition
Non-scouring limit: ≤ 3.0 m/s
Circular hydraulic elements: maximum DISCHARGE at d/D = 0.95 ; maximum VELOCITY at d/D = 0.81
Slope: steep enough for 0.6 m/s at design flow; flat starts are problematic
  • Design flow: peak hourly sewage (PF applied); pipes sized to run ½–¾ full (max design depth d/D = 0.75–0.8 — never full; the space above provides ventilation margin).
  • Minimum sewer size: 150 mm laterals (200+ mm mains); minimum cover 1.0 m (0.9–1.2 m under traffic); manhole spacing: 30 m for small sewers up to 150 m+ for large (≤ 0.3 m dia → 30 m; ≥ 1.2 m → 150–300 m).
  • Alignment: straight between manholes (avoid curves), follow the natural slope, cross below water mains with 0.5–1 m clearance (water mains stay above), avoid foundation proximity.
  • Survey: invert levels manhole to manhole; partial-flow diagrams (d/D vs Q/Qfull and v/vfull — the hydraulic-elements chart).

D. Shapes of Sewers

Fig 6.5 — Sewer shapes: circular, egg-shaped, horseshoe — partial-flow depths and why each is chosen
ShapeMerit
CircularBest hydraulic radius (max flow per area), structural strength — the standard
Egg-shaped (ovoid)Narrow invert keeps low flows fast — old combined sewers
Rectangular/boxLarge storm drains, tunnels; easy formwork
Horseshoe/archTunnels; good structural shape
Parabolic/U-shapedSpecial storm channels

E. Sewer Materials & Appurtenances

  • Materials: vitrified clay (corrosion-proof, brittle — small sewers), RCC/Hume (large mains), stoneware, PVC/HDPE (small modern), ductile iron (pressure/force mains), brick (old large sewers), GRP. Acid/sulphide resistance matters: H₂S → H₂SO₄ causes biogenic crown corrosion above the waterline — ventilate, use resistant materials, keep velocity up.
  • Joints: flexible rubber-gasket (modern), rigid cement (clay); infiltration/exfiltration controlled by water tests against code limits.
  • Appurtenances:
  • Manholes: at changes of grade/size/direction and at regular spacing (30 m small sewers); chambers with steps and heavy covers; drop manhole when the inlet sits > 0.6 m above the outlet (avoids scour); deep manholes for large sewers.
  • Catch basins/gullies (storm inlets), cleanouts, lamp holes (old), flush tanks, street inlets, inverted siphons (depressed sewer under a river/road — always full, needs scour velocity, two/three barrels), outfalls with screens.
  • Pumping stations (lift stations): wet well + pumps (submersible common), standby power, screening, controls; force mains pressurized at 0.6–3 m/s (min 0.6 to keep solids moving).
  • Construction: trenching (shoring/sloping), granular bedding, laying to laser grade, joint testing, backfill compaction; trenchless methods (microtunneling, pipe jacking) under roads/rivers; small-bore and simplified sewerage (solids-free/settled sewerage with interceptors) as low-cost Nepal options.
    • Fig 6.6 — Manhole with drop connection (inlet > 0.6 m above outlet) and the always-full inverted siphon under an obstruction
6.4 must-knows: sewage ≈ 80% of water supply; PF 1.5–3 (Harmon = (18+√P)/(4+√P), P in thousands); Manning n = 0.013; self-cleansing ≥ 0.6 m/s, non-scouring ≤ 3.0 m/s; Qmax at d/D = 0.95, vmax at 0.81D; design depth 0.75–0.8 D; min size 150 mm, min cover 1.0 m; manhole spacing 30 m (small sewers); drop manhole when inlet > 0.6 m above outlet; inverted siphon = depressed sewer, always full; H₂S → H₂SO₄ = crown corrosion above the waterline; separate = modern standard, combined = CSO risk.

6.5 Treatment and Disposal of Wastewater (ACiE0605)

A. Sewage Characteristics

  • Physical: temperature, colour (grey fresh → black septic), odour (H₂S rotten egg — septic), turbidity, solids (total, suspended, dissolved, settleable — Imhoff cone, 45–60 min settling).
  • Chemical: pH (fresh 7.3–7.5 alkaline; septic < 6.5); domestic BOD₅ ≈ 150 (weak) / 300 (medium) / 500 (strong) mg/L; COD ≈ 2–2.5× BOD; nitrogen (organic + NH₃ + NO₃ = TKN), phosphorus (detergents), chlorides, fats/oils/grease, sulphides.
  • Biological: pathogens — fecal coliform 10⁵–10⁸ MPN per 100 mL (millions).
  • Decomposition: aerobic (O₂ present → CO₂, NO₃ — fast, no odour, stable) vs anaerobic (→ CH₄, CO₂, H₂S, NH₃ — slower, odorous, yields biogas); facultative in between; septic = anaerobic dominance.
  • Nutrient cycles: nitrogen (organic → NH₃ → NO₂ → NO₃ nitrification; denitrification → N₂), carbon (→ CO₂/CH₄), sulphur (→ H₂S/SO₄).

B. Primary Treatment

  • Screening: coarse screens (> 50 mm spacing) + comminutors/shredders (cut solids, return to flow).
  • Grit chamber: horizontal-flow (constant velocity ≈ 0.3 m/s via proportional/Sutro weirs) or aerated (spiral roll); removes inorganic grit ≥ 0.2 mm (SG 2.65) protecting pumps; detention 40–60 s horizontal, 2–5 min aerated; velocity controlled so organic particles (low settling velocity) stay suspended; grit washer downstream.
  • Primary sedimentation (clarifier): detention 1.5–2.5 hr (2 hr typical); removes ≈ 60–65% SS and 30–35% BOD; circular (centre-feed scraper) or rectangular (chain-flight); primary sludge 4–6% solids to digesters.

C. Secondary (Biological) Treatment

ProcessPrincipleBOD removal / notes
Activated Sludge Process (ASP)Aerated suspended growth; return sludge; MLSS 1500–3000 mg/L; F/M 0.2–0.4 kg BOD/kg MLSS·d; SRT 5–15 d; aeration detention 4–8 hr85–95% BOD; oxygen ≈ 1 kg O₂/kg BOD; secondary clarifier + recycle R = 0.3–0.5Q; bulking risk (filamentous — keep SVI 50–150)
Trickling filterFixed film on rock/plastic media, rotary distributor; biofilm grazed by worms/larvae; recirculation; low energy75–90% (low/high rate); ponding/odour issues; simple operation; humus tank follows
RBC (rotating biological contactor)Disks rotate through sewage and airSimilar to trickling filter; modular, low power
Oxidation pond (facultative)Algae-bacteria symbiosis (algae release O₂ photosynthetically; bacteria use it); depth 1–1.5 m; detention 10–30 d; BOD load 100–300 kg/ha·d75–90%; cheap land-based — ideal for Nepal; maturation ponds follow (pathogen kill, 3–5 in series); anaerobic ponds first (3–5 m deep, 1–3 d) for strong waste
Aerated lagoonMechanical aeration, 3–4 m deep; HRT 2–6 dIntermediate between ASP and pond; suits cheap land
Constructed wetland / reed bedGravel + reeds (Phragmites), horizontal/vertical subsurface flowLow cost/energy; small communities; land-hungry; Dhulikhel-type Nepal systems
UASB (upflow anaerobic sludge blanket)Anaerobic granular sludge blanket — no aeration, biogas recovery; high-strength waste60–80% BOD; needs polishing; popular in warm climates
Fig 6.7 — The activated-sludge loop: aeration, settling, and sludge return

D. Sludge & Digestion

  • Sludge train: thickening (gravity/DAF → 2–5% solids) → stabilization (anaerobic digestion, mesophilic 30–35 °C, 25–30 d; biogas ≈ 0.75–1.1 m³/kg VS destroyed at 60–65% CH₄; thermophilic 50–55 °C is faster; two-stage high-rate) or aerobic digestion (small plants), lime stabilization, composting → dewatering (drying beds — Nepal common; centrifuge/belt press/filter press) → disposal (landfill, land application, incineration).
  • Septage (septic-tank sludge) — fecal sludge management (FSM) is Nepal's dominant sanitation chain — co-treatment in STPs or dedicated planted drying beds.

E. Disposal of Effluent — Dilution (Self-purification)

Oxygen sag curve (Streeter–Phelps 1925):
D_t = (k₁L₀/(k₂−k₁))(e^(−k₁t) − e^(−k₂t)) + D₀e^(−k₂t)
D = deficit (Osat − O); k₁ = deoxygenation rate (≈ 0.1–0.5/day, base e); k₂ = reaeration rate (≈ 0.2–1/day, rises with turbulence)
Critical time: tc = (1/(k₂−k₁)) ln[(k₂/k₁)(1 − D₀(k₂−k₁)/(k₁L₀))]
Critical deficit: Dc = (k₁/k₂)L₀ e^(−k₁tc)
Fig 6.8 — Oxygen sag (Streeter–Phelps): DO dips to Dc at tc, then reaeration wins — the river's four self-purification zones
  • Self-purification zones in a river: degradation (brown — turbid, high BOD) → active decomposition (grey — heavy pollution, oxygen minimum) → recovery (clearer) → clean water — the classic 4-zone question.
  • Reaeration helpers: turbulence, shallowness, cascades/aerators; higher temperature raises the rates but lowers DO saturation — hot polluted rivers are worst for fish.
  • Standards (Nepal discharge): BOD₅ ≤ 30–50 mg/L (category-dependent), SS ≤ 50, pH 5.5–9; irrigation reuse: BOD ≤ 100, fecal coliform < 1000/100 mL.
  • Land treatment: slow-rate irrigation (crop uptake), rapid infiltration (sandy soils — recharge), overland flow (sloped grass); removes BOD/N/P; watch clogging and groundwater contamination.
  • Marine/lake disposal: outfalls with diffusers rely on dilution; lakes suffer eutrophication (N and P — phosphorus usually limiting — algae bloom, DO crash).

F. On-Site Sanitation (Nepal core!)

Fig 6.9 — Septic tank + soak pit: scum/sludge zones, tees and baffle, effluent to soil absorption
  • Pit latrine: simple pit (0.9–1 m dia, 3–5 m deep), ventilated improved pit (VIP — vent pipe + fly screen, dark superstructure), offset pour-flush pit (Nepal standard double-pit alternating).
  • Septic tank: anaerobic settling + digestion; detention 12–36 hr (24 hr standard); sludge storage 6 months–3 yr (desludge every 1–3 yr); BOD removal ≈ 40–65% (about half); L:W = 2–4:1, water depth ≈ 1.5 m + 0.3 m freeboard; inlet tee, baffle, outlet tee; effluent must go to a soak pit — never directly to a drain or ditch.
  • Soak pit: covered pit (1–1.5 m dia, 2–3 m deep) filled with stone/brick aggregate; sized by soil percolation (seepage test); located ≥ 10–15 m from wells and the house (≥ 30 m from a deep well source where possible).
  • Double-pit pour-flush (Nepal standard): pits alternate roughly every 2 yr — one in use while the other rests/composts — sustainable FSM.
  • Other options: aqua privies, pour-flush + septic tank, community latrines, ecological sanitation (EcoSan — urine-diverting, composting).
  • Siting note: groundwater table ≥ 1.5 m below the pit bottom; clay soils need larger soak areas or piped disposal; flooding zones need raised platforms — sanitary-survey criteria.
6.5 must-knows: primary clarifier 1.5–2.5 h — 60–65% SS, 30–35% BOD; grit ≈ 0.3 m/s, 40–60 s; ASP MLSS 1500–3000 mg/L, F/M 0.2–0.4, 85–95% BOD, recycle 0.3–0.5Q, SVI 50–150; trickling filter = fixed film, low energy, humus tank; facultative pond 1–1.5 m deep, 10–30 d, algae-bacteria symbiosis; UASB 60–80% BOD + biogas; digestion mesophilic 30–35 °C, 25–30 d, biogas 60–65% CH₄; sag curve Dc = (k₁/k₂)L₀e^(−k₁tc), recovery needs k₂ > k₁; 4 self-purification zones; septic tank 24 h detention, BOD −40–65%, effluent → soak pit ≥ 10–15 m from wells; double-pit pour-flush = Nepal standard.

6.6 Concept of Environmental Assessment (ACiE0606)

A. Environmental Assessment Instruments (Nepal — EPA/EPR)

InstrumentFull formWhen required (Nepal)
BESBrief Environmental StudyProjects below the IEE threshold (EPR Schedule 1 — small scale)
IEEInitial Environmental ExaminationMedium scale (Schedule 2 — below EIA thresholds)
EIAEnvironmental Impact AssessmentLarge/significant (Schedule 3 — e.g., national highways, hydropower > 50 MW)
SEAStrategic Environmental AssessmentPolicies/plans (emerging)
EMPEnvironmental Management PlanMitigation/monitoring matrix — part of every EIA/IEE
  • EIA process: screening → scoping (ToR approval; Ministry for EIA, department/division for IEE) → baseline study → impact identification (checklists, Leopold matrix, networks) → prediction & evaluation → mitigation (EMP) → public hearing (mandatory for EIA) → report → review & approval (Ministry — MoFE) → implementation & monitoring → environmental audit.
  • Legal framework: Environment Protection Act 2053 (1997) with EPR 2054 (1997) — replaced by EPA 2076 (2019, authenticated 2076-06-24) and EPR 2077 (2020). Approving body: Ministry (MoFE) for EIA; departments for IEE/BES; ToR approval within 15 days; supplementary EIA if the proposal changes.
  • Impact categories: physical (land, air, water, noise), biological (forests, wildlife), socio-economic (displacement, cultural heritage, livelihoods); direct/indirect/induced; positive/negative; mitigation hierarchy: avoid → minimize → restore → compensate (offsets).
  • Environmental disasters (Nepal focus): earthquake (2015 Gorkha), GLOF (Tsho Rolpa lowering — risk-reduction case study), landslides/debris flows (monsoon), floods, fire, epidemics, industrial/hazardous spills. Mitigation: zoning, early warning, embankments, bio-engineering, insurance, preparedness plans, NBC enforcement.
6.6 must-knows: BES < IEE < EIA by scale (EPR Schedules 1/2/3); IEE approved by departments, EIA by the Ministry (MoFE) with mandatory public hearing; hydropower EIA > 50 MW; law: EPA 2076 (2019) + EPR 2077 (2020) replaced EPA 2053/EPR 2054; ToR approval within 15 days; process = screening → scoping → baseline → impacts (Leopold matrix) → EMP → hearing → approval → monitoring → audit; mitigation hierarchy: avoid → minimize → restore → compensate.

Numerical Traps Checklist (Chapter 6)

  • Peak factor direction: max daily (1.8) < max hourly (2.7) — don't swap; sources/plants use max daily, distribution mains/pumps use max hourly.
  • Alum vs alkalinity ratio: 0.5 mg/L as CaCO₃ consumed per mg/L alum — forgetting this causes a pH crash and poor floc.
  • HOCl vs OCl⁻ pH: more HOCl at LOW pH — high pH weakens chlorination (a reverse-intuition trap).
  • BOD vs COD magnitude: COD always ≥ BOD (some organics are non-biodegradable); ratio < 3 = biologically treatable.
  • Slow vs rapid sand: slow = biological, no coagulation, scraped clean; rapid = physicochemical, needs coagulated water, backwashed — never mix the cleaning methods.
  • Sewer hydraulic elements: Qmax at 0.95D, vmax at 0.81D — remember which is which.
  • Septic-tank effluent ≠ treated sewage: about half the BOD remains — soak pit, never direct discharge.
  • Streeter-Phelps k's: recovery needs k₂ > k₁; keep the base consistent (base e vs base 10 — factor 2.303!).
  • P & M alkalinity: P = T → pure hydroxide; P = 0 → pure bicarbonate — memorize the endpoints first.
  • EIA vs IEE approval level: Ministry (MoFE) for EIA vs departments for IEE — the roles are often reversed in options.

More Worked Examples (narrated)

Example — Population & demand projection

City 2021 population 200,000 growing 4%/yr, designed to 2041 (20 yr): P = 200,000×(1.04)²⁰ = 200,000×2.19 = 438,000. At 110 lpcd: average = 48.2 MLD; max daily = 86.7; max hourly = 130 MLD. Source and plant follow max daily; distribution mains and pumps follow max hourly.

Example — Reservoir sizing by mass curve

Hourly demand swings 2% (night) to 7% (morning peak) of the daily total: cumulative supply is flat (24-hr pumping) while cumulative demand zigzags; the maximum vertical gap gives the balancing storage ≈ 15–25% of daily demand for typical curves. Add 10% emergency + fire (e.g., 2 hr × 50 L/s = 360 m³) for total storage; then geometry (depth 3–5 m) and structural design (IS 3370 crack control, 0.2 mm).

Example — Chlorination math

Q = 20 MLD, dose 1.5 mg/L: Cl₂ = 20,000 m³ × 1.5 g/m³ = 30 kg/day. Bleaching powder (32% available): 30/0.32 = 94 kg/day. Hypochlorite dosing at 0.5% solution: 30/0.005 = 6000 L/day = 4.2 L/min pump. Target residual 0.3 after 30 min → chlorine demand = 1.2 mg/L.

Example — Pond series design

Q = 500 m³/d, BOD 300 mg/L → load 150 kg/d. Anaerobic pond at 300 g/m³·d volumetric load: V = 150,000/300 = 500 m³ → at 4 m depth, area 125 m² (detention 1 d). Facultative at 150 kg/ha·d: 1 ha at 1.2 m depth → detention 24 d. Maturation: two ponds of 0.5 ha for coliform reduction — the standard land-rich rural Nepal answer.

Example — Sag curve quick calc

L₀ = 25 mg/L, k₁ = 0.15, k₂ = 0.45, D₀ = 2, Osat = 9.2: tc = (1/0.3)ln[(3)(1 − 2×0.3/(0.15×25))] = 3.33×ln(2.52) = 3.08 d; Dc = (0.15/0.45)(25)e^(−0.462) = 5.25 mg/L → DO_min = 9.2 − 5.25 = 3.95 mg/L (fish stress — upgrade treatment upstream).

Example — Sewer slope selection

Lateral 150 mm serving 20 houses: peak ≈ 5 L/s. For 0.6 m/s with n = 0.013: R_full = D/4 = 0.0375 m; Manning gives S ≈ 0.005 (1 in 200) for v_full ≈ 0.61 m/s; at d/D ≈ 0.5 the velocity holds near 0.6 m/s. Lateral slopes of 1:100–1:200 are typical.

Extended High-Yield Additions (Exam-Focused Extras)

Water demand numericals

  • Population 50,000 @ 100 LPCD: average = 5 MLD; max daily = 1.8×5 = 9 MLD; max hourly = 2.7×5 = 13.5 MLD (consistent with 1.5 × max daily).
  • Geometric growth: P = 100,000(1.03)²⁰ = 180,600 → design at 181k → 18.1 MLD average (100 lpcd).
  • Fire (NBFU) at P = 100 thousand: Q = 4637×10×(1−0.1) = 41,733 L/min ≈ 60 MLD — huge, hence fire reserves live in reservoirs only.
  • Reservoir: max daily 9 MLD → balancing ≈ 30% (2.7 ML) + emergency 10% (0.9) ≈ 3.6 ML — within the ⅓–½ MDD rule.

Treatment numericals

  • Alum dose 30 mg/L at Q = 10 MLD: 300 kg/day (six 50-kg bags); alkalinity consumed = 15 mg/L as CaCO₃ (0.5×30); add lime if the raw water is short.
  • Jar-test optimum 25 mg/L → design dose 25–35 mg/L (seasonal margin).
  • Clarifier: Q = 10 MLD = 416 m³/hr; at vo = 40 m/d → A = 10,000/40 = 250 m² → dia 17.8 m; detention 2.5 hr → V = 1040 m³ → depth ≈ 4.2 m.
  • Rapid filters: 4 filters, rate 5 m/hr, Q = 10 MLD → total area 83.3 m² → each ≈ 21 m² (≈ 4.6 × 4.6 m); backwash 10 min at 40 m/hr ≈ 140 m³ per filter wash (≈ 1.5–3% of daily production at 24–48 hr runs — matches the 2–4% rule).
  • Chlorine: dose 2, demand 1.2 → residual 0.8 mg/L (pre-breakpoint arithmetic); compliance target 0.2–0.5 after 30 min contact.
  • BOD: sewage 200 mg/L at Q = 5 MLD → load 1000 kg/d; at F/M 0.3 and MLSS 2500 mg/L: V = 1000/(0.3×2.5) = 1333 m³ → aeration detention ≈ 6.4 hr.
  • Oxygen sag: L₀ = 20, k₁ = 0.1, k₂ = 0.3, D₀ = 1: tc = 5×ln(2.7) ≈ 4.97 d; Dc = (0.1/0.3)×20×e^(−0.497) ≈ 4.06 mg/L → minimum DO ≈ 5.1 mg/L.
  • Streeter-Phelps assumptions: steady state, plug flow, single point source, constant k's.

Sewer design numericals

  • Population 10,000, 100 lpcd, 80% return → average sewage 0.8 MLD; PF 2.5 → peak 2.0 MLD = 23.1 L/s; a 200 mm pipe (n = 0.013) at S = 0.005 carries Q_full ≈ 23 L/s; at d/D = 0.6, Q ≈ 0.7×Q_full ≈ 16 L/s < the 23.1 L/s peak → runs nearly full — upsize or steepen — practice partial-flow chart reading.
  • Self-cleansing 0.6 m/s → minimum slopes: 150 mm ≈ 1 in 150; laterals typically 1:100–1:200.
  • Inverted siphon: two barrels (one for low flow) to keep ≈ 0.9 m/s; head loss = water-level difference; always full and pressurized.
  • Manhole spacing: 150 mm sewer → 30 m; 600 mm → 90–120 m (code tables).

Rapid-Fire One-Liners (Last-Minute Revision)

  • Impurities: suspended (settle), colloidal (coagulate), dissolved (soften/adsorb), biological (disinfect).
  • Hardness (as CaCO₃): < 75 soft, 75–150 moderate, 150–300 hard, > 300 very hard; acceptable 200, permissible 600.
  • Alkalinity: P = 0 → all bicarbonate; P = M/2 → carbonate only; P = M → hydroxide only.
  • Fluoride ideal 1.0, max 1.5; arsenic 0.05 (NS)/0.01 (WHO); nitrate 45–50; iron 0.3; manganese 0.1 mg/L.
  • pH 6.5–8.5; turbidity < 5 NTU (1 ideal); TDS ~ 500–1000; DO 6–8 clean.
  • BOD₅ at 20 °C ≈ 68% of ultimate (k = 0.1/d); COD ≥ BOD always; MPN/membrane coliform — 0/100 mL drinking.
  • Diseases: waterborne (cholera/typhoid), water-washed (trachoma), water-based (guinea worm), vector (malaria/dengue).
  • Demand: Nepal rural 45 lpcd; peaks 1.8 daily / 2.7 hourly; design period 20–30 yr; fire Kuichling 3182√P L/min (P in thousands).
  • Population methods: arithmetic (old cities), geometric (fast-growing), decreasing-rate, logistic, master plan.
  • Intakes: submerged/wet/dry/tower; approach velocity 0.1–0.3 m/s; coarse screens > 50 mm, fine < 20 mm.
  • Pipes: CI/DI mains (100 yr), PVC/HDPE distribution, GI services; joints: spigot-socket, flanged (plant), push-on gasket, fusion HDPE.
  • Valves: sluice isolate, check NRV, air at summits, scour at valleys, PRV downhill, float tank level, globe throttling.
  • BPT where static head exceeds ≈ 50–60 m; service reservoir ⅓–½ of max daily demand (balancing + emergency + fire).
  • Distribution: dead-end (cheap, stagnant), grid-iron (best), ring, radial; min residual 8–10 m; NRW Nepal ≈ 25–30%.
  • Train: screen → aerate → coagulate-flocculate → settle → filter → chlorinate.
  • Alum pH 6.5–8.5; consumes 0.5 mg alkalinity/mg alum; rapid mix 30–60 s at G 700–1000; flocculation 20–30 min at G 20–80.
  • Clarifier: DT 2–2.5 hr, vo 30–50 m/d, weir ≤ 300 m³/m/d.
  • Slow sand: 100–200 L/m²/hr, biological schmutzdecke, scrape cleaning, feed < 50 NTU.
  • Rapid sand: 3000–5000 L/m²/hr, ES 0.45–0.7, UC 1.3–1.7, bed 60–90 cm, gravel 45–60, backwash expands 30–50%, terminal loss 1.8–2.5 m.
  • Chlorine: HOCl > OCl⁻ (better at pH < 7); breakpoint curve; contact 30 min, residual ≥ 0.2 mg/L; demand = dose − residual; THM byproducts; bleaching powder 30–35% available Cl₂; ozone/UV leave no residual.
  • Softening: lime-soda (both hardness types) vs zeolite ion exchange (brine regen, ~0 residual); aeration strips gases and oxidizes Fe/Mn.
  • Sewage ≈ 80% of supply; PF 2–3 (Harmon formula); self-cleansing 0.6, scour 3.0 m/s; design d/D ≤ 0.75–0.8; min size 150–200 mm; n = 0.013; Qmax 0.95D, vmax 0.81D.
  • Manholes 30 m small sewers, drop manhole > 0.6 m; inverted siphon under obstacles; grit chamber 0.3 m/s, 40–60 s, grit ≥ 0.2 mm SG 2.65.
  • Primary clarifier: 2 hr, 60–65% SS, 30–35% BOD.
  • ASP: MLSS 1500–3000, F/M 0.2–0.5, SRT 5–15 d, aeration 4–8 hr, R 0.3–0.5Q, SVI healthy 50–100, bulking = filamentous.
  • Trickling filter: rotary distributor, fixed film, recirculation; RBC disks; ponds: anaerobic (3–5 m) → facultative (1–1.5 m, algae-bacteria) → maturation (pathogens).
  • Sludge: thicken → digest (25–30 d mesophilic, biogas 60–65% CH₄) → drying beds; septage FSM is Nepal's chain.
  • Sag curve: Streeter-Phelps; k₁ deoxygenation, k₂ reaeration; critical-time formula; 4 zones (degradation → active decomposition → recovery → clean).
  • Septic tank 12–24 hr DT, L:W 2–4:1, desludge 1–3 yr, effluent → soak pit ≥ 10–15 m from sources; double-pit Nepal standard; EcoSan urine-diverting.
  • EIA Nepal: EPA 2053/2076 + EPR 2054/2077; screening → scoping → baseline → impacts → EMP → public hearing → approval (MoFE); IEE (department) vs EIA (ministry); Leopold matrix; monitoring & audit.
  • Mitigation hierarchy: avoid → minimize → restore → compensate; Nepal hazards: earthquake, GLOF, landslides, floods, fire, epidemics.

Deeper Concept Discussions

Water quality testing — methods & units table

ParameterMethod/InstrumentUnit
TurbidityNephelometer (Jackson candle — old JTU)NTU
ColourCobalt-platinum comparisonTCU/Hazen
pHGlass electrode / indicatorspH scale
HardnessEDTA titration / soap solution (Clark)mg/L CaCO₃
AlkalinityTitration — phenolphthalein (P) & methyl orange (T)mg/L CaCO₃
DOWinkler (iodometric), membrane electrodemg/L
BOD5-day incubation 20 °C, dilution methodmg/L
CODPotassium dichromate refluxmg/L
ColiformMPN (multiple-tube fermentation), membrane filtration, Colilert (enzyme)MPN/100 mL, CFU/100 mL
Residual chlorineDPD / orthotolidine (OTA — old), starch-iodidemg/L
SolidsOven 103–105 °C, muffle furnace 550 °C (volatile), Imhoff cone (settleable)mg/L
Iron/Mn/As/FSpectrophotometer/field kitsmg/L
  • Alkalinity relations (memorize): P = 0 → all HCO₃⁻; P < T/2 → HCO₃⁻ + CO₃²⁻; P = T/2 → all CO₃²⁻; P > T/2 → OH⁻ + CO₃²⁻; P = T → all OH⁻ — a recurring MCQ.
  • Why DO matters: fish need ≥ 4–5 mg/L; anaerobic decay produces H₂S and odour; a river's self-purification capacity is read from the DO sag.
  • Pathogen removal hierarchy: sedimentation (partial) → slow sand (good) → rapid sand (moderate — pre-chlorination helps) → disinfection (final barrier — CT logic: Giardia needs far more CT than bacteria).

Why each treatment step exists (concept chain)

  • Coagulation neutralizes the negative colloid charges (Zeta-potential reduction) — tiny particles never settle on their own (Brownian motion) — alum hydrolysis sweeps them into floc.
  • Filtration polishes turbidity to < 1 NTU so disinfection works (particles shield pathogens).
  • Chlorination is the final barrier — its residual travels through the network (why ozone/UV alone cannot protect mains).
  • Fluoridation (deficient areas) vs defluoridation (Nalgonda) — both one-markers.
  • Pre-chlorination aids taste/algae/iron; post-chlorination secures residual; superchlorination-dechlorination handles bad water.

Distribution system design logic

  • Design flow = max hourly demand at each node; fire flow checked separately at the worst point with max daily.
  • The reservoir floats on the system — fills at night, supplies peaks — pumps size to the average, not the peak (energy saving); that is the core benefit of storage.
  • Dead ends get flush hydrants/blow-offs; loops give reliability (path redundancy) — the grid-iron cost trade-off is a standard MCQ.
  • Minimum pipe size is driven by fire flow (100 mm), not by demand alone — an exam trap.
  • Calibration: hydrant fire-flow tests estimate available flow/pressure; EPANET is the modern Nepal utility tool.

Sewerage engineering insights

  • Why partial-flow design: capacity margin above design flow + ventilation space + the velocity peak near d/D 0.8–0.95; sewers are never designed full (except siphons).
  • Why minimum velocity: H₂S and grit problems start with deposition; why maximum: erosion of inverts and manholes.
  • Why manholes: access for cleaning equipment, ventilation, junctions; spacing grows with pipe size (machines clean larger pipes from farther apart).
  • Kathmandu is mostly separate-ish (storm drains + a growing sewer network); combined remnants overload treatment plants in the monsoon.
  • Force mains: check valves and air valves are critical; long force mains turn anaerobic (H₂S) — odour control by biofilters/chemicals.

Wastewater treatment — removal efficiencies summary table

UnitBOD removalSS removal
Screening + grit~5%~10%
Primary clarifier30–35%50–65%
ASP / trickling filter (secondary)85–95% total85–90% total
Facultative pond70–90%70–80%
Maturation pond+5–10%main job: pathogens (90%+ per pond series)
UASB (anaerobic)60–80%50–70%
  • Effluent standards (Nepal practice): BOD ≤ 30–50 mg/L, SS ≤ 50–100, pH 5.5–9; irrigation reuse coliform < 1000/100 mL — discharge and irrigation standards differ.
  • Nutrient removal (advanced): nitrification (longer SRT > 10 d, aerobic), denitrification (anoxic zone + carbon source), biological P removal (EBPR — anaerobic/aerobic cycling, PAOs) — recognize the terms.
  • Effluent disinfection: chlorination/dechlorination, UV (needs low SS), maturation ponds (cheapest — Nepal).

Environmental assessment factual extras

  • EPR 2077 schedule anchors: hydropower IEE 1–50 MW, EIA > 50 MW; hospitals BES 16–25 beds, IEE 26–100, EIA > 100; roads IEE ≤ 25 km, EIA > 25 km; water supply IEE 50,000–200,000 people, EIA > 200,000 — memorize the process; the exam asks roles and steps most.
  • Environmental audit (retrospective compliance) vs monitoring (ongoing measurement); EMP = mitigation matrix with responsibilities and cost.
  • Approving agencies: EIA — Ministry (MoFE); IEE — departments (DoR, DoED, DWSSM); scoping approved before baseline; public hearing for EIA (mandatory, local language).
  • Disaster mitigation examples: earthquake — NBC enforcement, retrofitting; GLOF — lake lowering (Tsho Rolpa) + early warning; flood — embankments, zoning, EWS; landslide — bio-engineering, drainage; epidemic — WASH, surveillance.
  • Institutions: MoFE (environment), DoHS (health), DWSSM (water supply), NWSC (urban water), WECS (water & energy commission), DEOC (emergency operations) — role-matching MCQs.

Quick Concept Cards (exam morning)

Card 1 — Quality

Suspended/colloidal/dissolved/biological; NTU < 1–5; pH 6.5–8.5; hardness as CaCO₃ (200/600); fluoride 1–1.5; arsenic 0.01–0.05; nitrate 45; iron 0.3; DO 6–8; BOD₅ ≈ 68% of ultimate; COD ≥ BOD; coliform 0/100 mL; 4 disease classes.

Card 2 — Demand & distribution

45 lpcd rural; peaks 1.8/2.7; Kuichling fire formula; geometric growth P(1+r)ⁿ; design 20–30 yr; intakes low velocity; air valves at summits, scour at valleys, check at pumps, PRV downhill; BPT beyond 50–60 m static; reservoir ⅓–½ max daily; dead-end/grid/ring/radial; NRW 25–30%.

Card 3 — Treatment

Train: screen → aerate → coagulate (30–60 s, G 700–1000) → flocculate (20–30 min, G 20–80) → clarify (2–2.5 hr) → filter (rapid 3000–6000 L/m²/hr, ES 0.45–0.7) → chlorinate (30 min, 0.2–0.5 residual). Slow sand biological 100–200. Alum needs 0.5× alkalinity. Breakpoint → free residual; THM byproducts. Softening: lime-soda vs zeolite (brine). Aeration strips gases, oxidizes Fe/Mn.

Card 4 — Sewerage & WWTP

Sewage ≈ 80% of supply; PF 2–3; v 0.6–3.0 m/s; d/D ≤ 0.75; min 150–200 mm; n 0.013; manholes 30 m+; drop > 0.6 m; grit 0.3 m/s, 40–60 s; primary 2 hr (35% BOD/60% SS); ASP (MLSS 1500–3000, F/M 0.2–0.5, SVI 50–100); ponds anaerobic 3–5 m → facultative 1–1.5 m → maturation; digesters 60–65% CH₄; sag curve k₁/k₂, 4 zones; septic 24 hr → soak pit ≥ 10–15 m; EIA screening → scoping → baseline → EMP → hearing → approve → monitor; mitigation avoid → minimize → restore → compensate; Nepal hazards: earthquake, GLOF, landslide.

Answer-Selection Heuristics for This Chapter

  • "Cheapest land-based sewage treatment for rural Nepal" → stabilization/maturation pond system (not ASP — energy and skills).
  • "Final barrier against pathogens" → chlorination (residual) — ozone/UV leave none.
  • "Why pre-chlorination?" → algae control, taste, iron oxidation — not primarily disinfection.
  • "Filter that removes bacteria without coagulation" → slow sand (schmutzdecke).
  • "Pipe material for corrosive-soil mains" → lined DI or PVC — not unlined steel.
  • "Valve preventing backflow to a pump" → check/NRV; "isolation" → sluice; "throttling" → globe.
  • "Highest household water use" → toilet flushing (~30%), then bathing — demand-management MCQs.
  • "Main cause of sewer corrosion" → H₂S → H₂SO₄ (crown); "of blockage" → grease + solids (FOG) at low velocity.
  • "Primary vs secondary sludge" → primary thick (4–6% TS), secondary thin (0.5–1.5%) — digestibility differs.
  • "Instrument for in-situ residual chlorine" → DPD colorimeter — not a turbidimeter.

  • The five alkalinity relations with P and T?
  • HOCl/OCl⁻ equilibrium vs pH, and the breakpoint curve shape?
  • Slow vs rapid sand: five differences (rate, biology, cleaning, feed quality, area)?
  • Sewer: 0.6/3.0 m/s, d/D 0.75, Qmax 0.95D, manhole spacing logic?
  • Grit chamber velocity 0.3 m/s — why not higher or lower?
  • ASP parameters (MLSS, F/M, SRT, SVI) and pond depths (anaerobic/facultative)?
  • Streeter–Phelps variables and the four river zones?
  • Septic tank: DT, L:W, desludging, soak-pit distance?
  • EIA steps in order and the approving authority in Nepal?

Rural Water Supply & Sanitation (RWSS) — Nepal-Specific Additions

Service levels & design norms (National Water Supply and Sanitation Level indicators)

LevelServiceTypical scheme
Basic (Level 1)45 lpcd, public point source within 15 min round tripGravity-flow spring scheme, standposts
Intermediate (Level 2)65 lpcd, partial private/yard connectionsGravity + BPTs + private taps
High (Level 3)Full house connection, 100+ lpcdUrban-style piped networks (NWSC)

Gravity-flow scheme components (typical Nepal hill scheme)

  • Source: spring box (intake with gravel pack, overflow, scour) or stream intake (check dam + intake); protection zone (fencing, recharge conservation).
  • Transmission main: HDPE/GI sized for max daily flow; air valves at summits, washouts at valleys, anchor blocks at bends (steep terrain!), stream crossings.
  • BPTs: roughly every 50–60 m of elevation drop; masonry tank + float-valve chamber.
  • RVT (reservoir tank): sized ⅓–½ of max daily demand (20–50% depending on 24-hr vs limited-hours supply); covered, vented, overflow + washout, tap stands.
  • Distribution: branched (dead ends acceptable in small schemes with washouts), PVC 20–32 mm service lines, private taps with optional meters.
  • Water safety plan (WSP): source-to-tap risk assessment, community governance (users' committee — WSUC), tariff for O&M, VLOM (village-level operation & maintenance) hardware.
  • Rainwater harvesting: roof catchment (tiles/GI — avoid thatch/lead paint), first-flush diverter, ferro-cement storage tank; sizing: demand × longest dry spell vs runoff (0.8 × rain × area × efficiency).

Sanitation chain & FSM (fecal sludge management)

  • Containment (double-pit/septic) → emptying (manual/Vacutug/Gulper) → transport → treatment (planted drying beds, co-composting, co-treatment in STP) → reuse/disposal (agriculture after composting).
  • Nepal context: only a few cities have sewers (Kathmandu partial, Biratnagar, and a handful more); > 80% rely on on-site systems — hence FSM is critical; septage BOD is 5–10× sewage — co-treatment needs careful dosing.
  • Nepal declared itself open-defecation-free (ODF) in 2019 — the CLTS (community-led total sanitation) campaign context.

Final Rapid Facts (last additions)

  • WHO water quantity: 20 lpcd minimum access, 50 low-health-risk, 100+ for full hygiene.
  • Chlorine contact tanks are baffled against short-circuiting (t₁₀/t₀ baffling factor; good baffling ≥ 0.7) — CT compliance.
  • Pipe-network calibration: hydrant fire-flow tests (pitot gauge) estimate available flow and pressure drop.
  • Metering: positive displacement for small domestic (accurate at low flow), electromagnetic/ultrasonic for bulk (no moving parts).
  • Sewer side-loads: kitchen grease traps (FOG), hospital disinfection, industrial pretreatment (BOD ≤ 300 mg/L class limits) before discharge to public sewers.
  • ASP modifications: step aeration, tapered, contact-stabilization, extended aeration (small plants, SRT 20–30 d), SBR (sequencing batch) — name-to-concept MCQs.
  • Trickling filter problems: ponding (clogged media), filter flies (Psychoda), odour.
  • Sludge drying beds: sand 150–300 mm + gravel + underdrains; loading 100–150 kg TS/m²·yr (Nepal climate); 15–20 d cycle; supernatant returns to the plant.
  • Effluent reuse in agriculture: BOD < 100, coliform < 1000/100 mL (WHO guideline) — drip vs furrow; landscape uses demand higher standards.
  • Household treatment options (Nepal): boiling, chlorine (Piyush), ceramic/biosand filters (Kanchan — iron nails for arsenic), SODIS (solar).
  • Sanitary survey: source risk, treatment integrity, cross-connections (backflow — air gap/vacuum breaker), storage hygiene — the WHO water-safety framework.
  • Watershed protection: source recharge (afforestation, gully control), no septic tanks in capture zones, agrochemical limits — prevention is the cheapest "treatment".

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (6.1–6.6)

Water Sources & Quality (6.1) — Course Facts

  • Impurity sizes: suspended > 1 micron (visible — bacteria, algae, clay, silt); colloidal 10⁻³–1 micron (charged, repel, do not settle — silica, alumina); dissolved 10⁻⁵–10⁻³ micron (arsenic, bicarbonates, lead, chloride — need a phase change to remove).
  • Groundwater formations: aquifer (yields water); confined/artesian aquifer (between two impermeable layers); unconfined (water table = phreatic surface); perched aquifer (local patches). Aquiclude — stores but does not transmit (clay); aquifuge — neither stores nor transmits (solid granite); aquitard — leaks slowly (sandy clay).
  • NEC OQ: "A porous formation that absorbs water but yields no appreciable supply" = aquiclude. "Water may not contain many impurities if its source is a spring along hill slopes."
  • Population forecast: rapidly growing city → geometric increase; large established city → arithmetic; logistic (Verhulst) for saturated growth; decreasing-rate for old cities.
  • Standards (course table): turbidity ≤ 5 NTU, pH 6.5–8.5, colour ≤ 5 TCU, residual chlorine 0.1–0.5 mg/L, nitrate ≤ 50 mg/L (blue-baby), fluoride ≤ 1.5 mg/L, temperature > 35 °C unsuitable. Algae control: copper sulphate or chlorine.
  • Microbiology: mesophiles grow at 25–40 °C (E. coli); Durham tubes detect coliform; the Thomas equation gives MPN/100 mL; coliform = fecal-contamination indicator.
  • Demand (course values): domestic 55–60% of total; rural 45 lpcd; fully plumbed house 112 lpcd; partially plumbed 65 lpcd; livestock < 20% of domestic — big animals 45 L/day, medium 20 L, birds 0.2 L. Fire: Kuichling Q = 3182√P, Buston Q = 5663√P (P in thousands, Q in L/min); Freeman ≈ 1136(P/10 + 10).

Intakes & Distribution (6.2)

  • Intake types: river, canal, reservoir, lake; best location = outer (concave) bank to avoid sediment, with sediment-exclusion devices; screens keep debris out.
  • Pipe life spans: cast iron ≈ 100 years; ductile iron > 100; cement concrete ≈ 75; prestressed concrete pipes for heads up to ~100 m; GI = zinc-coated (corrodes slowly); PVC/HDPE/PPR for small diameters; welded steel stronger and smoother than riveted.
  • Velocities in distribution mains: minimum 0.3 m/s (clean water self-cleansing), maximum 3 m/s; sewers minimum 0.6 m/s.
  • Fittings: plain socket joins same diameters; reducing socket joins different; union allows quick disconnection; elbows, tees, bends, adaptors.
  • Valves: sluice/gate (isolate), check/reflux (one-way), air relief (high points), scour/washout (low points), pressure reducing, butterfly, globe.
  • Break pressure tanks cut static pressure in long gravity mains (roughly every 50–60 m of residual head) — they prevent downstream bursts.
  • Service reservoirs: balancing + breakdown + fire + dead storage (four-compartment analysis); capacity ≈ 25–50% of daily demand (Nepal rural ≈ one-third to one-half day); outlet kept 10–15 cm above the floor.
  • Systems: dead-end/branch (cheap, stagnation), grid-iron (loops — repair without cutting supply), ring (one loop), radial (central source). Hardy-Cross / equivalent-pipe methods solve networks.

Treatment (6.3) — Course Values

  • Screening: coarse/bar screens spacing 50 mm or more (NEC OQ options: fine < 20 mm, medium 20–50, coarse > 50 mm), inclined at the intake for easy rack cleaning.
  • Sedimentation: plain SOR = 15–30 m³/day/m²; with coagulation 30–40 m³/day/m². Stokes settling vs = g(G−1)d²/18ν.
  • Coagulants: alum (most common), ferric chloride, ferrous sulphate + lime, PACl; optimum dose by jar test; coagulation (charge neutralisation) then flocculation (gentle mixing, G = 20–80 s⁻¹, detention 20–30 min).
  • Filtration: slow sand — 100–200 L/hr/m², effective size 0.2–0.35 mm, uniformity 2–3.5 (course: Cu 3–5), biological schmutzdecke gives the highest bacteriological efficiency, no coagulation, rural/small towns. Rapid sand — ≈ 3000–6000 L/hr/m² (30× SSF), ES 0.45–0.7 mm, Cu 1.3–1.7, needs coagulation-sedimentation, backwash ≈ 4% of filtered water; negative head if clogged.
  • Disinfection: chlorination — residual 0.2–0.5 mg/L after 30 min (breakpoint when ammonia present); super-chlorination for polluted water; ozone/UV leave no residual.
  • Miscellaneous: aeration (taste/odour, iron oxidation), defluoridation (Nalgonda/activated alumina), iron & manganese removal = aeration + sedimentation + filtration.

Sewers (6.4) — Course Formulas

  • DWF = (rate of water supply × population × return factor × peak factor); Nepal return factor = 80%; design uses peak flow.
  • Peak factors: domestic 6; lateral 2–6 (max 6 at low flows); branch 3; sub-main 3; main 2.5; outfall 2.
  • Storm flow (Rational): Q = CIA/360 (Q m³/s, i mm/hr, A ha); composite C = ΣCiAi/ΣAi; intensity by IDF or the British Ministry of Health formula: I = 760/(t+10) for 5–20 min; I = 1020/(t+20) for 20–100 min.
  • Shapes: circular (best full-flow hydraulics), egg-shaped/oval (combined systems — keeps velocity at low DWF), rectangular/box (storm drains), horseshoe. Partial-flow charts: maximum velocity at 0.81 depth, maximum discharge at 0.95 depth.
  • Materials: stoneware/vitrified clay (house sewers, acid-resistant), RCC (mains), brick (large), cast iron (pumping mains), PVC/HDPE (small). Appurtenances: manholes (40–150 m spacing by diameter), drop manhole (> 0.6 m difference), inverted siphon (depressed sewer), catch basins, street inlets, regulators, flushing tanks.
  • Separate — two sewers; combined — one; partially separate (storm overflows, sanitary treated). Self-cleansing ≥ 0.6 m/s; non-scouring ≤ 3 m/s.

Wastewater Characteristics & Treatment (6.5) — Course Values

  • Physical: fresh sewage light brown → grey → black (stale); fresh odourless, then H₂S rotten-egg (anaerobic); average temperature ≈ 20 °C; high temperature indicates industrial waste.
  • Chemical: fresh sewage alkaline pH 7.3–7.5, falls as acids form; TKN = organic + ammonia nitrogen; COD > BOD always; BOD by dilution at 20 °C for 5 days; BOD₅ ≈ 68% of ultimate; minimum DO for fish survival = 4 ppm.
  • Solids: total solids dried at 103–105 °C for 24 h; volatile/fixed at 600 °C (muffle furnace, 30 min); settleable by Imhoff cone.
  • Primary: screening → grit chamber (0.3 m/s, grit ≥ 0.2 mm, 40–60 s, proportional/Sutro weirs) → primary sedimentation (1.5–2.5 h; removes 60–65% SS, 30–35% BOD).
  • Secondary (biological): ASP — aeration 4–8 h, F/M 0.2–0.5, MLSS 1500–3000 mg/L, SVI = 50–150 mL/g (bulking > 200); trickling filters (fixed growth, recirculation); oxidation ponds (detention 2–6 weeks, depth 1–1.8 m, algae-bacteria symbiosis); septic tank (24 h detention, effluent to soak pit); Imhoff tank (two-storey digestion).
  • Disposal by dilution: oxygen sag curve (Streeter-Phelps: k₁ vs k₂; critical point where deficit rate = reaeration rate); self-purification zones: clean → degradation → active decomposition → recovery → clean.
  • Sludge disposal: digestion (anaerobic, mesophilic ~35 °C), drying beds, lagoons, incineration, land application. Solid waste: generation → collection → transport → disposal (sanitary landfill, composting, incineration, open dumping).

Environmental Assessment (6.6) — Course Schedule Values (EPA 2076 / EPR 2077)

  • Instruments: BES (Schedule 1), IEE (Schedule 2), EIA (Schedule 3). EPA authenticated 2076-06-24 (11 Oct 2019); EPR 2077. ToR approval before BES/IEE; scoping document + ToR for EIA; EMP required before implementation; supplementary EIA if the proposal is revised.
  • BES examples: plantation 10–50 ha; river mining ≤ 50 m³/day; hospital 16–25 beds; bridge 50–250 m; local roads; buildings 7–10 storeys; teaching hospital ≤ 50 beds.
  • IEE examples: plantation 50–500 ha (Terai) / 50–250 ha (hill); river mining > 50 m³/day; water supply for 50,000–200,000 people; bridge > 250 m; roads ≤ 25 km; buildings 5,000–10,000 m² built-up; teaching hospital 50–100 beds; hydropower 1–50 MW.
  • EIA examples: plantation > 500 ha (Terai)/> 250 ha (hill); national parks/conservation areas; water supply > 200,000 people; roads > 25 km; buildings > 10,000 m²; teaching hospital > 100 beds; hydropower > 50 MW.
  • Approvals: national-priority/investment-board/multi-province projects — prescribed body for BES/IEE, Ministry (Forest & Environment) for EIA; provincial matters → provincial bodies; local matters → local bodies (BES/IEE), provincial body for EIA. ToR within 15 days; public notice in a local newspaper; non-compliance bars report preparation up to 5 years.
  • Disaster types & mitigation: natural (earthquake, flood, landslide, GLOF, fire, epidemic) vs human-induced; mitigation = structural (retrofitting, embankments, hazard-resistant codes) + non-structural (land-use planning, early warning, insurance, preparedness training).
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): coarse-screen spacing ≥ 50 mm; SOR plain vs coagulated (15–30 vs 30–40); COD always > BOD; fresh sewage alkaline (7.3–7.5); return factor 80% (Nepal); peak-factor ladder 6 → 2; aquiclude (clay) vs aquifuge (granite); BES/IEE/EIA schedule boundaries — hospital 16–25 / 26–100 / > 100 beds and hydropower < 1 / 1–50 / > 50 MW.
