NEC License Exam — High-Yield Notes (v5.5 edition)

Chapter 7: Application of Water Resources Engineering (ACRE07)

NEC License Exam (1-Mark MCQ Focus) | NEC prep-course edition — v5.5

This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

7.1 Water Demand Estimation for Irrigation (ACiE0701)

A. Crop Water Requirement (CWR)

CWR = ETc = Kc × ET₀ (crop coefficient × reference evapotranspiration)
ET₀ by Penman–Monteith (FAO-56 standard), Blaney–Criddle (temperature based), or pan evaporation: ET₀ = Kp × Ep
Net irrigation requirement: NIR = ETc − effective rainfall (Pe) (+ leaching if needed)
Gross irrigation requirement: GIR = NIR / irrigation efficiency
Field irrigation requirement (FIR) adds percolation losses in the field
  • ETc factors: climate (ET₀), crop type and stage (Kc varies: initial 0.3–0.5, mid-season 1.0–1.2, late 0.5–0.8), soil, management.
  • Effective rainfall: the portion stored in the root zone and usable by the crop (USDA/SCS method, 80% dependability); runoff and deep percolation are excluded.

B. Command Areas, Irrigation Intensity

  • Gross command area (GCA): the total area commanded — irrigable by gravity flow — from the canal (includes uncultivable land).
  • Culturable command area (CCA): GCA minus uncultivable land (forest, waste, homesteads) — the basis for water requirement.
  • Cultural (non-cultivable) commanded area: villages, ponds and similar.
  • Irrigation intensity: (irrigated area in a season / CCA) × 100%; annual intensity sums the seasons — e.g., monsoon paddy 70% + winter 35% + spring 20% = 125%.
  • Time factor: the fraction of the outlet command irrigated at once (rotation); capacity factor: actual supply ÷ full supply demand.

C. Duty and Delta

Fig 7.1 — Duty–delta: 1 cumec for B days over D ha gives depth Δ = 8.64B/D (D = 8.64B/Δ)
Fig 7.2 — Field irrigation methods: furrow, sprinkler, drip and border/basin — application efficiencies and selection
Delta (Δ): total depth of water applied to a crop over its base period (m)
Duty (D): area irrigated per unit continuous discharge (ha/cumec) — British/Nepal convention
Relation: Δ = 8.64 B / D (B = base period in days, Δ in m, D in ha/cumec)
Derivation: 1 cumec flowing for B days delivers 86400×B m³ over 1 ha (10⁴ m²) → depth 8.64B m; spread over D ha → Δ = 8.64B/D
  • Delta examples: rice 120–150 cm (B ≈ 120 d), wheat 40–50 cm (B ≈ 120 d), sugarcane 120–180 cm (B ≈ 300+ d).
  • Higher duty = more efficient (more area per cumec). Duty improves with efficient methods (drip > sprinkler > flood), canal lining, better scheduling, and crop choice.
  • Duty varies along a canal: duty increases downstream — flow is progressively diverted at laterals while the served area accumulates, so the remaining flow commands more area.

D. Irrigation Efficiencies & Losses

EfficiencyDefinitionTypical
Conveyance efficiency ecWater delivered to the field / water diverted at the head70–90% (Nepal unlined canals 60–75%)
Application efficiency eaWater stored in the root zone / delivered to the field50–70% flood; 75–85% sprinkler; 90%+ drip
Storage efficiencyWater stored / water needed to fill the root zone—
Water use efficiencyCrop yield / water usedkg/m³ (productivity view)
Overall project efficiencyec × ea35–60% conventional
  • Losses: seepage (percolation from unlined canals — the biggest), evaporation, weed transpiration, operational waste (overtopping, poor timing), end spills.
  • Waterlogging: the water table rises into the root/aeration zone (generally within about 1.5–2 m of the surface). Causes: seepage, over-irrigation, poor drainage. Effects: aeration loss, salt accumulation ("white alkali"), yield drop. Remedies: lined canals, surface/subsurface drainage, crop rotation, reduced application.
  • Soil salinity: problematic when EC > 4 dS/m; leaching requirement LR = ECw/(5·ECe − ECw) — the extra water needed to flush salts; gypsum reclaims sodic (high-Na) soils; SAR = Na⁺/√((Ca²⁺+Mg²⁺)/2) classifies irrigation water.

E. Soil–Moisture–Irrigation Relationship

Available water AW = FC − PWP (field capacity minus permanent wilting point)
FC ≈ 0.1 (sand) to 0.4 (clay) L/L; PWP ≈ half of FC (roughly)
Readily available water RAW = AW × p (depletion fraction 0.4–0.7 by crop)
Irrigate when soil moisture depletes to RAW; application depth d = (FC − θcurrent) × root depth
Irrigation frequency = RAW / daily ETc
  • Depth & frequency: deep soils take less frequent, larger applications; shallow and sandy soils need frequent light ones. Root zones run 0.5–1.5 m (paddy shallow, wheat about 1–1.2 m).
  • Moisture constants: saturation → field capacity (after gravity drainage 1–3 d; tension −1/3 bar) → permanent wilting point (−15 bar) → hygroscopic (oven dry). Water available to plants lies between FC and PWP.
  • Infiltration/intake families: USDA basic intake rate classes (0.1–2.0 in/hr) guide the choice of border, basin or furrow irrigation by soil texture and slope.

F. Design Discharge for Canals

Q_canal = peak concurrent crop demand ÷ project efficiency (+ transmission losses)
Kennedy: V₀ = 0.55 m y^0.64 (m = critical velocity ratio ≈ 1.1)
Lacey regime equations: P = 4.75√Q ; V = (Qf²/140)^⅙ ; R = 2.5V²/f ; S = f^(5/3)/(3340·Q^⅙) ; f = 1.76√d(mm)
Design capacity = peak concurrent crop demand × (1/efficiency) + losses
  • Rotation vs continuous supply: rotation (warabandi, Nepal "pakho") concentrates flow into full-depth turns — better application efficiency and equity; continuous thin supply wastes water.
  • Canal capacity design steps: crop plan & areas → monthly/10-daily water requirement (duty table) → peak concurrent requirement → divide by project efficiency → add transmission losses (0.6–2.5 m³/s per 10⁶ m² of wetted area) → design discharge at each node. Capacity decreases from head to tail as offtakes draw water.
7.1 must-knows: CWR = Kc·ET₀; NIR = ETc − Pe; GIR = NIR/efficiency; Δ = 8.64B/D (rice 1.2 m, B ≈ 120 d); duty increases downstream, canal capacity decreases; GCA ⊃ CCA; intensity sums seasons (70+35+20 = 125%); efficiencies: conveyance 70–90%, application flood 50–70/drip 90+, overall 35–60%; waterlogging = water table within ~2 m; salinity EC > 4 dS/m, LR = ECw/(5ECe − ECw); AW = FC − PWP, RAW = p·AW, frequency = RAW/ETc; Kennedy V₀ = 0.55my^0.64; Lacey P = 4.75√Q, f = 1.76√d(mm); design Q = peak concurrent demand ÷ efficiency + transmission losses.

7.2 Water Conveyance Structures (ACRE0702)

A. Canal Design

  • Alignment: contour canals follow the contour (least excavation, command on one side); watershed/ridge canals serve both sides but cost more and need cross-drainage; side-slope canals suit hill terrain (Nepal). Balance cut and fill; avoid unstable slopes, high embankments and village displacement.
  • Canal sections: trapezoidal is standard (side slope 0.5:1 in rock to 1.5:1 in loose soil; lined canals steeper); full supply depth with freeboard 0.3–0.9 m by discharge; berms, dowla (embankment), service road, inspection path.
  • Longitudinal slope: flatter than the terrain — the gradient is chosen for a regime velocity (0.3–1 m/s); where the terrain is steeper, falls/drops (vertical drop, rapids, chutes, cascades) dissipate the surplus energy.
  • Lining: cement concrete 50–100 mm (1:2:4), brick lining, CC blocks, masonry, geomembrane with cover. Benefits: seepage cut 80–95%, weed control, higher velocity (n ≈ 0.014 vs 0.025 unlined), smaller section, less waterlogging. Expansion joints every 2.5–3 m against temperature cracking.
  • Silt control in canals: excluders/ejectors at headworks (see 7.3), settling basins (hydropower), sluicing, curvature near the head, drawdown flushing; Kennedy/Lacey regime design promotes self-clearing.

B. Tunnels (hydraulic)

TypeFlow condition
Pressure tunnelFull flow (penstock/pressure shaft to turbines); internal water pressure — steel liner where the head is high
Non-pressure (free-flow) tunnelPart-full gravity — headrace tunnels (the Nepal medium-hydropower standard)
  • Tunnel stability: rock mass rating (RMR/Q-system) selects support — rock bolts, shotcrete, steel ribs, concrete lining; squeezing ground occurs in weak Himalayan schist. Lining thickness follows internal pressure and external ground load.
  • Protection: drainage holes, consolidation and contact grouting, waterproofing, portal slope protection, ventilation, probe drilling ahead for water inflow.
  • Headloss: free-flow tunnels are designed like canals (Manning); pressure tunnels use Darcy friction plus bends; surge protection ties into the surge tank.
  • Nepal examples: Melamchi tunnel 27.5 km (water supply), Kaligandaki A headrace, many 1–8 km headrace tunnels — geology lessons: squeezing, inflow, faults.
  • Course tunnel facts: circular section is best structurally; egg-shaped suits stratified soft laminated rock; heading-and-benching for soft rock (heading 3–3.5 m ahead); full-face method up to ≈ 3 m dia; NATM = sequential excavation with flexible supports and monitoring. Minimum sizes: circular > 2.0 m; other shapes > 1.9 m wide × 2.1 m high. Velocities: unlined 2–2.5 m/s, concrete-lined 4–5, steel-lined up to 9 m/s.

C. Forebay & Surge Tanks

  • Forebay: a small reservoir at the end of the headrace tunnel/canal before the penstock — provides short (peaking) storage, settling, water-level control, trash rack and an escape/spill weir; connects to the penstock intake (bell mouth + gate).
  • Surge tank (surge shaft): a chamber near the turbine end of the pressure tunnel — absorbs water hammer on load rejection (governor closes wicket gates) and improves governor stability. Types: simple (open), restricted-orifice (throttled), differential (internal riser + annular), one-way.
  • Sizing: mass-oscillation (Thoma) analysis — tank area must exceed the Thoma stable area; maximum/minimum surge levels set the tank top and bottom.
  • Trash racks at intakes: bar spacing 50–150 mm (finer for Pelton), approach velocity ≤ 0.9–1.2 m/s, cleaning rakes.
  • Course formulas: forebay minimum submergence hs = 1.5Vp²/2g (or 0.5Vp√D); forebay spillway length L = Q/(C·H^1.5) with C = 1.7 sharp-crested, 2.2 ogee. Surge-tank up-surge Zmax = Vt√(Lt·At/(g·Ast)) with corrections (1 − 2P/3 + P²/9) up and (1 − 2P) down, P = hf/Zmax.

D. Penstocks & Pressure Shafts

Fig 7.3 — Forebay–surge tank–penstock–powerhouse: surge tank protects against water hammer
Wall thickness (thin cylinder): t = pD/(2σ_allow) + corrosion allowance
Economic penstock diameter: minimize (capital cost + energy value of headloss) — hf = fLV²/2gD; typical velocity 4–7 m/s (economic ≈ 5–6); headloss target 2–4% of gross head
Anchorage blocks resist thrust at bends (hydrodynamic + static); expansion joints every ~50–100 m; air valves at summits, drain valves at lows
Water hammer: p = ρcV (instant closure) — governor closure time vs critical 2L/c — surge tank or relief valve if critical
  • Materials: steel plate (rolled), ductile iron (small), GRP/RCC for low head; buried vs exposed; pressure shafts (steel liner in tunnel with backfill concrete + grouting — the rock shares internal load).
  • Course formula: penstock thickness t = P·R/(σ·η − 0.6P) + 0.15 cm corrosion allowance; economical diameter from V_eco = 0.125√(2gH).
  • Bifurcations/Y-pieces split flow to multiple turbines; rust protection by paint systems and cathodic protection.

E. Hydraulic Transients (Water Hammer)

Elastic theory (Joukowsky): ΔH = cV₀/g (head rise); c = wave speed = √(K/ρ)/√(1 + (K/E)(D/t)ψ)
c in steel penstocks ≈ 800–1200 m/s
Phase time 2L/c — Allievi charts; rigid-column (mass oscillation) analysis covers the slower surge-tank behaviour
Protection: surge tanks, air chambers, relief valves, bypass, slow-closing governors (jet deflectors for Pelton)
  • Load rejection sequence: electrical trip → governor closes guide vanes → decelerating water → pressure rise (then a negative surge after reflection). Rapid start risks negative pressure/cavitation — turbine ramping limits apply.
  • Hydrodynamic pressure on anchors/bends: pA = ρQΔV (momentum change) plus wave loads — anchor blocks designed for normal and emergency closure.

F. Regulating & Cross-Drainage Structures

StructureFunction
Head regulatorControlled offtake from main canal to branch/distributary (gates + sill)
Cross regulatorAcross the main canal — raises upstream water level for offtakes, controls main flow
Falls/declinesDissipate surplus bed slope (vertical drop, rapid, chute, flumed fall with cistern + baffle)
Outlets (sluice/pipe)Deliver canal water to the watercourse — pipe outlet, APM (subsoil pipe outlet), open flume; semi-modules keep discharge constant over a range of water levels
AqueductCanal ABOVE the drainage (drain passes under in free-flow barrels)
Siphon aqueductCanal above; drain passes UNDER PRESSURE (drain HGL above barrel soffit) — uplift design required
SuperpassageDrain ABOVE the canal (canal in barrel below)
Siphon superpassageCanal under pressure below the drain
Level crossingDrain & canal cross at the same level — gated junction (rare, operation-heavy)
Inlet/outletSmall drain let into the canal / canal water spilled to a drainage — low structures
Fig 7.4 — Cross-drainage works: aqueduct, siphon aqueduct, superpassage and level crossing — picked by relative bed levels
  • Regulator gates: vertical lift or stop logs; flow control by gate opening (free/submerged flow formulas).
  • Fall design: vertical drop (Sarda type — triangular crest, popular in UP/Nepal), rapids; energy dissipated in a cistern sized like a stilling basin (jump check by Froude).
  • Surface drainage of the command: field drains → collectors → main drain → outlet; subsurface drains 1–1.5 m deep at 30–50 m spacing (mole drains in clay). Irrigation without drainage breeds waterlogging and salinization.
CD-works selection logic: relative bed levels decide the type (canal above vs drain above; pressure vs free flow). Siphon types need uplift checks on floors (Khosla logic again). Identify by bed-level relation — recurring NEC diagrams.
7.2 must-knows: contour canal = one-side command, watershed = both sides; lining: CC 50–100 mm, seepage cut 80–95%, n ≈ 0.014, joints 2.5–3 m; tunnels: circular best structurally, min circular > 2.0 m, velocities unlined 2–2.5 / lined 4–5 / steel 9 m/s, NATM = sequential flexible excavation; forebay hs = 1.5Vp²/2g, spillway L = Q/(C·H^1.5), C = 1.7 sharp / 2.2 ogee; surge tank absorbs water hammer + stabilizes governor (Thoma minimum area), types simple/restricted-orifice/differential; penstock t = pD/2σ, V_eco = 0.125√(2gH), velocity 4–7 m/s, headloss 2–4% of gross head; water hammer ΔH = cV/g, critical closure 2L/c; CD works by bed level: aqueduct (canal over, drain free), siphon aqueduct (drain pressurized), superpassage (drain over), level crossing (same level, gated).

7.3 Diversion Headworks (ACiE0703)

A. Components of Weir/Barrage

Fig 7.5 — Diversion headworks: piles, floor, undersluices, weir bays, divide wall, head regulator
  • Diversion headworks parts: weir/barrage (raises the water level), undersluices (pocket scouring, sluicing silt, passing the flood portion), divide wall (separates undersluice from weir bays), fish ladder, canal head regulator, silt excluder/ejector, guide banks and approach embankments, marginal bunds, river training works.
  • Weir vs barrage: weir — raised crest with small shutters, flow over the crest; barrage — low crest with full-height gates (precise level and flow control, often carries a road bridge) — the modern choice.
  • Weir crest types: vertical drop, broad crest, ogee, sloping glacis with cistern (the Sarda fall is a canal fall, not a weir type); masonry weirs with vertical/sloping profiles.
  • Component details: crest (shutters 1–1.5 m), upstream and downstream impervious aprons with cutoffs at the ends, talus/block protection, cistern (energy-dissipation basin with friction blocks/baffle), guide walls.
  • Course facts: undersluice crest 1–1.2 m lower than the weir crest; fish-ladder velocity ≈ 0.3 m/s (up to 3 m/s for strong fish); head regulator angle with the weir axis 90°–110° (110° controls silt better).

B. Seepage Theories (applied to weir floors)

Fig 7.6 — Seepage creep path under a weir floor: length L vs head H (Bligh), refined by Khosla theory
TheoryBasisDesign use / limits
Bligh's creep (1910)Creep length L = total floor length + 2× depth of each cutoff; safety requires L ≥ C·H (C: boulders/shingle 5–8, coarse-grained sand 12, fine micaceous sand 15)First theory; equal weight to horizontal and vertical creep; gives floor length and cutoff depth; uplift ordinate increased 33% for safety, floor t = h/(G−1)
Lane's weighted creep (1934)Horizontal creep weighted ⅓: Lw = b/3 + 2(d₁+d₂+d₃) ≥ C′·HRefined creep (vertical seepage 3× more effective); still crude
Khosla's theory (1936)Method of independent variables — exact Laplace solution for composite floors decomposed into standard forms (pile at end, intermediate pile, depressed floor); corrections for interference, floor thickness, slopeGives uplift pressures at key points (E, D, C) and exit gradient GE = H/d × 1/(π√λ) — the modern design basis
Khosla exit gradient: GE = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ) ; d = downstream cutoff depth; λ = (1+√(1+α²))/2 with α = b/d
Safety: GE ≤ ic/FOS (ic ≈ 1 for sand; FOS 4–5) — sets the downstream cutoff depth
Uplift: pressure head at a floor point = φ·H (φ from Khosla's curves, corrected); floor thickness t from uplift balance — thicker where φ is higher (upstream)
Fig 7.7 — Khosla uplift: pressure ordinates under the floor are highest at the u/s pile — floor thickness follows h/(G−1)
  • Corrections in Khosla: (1) mutual interference of piles C = 19√(D/b′)·(d+d′)/b % (up for one point, down for the other); (2) floor thickness (pressures at top vs bottom); (3) sloping floor (depresses the pressure curve — chart correction).
  • Exit gradient governs the downstream pile depth; uplift governs floor thickness (thickest upstream).
  • Safe exit gradients (Khosla): shingle 1/4–1/5, coarse sand 1/5–1/6, fine sand 1/6–1/7 — FOS 4–6 on ic ≈ 1, i.e. design GE ≈ 0.14–0.25.
  • Failures on pervious foundations: piping/undermining (exit gradient lifts particles at the downstream end — longer creep path + deeper downstream pile prevent it) and uplift rupture (thicker impervious floor + upstream pile).

C. Silt Control Structures

Fig 7.8 — Silt excluder (before canal entry) vs ejector (in canal downstream)
  • Silt excluder: tunnels in the undersluice pocket under the head regulator sill — draws the silt-laden bottom layer to the undersluices before the canal entry; tunnel capacity ≥ 20% of canal discharge.
  • Silt ejector (extractor): built on the canal bed downstream of the regulator — removes silt that has already entered, escaping it back to the river. Prevention (excluder) is cheaper than cure (ejector).
  • Settling basin (desilting basin): an enlarged chamber slows the flow (0.02–0.1 m/s — below the settling velocity of the design particle) so sediment settles; continuous or intermittent flushing; dual basins allow continuous operation. Design particle: 0.2 mm for Pelton (high head), 0.3–0.4 mm for Francis — remove particles harder than the turbine material.
  • Vortex tubes and sediment traps serve small intakes; reservoir sediment management: flushing, sluicing, density-current venting, watershed erosion control.

D. Design of Weir/Barrage (floors & crest)

Bligh floor length: L = C·H — H = maximum seepage head (worst case: high flood upstream, lowest downstream water level)
Cutoff depths: upstream pile ≈ 0.33–0.5 H (typically 2–3 m); downstream pile deeper — set by the exit-gradient check (piping defence)
Crest level: pond level + shutter height; waterway ≈ Lacey regime perimeter P = 4.75√Q (± 10–20%)
Floor thickness: by uplift (Khosla); glacis profile ≈ 1:2–1:3 into the cistern; cistern level & length set the jump
  • Energy dissipation downstream: hydraulic jump formed on the glacis (tailwater controlled), cistern with friction blocks + end sill; match the tailwater curve to the jump curve (deficient → deepen cistern or add a sill; excess → saddle/upstream sill).
  • Weir stability: overturning/sliding (rarely critical — broad base), uplift (floor thickness), flotation during construction dewatering, piping (exit gradient).

E. Energy Dissipaters (summary of devices)

  • Stilling basin (jump — USBR II/III adaptations), roller bucket (SR type), ski-jump/flip bucket (plunge pool), plain apron, baffle piers & end sills, canal-fall drops, plunge pools with riprap, stepped chutes (small).
  • Selection by head & tailwater: jump basins for moderate head with stable tailwater; ski-jump for high dams/narrow valleys (flip clear of the toe); roller bucket for deep tailwater.

F. Stability Analysis of Dams (gravity — conceptual)

Gravity dam forces: weight W; water thrust P = ½γH² at H/3; uplift U (triangular — reduced by drains); silt P_s = ½γs·Ka·h²; ice, wave, seismic, temperature
Checks: overturning FOS ≥ 1.5 (course: ≥ 1.6); sliding FOS ≥ 1.5 (μ ≈ 0.7–0.75; shear-friction factor SFF = (μΣV + cA)/ΣH ≥ 3.6 per IS 6512); no tension at the upstream face — resultant within the middle third (e ≤ B/6)
Elementary triangular profile: base B = H/√(G−c) (G = sp. gravity of masonry, c = uplift coefficient; without uplift B = H/√(G−1)); practical gravity bases ≈ 0.7–0.8H
  • Low vs high dam: a high dam's base widens mainly because of uplift; the drainage gallery cuts uplift by roughly 30–50%.
    • Fig 7.9 — Gravity dam forces: water thrust at H/3, uplift triangle, self-weight — resultant kept inside the middle third
  • Embankment (earth) dam stability: slip-circle checks for steady seepage (FOS ≥ 1.5), sudden drawdown, construction pore pressure and earthquake (≈ 1.2); seepage control by filters and toe drains; failure modes — slope slip, piping, foundation shear, and overtopping (the most common dam failure worldwide).
  • Nepal dams: most hydropower is run-of-river (weirs/barrages); Kulekhani (1982) is Nepal's only major storage scheme — ≈ 114 m rockfill dam; Babai and Rani-Jamara are irrigation barrages.
7.3 must-knows: weir = high crest + small shutters, barrage = low crest + full gates; undersluice crest 1–1.2 m lower; fish ladder ≈ 0.3 m/s; head regulator 90–110° to weir axis; divide wall separates undersluices; Bligh L = C·H (C 5–15), uplift +33%, floor t = h/(G−1); Lane weights horizontal ⅓; Khosla GE = (H/d)·1/(π√λ), λ = (1+√(1+α²))/2 — downstream pile governs GE, uplift governs floor thickness (upstream thickest); 3 corrections: interference 19√(D/b′)(d+d′)/b, thickness, slope; failures: piping (exit gradient) vs uplift rupture; silt excluder u/s = prevention (tunnels ≥ 20% canal Q), ejector d/s = cure; waterway P = 4.75√Q; scour R = 1.35(q²/f)^⅓; gravity dam: overturning ≥ 1.5 (course 1.6), no tension e ≤ B/6, B = H/√(G−c); earth dam: overtopping = most common failure.

7.4 River Training Works (ACiE0704)

A. River Stages & Need

  • Stages: low water, freshet (monsoon high), flood. Meandering cause: excess energy/sediment imbalance — helical secondary flow erodes the outer bank and deposits point bars on the inner — sinuosity grows until cutoffs and oxbows form.
  • Objectives: flood protection (embankments), navigation depth, sediment control, protection of structures (intakes/bridges — Nepali practice: guide bunds at bridge sites), bank stabilization, land reclamation.
  • Classification: training for discharge (high flood — embankments), for depth (navigation — groynes/locks), for silt (training walls), and by works type: embankments (levees), guide banks (Bell's bunds), spurs/groynes, pitched islands, revetments, bio-engineering.

B. Design of River Training Works

Guide banks (Bell's bunds)

  • Earth core with stone pitching; straight (Bell) or hooked shapes — straight is typical. Upstream arm ≈ 1.0–1.5× bridge length L, downstream ≈ 0.2–0.4L; top width 6–9 m; side slopes 1.5:1–2:1; freeboard 1–1.5 m. Launching apron: stone ~1–1.2 m thick laid at the toe, width ≈ 1.0–1.5× anticipated scour depth — it settles into the scour hole as the river undermines it.
  • Scour depth: Lacey normal scour R = 1.35(q²/f)^⅓ below HFL; foundations and aprons go below the deepest scour (piers commonly designed for 2× normal scour).

Levees (embankments/flood dykes)

  • Earthen flood embankments designed to a return-period flood; freeboard 1–1.5 m; side slopes 2:1–3:1 by material; seepage handled with filters/berms; settlement allowance included. A confined river raises flood levels downstream (the problem is transferred, not removed); drainage sluices and escapes are needed.

Spurs/Groynes

  • Attracting spurs point downstream (draw flow toward the bank, scour near the head — deepen a channel), repelling spurs point upstream (push flow away from the bank — protect it), perpendicular spurs deflect.
  • By permeability: impermeable (rockfill/earth with stone pitching — siltation behind), permeable (tree/brushwood, bamboo; Nepal "porcupine" screens — silt trap and velocity reducer); special shapes: T-head, hockey-stick, Denehy T-head.
  • Spacing 2–4× spur length (depends on angle and function); heads heavily armoured; scour at the head (jet effect) — riprap + launching apron.

Bank protection

  • Revetments: dry stone pitching 30–50 cm thick; riprap graded, thickness ≥ 2×D50; gabions (Nepal standard), concrete blocks, sand-cement bags (economy); geotextile filter underneath; toe protection essential; bio-engineering (vetiver, bamboo, brush layering — combined civil-bio Nepal practice).
  • Watershed management (upstream): afforestation, terracing, check dams, gully plugs, contour bunding — reduces sediment yield and flood peaks. Sediment yield in Nepal hills is high (fragile geology, deforestation).
Fig 7.10 — River training works: guide bank with launching apron, attracting vs repelling spurs, scour at the head
7.4 must-knows: meandering = helical secondary flow (outer bank erodes, point bars inside); training classified for discharge/depth/silt; guide bank (Bell's bund): u/s arm 1.0–1.5L, d/s 0.2–0.4L, top 6–9 m, freeboard 1–1.5 m, launching apron 1–1.5× scour depth; Lacey scour R = 1.35(q²/f)^⅓ below HFL (piers designed 2×); spurs: attracting points d/s (scours channel), repelling points u/s (protects bank), spacing 2–4× length; permeable spur = Nepal porcupine; revetments: pitching 30–50 cm, riprap ≥ 2×D50, geotextile filter, toe protection; watershed treatment u/s: afforestation, terracing, check dams.

7.5 Power and Energy Potential Study (ACRE0802)

A. Power & Energy

P (kW) = 9.81 × Q × H × η (Q m³/s, H net head m, η overall 0.8–0.9)
≈ 8 × Q × H (rule of thumb)
Energy E (kWh) = average power × hours; firm energy = available at the design reliability level; secondary energy = seasonal excess
Net head = gross head − losses (trash rack, conduit, surge) − tailwater variation

B. Types of Hydropower Plants

BasisTypes
StorageRun-of-river (RoR — daily pondage at most, Nepal standard), pondage (daily storage), reservoir/storage (seasonal — peaking)
HeadLow (< 15 m), medium (15–50 m), high (> 50 m)
Capacity (Nepal)Micro ≤ 100 kW; Mini 101–1000 kW; Small 1–10 MW; Medium 10–100 MW; Large > 100 MW
ConveyanceCanal type, tunnel type, mixed; Nepal high-head schemes convey 70–80% of gross head via tunnel/penstock
Dam positionDam-toe (powerhouse at the dam), valley dam, diversion type

C. Components of Hydropower Projects

  • Headworks: weir/barrage + undersluices + intake (trash rack, gate) + settling basin + flushing system.
  • Conveyance: headrace canal/tunnel → forebay/surge tank → penstock/pressure shaft → bifurcation.
  • Powerhouse (surface/underground): turbines + generators + governors + transformers + switchyard + control room + auxiliaries (cooling, drainage, EOT crane, compressed air).
  • Tailrace: returns flow to the river.
  • Switchyard/transmission: step-up transformer (11 kV generation → 33/66/132/220 kV grid), lines, switchgear, protection.
  • Others: fish pass/ladder, spillway (dams), access roads, colonies, spoil management.

D. Reservoirs & Regulation

  • Storage zones: dead storage (sediment/intake level), live/active storage (drawdown for power/irrigation), flood surcharge (spillway), buffer; gross = the sum. Yield by mass curve (Rippl) — sequential firm yield; storage-yield curves.
  • Regulation: rule curves (seasonal guide levels), firm energy from sequential flow simulation, peaking within pondage, flood-control vs storage trade-offs, sedimentation (trap efficiency vs capacity-inflow ratio — the Brune curve; large reservoirs trap 90–100%), dead-storage life 50–100 yr design.
  • Losses: evaporation (pan × coefficient), seepage; bank and valley storage concepts (effective flood-mitigation storage = live + surcharge − valley storage).

E. Load Analysis

Load curve: power vs time; load duration curve (LDC): sorted descending
Load factor LF = average load / peak load (0.45–0.6 typical)
Capacity (plant) factor CF = average output / installed capacity (Nepal RoR ≈ 0.5–0.7, wet-season heavy; course range 0.25–0.7)
Plant use factor, diversity factor (> 1 — sum of individual peaks ÷ system peak), coincidence factor = 1/diversity, demand factor, power factor kW/kVA (0.8–0.9)
Firm power = available 100% of the time; RoR design discharge commonly Q40 (40% exceedance) to Q60
  • Installed capacity fixing: firm flow (FDC exceedance) × net head for RoR; peaking pondage from energy storage ÷ peak hours; economic optimization (marginal cost of an extra MW vs revenue); grid demand & energy balance. Course marginal-benefit form: 8.76 × ΔP × energy rate vs annualized cost.
  • Peaking RoR (Nepal standard): pondage stores hours of dry-season flow to run 4–6 hr peaks; tailwater fluctuation and environmental flow constrain operation.
    • Fig 7.11 — Load-duration and Rippl mass curves: load factor, firm power, and the storage for firm yield

F. Hydropower Development in Nepal

  • History: Pharping (Chandrajyoti) 1911 — 500 kW, the first; Sundarijal 1936 (640 kW); Trishuli 1967; Kulekhani I 1982 — 60 MW (first storage); Khimti 2000 — 60 MW (first IPP); Kaligandaki A 2002 — 144 MW (largest until recently); Upper Tamakoshi 2021 — 456 MW (largest now).
  • Potential: theoretical ≈ 83,000 MW; technically feasible ≈ 44,000 MW; economically viable ≈ 42,000 MW. Installed capacity passed 3,000 MW by the mid-2020s — wet-season surplus, dry-season deficit with imports from India.
  • Institutions: Department of Electricity Development (DoED — licensing; survey licence 5 yr, generation licence 35 yr domestic / 30 yr export), Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA — utility), Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC), IPPs (IPPAN), Ministry of Energy (MoEWRI).
  • Policy/Legal: Electricity Act 2049 (1992), Electricity Regulation 2050, Hydropower Development Policy 2058 (2001), Water Resources Act 2049. Royalties: capacity royalty Rs 100/kW-yr for the first 15 years; energy royalty 2% of sales for the first 15 years, 10% after; local area development funds.
  • PPA & tariffs: NEA PPA with dry/wet season differentiation (dry premium), take-or-pay concepts, currency indexation — concept level.
  • Export: India power trade (PTA 2014; 10 GW target), tri-nation Bangladesh transit, SAARC grid; cross-border 400 kV Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur corridor.
  • Challenges: seasonal variation, transmission constraints, GLOF/sediment/landslides, financial closure, land acquisition, geological risk (squeezing tunnels), climate change on glacier-fed flows.
7.5 must-knows: P = 9.81QHη ≈ 8QH kW; plants: RoR (Nepal standard) / pondage / storage; size ladder micro ≤ 100 kW, mini ≤ 1 MW, small ≤ 10 MW; chain = headworks → headrace → forebay/surge → penstock → powerhouse → tailrace → switchyard (11 → 33/66/132 kV); storage zones dead/live/surcharge, firm yield by Rippl mass curve; LF = avg/peak (0.45–0.6), CF = avg/installed (RoR 0.5–0.7), diversity > 1; RoR design discharge Q40–Q60; Nepal: potential 83,000 → technical 44,000 → economic 42,000 MW; milestones Pharping 1911 (500 kW, first), Kulekhani 1982 (60 MW, first storage), Khimti 2000 (first IPP), Kaligandaki A 144 MW, Upper Tamakoshi 456 MW (largest); DoED survey 5 yr, generation 35/30 yr (export); Electricity Act 2049; royalties capacity Rs 100/kW-yr, energy 2% → 10%.

7.6 Hydro-electric Machines and Powerhouse (ACiE0806)

A. Turbines — Types & Performance

Fig 7.12 — Turbine family: Pelton buckets, Francis mixed-flow runner, Kaplan axial blades — bands of specific speed Ns
Impulse (Pelton)Reaction (Francis/Kaplan/Propeller/Deriaz/Bulb)
Pressure energy → kinetic at the nozzle (atmospheric casing); bucket impact; high head, low flow (150–2000 m); no draft tube; jet deflector on rejectionPressure + velocity used at the runner (water stays pressurized); draft tube recovers exit head; low-medium head; spiral casing + guide vanes regulate
TurbineHead rangeSpecific speed Ns (metric hp; kW in brackets)Notes
Pelton150–2000 m10–35 (8.5–30 kW; multi-jet 35–60 / 30–51)Impulse; bucket angle ≈ 165°; jet ratio D/d = 11–25
Francis30–600 m60–300 (51–225 kW)Mixed (radial-axial) flow; most common worldwide; spiral casing, stay & guide vanes
Kaplan2–40 m300–1000 (225–860 kW)Axial, adjustable blades + wicket gates (double regulation); low head, large Q
Propeller2–40 m300–1000 (225–860 kW)Fixed blades (single regulation); efficiency drops off-design
Deriaz (diagonal)20–90 m—Adjustable diagonal blades (between Francis and Kaplan)
Bulb/tubular2–25 m600–1000Horizontal Kaplan in the water passage — very low head RoR
Crossflow (Michell–Banki)2–60 m10–80Simple — the Nepal micro-hydro workhorse; good part-flow efficiency
Specific speed: Ns = N√P / H^1.25 (P in kW per runner, N rpm, H net head m; 1 hp = 736 W)
Bands with P in kW: Pelton 8.5–30 single jet / 30–51 two or more jets, Francis 51–225, Kaplan/propeller 225–860 — same bands in hp: 10–35 / 35–60 / 60–300 / 300–1000
Efficiency curves: Pelton — flat peak (jet regulation); Kaplan — flat (double regulation); Propeller — steep off-design drop; Francis — moderate
Cavitation: Thoma number σ = NPSH/H = (Hatm − Hvap − Hs)/H ≥ σ_critical — sets the maximum suction height Hs (setting by sigma chart)
Runaway speed on load rejection ≈ 1.6–2.2× rated (Pelton ≈ 1.8×); the governor keeps speed within limits

B. Turbine Selection

  • By head and specific speed (chart); by discharge variation (Kaplan double regulation flat; Pelton multi-jet; Francis narrower); by sediment (abrasion-resistant coatings; Pelton needles and Francis runners wear in Nepal's rivers); by cavitation margin; by cost and O&M skill.
  • Pelton preliminary design: jet velocity Vj = Cv√(2gH) (Cv ≈ 0.97–0.99); bucket speed u = 0.46–0.48 Vj; u = πDN/60; jet diameter d = √(4Q/(πVj·n_jets)); bucket width ≈ 3.5d; number of buckets Z = 15 + D/(2d) (≈ 15–22); efficiency 85–90%.
  • Francis preliminary design: Ns → speed and runner diameter via constants; guide-vane and runner geometry from velocity triangles; elbow draft tube recovery ≈ 70–85% of exit kinetic energy; efficiency 90–94% modern.
  • Head–turbine matching (course): ≤ 15 m — Kaplan/propeller; 15–60 m — crossflow (micro-hydro); 60–150 m — Francis; > 350 m — Pelton.
  • Governors: mechanical-hydraulic (classic), electro-hydraulic, digital; actuate wicket gates (reaction) or needle + deflector (Pelton); transient speed rise ≤ 50%; isolated-grid droop 5% standard; design checks penstock inertia and flywheel effect GD².

C. Scroll Case & Draft Tube

  • Spiral (scroll) case: wraps the guide vanes with uniformly decreasing area (constant-velocity design) for even velocity distribution; stay ring carries load; steel or concrete (low head).
  • Draft tube: a diffuser below the runner recovering kinetic energy as pressure (and gaining elevation to tailwater). Types: straight conical, elbow (most common — saves excavation), Moody spreading, bullet. Recovery 70–85%; divergence cone angle 7–10° avoids separation.

D. Generators & Governor Auxiliaries

  • Generator types: synchronous — salient-pole for low-speed hydro (< 300 rpm), cylindrical-rotor for turbo sets; static or brushless excitation; kVA = kW/power factor (hydro PF 0.8–0.95); generation voltage 3.3/6.6/11 kV typical for medium plants.
  • Cooling: air (most), water (large); insulation class F with class B temperature-rise practice; flywheel effect (GD²) added for stability (micro-hydro flywheels).
  • Auxiliaries: governor oil-pressure units, compressed air (brakes, governor accumulator), cooling water (self-consumption ≈ 0.2–0.5% of Q), drainage & dewatering (tailrace stop logs + pumps), fire protection (CO₂/water mist).
  • Transformers & switchyard: step-up 11 → 33/66/132 kV; breakers, isolators, CT/PT, protection (differential, overcurrent, earth fault); control & SCADA; earthing and lightning protection.

E. Pumps & Pumping Systems

Pump head: H_m = H_static + losses; pump H–Q curve falls, system curve rises → operating point at the intersection
Pump specific speed: Ns = N√Q / H^0.75 — radial (centrifugal) < 30, mixed 30–100, axial > 100 (metric)
Cavitation: NPSHa = Hatm + hsuction − Hvap − hlosses > NPSHr (margin 0.5–1 m)
Affinity laws: Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³
Series adds head (same Q); parallel adds Q (same H); centrifugal pumps need priming; BEP efficiency 70–90%
  • Types: centrifugal (radial — most common), mixed flow, axial (high Q, low H), reciprocating (dosing), jet/air-lift, submersible, vertical turbine/deep-well, hand pumps (Nepal Terai — Tara/Afridev), solar pumps (rural WSS trend).
  • WR applications: drainage/dewatering, water-supply boosting, irrigation lift schemes, seepage control, powerhouse services; sewage pumps (non-clog), sludge pumps.
  • Field testing: V-notch/weir for discharge, pressure gauges, power meter — efficiency = water hp/shaft hp; characteristic curves from the factory test.

F. Powerhouse — Types, Layout & Dimensions

  • Types: surface (open/outdoor/semi-outdoor), underground (the Nepal Himalaya standard — rock cavern protection; e.g., Upper Tamakoshi), dam-toe, semi-underground, floating, in-river bulb.
  • Surface powerhouse blocks: machine hall (turbine-generator bays + EOT crane), control room, auxiliary bay, service bay, draft-tube gate area, substructure (spiral case/draft-tube concrete), tailrace. Unit bay spacing 12–20 m in medium plants (set by spiral-case/draft-tube concrete); crane sized for the heaviest lift (generator rotor); crane rail height from rotor transport clearance.
  • Underground powerhouse: cavern span 15–25 m by rock quality; support with rock bolts, shotcrete, lining; two escape routes; ventilation; rock cover for unlined pressure tunnels ≥ 0.8–1.0× static head (Norwegian criterion); drainage and seepage handling.
  • Micro hydro powerhouse (Nepal rural): simple structure, crossflow turbine + induction generator with an ELC (electronic load controller) — the village-electrification classic.
  • Tailwater & flood design: powerhouse floor above the design flood (or flood walls), draft-tube gates for dewatering, tailrace deck protection, drainage sump pumps.
7.6 must-knows: Pelton impulse 150–2000 m, Ns 10–35 hp (8.5–30 kW), no draft tube, deflector on rejection; Francis 30–600 m, Ns 60–300; Kaplan 2–40 m, Ns 300–1000, double regulation; crossflow 2–60 m = micro workhorse; Ns = N√P/H^1.25; Pelton Vj = Cv√(2gH), u = 0.46–0.48Vj, Z = 15 + D/2d, η 85–90%; draft tube recovery 70–85%, cone 7–10°; Thoma σ sets suction height Hs; runaway 1.6–2.2× rated; generator salient-pole < 300 rpm, PF 0.8–0.95, 11 kV; pumps Ns = N√Q/H^0.75 (radial < 30, axial > 100), affinity Q∝N H∝N² P∝N³, series adds head / parallel adds Q, priming needed; powerhouse: underground = Nepal standard, bay 12–20 m, crane sized for the heaviest rotor, floor above design flood; micro hydro = crossflow + induction generator + ELC.

Extended High-Yield Additions (Exam-Focused Extras)

Irrigation numericals

  • Delta for rice: B = 120 d, duty 860 ha/cumec → Δ = 8.64×120/860 = 1.21 m (typical 1.2 m). Wheat: duty 1800, B = 120 → Δ = 0.576 m ≈ 58 cm.
  • Duty-to-discharge: CCA 5000 ha, intensity 60% paddy (Δ = 1.2 m, B = 120 d): area 3000 ha → D = 8.64×120/1.2 = 864 ha/cumec → Q = 3000/864 = 3.47 cumec; gross at 60% efficiency: 5.8 cumec.
  • ET: ET₀ = 5 mm/d, Kc = 1.1 → ETc = 5.5 mm/d; Pe = 1 mm/d → NIR = 4.5 mm/d; at 50% efficiency → GIR = 9 mm/d = 90 m³/ha·d.
  • RAW: FC 0.32, PWP 0.16, root 0.8 m, p = 0.5: AW = 128 mm, RAW = 64 mm; at ETc 5.5 → frequency ≈ 12 d; delivered depth = 64/0.6 ≈ 107 mm.

Headworks numericals

  • Bligh: H = 4 m, C = 12 → required creep L = 48 m; with two cutoffs of 3 m each, floor = 48 − 12 = 36 m.
  • Khosla exit gradient: H = 4, d = 3, α = b/d = 8 → λ = (1+√65)/2 = 4.53 → GE = (4/3)/(π×4.53) = 0.094; FOS = ic/GE ≈ 10.6 — safe.
  • Uplift: at a floor point φ = 0.35, H = 4 m → pressure head 1.4 m; balancing floor self-weight: t = 1.4/(2.4−1) = 1.0 m (plus safety factor) — the RCC floor design pattern.
  • Lacey waterway: Q = 3000 cumec → P = 4.75√3000 = 260 m; provide 270–285 m of weir bays.
  • Scour: q = 3000/260 = 11.5 m²/s; f = 1.0 → s = 1.35(11.5²)^⅓ = 6.9 m below HFL → cutoffs/aprons below 6.9 m + margin.

Hydropower numericals

  • Q = 10 m³/s, H = 200 m, η = 0.85: P = 9.81×10×200×0.85 = 16.7 MW.
  • Energy: 16.7 MW × CF 0.6 × 8760 = 87.8 GWh/yr.
  • Pelton: H = 400, Cv = 0.98 → Vj = 86.8 m/s; u = 0.46×86.8 = 39.9; N = 500 rpm → D = 60×39.9/(π×500) = 1.52 m; 4 jets of 0.5 m³/s: d = 86 mm; jet ratio D/d = 17.7 ✓ (11–25).
  • Ns check Francis: P = 20,000 kW, N = 300, H = 150 → Ns = 300×141.4/525 ≈ 81 — squarely in the Francis band 51–225 kW (60–300 hp) ✓ — P in kW gives Ns in kW units (150^1.25 = 525).
  • Penstock: D = 2 m, p = 2.45 MPa, σ_allow = 140 MPa: t = 2.45×2/(2×140) = 17.5 mm → provide 18–20 mm + corrosion allowance.
  • Surge tank: Thoma area stability — A > A_Thoma (qualitative exam question).
  • Pump: Q = 50 L/s, H = 60 m, η = 0.7 → P = 42 kW motor.

Rapid-Fire One-Liners (Last-Minute Revision)

  • ETc = Kc·ET₀; NIR = ETc − Pe; GIR = NIR/efficiency; ET₀ by Penman-Monteith or pan (Kp).
  • GCA ⊃ CCA; irrigation intensity = seasonal irrigated/CCA; annual sums can exceed 100%.
  • Δ = 8.64B/D; duty increases downstream; rice Δ ≈ 1.2 m; kor watering = first watering, kor period = base period.
  • Efficiencies: conveyance 70–90%, application flood 50–70/drip 90+, overall 35–60%.
  • Waterlogging: water table in the root zone; salinity EC > 4 dS/m; remedies: lining + drainage.
  • AW = FC − PWP; RAW = p×AW; frequency = RAW/ETc.
  • Canal lining: CC 50–100 mm, seepage cut 80%+, n → 0.014, joints 2.5–3 m.
  • Tunnels: circular best structurally; velocities unlined 2–2.5, lined 4–5, steel 9 m/s; NATM = flexible sequential excavation.
  • Forebay hs = 1.5Vp²/2g; surge tank = water hammer + governor stability; Thoma minimum area.
  • Penstock t = pD/2σ (+ allowance); economic dia by cost + energy loss; velocity 4–7 m/s; anchors at bends; air valves at summits.
  • Water hammer ΔH = cV/g; critical closure 2L/c; protection: surge tank/air chamber/relief valve/deflector.
  • CD works by bed levels: aqueduct (canal over drain, free), siphon aqueduct (drain pressurized), superpassage (drain over canal), siphon superpassage, level crossing.
  • Head regulator offtakes; cross regulator raises level; Sarda-type falls; semi-module outlets give constant Q.
  • Subsurface drains 1–1.5 m deep, 30–50 m spacing — "irrigation without drainage breeds waterlogging".
  • Headworks: weir/barrage + undersluices (+1–1.2 m lower crest) + divide wall + fish ladder (0.3 m/s) + regulator (90–110°) + guide banks.
  • Bligh L = C·H (equal weights, 33% uplift margin); Lane weights horizontal ⅓; Khosla exact — GE = H/d·1/(π√λ), only the downstream pile governs; uplift governs floor thickness (upstream thicker).
  • Excluder (upstream, prevention, ≥ 20% canal Q) vs ejector (downstream, cure); settling basin: 0.2 mm for Pelton, 0.3–0.4 for Francis.
  • Weir waterway ≈ 4.75√Q; scour s = 1.35(q²/f)^⅓; launching apron 1–1.5× scour depth.
  • Gravity dam: overturning ≥ 1.5 (course 1.6), sliding via μ 0.7–0.75, no tension (middle third), elementary B = H/√(G−c).
  • Earth dam failures: overtopping (most common worldwide), piping, slope slips (FOS 1.5 steady / 1.2 drawdown-EQ).
  • P = 9.81QHη ≈ 8QH; LF = avg/peak; CF = avg output/installed (RoR 0.5–0.7); diversity > 1.
  • RoR design discharge Q40–Q60; pondage = peak hours × peak flow.
  • Nepal: Pharping 1911 (500 kW) first; Kulekhani 1982 (60 MW) first storage; Khimti 2000 first IPP; Kaligandaki A 144 MW; Upper Tamakoshi 456 MW (2021); potential 83,000/44,000/42,000 MW; DoED licenses (5/35/30 yr), NEA utility, ERC regulator; royalty: capacity Rs 100/kW-yr, energy 2% → 10%.
  • Turbines: Pelton 150–2000 m (Ns 10–35 hp / 8.5–30 kW); Francis 30–600 m (60–300 / 51–225); Kaplan 2–40 m (300–1000 / 225–860); crossflow for micro.
  • Pelton: u = 0.46Vj, D/d 11–25, buckets Z = 15 + D/2d; deflector on rejection; no draft tube.
  • Francis draft-tube recovery 70–85%; Thoma σ sets setting depth; runaway 1.6–2.2×.
  • Generator: salient pole (low speed), PF 0.8–0.95, 11 kV typical; class F insulation; GD² stability.
  • Pumps: radial/mixed/axial by Ns; NPSHa > NPSHr; affinity Q∝N, H∝N², P∝N³; series head, parallel flow.
  • Powerhouse: underground is Nepal's standard (rock cover, ventilation, two escapes); bay 12–20 m; crane = heaviest rotor; floor above design flood.
  • Micro hydro: crossflow + induction generator + ELC — Nepal village classic.
  • E-flow: 10% of minimum monthly flow (GoN standard); monsoon shutdowns on high-sediment rivers.

Deeper Concept Discussions (Chapter 7)

Why duty-based design works

  • Duty compresses crop + soil + climate into one number (ha per cumec) — canal capacity = area ÷ duty. The modern FAO approach computes 10-daily crop water balances, but duty survives in Nepali/Indian practice — the exam uses both.
  • Duty increases downstream; capacity decreases downstream (offtakes). Do not mix the two directions.
  • Warabandi rotation (Nepal "pakho") improves equity — each outlet gets a full-flow turn instead of a thin continuous trickle (less seepage per unit delivered).

Cross-drainage selection worked logic

  • Canal FSL above drain HFL, drain bed below canal bed → aqueduct (free-flow drain barrels under the canal).
  • Canal above but drain HFL above the barrel soffit → siphon aqueduct (pressurized drain) — uplift designed under the canal floor (Khosla logic again).
  • Drain above the canal → superpassage; canal pressurized below → siphon superpassage.
  • Level crossing (gated, same level) and inlet/outlet (minor drains) — rare, definition items.

Khosla corrections — the three adjustments

  • Mutual interference: C = 19√(D/b′)·(d+d′)/b % — applied up or down depending on the point; negligible for widely spaced piles.
  • Thickness of floor: charts give pressures at floor top — correct for the thickness to the bottom.
  • Sloping floor: a slope of 1:n between piles depresses the interpolated pressure curve (chart correction).
  • Safe exit gradients: shingle 1/4–1/5, coarse sand 1/5–1/6, fine sand 1/6–1/7 (FOS 4–6 → design GE ≈ 0.15–0.25).
  • Why the downstream cutoff is deepest: exit gradient (piping — the last defence) depends inversely on d; the upstream pile seals entry and lengthens creep.

Weir vs barrage — design philosophy

  • Weir: cheap, passive (shutters fall at high flood — an operational risk), fixed pond level. Barrage: gates control the pond over a range, better sediment control (bigger undersluice share), road-bridge benefit, higher cost — Nepal's newer headworks (Babai) are barrage-type.
  • Gates: vertical lift, radial (tainter — lower hoist capacity, reacts at the trunnion), stop logs; hoists electric or manual.
  • Sloping-glacis weirs force the jump on the glacis by cistern/tailwater control — friction blocks + end sill (USBR-type basins adapted).

  • Sediment & turbines: Nepal's glacier-fed rivers carry quartz (hardness 7) that erodes Francis runners and Pelton needles — erosion worsens with jet velocity, so high-head plants target finer removal (0.15–0.2 mm); HVOF tungsten-carbide coatings; seasonal sand-trap flushing; monsoon shutdowns.
  • Governor stability: penstock water starting time T_w < 2.5 s and T_w < T_m/3 rule of thumb; surge tanks reduce T_w; no-load opening and damping tuned at commissioning.
