  • RAW: FC 0.35, PWP 0.15, root 1.0 m, p = 0.5 → 100 mm; at 5 mm/d → 20-day rotation.
  • Canal: Q = 2 cumec, n = 0.014, b = 1.5, y = 1.0, z = 1: A = 2.5, R = 0.577; for V = 0.8 m/s → S = 1/3830 — regime slope math (S = (Vn/R^⅔)²).
  • Bligh: H = 3.5, C = 12 → L = 42 m; with two cutoffs × 2.5 m → floor = 42 − 10 = 32 m.
  • Khosla: H = 3, d = 2.5, λ = 4: GE = (3/2.5)/(π×4) = 0.0955; FOS = 10.5 ✓.
  • Uplift t: φH = 1.8 m head: t = 1.8/(2.4−1) = 1.29 m (add factor).
  • Lacey waterway Q = 1200: P = 4.75×34.6 = 164 m; provide ~170–180 m.
  • Scour: q = 7.06, f = 1.1 → s = 1.35×(45.3)^⅓ = 4.8 m below HFL.
  • Power: Q = 5, H = 120, η = 0.85 → 5.0 MW.
  • Energy: 5 MW × 0.65 × 8760 = 28.5 GWh/yr.
  • Pelton D: u = 0.46×0.98×√(2×9.81×300) = 34.6 m/s; N = 375 → D = 1.76 m.
  • Jet dia: 1.5 m³/s in 2 jets → d = 113 mm; D/d = 15.6 ✓.
  • Penstock t: H = 350 m (3.43 MPa), D = 1.8, σ = 130 → 23.7 mm → 26 mm with allowance.
  • Water hammer: c = 1000, V = 5 → ΔH = 509 m — instant closure impossible; slow close/surge tank mandatory.
  • Ns: P = 8000 kW, N = 500, H = 200 → Ns = 59.5 (200^1.25 = 752) — too high for single-jet Pelton → ~3 jets (≈34 per jet) or Francis.
  • Pump: Q = 20 L/s, H = 40, η = 0.65 → 12.1 kW.
  • Forebay pondage: 3 MW × 4 h at H = 150, η = 0.85 → volume = 43,200 MJ ÷ (9.81×150×0.85 kJ/m³) ≈ 34,500 m³ (12 MWh = 43,200 MJ).
  • Load factor: energy 500 GWh, peak 100 MW → avg 57 MW → LF = 57%.

Last-Mile Memory Hooks (Chapter 7)

  • Duty↔delta: Δ = 8.64B/D — "8.64 = 86,400 s ÷ 10,000"; B in days, D in ha/cumec, Δ in m.
  • Kennedy vs Lacey: Kennedy = one formula (V₀ = 0.55my^0.64, upper Punjab); Lacey = complete regime theory (P = 4.75√Q, f = 1.76√dmm) — paired every year.
  • Bligh vs Lane: same creep idea; Lane weights horizontal ×⅓ (shorter floor); Khosla replaces both (independent piles + corrections).
  • Exit gradient order: fine sand worst; deeper downstream cutoff cuts GE fastest.
  • Settling basin removal: 0.2 mm trap for Pelton (high head), 0.3 mm Francis; trap ratio 20 → 90–95% removal.
  • Turbine Ns ladder: Pelton (10–35 hp) < Francis (60–300 hp) < Kaplan (300–1000 hp) — kW: 8.5–30 < 51–225 < 225–860; the higher the head, the lower the Ns.
  • Pondage vs storage: pondage = hours–days (diurnal peaks, RoR forebay); storage = seasonal (reservoir).
  • CD one-liner: drain under + free = aqueduct; drain under + pressurized = siphon aqueduct; canal under = superpassage.
  • Approximation sanity check: P(kW) ≈ 8 × Q × H — Q = 2, H = 60 → 960 kW.

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (7.1–7.6)

Irrigation & Water Requirements (7.1) — Course Formulas

  • Demand chain: CIR = Cu − Re; NIR = CIR + LR + PSR + NWR; FIR = NIR + application losses; GIR = FIR + conveyance losses. Consumptive use Cu = ET + plant-metabolism water.
  • Kor watering = first watering after the plant has grown a few cm; kor depth Δ = 8.64B/D; kor period = the base period of the crop.
  • Water-distribution efficiency ηd = (1 − y/yavg)×100; readily available soil moisture = γd·D·(FC − OMC)/γw; irrigation interval = depth required / crop ET.
  • Methods: furrow — depth 8–30 cm, wets 20–50% of the surface; sprinkler — 80–85% application efficiency; drip > 90% (most efficient); border/basin flooding least efficient.
  • Semi-arid regions (25–50 cm rain/yr) grow inferior crops without irrigation; Zaid crops grow March–June; SAR classifies irrigation water; salinity = accumulation, leaching = washing out.
  • Canal design: lined trapezoidal canals for discharges above 85 cumecs; A = BD + D²(θ + cotθ), P = B + 2D(θ + cotθ); most efficient triangular section R = y/2√2.
  • Tractive force theory: bed shear τ₀ = γw·R·S; side shear τ₀′ = 0.75γwRS; tractive-force ratio K = √(1 − sin²θ/sin²φ).
  • Lacey's regime theory (unlined alluvial canals): f = 1.76√d(mm); v = (Qf²/140)^⅙; P = 4.75√Q; R = 2.5v²/f; normal scour depth R = 1.35(q²/f)^⅓.

Conveyance & Cross-Drainage (7.2)

  • Canal lining reduces seepage, prevents weeds, allows higher velocity/smaller section; economy = water saving vs cost.
  • Tunnels: circular best structurally; egg-shaped for stratified soft laminated rock; heading-and-benching for soft rock (heading 3–3.5 m ahead); full-face up to ≈ 3 m; NATM = sequential excavation, flexible supports, monitoring. Minimum sizes: circular > 2.0 m; others > 1.9 m wide, 2.1 m high. Velocities: unlined 2–2.5 m/s, concrete-lined 4–5, steel-lined to 9 m/s.
  • Forebay: hs = 1.5Vp²/2g (or 0.5Vp√D); depth H = hs + Dp + settling depth + freeboard; spillway L = Q/(C·H^1.5), C = 1.7 sharp-crested, 2.2 ogee.
  • Surge tank: stores water at load rejection until the penstock flow decelerates: Zmax = Vt√(Lt·At/(g·Ast)); up-surge ×(1 − 2P/3 + P²/9), down-surge ×(1 − 2P), P = hf/Zmax. Types: simple, restricted-orifice, differential.
  • Penstock: t = P·R/(σ·η − 0.6P) + 0.15 cm; economical diameter V_eco = 0.125√(2gH); critical closure Tc = 2L/Vc; wave speed Vc = √(K/ρ)/√(1 + DK/(tE)); relief: surge tanks, relief valves, slow closure.
  • Regulating structures: canal head regulator, cross regulators, distributary head regulators; outlets — pipe, APM (subsoil), open flume; vertical-drop/canal falls dissipate energy.

Diversion Headworks & Seepage Theories (7.3) — Course Values

  • Components: weir/barrage, undersluices, divide wall, fish ladder, head regulator, silt control works, guide banks, marginal bunds, sheet piles, impervious & pervious floors.
  • Weir vs barrage: weir — high crest, small shutters; barrage — low crest, large adjustable gates; barrage flushes silt better and controls more precisely.
  • Undersluices: crest 1–1.2 m lower; scour the pocket, pass floods, keep supplies during repairs. Divide wall: at right angles to the weir axis. Fish ladder: pool-and-weir, ≈ 0.3 m/s. Head regulator angle 90°–110° (110° best for silt).
  • Silt excluder — river bed, upstream of the head regulator (prevention). Silt ejector — canal bed, downstream (cure).
  • Guide bank (Bell's bund) — forces a straight river approach; launching aprons protect the toe; marginal bunds protect upstream land.
  • Failures on pervious foundations: piping (exit gradient — prevent with longer creep + downstream piles) and uplift rupture (thicker floor + upstream piles).
  • Bligh: L = b + 2(d₁+d₂+d₃) ≥ C·H_L; floor t = h/(G−1) with the uplift ordinate increased 33% for safety. Lane: L = b/3 + 2(d₁+d₂+d₃) ≥ C₁·H_L. Khosla: independent variables + 3 corrections; GE = (H/d)·1/(π√λ), λ = (1+√(1+α²))/2; only the downstream pile controls GE; pressures at key points E, D, C from curves.
  • Energy dissipators: USBR stilling basins (Type I: Fr < 1.7; Types II & III with baffle blocks); roller bucket for deep tailwater; flip bucket for shallow.
  • Dam stability: P = ½γH²; silt ½γs·Ka·h²; uplift kγw(h + H − h/3); overturning FS = Mr/Mo ≥ 1.6; eccentricity e = B/2 − x, base stress Pn = (ΣV/B)(1 ± 6e/B), no tension: e ≤ B/6; minimum base B = H/√(G−K).

Hydropower & Powerhouse (7.5–7.6) — Course Values

  • Power P = ηγQH (kW; η ≈ 0.8–0.9 overall).
  • Nepal potential: theoretical ≈ 83,000 MW; technically feasible ≈ 44,000 MW; economically feasible ≈ 42,000 MW. World: China 421 GW > Brazil 110 GW; largest plant: Three Gorges (22.5 GW).
  • Nepal milestones: Pharping 1911, 500 kW (first); Kulekhani I 1982, 60 MW (first storage, Makawanpur); Khimti 2000, 60 MW (first IPP); Upper Tamakoshi 2021, 456 MW (largest).
  • Institutions: NEA (state utility); DOED licenses — survey 5 years, generation 35 years (domestic) / 30 (export).
  • Factors: load factor = avg/peak (≤ 1); plant (capacity) factor = avg/capacity (0.25–0.7); utilization factor 0.4–0.9; power factor kW/kVA (0.8–0.9); diversity factor > 1; coincidence = 1/diversity. Firm power available 100% of the time.
  • Installed capacity choice: marginal benefit = 8.76 × x% × energy rate vs marginal cost (annualized + O&M) — add capacity until they balance.
  • Head-turbine matching: ≤ 15 m Kaplan/propeller; 15–60 m crossflow; 60–150 m Francis; > 350 m Pelton. Ns rises from Pelton (10–35 hp single jet) to Kaplan (300–1000 hp).
  • Components: intake, headrace, forebay, penstock, powerhouse (surface/semi-underground/underground), tailrace. Generators: synchronous, salient-pole at low/medium speed. Governors: mechanical-hydraulic, electric, microprocessor ELC (micro-hydro).
  • Reservoir terms: bank storage; valley storage; effective flood storage = live + surcharge − valley; trap efficiency 90–100% (large reservoirs); capacity-inflow ratio CIR = capacity/annual inflow.
  • Spillways: ogee (nappe profile), chute, side-channel, shaft/morning-glory, siphon; Q = C·L·He^1.5. Stilling basin L/B = 4–10, depth/width 1–1.5, basin depth 3–5 m; sediment load S = Q·T·C; sediment volume = load/density × packing factor (a = 0.36 for d > 1 mm, 0.44 for 0.1–1 mm, 0.51 for < 0.1 mm).
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): excluder (upstream) vs ejector (downstream); Bligh (equal weighting, 33% uplift margin) vs Lane (⅓ horizontal) vs Khosla (exit gradient, downstream pile governs); 83,000 vs 44,000 vs 42,000 MW potential ladder; Pharping 500 kW 1911 vs Upper Tamakoshi 456 MW 2021; bucket type ↔ tailwater depth (roller = deeper, flip = shallower); weir (high crest, small shutters) vs barrage (low crest, large gates).

Chapter 8: Rural Engineering (ACRE08)

NEC License Exam — High-Yield Notes (v5.5 edition)

Chapter 8: Rural Engineering (ACRE08)

NEC License Exam (1-Mark MCQ Focus) | NEC prep-course edition — v5.5

This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

8.1 Rural Roads (ACRE0801)

A. Rural Road Concepts & Classification

A rural road is any road that is not a national highway or feeder road. Its job is to connect villages to each other and to markets, so it carries little traffic but gives essential access.

Nepal splits its road network into two systems. The Strategic Road Network (SRN) — national highways and feeder roads — is managed by the Department of Roads (DoR). Everything else, the Local Road Network (LRN) — district, urban and village roads — falls under DoLI (formerly DoLIDAR/DoLID). The exam regularly asks which agency owns which network.

ClassRoleExample
National Highway (NH)East–west and north–south arteries, capital to regionsMahendra, Prithvi, Araniko
Feeder Road (FR)Links NH to district HQ and major towns—
District Road (DR)Inside the district: HQ to villages—
Urban Road (UR)Inside municipal areas—
Village / local roadVillage-to-village and market access (LRN)Most rural roads

Functional classification ranks roads by the balance of movement and access: arterials carry through traffic, collectors do both, and local roads mostly provide access. A rural road is a local or collector road. Nepal's DoR rural standards grade local roads into Classes A, B, C and D by traffic and importance, with design speeds of roughly 20–40 km/h in the hills. A trail is only a foot or mule track; a rural road must be at least jeep/tractor passable, with a formation width of about 3 m or more in the hills.

B. Alignment Survey

Alignment design moves through three field stages:

StageWhat happens
ReconnaissanceMap and imagery study plus a rapid walk-over; fix control points (pass/saddle, river crossing, market), avoid unstable ground, and stake a 50–100 m wide corridor strip.
Preliminary surveyTraverse the chosen corridor with theodolite/total station; take levels, cross-sections and soil/borrow samples; compare alternatives.
Final location & detailed surveyPeg the centre line (20 m spacing on plain, 10–20 m in hills, 5 m on curves); take L-sections and cross-sections at 20–30 m; record land acquisition details.

What controls an alignment: obligatory points (a bridge site, a saddle, a market town), the steepest gradient vehicles can climb, slope stability, drainage and bridge sites, minimum curve radius, earthwork cost balance, and environmental constraints such as forests and settlements.

Hill alignment rules: follow the contours; keep to the stable side of the valley away from seeping concave slopes that feed landslides; choose side-long ground with a uniform transverse slope (ideally under 20–30°; above 40° becomes costly); cross ridges at saddles; and in river routes stay above the high flood level (HFL). Alternatives are compared on earthwork quantity, number of structures, length, maximum grade, land cost and stability risk. The mass-haul (excess–deficit) curve balances cut and fill, and lead and lift terms price the earthwork — both are favourite one-mark questions.

C. Design Criteria (Nepal Rural/Local Road Standards)

ParameterPlain/RuralHill Rural (typical)
Design speed40–50 km/h20–30 km/h
Carriageway (single lane)3.5–3.75 m3.0–3.5 m
Shoulder1.0–1.5 m each side0.5–1.0 m / drain
Formation width7.5–9.0 m4.5–6.5 m
Max gradient5–6% (ruling ~3.3%)8–10% (exceptional 12%)
Min curve radius (V = 20 km/h)≈ 15–20 m (with superelevation)≈ 15 m absolute min (hairpin ≥ 14–15 m)
Camber2.5–3.5% gravel, 2% bitumen3–5% gravel + inner drain slope

D. Geometric Design Essentials

Fig 8.1 — Rural road cross-section: camber, shoulders, side drain, compacted subgrade
  • Superelevation banks the pavement into a curve. Design it as e = V²/(127R) − f, cap it at emax = 0.07, and for mixed traffic use the practical compromise e = V²/225R (Nepal follows the IRC approach).
  • Extra widening at a curve has two parts — mechanical and psychological: We = nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R), with n lanes and wheelbase l = 6.1 m. A single-lane road takes the full widening at the curve.
  • Setback distance is the clearance cut back into a hillside so drivers can see the SSD length around a curve against a cut face.
  • SSD = reaction distance + braking distance = 0.278V·t + V²/(254f), with f = 0.35–0.4 and t = 2.5 s. Overtaking sight distance (OSD) works out at roughly 2×SSD plus the overtaking-time terms.
  • Vertical curves smooth grade changes: summit curve length L = K×A, where K comes from the sight-line requirement; valley curves are designed for headlight sight distance.
  • Grade compensation on hill curves recovers speed lost to curvature: compensation = (30+R)/R percent, capped at 75/R %, deducted from the ruling gradient on sharp curves.
  • Hairpin bends: minimum radius 14 m on stable ground, successive hairpins separated by about 40–60 m, and the gradient inside the bend limited to about 4%.

E. Cross-Drainage Structures

Water crossing a road needs the right structure for its size and flow:

StructureWhere usedKey fact
Causeway / vented causewaySeasonal streams on low-volume roadsCheapest; submersible in flood; a vented causeway lets normal flow pass underneath
Culvert (pipe, slab, box)Span under 6 mOne or multiple cells; pipe for small flows, slab/box for larger
BridgeTotal span ≥ 6 mMinor ≤ 20 m, major 20–60 m, long-span > 60 m

Cost rises in the order causeway < culvert < bridge. A scupper (the syllabus's "scooper") is an opening in the parapet that drains rainwater off a bridge deck. Structures are sized for a design flood — about 1-in-25 years for rural culverts and 1-in-50/100 for bridges — with the waterway checked by Lacey's regime perimeter P = 4.75√Q in alluvial streams, plus HFL, scour depth and afflux. Slope protection includes stone pitching, gabion and dry-masonry walls, check dams in gullies, toe (tooth) walls, and the drain family: side drains, catch drains, chutes and cross drains.

F. Bio-Engineering for Slope Protection

Bio-engineering uses live plants — grasses, shrubs and trees — alone or with small structures to stop shallow slope failures and surface erosion. It is cheap, self-repairing and environment-friendly, and Nepal (DoLIDAR/DoR manuals) is a recognised pioneer.

How plants protect a slope. Hydrologically they intercept rain, slow runoff, let water soak in evenly and dry the soil by transpiration. Mechanically their roots bind and reinforce the soil. The limits matter: vegetation only holds the top 1–2 m — a deep-seated landslide still needs a retaining structure, so the two are combined into a "bio-technical" approach.

TechniqueWhat it is
Grass seeding / turfingCovers bare surface quickly against raindrop erosion
Grass lines (vertical rows)Rows planted down the slope to guide drainage
Brush layeringLive branches laid in horizontal trenches across the slope
PalisadesRows of live vertical cuttings that sprout
StoolingPlanted stakes that resprout (e.g. Ficus, Erythrina)
Live check damsLiving barriers in gullies
Tree plantingDeep rooting for long-term reinforcement

Common Nepal species: Napier grass, Amriso (broom grass, Thysanolaena), Khar, Erythrina (Phaledo), Ficus, Alnus (Uttis) and Leucaena. Species are chosen by local availability and root depth.

G. Construction & Maintenance of Rural Roads

Construction sequence: clearing and grubbing → earthwork (cut/fill, mass-balanced) → subgrade preparation and compaction → sub-base/base (gravel or WBM) → surface (gravel seal or bituminous) → drainage and protection works.

WBM (Water Bound Macadam) is the classic rural base course. It is laid in three layers, each 75–100 mm compacted, with screenings and binding material added, watered and rolled. Coarse aggregate sizes step down by grade: 90 mm (grade 1), 63 mm (grade 2), 53 mm (grade 3). Compaction targets come from the Proctor test — field density at 95% MDD for subgrade and 98%+ for base.

Maintenance types: routine work (annual grading, pothole patching, drain clearing — budgeted at 4–6% of construction cost per year), periodic work (regravelling every 3–5 years, resealing every 5–8), emergency repairs after monsoon damage, and special repairs.

Nepal practice: the Green Roads approach builds with the environment — mass-slumping avoided, slopes vegetated as construction proceeds, half-bench cut-and-fill in the hills. Community and food-for-work programmes (DoLIDAR) and labour-based technology (LBT) suit rural Nepal: jobs are created with little capital. Typical gravel-road defects are potholes, ruts, edge break, corrugations, dust, and gravel loss of 10–25 mm per year under traffic.

Key numbers: hairpin minimum radius ≈ 14 m; minimum radius from R = V²/(127(e+f)); superelevation e ≤ 0.07 (rural, no snow) with e+f ≤ 0.20; grade compensation at sharp curves.
8.1 rapid numbers: single-lane carriageway 3.5 m; hill formation 4.5–6.5 m; ruling gradient hill ≈ 5%; limiting 8%; hairpin R ≥ 14 m; camber gravel 3%; SSD f = 0.35; WBM layer 75–100 mm; routine maintenance 4–6% of capital cost per year.

8.2 Trail Bridges (ACRE0802)

A. Trail Bridge Types

Fig 8.2 — Suspension (deck + stiffening truss on hangers) vs suspended (deck hung straight from cable)
Fig 8.3 — Suspension-bridge components: anchorage, pylons, main cables, hangers, stiffening truss — LSTB loading norms

Trail bridges carry people — and where needed animals — across rivers where there is no road bridge. Nepal's Trail Bridge Sub-Sector (TBSSP/DoR) classifies them by span:

TypeSpanDeckNotes
Suspended bridgeup to ~120 mWalkway cables + netting + cross planksFlexible; deck hangs straight from the cables; sags and "waves" as you walk; Nepal's most common short-span type
Suspension bridge120–500 m (LSTB)Stiffening truss hung on main cables by hangersUpward-cambering walkway; gentle sag ≈ 1/10–1/12 of span; components: anchorages, towers, main cables, hangers, deck truss, wind bracing
Steel truss bridgeup to 32 m (standard designs 16–32 m)Truss on abutmentsWhere foundations are good
RCC slab/box, timber, laddervery short—Local crossings; ladder = temporary

Design loading (Nepal trail-bridge standards): a uniformly distributed crowd load of about 3.5–5 kN/m² (course norm 400 kg/m² ≈ 3.9 kN/m²) plus concentrated animal/livestock loads of 1.5–3 kN, together with wind load. Trail bridges carry no vehicular loading.

B. General Standards (Nepal Trail Bridge Standards)

ParameterShort Span (SSTB ≤ 120 m)Long Span (LSTB > 120 m)
Clear deck width1.0–1.5 m (typical 1.2–1.4 m)≈ 1.2 m
Max live load (UDL)≈ 3.5–5 kN/m² (norm 400 kg/m²)≈ 3.5–4 kN/m²
Sag/span ratio1/12 (suspended 1/10–1/12)1/10–1/12
Max approach gradient≤ 8–10%≤ 8%
Freeboard above HFL≥ 1.5–2 m≥ 2–3 m
DocumentsSSTB Standard + Technical Hand Book (Vol I Survey & Design, II Forms, III Drawings) — designed by sub-overseer, approved by engineerLSTB Technical Manual (Vol A Design, B Survey, C Drawings) — surveyed and designed by an engineer, executed by overseer
  • Components of a suspension bridge: anchorage (gravity/tunnel/rock), pylons, main cables, hangers, stiffening truss, handrail, cross girders, deck planks or steel grating, wind bracing, tower-top saddles and cable bands.
  • Anchorage types: a gravity block resists cable pull by its own weight; a tunnel/rock anchorage ties the cables into sound rock. Rock anchorage is preferred in the Nepal Himalaya — cheap and reliable where rock is available.
  • Cable material: galvanised steel — locked-coil strand (older, stiff) or stranded rope (6×19 / 6×37 construction). Design factor of safety on cables ≈ 3.0–3.5. Sag is adjusted with turnbuckles/tensioning.
  • Site investigation covers river width and HFL, bank stability, rock for anchorage, approach alignment, catchment flood and debris, material availability, animal-traffic needs and distance to the nearest alternative crossing (site selection standard: minimum 500 m from an existing crossing).
  • Site selection favours: a narrow gorge (shorter span), high firm banks (freeboard without tall towers), stable rock for anchorage, straight approach trails on both banks, and a position safely out of debris-flow fans.
  • Construction and maintenance: anchor concreting → tower erection → cable hauling/spinning → deck joists → decking. Upkeep means cable wire-brushing and re-greasing, plank and hanger replacement, anchor-crack monitoring and load-restriction signage. Typical defects: plank rot, hanger corrosion, anchor seepage.
Exam trap — suspension vs suspended: "-ion" = stiffened deck on main cables (long span, LSTB > 120 m); "-ed" = the flexible deck-cable net itself (≤ 120 m). Course norms for trail bridges: live load 400 kg/m², design wind 160 km/h, design life ≥ 50 years, and the windguy system only on LSTB.
Memory hooks: Suspension = stiffened deck + cables above (120–500 m); suspended = flexible cable-net deck (≤ 120 m); sag ≈ L/10–L/12; cable FoS ≈ 3; deck width ≈ 1.2 m; live load 400 kg/m²; wind 160 km/h; life ≥ 50 yr; SSTB ≤ 120 m, LSTB > 120 m.

8.3 Farm Machinery and Post-Harvesting (ACRE0803)

A. Tillage & Field Equipment

Tillage prepares the seedbed in two stages. Primary tillage opens the ground — mould-board plough, disc plough, country plough (a mould-board inverts the furrow to roughly 20–30 cm depth; a disc plough rolls instead of slides, so it copes better with hard, sticky, trashy or stony soil). Secondary tillage refines it — harrows and cultivators break clods and kill weeds, and a rotavator (PTO-driven rotary tiller) finishes the seedbed in a single pass.

Nepal's small farms still rely on indigenous tools: the kodalo (spade), kuto (hoe) and the wooden country plough (hal) drawn by oxen. For sowing, a seed drill places seed at controlled depth and spacing (far better germination than broadcasting) and can add fertiliser; a planter spaces row-crop seed exactly. Harvesting runs from the sickle to reapers and binder-reapers up to the combine, which reaps, threshes and cleans in one pass — mini-combines are spreading across the Terai. Threshing separates grain from the ear (manual beating, animal treading, or beaters/axial-flow threshers — drum speed 700–1000 rpm for paddy) and winnowing blows the husk away; multi-crop threshers handle wheat, paddy and mustard.

Draft and power: draft is the pull force needed; a pair of oxen delivers roughly 0.5–1 hp, and 8–12 hp power tillers (walking tractors) are the smallholder workhorse of the mid-hills and Terai. Tractor work is rated through the PTO (power take-off) shaft.

B. Water Mill, Wind Mill (Traditional & Improved)

  • Ghatta (traditional water mill) — the wooden horizontal-axis turbine of the mid-hill streams: an open flume under roughly 2–5 m head turns a vertical stone runner to grind grain. Efficiency is under 20% and output 0.5–3 kW; thousands are still working.
  • Improved Water Mill (IWM) — the same site upgraded: a steel axial or crossflow runner, better bearings, and a belt drive that can also power a rice huller, oil press or a small dynamo producing 3–5 kW of electricity. Supported by AEPC/REDP programmes, an IWM roughly doubles the output and can share its canal for irrigation.
  • Wind mills — the multi-blade American wind pump turns high torque at low speed, ideal for lifting water with a piston pump; the cheap sail-type mill has had Terai trials; the propeller type generates electricity. Pumping needs wind above about 3–5 m/s and power generation above 6 m/s. Nepal's wind potential is site-specific — the Kagbeni–Mustang corridor is the famous windy valley. Wind power grows with the cube of velocity (P = ½ρAV³), and hub height is kept ≥ 10–15 m to catch smoother, faster wind.
  • Water lifting without fuel — the treadle pump (human-powered, Terai irrigation) and the hydraulic ram, which uses its own water-hammer impulse to push a small share of the water 10–20× higher than the source fall, needing no external energy at all. Solar pumps are increasingly common for drinking water.

C. Processing Equipment

  • Rice mills come in three generations: the single-pass huller (high breakage, ≈ 60–65% head-rice recovery), the two-stage sheller + polisher, and the modern rubber-roll sheller + whitener (≈ 68–72% recovery).
  • Other village agro-machines regularly asked in the exam: flour mills (plate/roller), oil expellers (ghani, rotary or screw press), paddy parboiling tanks, batch/continuous and solar driers, dal mills and spice grinders.
  • Post-harvest losses for grain (approximate): harvesting 1–3%, threshing 2–4%, drying 1–2%, storage 3–8% — totalling ≈ 5–15%, worse in Nepal with poor moisture control and rodents.

D. Grain Storage Structures

Why storage design matters: grain must be kept dry and cool, sealed against rodents, birds and insects, easy to load and unload, and cheap per tonne. Safe moisture content is 12–14% for cereals (paddy 14%, wheat 12%, maize 13%) and about 8% for pulses and oilseeds — above these, fungi and insects take over. Capacity arithmetic is volume = mass ÷ bulk density, with paddy ≈ 550–600 kg/m³, wheat ≈ 750–800 kg/m³ and shelled maize ≈ 700–750 kg/m³.

Storage typeExamplesNotes
Traditional (Nepal)Bhakari, Deuri, Kotho (bamboo/mud), Ghyam pits, gunny bags on tak platformsCheap but rodent- and moisture-prone
Improved small storesPusa bin (mud + polythene, hermetic), metal drums, ferro-cement and bamboo-reinforced mortar binsHermetic storage kills insects by CO₂ build-up
Bag godownsStacks on dunnage 15 cm off the floor, 50 cm from walls; aisle 1–1.5 m; stack height ≤ 8–10 bagsLouvred ventilation + fumigation sealing; RCC damp-proof floor
Large storageWarehouses, steel/RCC silos (flat-bottom or hopper, with aeration and fumigation), CAP (cover and plinth), cold storesSilos for bulk traders; CAP for short-term bag surplus

Storing farm inputs safely: fertiliser stays dry and ventilated, separated by type and away from seed and pesticides (urea and CAN are hygroscopic and need sealed handling). Seed keeps its viability cool and dry — below about 20 °C and 60% RH — and Harrington's rule says every 1% moisture drop or 5 °C drop roughly doubles seed life. Pesticides are locked in a ventilated room with a bunded floor, stored away from food, feed and fertiliser, with poison labelling and PPE (regulated under Nepal's Pesticide Act and Plant Quarantine rules). Store siting keeps at least 30 m from dairy and poultry farms and about 150 m from factories.

E. Cold Storage System (Dairy & Perishables)

A cold chain — pre-cooling → cold store → refrigerated transport → market — extends shelf life by slowing respiration and microbial growth. The cooling load has four parts: product load (field heat plus respiration — field heat dominates the initial pull-down), transmission through walls and roof (Q = U·A·ΔT), infiltration (door openings, air changes), and equipment/people loads.

CommodityStorage TApprox. shelf life
Potato (seed, high hills)2–4 °C (cold store; curing 10–15 °C)6–10 months
Apple0–4 °C, RH ≈ 90%4–6 months
Milk (raw)≤ 4 °C, chilled within 2 h of milking24–48 h
Butter/ghee−10 to −20 °C6–12 months
Leafy vegetables0–4 °C, RH ≈ 95%days–2 weeks
Frozen meat/fish−18 to −25 °C3–12 months

The vapour-compression refrigeration cycle runs compressor → condenser → expansion valve → evaporator. Refrigerants: R-134a, R-404A and ammonia (NH₃ — efficient but toxic) for large plants. Walls and roof use 50–150 mm PUF/EPS insulated panels with the vapour barrier on the warm side. Relative humidity is held at 85–95% for most vegetables — drier air wilts them — using humidifiers and careful defrost management. In Nepal, cold stores cluster in the Terai (potato and vegetables), dairy chilling centres follow the milk-collection routes, and solar-PV cold rooms are emerging for off-grid hills.

8.3 rapid numbers: safe MC: paddy 14%, wheat 12%, maize 13%; paddy bulk density ≈ 575 kg/m³, wheat ≈ 780 kg/m³; rubber-roll recovery ≈ 70%; total grain PHL ≈ 5–15%; potato store 2–4 °C; milk ≤ 4 °C; hydraulic ram lifts water 10–20× the source fall; IWM electricity 3–5 kW.

8.4 Rural Water Supply and Sanitation (ACRE0804)

A. Rural Water Supply Systems & Types

Rural schemes pick the technology the source allows: gravity flow (source uphill of the community — the standard Nepali hill scheme, no power needed), lift/pumped supply (hand pumps, solar or electric pumps where the source sits below the village), rainwater harvesting from roof catchments where springs fail, spring/stream intakes, shallow and deep tubewells in the Terai, and combinations of these.

Service levels (Nepal): basic supply is 45 L/person/day, intermediate ≈ 65, and high/fully plumbed 100+ (urban norms run 100–135). The course pptx's design rule for public taps: one tap stand for every 8–10 households, with the fetching distance no more than 200 m horizontally and 50 m vertically. Under SDG wording, "basic service" means an improved source within a 30-minute round trip, available when needed and meeting quality standards.

B. Quantity & Quality Considerations

  • Demand build-up: domestic 45 lpcd as the base, plus institutions (school 15–20 lpcd per student; health post 200–400 L/day), livestock (cattle 40–60 L/day, buffalo 60–80, goat 8–10, poultry 0.1–0.2), small non-domestic uses, and 15–20% unaccounted-for losses.
  • Peak factors: max-day ≈ 1.5–2× average; peak-hour ≈ 2–3× average hourly. Rural gravity systems size the source on max-day demand and check pipes on peak flow; fire demand is rarely considered in rural Nepal.
  • Quality risks in the rural setting: for springs and streams it is bacteriological (E. coli) first — so disinfection is essential; Terai tubewells add iron/manganese (aesthetic and health) and arsenic (Nepal standard 0.05 mg/L — tighter WHO value 0.01); turbidity < 5 NTU; pH 6.5–8.5; ammonia and nitrate signal latrine contamination nearby.
  • Rural treatment package: protect the source, then keep it simple — roughing filter + slow sand filter where turbid (the Nepal standard combination), chlorination with bleaching powder in the RVT or at the tap keeping 0.2–0.5 mg/L free residual chlorine, plus household options: SODIS, ceramic candle filters, and arsenic-removal filters in the Terai.

C. Groundwater Development & Tubewell Technology

Fig 8.4 — Tubewell in an unconfined aquifer: casing, screen, gravel pack, cone of depression
  • Aquifer types: unconfined (open water table), confined/artesian (potentiometric surface above the aquifer), and semi-confined (leaky). The Terai is a thick alluvial multi-aquifer system recharged at the Bhabar zone along the Chure foothills.
  • Wells by depth: dug wells (1–3 m dia, shallow, bucket or hand pump), shallow tubewells (< 40–60 m, 10–20 cm dia, hand or centrifugal pump) and deep tubewells (60–300 m, turbine/submersible, yielding 20–100 m³/h).
  • Tubewell components: casing pipe; well screen — the slotted intake, with aperture matched to the aquifer grain size and 10–20% open area; gravel pack around the screen (pack grain ≈ 4–6× the aquifer d₅₀, thickness typically 50–100 mm); sand trap; riser pipe; pump. Well development pumps out the drilling fluid and fines until the water runs clear.
  • Design basics: yield comes from a pumping test (step-drawdown, then constant-rate); specific capacity = Q ÷ drawdown; drawdown cone and radius of influence follow the Thiem/Dupuit equations; well losses split into laminar (formation) and turbulent (screen/well) parts.
  • Hand pumps (Nepal): the India Mark II/III for deeper wells (cylinder to ~45 m water column) and the Afridev — a VLOM (Village Level Operation & Maintenance) pump preferred in the Terai for its simple, village-repairable parts.
  • Sanitary protection: grout a sanitary seal in the top 3–6 m, build a platform and apron with drainage, keep the wellhead above flood level, and separate latrines by at least 30 m (Nepal guideline) — 10–30 m is the commonly cited band.

D. Ferro-Cement Tank

Ferro-cement is rich mortar (1:2 to 1:3, w/c ≈ 0.4–0.45) plastered over layers of welded wire mesh and chicken mesh wrapped on light skeletal steel bars, making a shell only 20–40 mm thick. It is strong in tension, crack-resistant, light (therefore earthquake-tolerant) and buildable by skilled masons with local materials and no heavy plant — which is why it is Nepal's standard small rainwater tank.

  • Uses: RVTs and rainwater jars of 1–10 m³, water tanks up to ≈ 20 m³, latrine slabs and linings, and even biogas domes.
  • Design/cure: 4–6 mesh layers for tanks, wet curing ≥ 14 days, inside coated with waterproof slurry or cement paint, plus a lid, tap, overflow, drain and air vent.
  • Rainwater harvesting (RWH) train: clean GI/tile roof → gutter → first-flush diverter (discards the first ~1 mm of runoff — about 3 minutes of rain) → ferro-cement tank or RVT → tap + overflow.
  • RWH sizing: annual supply = roof area × rainfall × runoff coefficient (GI ≈ 0.9, tile 0.8–0.9); demand = persons × lpcd × days; the tank covers the dry-season deficit, sized from a cumulative mass diagram or the dry-month demand method.
    • Fig 8.5 — Rainwater harvesting train: roof → gutter → first-flush diverter → ferro-cement RVT (lid, tap, overflow)
  • Exam-style example: roof 60 m², GI (0.9), rainfall 1500 mm → harvest = 60 × 1.5 × 0.9 = 81 m³/yr. A family of 5 at 45 lpcd needs ≈ 82 m³/yr — marginal, so storage must carry the dry months.

E. Design Criteria of Rural Water Supply & Sanitation Schemes (Nepal)

  • Design period: 15 years for rural schemes (DWSSM standard), and the source yield must last that long; population is projected geometrically over the short horizon.
  • Gravity-flow components (course order): intake (spring box, stream intake, or infiltration gallery) → collection chamber → interruption chamber (IC) and break pressure tank (BPT) → sedimentation/desanding if turbid → RVT (reservoir tank) → distribution main → tap stands, plus air valves at summits, washouts at low points and isolation valves. A BPT discharges to atmosphere to break static pressure when the line exceeds the pipe's pressure rating; in a transmission line the same function is called an interruption chamber (no float valve), and a reservoir can itself act as a BPT — ferro-cement BPTs are preferred for economy.
  • RVT capacity: typically 25–50% of daily demand (about 1/3 to 1/2 of max-day demand), placed so taps get a working static head — keep the maximum static head at taps below ≈ 25–30 m; where head builds up without a suitable RVT site, break-pressure tanks are inserted roughly every 50–60 m of head.
  • Pipe design: HDPE (PN4/6/10 classes) buried with ≥ 60 cm cover, working velocity 0.5–1 m/s, sized by Hazen–Williams or standard flow tables, with thrust blocks at bends on pressure mains.
  • Tapstand: 1 per 8–10 households (≤ 200 m horizontal / 50 m vertical fetching distance), tap discharge ≈ 0.15–0.2 L/s.
  • Water Safety Plan (WSP): now the mandatory concept — hazards identified from catchment to tap, control measures and monitoring applied, in a simplified rural form.
  • Community management: the WUSC (Water Users & Sanitation Committee) owns operation and maintenance, funded by a monthly per-tap tariff, with a village maintenance worker (VMW). Functionality is judged by the share of taps working and water quality compliance.

F. Survey of Rural Water Supply Systems

  • Pre-feasibility survey: measure the source yield (volumetric or weir method — always the dry-season minimum), spot-test quality, census households (people, livestock, existing sources, willingness to pay), run a topographic survey for the pipeline L-section, check land for tanks and material access, and help form the WUSC.
  • Design survey outputs: the scheme report — source and yield certificate, demand calculation, hydraulic design (pipe schedule, tank sizes), cost estimate, tariff proposal, O&M plan, WSP, and environmental screening (IEE/EIA per the EPA schedules, with cost thresholds applied).

G. Design of a Typical Rural Gravity Flow Scheme (Worked Concept)

  • Steps: demand (45 lpcd × projected population × 1.15 for losses) → source check (dry-season yield ≥ max-day demand) → intake → pipeline routing (follow contours, avoid unstable slopes, HDPE buried) → RVT sizing and siting on the hydraulic grade line → branch distribution (rural standard; loops only where reliability justifies) → tap stands → residual chlorine and WSP.
  • Worked example: population 500 → design population 700; Qavg = 700 × 45 = 31.5 m³/d; +15% losses → 36 m³/d ≈ 0.42 L/s average; max day ×1.7 → ≈ 0.72 L/s — so the spring must yield ≥ 0.72 L/s in the dry season. RVT = 12–18 m³; a 40 mm PN10 HDPE main (ID ≈ 35 mm) at ≈ 0.7 m/s carries the peak — a 50 mm main would run at only ≈ 0.4 m/s; at 0.15 L/s per tap, about 5 tap stands serve the village.

H. Rural Sanitation

  • Sanitation ladder (SDG): open defecation → unimproved → limited (shared) → basic (improved, not shared) → safely managed (excreta safely treated/disposed). Nepal declared nationwide ODF in 2019.
  • Simple pit latrine: pit 0.9–1.2 m dia (or 1 m × 1 m), 2–3 m deep, lined above the groundwater, covered by a slab with a pan and a superstructure. The pit is "full" when digested sludge reaches 50 cm below the top; it is then closed with a 50–75 mm earth layer, and the filled pit can be reused after 2 years. Solids accumulate at 0.04–0.05 m³/person/yr (the design rule is V = NRT, N users × rate R × period T, with a design period of at least 2 years), so a 3 m³ pit serving 5 people lasts ≈ 12–15 years.
  • VIP latrine: a pit privy improved with a 90 mm vent pipe (with fly screen) that pulls odours out and stops flies breeding — the standard on-site upgrade.
  • Septic tank: settles and anaerobically digests blackwater. Course design criteria: detention time 1–3 days (24 h typical), minimum width 0.75 m, freeboard 0.3–0.45 m, minimum effective depth 1 m, L:B = 2–4. Effective volume = V₁ (settling, Q×t) + V₂ (sludge digestion, 0.0425 m³/person) + V₃ (sludge storage, Cds×N, e.g. 0.085 m³/person at a 3-year cleaning interval). Two chambers with a baffle are preferred; desludge every 6 months to 3 years (practice: 2–3 years); never let disinfectants, soaps or kitchen water in — they kill the digestion.
  • Soak pit: receives septic effluent and lets the soil absorb it. Design range: diameter 0.9–3.5 m, effective depth > 1 m, GWT at least 2 m below the pit bottom; no groundwater source within a 60 m radius; multiple pits 3× the largest diameter apart. Absorption area: A = Q ÷ I, with I = 130/√Tr (L/m²/day) from the percolation test (Tr = 25 min/cm → I ≈ 26 L/m²/day, inside the usual 10–30 L/m²/day band). Loading limits run ≈ 10–30 L/m²/day of sidewall + bottom area; keep 15–30 m from wells and out of clay or a high water table (use a soakage trench instead).
  • Construction practice: pit lining above the water table, a slab with a 50 mm minimum water-seal pan, a vented fly screen (VIP), a handwashing station (mandatory for ODF+), and twin pits alternating with 1–2 year rest — the composted pit becomes safe soil conditioner (Nepal onsite-sanitation guideline).
  • Rural solid waste: generation ≈ 0.1–0.3 kg/cap/day (urban Nepal ≈ 0.4–0.5). The preferred rural route is household composting, then communal pits; collection and transport move waste to landfill or controlled dumping. The hierarchy: reduce → reuse → recycle → compost → engineered landfill; open burning is avoided.
8.4 rapid numbers: basic supply 45 lpcd; design period rural 15 yr; max-day factor 1.5–2.0; residual Cl₂ at tap 0.2–0.5 mg/L; arsenic Nepal std 0.05 mg/L; RWH runoff coeff GI 0.9; ferro-cement shell 20–40 mm; septic detention 24 h (1–3 d band); soak pit I = 130/√Tr ≈ 10–30 L/m²/d; latrine–well distance ≥ 30 m preferable (10–30 m band); tapstand per 8–10 HH.

8.5 Rural Energy (ACRE0805)

A. Rural Electrification (Nepal)

  • Framework: NEA grid expansion plus community rural electrification (CRE), where NEA supplies through user committees; isolated mini-grids from micro hydro and solar; and off-grid solar home systems under AEPC (Alternative Energy Promotion Centre), which also channels the Rural Energy Policy 2006 subsidies. National electrification has passed 90%, grid-dominated.
  • Rural distribution chain: 33/11 kV substation → 11 kV feeder → 11/0.4 kV transformer (25–100 kVA rural) → 3-phase 4-wire LV at 400/230 V; voltage drop kept within ±5–10%; losses are both technical and non-technical (theft/metering).
  • Load management: a rural household connects ≈ 200–500 W and the village load factor is low (≈ 0.2–0.3); productive end uses (hullers, cold stores, pumping) raise the load factor and scheme revenue.

B. Solar Energy

  • Resource (Nepal): ≈ 4.5–5.5 kWh/m²/day of solar insolation with about 300 sunny days a year; the Terai and trans-Himalaya (Mustang, Dolpo) are highest.
  • PV chain: cell (mono/poly Si) → module (cells in series) → array (modules in parallel). Ratings assume standard test conditions (1000 W/m², 25 °C); output falls ≈ 0.4–0.5%/°C above 25 °C; typical cell efficiency 15–20%.
  • Solar home system: 20–60 W panel + deep-cycle battery (limited to ≈ 50% depth of discharge for long life) + charge controller + DC lamps. Sizing: Wp = daily Wh demand ÷ (peak sun-hours × system efficiency 0.6–0.75).
  • Battery sizing: Ah = daily Wh ÷ system voltage ÷ DoD ÷ inverter efficiency, with 1–3 days autonomy; flooded batteries need topping up and terminal cleaning.
  • Solar pumping: PV array + controller + DC/AC submersible pump; flow = available energy ÷ (ρgH) — ideal for remote hill drinking water.
  • Solar thermal: box (direct) and chimney (indirect) dryers, parabolic cookers, and SODIS — 6 h of sun (UV) pasteurises water at 60–65 °C.

C. Bioenergy

  • Biogas: anaerobic digestion of cattle dung yields gas of 55–65% CH₄ (course capsule ≈ 60%) with CO₂. Nepal's household workhorse is the fixed-dome GGC 2047 (modified Chinese) model in 4, 6, 8, 10 m³ sizes; the floating-drum Indian KVIC is the alternative. Gas yield ≈ 0.03–0.04 m³ per kg of dung; the Nepal norm sizes a 6 m³ plant for ≈ 30–35 kg dung/day from 3–4 cattle (a cow gives 10–12 kg collectible, a buffalo ~15). Retention time is 30–40 days in warm Terai and 50+ days in the colder hills (temperature must stay above ≈ 15 °C; mesophilic ≈ 30–35 °C).
  • Plant parts: inlet, digester dome, gas holder (dome top), outlet/displacement pit, slurry compost pit, gas pipe with water trap and safety arrangements; appliances — a biogas stove burning 0.3–0.5 m³/h and (poor-efficiency) lamps.
    • Fig 8.6 — Fixed-dome biogas plant (GGC 2047): inlet, gas dome, digester, outlet, slurry to compost — 6 m³ ≈ 30–35 kg dung/day
  • Benefits: ≈ 2–3 tonnes of fuelwood saved per plant per year, slurry as fertiliser, smoke-free kitchen; AEPC subsidies and credit mechanisms support them. Nepal has installed over 400,000 plants — historically world-leading per capita.
  • Improved Cooking Stove (ICS): the 2-pot metal/clay chimney stove reaches 15–25% efficiency against 5–10% for an open fire, cutting fuelwood ≈ 30% and indoor smoke; parts — combustion chamber, pot seats, chimney with damper, fire door.
  • Other bioenergy: residue briquetting, small gasifiers, and the improved water mills of 8.3.

D. Micro-Hydro Design & Construction (Rural)

Fig 8.7 — Micro-hydro scheme layout: intake → canal → forebay → penstock → powerhouse, P ≈ 8QH kW
  • Definition (Nepal): micro < 100 kW, mini 100–1000 kW, small < 10 MW. A micro-hydro plant (MHP) is typically 5–100 kW, run-of-river; Nepal has 3,000+ installed under AEPC's subsidy programme.
  • Components: intake (gravel trap + trash rack) → contour canal → forebay with desanding basin → spillway → penstock (HDPE/MS) → powerhouse (turbine + generator + ELC + switchboard) → tailrace; local 3-phase 400 V or small 11 kV transmission.
  • Turbines by head: Pelton or crossflow above ≈ 30–50 m; crossflow is the village workhorse for low-to-medium heads (≈ 2–30 m, small-to-medium flows); propeller types for very low heads; pico-propellers use canal drops.
  • Generation: synchronous generators for larger/grid plants; village MHPs use the cheap, robust induction generator, which needs reactive excitation from capacitors and an ELC (electronic load controller) dumping surplus to a ballast load — the ELC holds frequency constant by balancing load, while excitation holds voltage.
  • Measuring head and flow: head by level survey (level/clinometer/altimeter); flow by float method, weir (rectangular or V-notch) or bucket method; the design flow is an exceedance flow (e.g. Q40–Q60 — available 40–60% of the time), a compromise between output and cost.
  • Power: P = 9.81 × Q × H × η, with overall η ≈ 0.5–0.7 including generator and drive (V-belt drive loses 3–5%); the handy site rule P(kW) ≈ 8·Q·H for η ≈ 0.8 before overall losses.
  • Example: Q = 0.15 m³/s, H = 25 m, η = 0.6 → P = 9.81 × 0.15 × 25 × 0.6 ≈ 22 kW — enough for roughly 60–100 households at 100 W average.
  • Construction: community labour contribution; civil works in masonry and RCC; penstock anchored with blocks every 6–10 m and thrust blocks at bends; commissioning tests the load-rejection response of the ELC.
  • O&M: monsoon debris clearing, trash-rack cleaning, penstock leak repair, bearing lubrication; tariffs flat or metered; productive end uses raise the load factor from ≈ 0.25 toward 0.4.

E. Water Mills & Wind Mills (rural recap)

  • Improved ghatta: steel axial/crossflow runner replaces the wooden one — grinding, hulling and 3–5 kW electricity from one canal; subsidised upgrade; water rights (pani mukiya) settled by community agreement.
  • Wind: small wind–solar hybrids power telecom and health posts; multi-blade windmills pump water in the Terai; hub height ≥ 10–15 m keeps the rotor above ground turbulence.
8.5 rapid numbers: Nepal solar ≈ 4.5–5.5 kWh/m²/day; MHP = < 100 kW; overall MHP η ≈ 0.5–0.7; biogas CH₄ 55–65%; 6 m³ plant ≈ 30–35 kg dung/day; retention 30–40 d; ICS efficiency 15–25% vs open fire 5–10%; battery DoD 50% for long life; P = 9.81QHη.

8.6 Rural Housing (ACRE0806)

A. Rural Housing & Types

A rural house must serve the family's livelihood, suit the climate, stay affordable and — often forgotten — be seismically sensible. Nepal's stock runs from traditional stone-in-mud with thatch (hills) and brick/mud (Terai) through timber-frame to modern stone-in-cement and RCC buildings; low-income approaches include site-and-services and core houses. NBC applies mainly to urban construction, so rural practice follows simplified seismic guidelines.

Fig 8.8 — Rural housing seismic bands: plinth, sill, lintel, roof bands with corner reinforcement (simplified NBC)

Appropriate-technology design checklist: local materials (stone, timber, bamboo, mud); simplified NBC 105 seismic principles — plinth, sill, lintel and roof bands plus corner reinforcement in good mortar; climate response (windows to the south for winter sun in the hills, orientation to prevailing winds); ventilation and daylight from openings ≈ 10–15% of floor area; sanitation (separate kitchen, cattle away from the dwelling, latrine); water supply; plinth 450–600 mm above ground (higher in flood zones); and affordability — mud mortar is cheapest.

B. Farm Buildings — Purpose & Types

  • Purpose: protect animals, crops and machines; make workflow and hygiene efficient; storage. Types: residence, cattle shed, poultry house, goat/swine sheds, feed/fodder store, machinery shed, manure pit, biogas plant, hay stack.
  • Site selection: elevated and well-drained, near water, leeward (downwind) of the dwelling for animal sheds, accessible for inputs and markets, with room to expand, away from flood and landslide. Grain stores sit at least 30 m from dairy/poultry farms and ~150 m from factories.
  • Orientation (Nepal): long axis east–west limits summer sun load and eases cross-ventilation; sheds open south/southeast for sun; in cold areas the north side stays enclosed. For dairy shade structures the course text is explicit: E–W keeps feed and water troughs shaded all day; N–S dries the floor faster and is chosen when paving is too costly.

C. Dairy Cattle Housing

  • Systems: stanchion/tie (restricted), loose housing (open lot + shelter), and stall feeding — zero grazing — the common Nepal pattern.
  • Space standards (course figures): sun-shade structure 2.5–3 m² per head; shaded feeding area 3–4 m²/cow; roof area ≈ 3 × 7 m per 10 cows with 3 m roof height; cross-tied cow 3.5–4.5 m² covered (buffalo slightly more); stall 1.1–1.2 m wide × 1.7–2.0 m long; manger height ≈ 0.5–0.6 m; feed alley 1.2–1.5 m; central drain sloping 1–2% to the gutter; milking bay; calving box 10–12 m²; calf pen 1.5–2 m²/animal.
  • Height and roof: eaves 2.4–3.0 m, ridge 3.5–4.5 m; gable roofs beat single pitch because they allow a centre vent; a woven mat under CI sheet cuts radiant heat; floors are grooved concrete at 1.5–2% (1:40–1:60) to drains.
  • Comfort: cross-ventilation with adjustable winter openings (≈ 10% of floor); cattle comfort 10–20 °C; buffaloes suffer heat stress and need wallow/water access.

D. Poultry Housing

Systems: deep litter (bedding 10–15 cm of rice husk/sawdust), battery cage, slatted or wire floor, combination, and free-range/backyard. The course's stocking table (layers, per m²): fold system 2; deep litter 3–4 (low density) to 5–7 (high); wire floor 7–8 (up to 9–10); combination floor 5–6 (7–8); cage including alleys 8–12 (up to 15–25). Chicks stock at 15–20 birds/m² for weeks 1–4.

  • Feeder/drinker space: linear feeder ≈ 5 cm/bird broilers, 7.5 cm layers; one tube drinker per ~40–50 birds or nipples at 8–10 birds each.
  • Brooding climate: start 32–35 °C in week 1, then step down ≈ 3 °C per week to ambient by week 3–4; RH 50–70%; ammonia below 20 ppm; the brooder house has no ridge ventilation opening (layers' houses do).
  • Lighting: layers need ≈ 16 h/day of light for production; pullets transfer to the laying house at 17–18 weeks; laying starts at 20–24 weeks of age.
  • Structure: house width kept under 9–12 m for natural ventilation; eaves 2–2.4 m, ridge 3–3.5 m; roof overhang ≈ 0.5 m; local materials fine (bamboo, timber) with a concrete apron for rat-proofing, wire mesh against predators, and insulated or thatch roofing (fire risk noted); the brooder section is separated; long axis E–W.

E. Goat & Swine Housing

  • Goats hate wet floor — give them a dry, well-ventilated shed with an elevated slatted floor (timber/bamboo slats, 1.5–2.5 cm gaps) raised about 0.75–1 m, so manure drops through. Floor area: adult goat ≈ 0.8–1.2 m² (slatted 0.7–0.9), kids 0.4–0.5; partitions and fences 1.2–1.5 m high (goats jump); feed rack, water trough and a separate buck pen complete the unit.
  • Swine need a concrete floor sloped to a drain and cooling in heat (wallow or shade). Space: grower 0.7–0.9 m², adult 1.5–2.5 m², sow with litter (farrowing pen) 4–6 m² with a 30–34 °C creep area for piglets; walls 1.2–1.5 m high; shaded open run; trough along the wall; strict biosecurity (African swine fever — restricted entry, disinfection).

F. Environmental Considerations in Planning Farm Buildings

  • Waste quantities (what the design must absorb): a cow voids ≈ 10–12 kg dung + 8–10 L urine daily (a buffalo ≈ 15 kg); a 1000-bird broiler flock ≈ 1–1.5 t litter per batch. Dung to biogas or compost; urine (a potent fertiliser — rich in N and K) drained to a soak pit via open covered channels; poultry litter (bedding + droppings) to fertiliser after rest; dead animals buried ≥ 1 m deep, covered with lime, away from wells — or incinerated; milking areas washable with clean water. Manure stored in the open loses ≈ half its nitrogen to volatilisation — cover the heap or shed it.
  • Sanitation link: animal sheds and manure pits are pollution sources — keep leachate ≥ 30 m from water sources, drain shed wash-water through a screened trap before discharge, and never site the dairy above the well on the same aquifer path.
  • Water and drainage: livestock demand (cattle 40–60 L/day and up); sheds graded 1–2% with no ponding; manure removed every 5–7 days to break the fly lifecycle.
  • Climate response: shade trees to the west, roof overhang 0.6–1 m, white/insulated roofs against heat, windbreaks to the north in cold zones; avoid humid fog pockets that bring respiratory disease.
  • Zoning: clean/dirty separation — dwelling upwind and uphill, sheds downwind; manure pit ≥ 15–30 m from dwelling and well; leachate kept ≥ 30 m from water sources; the biogas plant sits between cattle shed and kitchen.

G. Selection of Materials for Low-Cost Farm Buildings

  • By element: foundation — stone masonry in mud/cement; wall — stone in mud mortar (good thermal mass for hills), bamboo-mud wattle, brick; roof — GI sheet (durable but hot — insulate), thatch (cheap, fire risk), tile, or ferro-cement channels; floor — compacted earth (cheapest), brick flat soling + mud, or washable concrete for milking and poultry houses.
  • Selection criteria: cost, local availability, strength and durability, climate fit, washability/hygiene (dairy and poultry), fire behaviour, seismic bands even in mud buildings, and owner maintainability. Appropriate-technology options include stabilized earth blocks, rat-trap bond and bamboo trusses.

H. Construction of Farm Buildings (summary of good practice)

  • Setting out by the 3-4-5 method; compacted plinth fill with DPC; plinth, lintel and roof bands even in mud construction for seismic safety; timber/steel trusses tied down against wind; drainage and aprons around every shed. Sequence: foundation → plinth → walls → roof → floors → fittings → services (water, power, waste).
  • Farmers' residence: zone the homestead — living core, kitchen with flue, store, and cattle attached but separated by a store or veranda (less smell and flies); high plinth; multi-use verandah; rainwater tank; latrine and handwashing; kitchen garden. Cattle, poultry, goat and swine housing follow C–E above; the recurring construction themes are drainage slope, ventilation, rodent-proofing and biosecurity.
8.6 rapid numbers: cow stall 1.2 × 1.8 m; shade 2.5–3 m²/head, 3–4 m²/cow; broiler deep litter 10–12/m² (meat birds); layer 3–4 (up to 5–7)/m² (course table); brooding 32–35 °C; goat 0.8–1.2 m² slatted; sow farrowing 4–6 m²; plinth 450–600 mm; opening area ≈ 10–15% floor; manure pit ≥ 15–30 m from dwelling/well.

Deeper Concept Discussions (Chapter 8)

Why rural roads fail early in Nepal (and how standards prevent it)

  • Monsoon concentration: 80% of the rain falls in 4 months — undersized drains saturate the road, gravel washes out and cut slopes slump. The standard response: a side drain in every cut, cross-drainage at every gully (never stretch a culvert), and slope stabilisation concurrent with construction — the Green Road approach.
  • Mass balancing: balancing cut and fill along the contour cuts both haul cost and spoil dumping (a slide trigger). Half-bench sections where fill can be keyed and vegetated; full bench only in hard rock with retaining structures.
  • Maintenance economics: one rupee spent on maintenance saves about four in reconstruction — routine budgets run 4–6% of capital per year, and community maintenance groups (CMG) deliver the labour in DoR rural projects (the Road Board remains a pending bill).

Suspension vs suspended bridge — mechanics comparison

AspectSuspensionSuspended
DeckStiff truss hung by hangersFlexible deck-cable net (planks + netting)
Span range120–500 m (LSTB)≤ 120 m (SSTB)
Sag≈ L/10–L/12 (cable tension T = wL²/(8s))Larger relative sag, more deflection
StiffnessTruss resists local loads → smootherDeflects under walking — the "wave"
Cost/complexityHigher (more steel, bigger anchors)Lower — community-maintainable
  • Main-cable tension T = wL²/(8s) (w = UDL, s = sag): halving the sag doubles the tension, so sag choice trades cable size against deck motion. Anchorage design checks overturning and sliding with safety factors.

Biogas plant sizing worked logic

  • Dung per cow ≈ 10–12 kg/day (buffalo ≈ 15); gas yield ≈ 0.03–0.04 m³ per kg of dung at a 30–40 day retention. The Nepal sizing norm (which allows for what is actually collectible) puts 3–4 cattle ≈ 30–35 kg/day on a 6 m³ plant; the course capsule's short form: 1 kg dung ≈ 0.04 m³ gas, a 1 m³ ≈ 20–25 kg dung/day plant for small digesters.
  • Retention time = digester volume ÷ daily slurry feed (dung + equal water) — 30 days Terai, 40–50 days hills; colder means a bigger digester or insulation, and an underground dome helps.

RWH tank sizing quick method (dry-month demand)

  • Compute the monthly roof harvest; find the longest run of months where demand exceeds supply; the tank volume = cumulative deficit + dead storage; and check the tank is larger than the biggest single-month harvest so transition-month rain is not spilled.

20 More Rapid Numericals (answers inline)

  • SSD at 40 km/h, f = 0.35: reaction 0.278×40×2.5 = 27.8 m + braking 40²/(254×0.35) ≈ 18 m → ≈ 46 m (with f = 0.4, ≈ 43 m — exam accepts ~45 m).
  • Superelevation, V = 30, R = 40: e = V²/225R = 900/(225×40) = 0.10, but emax = 0.07 → provide 0.07 and let friction carry the rest (concept answer: e_max = 7%).
  • Extra widening: single lane, R = 30, V = 30: We = 1×6.1²/(2×30) + 30/(9.5√30) = 0.62 + 0.58 = 1.2 m.
  • Suspension cable: L = 120 m, w = 4 kN/m, s = 12 m: T = 4×120²/(8×12) = 600 kN per main cable (with half the deck load per cable plane).
  • Cable FoS: ultimate 1960 kN vs working 600 kN → 3.3 ✓.
  • Sag ratio: s = 10 m, L = 120 m → 1/12 ✓ (Nepal standard).
  • RWH: roof 80 m², rainfall 1200 mm, GI 0.9 → 80×1.2×0.9 = 86.4 m³/yr.
  • Tank for a 15-day dry gap, family 6 × 45 lpcd: 6×45×15 = 4.05 m³ → provide a 5 m³ ferro tank.
  • Solar sizing: 300 Wh/day, PSH 5, η 0.7 → Wp = 300/(5×0.7) = 85 Wp → 100 W module.
  • Battery: 300 Wh, 12 V, DoD 0.5 → 300/(12×0.5) = 50 Ah → 75–100 Ah for cycle life.
  • Biogas: 30 kg dung/day ≈ 1.0–1.2 m³ gas/day; the Nepal standard table (slurry volume + safety margin) puts 30 kg/d on a 4 m³ plant — quote the standard table.
  • MHP: Q = 0.2, H = 20, η = 0.6 → P = 9.81×0.2×20×0.6 = 23.5 kW.
  • Design population 600, 45 lpcd, 15% loss: 600×45×1.15 = 31 m³/d = 0.36 L/s; max day ×1.7 ≈ 0.61 L/s.
  • RVT = 40% of 31 ≈ 12.5 m³.
  • Septic tank, 8 users, 100 lpcd, cleaned every 3 yr: V₁ = 0.8×1 = 0.8 m³; V₂ = 0.0425×8 = 0.34 m³; V₃ = 0.085×8 = 0.68 m³ → total 1.82 m³ (adopt ≈ 2.4 × 0.8 × 1.4 m with freeboard).
  • Soak pit for the same 8-user tank (effluent 800 L/d, Tr = 25): I = 130/25 = 26 L/m²/d → A = 800/26 ≈ 30.8 m² → 2 pits of Φ 2.5 m, effective depth 2 m (A = n·π·Φ·d ✓), overall depth 2.5 m with 0.5 m freeboard.
  • Grain store: 10 t paddy at ρ = 575 → 17.4 m³ → a 3 m dia × 2.5 m bin ≈ 17.7 m³ ✓.
  • Cold-store pull-down: 5 t potato, cp = 3.5 kJ/kg·K, ΔT = 20 → field heat = 5000×3.5×20 = 350 MJ ≈ 97 kWh (over 24 h ≈ 4 kW of cooling).
  • Culvert flood: catchment 2 km², rational C = 0.4, i = 50 mm/h → Q = 0.278×0.4×50×2 = 11.1 m³/s.
  • Wind pump: 40 m³/day lifted 10 m → E = 40 000 kg × 9.81 × 10 = 3.92 MJ ≈ 1.09 kWh/day mechanical — a multi-blade windmill manages this at a 4 m/s mean wind.

Worked Design Walkthrough: A 20 kW Micro Hydro Plant

  • Site data: stream with Q40 = 0.18 m³/s (measured by V-notch with float checks), gross head 30 m (level survey), village of 150 households 1.2 km below.
  • Power check: P = 9.81 × 0.18 × 30 × 0.65 ≈ 34 kW gross potential → design capacity chosen at 20 kW (penstock headloss ~8%, part-flow months) — installed capacity follows the demand and load survey, not the maximum water.
  • Selection: H = 30 m, Q = 0.18 → crossflow (or 2-jet Pelton); low specific speed — crossflow chosen for village O&M simplicity.
  • Canal: 400 m contour canal, trapezoidal stone masonry, S = 1/1000, capacity 0.25 m³/s (design flow + spill margin); forebay + desanding basin (two cells; 0.5 mm removal is acceptable for a crossflow); spillway returns excess to the stream.
  • Penstock: HDPE PN10 — 200 mm gives V = 0.18/(π×0.1²) = 5.7 m/s (too high) → 250 mm gives V ≈ 3.7 m/s ✓ (inside the 3–5 m/s band); anchor blocks every 8 m, thrust blocks at bends, air valve at the summit.
  • Powerhouse: crossflow turbine + 20 kW induction generator + ELC ballast; switchboard with kWh meters per household group; tailrace returns the flow; 3-phase 400 V transmission 1.2 km to the village with sag and clearance per NBC/NEA LV rules.
  • Tariff & management: flat monthly per bulb or metered; MHP committee; productive loads (a 3 kW huller, daytime welding) lift the load factor from 0.25 → 0.4, improving revenue and payback.

Worked Design Walkthrough: 10-household Septic Tank + Soak Pit

  • Flow: 10 HH × 5 persons × 70 L/d of black+grey to the septic ≈ 3.5 m³/d → a 24 h tank needs 3.5 m³ of settling volume plus digestion and storage terms — total ≈ 6–7 m³ twin-chamber, or per-household 2 m³ tanks with a shared soak trench (village layouts prefer sharing where land allows).
  • Soak pit: effluent 60% of 3.5 = 2.1 m³/d at 20 L/m²/d → 105 m² needed — too big for one pit. Two 1.5 m × 3 m pits give (π×1.5×3 + 1.8) ≈ 15.9 m² each = 31.8 m² total → 66 L/m² — overloaded. Four pits or a 30 m drainage trench are required — the worked lesson: keep greywater out of the septic system in dense settlements.
  • Distance checks: ≥ 30 m from wells; tank ≥ 5–7 m from the house foundation; desludging access; vent on the tank cover.

Worked Design Walkthrough: Rural Road Cross-Section in Mid-Hills

  • Given: jeep track, hill terrain, design speed 20 km/h, side-long slope 30°.
  • Section: carriageway 3.5 m gravel + 0.5 m shoulders = 4.5 m formation; cut slope 1:1 (soil) with catch drain; fill side on dry stone retaining/keyed fill with bio-engineering (brush layer + grass lines); side drain 0.6 × 0.6 m stone-pitched, gradient = road grade (min 0.5%); cross drains every 60–80 m on grade; culverts at all gullies (min 600 mm dia or 0.9 × 0.6 box).
  • Curve at R = 20 m: e = V²/225R = 400/(225×20) = 0.089 → cap 0.07 + friction; widen 1.3 m on the inside; apply grade compensation; check the 30 m SSD against the cut face — provide a benched sight line, or a mirror and mandatory warning signs at a blind hairpin.
  • Mass diagram: balance cut and fill within ~200 m leads (headpan labour works within 50–100 m, tractors longer); surplus is spoiled on stable benches and vegetated — never tipped over the fill slope (slide trigger).

Last-Mile Memory Hooks (Chapter 8)

  • Suspension vs suspended: "-ion" = truss-stiffened long span; "-ed" = flexible short span — one letter separates two bridge families.
  • Rural design-speed ladder: hill 20–30 < plain rural 40–50 < NH 80–100 km/h — gradients run the other way (hill allows 8–10% vs plain 5–6%).
  • 45–65–100: rural basic 45 lpcd, intermediate 65, urban ~100 — Nepal's service-level ladder.
  • Turbine-by-head ladder (rural): low head < 10 m → propeller/crossflow; 10–50 → crossflow/Francis; > 50 → Pelton.
  • Bio-engineering rule: vegetation holds the top 1–2 m; structures hold the rest — combined = bio-technical.
  • Battery 50% DoD, panel derate ×0.7, PSH 4.5–5.5 (Nepal) — three solar sizing constants.
  • Storage moisture ceiling: "12–14 for cereals, 8 for pulses/oilseeds" — cross it and fungi/insects follow.
  • The sanitation triple: septic 24 h / desludge 2–3 yr / soak 10–30 L/m²·d.
  • Farm shed spacing ladder: manure pit 15–30 m ≈ latrine-to-well 30 m > septic-to-house 5–7 m > sheds downwind of dwelling — closest = septic, farthest = manure/waste.
  • Exam trap pairs: suspension vs suspended; duty vs delta (Ch 7 echo); micro vs mini (< 100 vs 100–1000 kW); causeway vs bridge (submersible vs bridged); deep-litter densities (broiler 10–12 vs layer 5–7 per m²).

Prep-Course Grounding — Rapid-Fire Capsule for Rural Engineering (8.1–8.6)

8.1 Rural Roads — Capsule One-Liners

  • Rural road classes (Nepal DoLIDAR/DoR practice): District Core Road Network → Upgrading → Farm roads (earthen, dry-season) < Village roads (gravelled, all-season) < District roads (bituminous). Strategic Road Network (SRN) = DoR; Local Road Network (LRN) = DoLI/DoLIDAR (now DoLI).
  • Single-lane earthen/gravel rural road: carriageway ≈ 3.5 m (2.75 m minimum for one vehicle), shoulder 0.5–1.0 m each side, camber 3–5% earthen (2.5% gravel, 2% bituminous).
  • Alignment: ruling gradient 5–6% (hill rural), max 8–10% with hairpins avoided; superelevation e = V²/(225R) for mixed traffic (rural e ≤ 7%); extra widening We = nl²/2R + V/(9.5√R).
  • Sight distance: SSD = vt + v²/2gf; rural design speed 30–40 km/h in rolling terrain.
  • Cross-drainage: culvert (pipe/box, < 6 m), causeway/vented causeway (submersible, flash floods, economical — vented lets normal flow pass), ford, bridge (> 6 m span).
  • Slope protection: bio-engineering (vetiver, bamboo, napier — cheap, self-repairing, eco-friendly) + civil works (gabion and retaining walls, stone pitching, breast walls, side and catch-water drains). Gradient control and drainage = "water is the enemy of roads."
  • Maintenance: routine (drains, potholes), periodic (regravelling 3–5 yr), special (flood damage); labour-based technology preferred in rural Nepal (green roads — avoid mass blasting).

8.2 Trail Bridges — Capsule One-Liners

  • Types: suspension (LSTB > 120 m), suspended (SSTB, ≤ 120 m), steel truss (up to 32 m; standard designs 16–32 m), cantilever, drop-down suspended (small spans).
  • SSTB (short span): span up to 120 m (wooden-deck types commonly 12–60 m), wire-rope main cables, deck width ≈ 1.0–1.2 m, live load ≈ 3.5–4 kN/m² (course norm 400 kg/m²) with a 5 kN concentrated allowance.
  • LSTB (long span): 120–250+ m suspension with stiffening truss; H-frame pylons at both banks; sag ≈ 1/10–1/12 of span; gravity/tunnel/rock anchorage; windguy system only on LSTB.
  • Site selection: narrow gorge, high banks (freeboard ≥ 2 m above HFL or per standard), stable banks, aligned with approach trails, minimum 500 m from the nearest existing crossing.
  • Design parameters: dead load (cables, deck, railing), live (pedestrian 400 kg/m² + livestock), wind (norm 160 km/h), snow (high hills), temperature, seismic; wire rope (6×19 or 6×37) FoS ≥ 3.0–3.5; sag set by turnbuckles/tensioning; design life ≥ 50 years.
  • Construction: anchorage concreting → tower erection → cable pulling → deck joists → decking; maintenance: cable greasing, plank replacement, painting, anchor-bolt checks.

8.3 Farm Machinery & Post-Harvest — Capsule One-Liners

  • Tillage: primary (mould-board plough inverting 20–30 cm; disc plough 3–10 discs of 60–75 cm) vs secondary (harrow, cultivator); animal draft ≈ 0.5–1 hp per pair; power tiller 8–12 hp common in the Nepal Terai.
  • Water mill (ghatta): traditional horizontal wooden turbine, head 2–5 m, output 0.5–3 kW; improved ghatta (metal runner) doubles output and yields 3–5 kW, doubling as oil expeller/huller; multi-blade American windmill pumps water (low tip-speed), propeller type generates.
  • Intercultural tools: khurpi, spade; harvesting: sickle; threshing: manual beating, ox-treading, thresher (drum 700–1000 rpm for paddy); winnowing by chaff separator.
  • Processing: rice mill (huller/polisher), maize sheller, oil expeller (ghani/expeller), flour mill (plate/roller); post-harvest losses ≈ 5–15% of grain when stored poorly.
  • Grain storage design: moisture < 12–14% for safe storage; aeration against pests; bag storage (flexible, ventilated) vs bulk (silos/bins — metal, ferro-cement, brick); hermetic storage kills insects by CO₂ build-up; raised plinth + rat-proofing (metal collar/overhang); volume = mass ÷ bulk density (paddy ≈ 580, wheat ≈ 800 kg/m³).
  • Cold storage: dairy/perishables at 0–4 °C (milk 4 °C, vegetables 0–5 °C, fruits 0–13 °C); PUF/thermocole insulation with vapour barrier; refrigeration load = product + transmission + infiltration + equipment (Q = U·A·ΔT); rural dairy rule — milk chilled within 2 h of milking.
  • Fertilizer/pesticide store: dry, ventilated, pesticide room with bunded floor, away from water sources.

8.4 Rural Water Supply & Sanitation — Capsule One-Liners

  • Nepal rural demand = 45 lpcd (basic "access" standard 25 lpcd); design period rural WSS = 15 years; service ladder 45 → 65 → 100+ lpcd.
  • Gravity-flow scheme: intake (spring/river) → transmission main → interruption chamber / break-pressure tank (roughly every 50–60 m of head) → distribution → tap stands (1 per 8–10 households, 0.15–0.2 L/s per tap, fetching ≤ 200 m horizontal / 50 m vertical).
  • Source protection: spring-protection boxes, fencing, intake above contamination, buffer zone; sanitary survey before design.
  • Rainwater harvesting: supply = roof area × annual rainfall × runoff coefficient (GI 0.9, tile 0.8–0.85); tank sized for the dry-period deficit; first-flush diverter mandatory; ferro-cement tank shell 20–40 mm of rich (1:3) mortar over chicken/weld mesh — economical up to ≈ 20 m³.
  • Tube wells: shallow (hand pump, ⌀ 100–150 mm, 10–30 m, India Mark II/III) vs deep (motorised); well development removes drilling fluid; gravel pack graded 2–3× the screen slot sizing; sanitary seal in the top 3 m.
  • Sanitation (service ladder): the Nepal sanitation ladder runs open defecation → simple pit latrine (single pit for impermeable soil; double/twin-pit alternating — one pit in use while the other digests for 1–2 years, then emptied as safe compost; no desludging machinery needed) → improved pit/VIP (vent pipe + fly-screen carries odours and flies away; dark interior) → pour-flush with pan and water seal (50 mm minimum water seal; no need for water for flushing — a mug suffices) → septic tank + soak pit for blackwater (detention 12–36 h, standard 24 h) → flush toilet with sewerage where a network exists. Twin-pit logic: pits alternate — fill one, seal it for ~1–2 years of anaerobic digestion (volume drops ~50%, pathogens die off), then switch; the digested soil-like humus is safe to handle. Soak pit: a covered pit (1–2 m Φ, 1.5–3 m deep) with a porous lining of dry brick/stone packed in layers; septic effluent percolates through the soil where aerobic bacteria finish the treatment; sized from I = 130/√Tr ≈ 10–30 L/m²/day (percolation test); soakage trench (0.5–0.6 m wide, 0.6–1 m deep, gravel-filled, laid to fall 1:200–1:400) replaces pits in clay or high water table. Ecosan (ecological sanitation): dry, waterless, separates urine and faeces — ash dehydrates faeces, urine (rich in N) is diluted 3:1 as fertiliser; suitable where water is scarce or the water table high. Desludging every 2–3 years; latrine ≥ 30 m from the water source (10–30 m band, 30 m preferable) and downhill of it; latrines also ≥ 15 m from kitchens/dining and above the 10-year flood level where relevant. ODF (Open Defecation Free) verification and post-ODF total sanitation are the Nepal campaign milestones.
  • Solid waste: rural generation 0.2–0.4 kg/cap/day (urban 0.5+), of which the organic fraction is ≈ 60–65%; collection (communal bins, door-to-door), transport, disposal: sanitary landfill (lined, daily cover), composting of the organic fraction (a 1 m³ digester ≈ 20–25 kg dung/day ≈ 0.4 m³ gas), incineration for health-care waste, vermicomposting.

8.5 Rural Energy — Capsule One-Liners

  • Micro-hydro (< 100 kW; mini 100–1000 kW): intake → canal → forebay/desanding → penstock → powerhouse (crossflow/Pelton turbine, ELC governor); Nepal > 3,000 MHPs (AEPC subsidy programme); crossflow suits ≈ 2–30 m heads.
  • Solar: PV cell efficiency ≈ 15–20%; solar home systems 20–40 Wp typical rural Nepal (AEPC subsidy); solar lanterns and pumping (array + MPPT controller + DC pump); peak sun hours Nepal ≈ 4.5–5.5 kWh/m²/day.
  • Biogas: fixed-dome (Chinese/GGC 2047 — most common in Nepal) vs floating-drum (Indian KVIC); 1 kg dung ≈ 0.04 m³ biogas; ≈ 60% CH₄; digester 4–8 m³ for a 4–6 cattle family; slurry = fertiliser; mesophilic digestion ≈ 30–35 °C.
  • Improved cooking stoves (ICS): chimney + damper, 20–30% efficiency vs ≈ 10% open fire; cuts indoor air pollution and fuelwood use by 30–50%.
  • Rural electrification: grid extension vs isolated MHP mini-grids; ELC ballast for frequency/load management; tariff funds O&M.
  • Wind: multi-blade water pumping (low tip-speed) vs 2–3-blade propeller for electricity; wind power P = ½ρAV³ (cubic with velocity!); Nepal feasibility concentrates in the Kaligandaki corridor.

8.6 Rural Housing & Farm Buildings — Capsule One-Liners

  • Rural housing types: traditional (mud-bonded brick/stone, thatch), improved (RCC band + CGI), appropriate-technology housing (stabilized mud blocks, rat-trap bond, ferro-cement elements).
  • Dairy cattle housing: shade 2.5–3 m²/head, shaded area 3–4 m²/cow; covered floor ≈ 4–5 m² per adult cow + paddock; floor slope 2–3% to drain; manger 0.5–0.75 m high; stall ≈ 1.2 × 2 m; E–W orientation; roof height 2.5–3 m; gable roof with centre vent.
  • Poultry housing: deep-litter stocking 3–4 (low) to 5–7 (high) layers/m² (broilers 0.09–0.14 m²/bird); cage 0.06–0.08 m²/hen; feeder 5–7 cm/bird; brooding 32–35 °C first week; 16 h light for layers; long axis E–W.
  • Goat/swine housing: goat 1–1.5 m²/animal on raised slats (0.75–1 m above ground, slat gap 1.5–2 cm); swine pen 2–3 m²/sow with wallow/dunging area, creep area 30–34 °C for piglets.
  • Farm building planning: ventilation, drainage, orientation to prevailing wind, insulation, waste management (dung → biogas), fodder/grain store adjacency; low-cost materials: stabilized earth blocks, bamboo trusses, ferro-cement tanks, CGI sheets.
  • Service buildings cluster: residence upwind/uphill of the cattle shed; manure pit > 30 m from the well; biogas plant between cattle shed and kitchen.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): 45 lpcd + 15-year design period (rural WSS pair); SSTB ≤ 120 m wooden-deck types vs LSTB > 120 m suspension; causeway = submersible crossing; vented causeway lets normal flow pass; crossflow turbine for low-to-medium micro-hydro heads; fixed-dome GGC 2047 biogas model; ELC for mini-grid frequency control; deep-litter layer densities 3–7 birds/m² (broiler 10–12).
