This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

9.1 Highway Planning and Survey (ACiE0901)

A. Modes of Transport

Five modes move the world's traffic: road, rail, air, water and pipeline — plus ropeways, which matter in Nepal for hill cargo. Each has a different cost structure: road is cheap to build for low volumes but costly to operate; rail is the reverse (high fixed cost, low running cost); air is fastest and costliest; water is cheapest for bulk; pipeline runs continuously for fluids.

Why roads dominate: door-to-door flexibility, low capital for low traffic volumes, and they feed every other mode. The price is accidents, congestion, and higher energy per tonne-km than rail or water for bulk goods. In Nepal roads carry over 90% of passengers and freight — the railway is still nascent (the Janakpur–Jaynagar line), ropeways are re-emerging for cargo, air links the hills, and water transport is negligible.

B. History of Road Development in Nepal

MilestoneRouteWhen / notes
First vehicular roadRaxaul (India) – Birgunj – Amlekhgunj~1927
First national highwayTribhuvan Rajpath (Kathmandu–Hetauda/Birgunj)Built 1953–56 with Indian aid
Araniko RajmargKathmandu–Kodari (China border)1963–68, Chinese aid
Mahendra (East–West) HighwayKakarbhitta to Kanchanpur (Mahendranagar), ~1,000+ kmConstructed 1960s–70s with Indian cooperation
Prithvi HighwayNaubise–PokharaCompleted 1974, Chinese aid

Later additions: Siddhartha (Butwal–Pokhara), Mechi, Koshi, B.P. Koirala (Biratnagar area), Dharan–Hile/Dhankuta, Karnali, the Madan Bhandari (inner-Terai) highway under development, and the Kathmandu–Nijgadh Fast Track under construction as an expressway-standard link.

Today's network: roughly 70,000+ km of roads in total, of which the Strategic Road Network (SRN) under DoR is ≈ 12,898 km (course data) — about 80% of the network is Local Road Network (LRN). Road density remains among the lowest in South Asia but is growing fast.

C. Classification of Roads

  • By function (IRC/DoR): Expressway, National Highway (NH), Feeder Road (FR) — the state-highway/MDR analogue — then District Road (DR) and Urban Road (UR), with LRN local roads below. Nepal's DoR runs NH + FR as the SRN.
  • By traffic (NRS 2070 classes, 20-yr perspective ADT): Class I (expressway) > 20,000 PCU/day; Class II (arterial) 5,000–20,000; Class III (collector) 2,000–5,000; Class IV (local) < 2,000 — the course's heavy/medium/light banding maps onto these; by surface: paved (bituminous, cement) vs unpaved (gravel, earthen); by season: all-weather vs fair-weather.
  • Nagpur classification (historic India, still quoted): NH, SH (State), MDR (Major District), ODR (Other District), Village roads — Nepal's older documents mirrored it.
  • Expressway: fully access-controlled, divided carriageway, highest design speeds — Nepal's Fast Track is planned to this standard.
Fig 9.1 — How Nepal's roads are classified: the hierarchy that sets every design standard

D. Road Survey (Engineering Surveys for Highway)

Fig 9.2 — The four phases of highway engineering surveys — map study to final location & DPR

Highway engineering surveys run in four classic phases:

PhaseWhat happens
Map studyTopographic maps (1:50,000 for Nepal) and imagery; mark 2–3 possible alignments between termini, avoiding villages, forests and unstable ground.
ReconnaissanceField walk/drive of the corridor: grades, crossings, materials, landslide zones, water; simple instruments (compass, abney level/clinometer, altimeter); output — alternative strip maps and a report.
Preliminary surveyTraverse the chosen corridor (total station), levelling, cross-sections every 50–100 m (100–200 m on plain), soil profile and borrow pits, drainage data (HFL, catchments); compare alternatives and pick the final alignment with a detailed project report.
Final location & detailed surveyPeg the centre line (20 m plain / 10 m hill / 5 m on curves), L-section, cross-sections at 20–30 m, land acquisition plans, utility mapping, detailed drainage survey.
  • Instrumentation: total station, DGPS and drone photogrammetry are the modern kit; levelling gives profiles; traffic counts and origin–destination surveys run during the preliminary phase.
  • Comparing alternatives: weigh length, earthwork, structures, land cost, maximum grade and travel-time savings — the economic choice is the lowest total annual cost (capital + maintenance + user costs), evaluated by benefit–cost or NPV (the Chapter 10 link).
  • Alignment controls: obligatory points (river crossing, saddle, tunnel portal), gradient, sight distance, stability, drainage, land use and cost, the number of cross-drainage works, and environmental/social factors (resettlement).
  • A good alignment is: shortest, safest, cheapest (least earthwork and structures), aesthetic, easy in gradient and geometry, and leaves room for future upgrading.
  • Nepal Road Standard (DoR, first issued 2027 BS, updated NRS 2070): roads are classed I–IV by terrain and traffic, with design speeds from 120 km/h (plain, Class I) down to 20 km/h (steep, Class IV) — the class table sits in the grounding capsule below.
Exam favourites: first road = Raxaul–Birgunj (1920s); first highway = Tribhuvan Rajpath; the great east–west artery = Mahendra Highway; Kathmandu–Kodari = Araniko; Kathmandu–Pokhara = Prithvi.
9.1 rapid numbers: pegging interval 20 m (plain), 10 m (hill), 5 m (curves); cross-sections every 20–30 m in detailed survey; first highway: Tribhuvan Rajpath (1956); East–West = Mahendra Highway; total road ≈ 70,000+ km, SRN ≈ 12,898 km (DoR).

9.2 Geometric Design of Highway (ACiE0902)

A. Design Controls & Criteria

  • Design vehicle: key dimensions — car 1.0 PCU baseline; bus/truck 2.5 m wide; the WB-15/WB-19 articulated trucks set turning radii. Design speed is the master control (chosen by terrain and road class); design traffic is PCU-based with growth rates of 5–7.5% (typical 5–7%); design hour volume for planning = the 30th-highest hourly volume (DDHV).
  • PCU factors (IRC, approximate): car 1.0, bus/truck 3.0, motorcycle 0.5–0.75, cycle 0.5, rickshaw 1.5–2.0, tractor-trailer 4.5, animal cart ≈ 3.0.
  • Cross-section elements: carriageway, shoulders (1.0–2.5 m), footpath, median on divided roads, and the right of way (land width). IRC ROW: NH 45 m open / 30 m built-up; SH 30/20; MDR 25/15; ODR 15/12; VR 12/9. Nepal DoR ROW per NRS 2070 (verified): National Highway 50 m, Feeder Roads 30 m, District Roads 20 m. Then side drains, embankment slopes, boundary stones.
  • Camber is the crossfall that drains the surface — NRS 2070 Table 11-3 (the course/PANA set): cement concrete 1.5–2%, bituminous 2.5%, gravel 4%, earthen 5% (the IRC textbook band runs a shade flatter: thin bituminous 2–2.5%, high-type bituminous 2%, gravel 2.5–3.5%, earth 3–4%). It is steeper for the rougher, more pervious surfaces (earth, gravel) and for heavy-rain areas; a smooth, impervious surface drains even at a flat camber. Shapes: parabolic (common), straight, combined.
  • Carriageway width: 3.75 m single lane (Nepal practice 3.5 m), 7.0–7.5 m two lanes; shoulders ≥ 1.0–2.5 m by class.

B. Highway Curves — Horizontal

Fig 9.3 — Superelevation: outer edge raised through a transition spiral; e ≤ 7%, friction f = 0.15
  • Speed ↔ radius: R = V²/(127(e+f)) with V in km/h; emax = 0.07, design side friction f = 0.15; the mixed-traffic comfort rule is e = V²/225R.
  • Superelevation design steps (IRC): (1) compute e for 75% of design speed: e = (0.75V)²/127R, capped at 0.07; (2) check the friction left for full speed: f = V²/127R − e ≤ 0.15; (3) if it exceeds 0.15, limit e = 0.07 and re-check; (4) for mixed traffic provide the equilibrium e = V²/225R, attained gradually by rotating the pavement.
  • Transition curve length (spiral / cubic parabola): Ls = 0.0215V³/(CR) from comfort, with C = 80/(75+V) m/s³ (IRC); also checked against the rate of superelevation rotation — 1 in 150 (plain), 1 in 100 (built-up), 1 in 60 (mountainous).
  • Extra widening: We = nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R) — the mechanical part uses wheelbase l = 6.1 m (standard commercial vehicle), the psychological part is the V/(9.5√R) term.
  • Setback distance: the clearance m = R − (R−d)·cos(β/2), where β is the sight-line angle subtending the sight distance and d the distance to the obstruction — needed where cut slopes or trees block SSD (or OSD) on curves; a hill-road staple.
  • Vertical curves: summit (crest) for SSD with s < L: L = NS²/4.4 (and L = 2S − 4.4/N when s > L); valley by the headlight criterion: L = NS²/(1.5 + 0.035S). N is the deviation angle |g₁−g₂|/100 — a dimensionless decimal; K = L/N.
  • Gradients (IRC): ruling — plain 3.3% (1 in 30), mountainous 5% (1 in 20), steep 6% (1 in 16.7); limiting — plain 5%, mountainous 6%, steep 7%; exceptional (short stretches only) — plain 6.7% (1 in 15), mountainous 7%, steep 8%; minimum for drainage ≈ 0.2–0.5% (NRS 2070 fixes 0.5%). NRS also eases the maximum gradient by 0.5% for every 500 m rise above mean sea level. In Nepal hill practice — rural roads under NRRS in particular — exceptional gradients up to about 12% are tolerated on very short steep stretches (course/hill-practice value), and NRS 2070 backs that: Table 10-1 sets the maximum gradient at 12% for the 20 km/h design speed, easing to 10% at 30, 9% at 40, 7% at 60, 6% at 80, 5% at 100 and 4% at 120 km/h, with Table 10-2 capping the length of each critical grade. The "8% exceptional" ceiling is IRC's terrain-based value, not NRS's.
  • Grade compensation on curves claws back speed lost on sharp curves: compensation = (30+R)/R %, capped at 75/R % — applied on curves within the compensation limit, and not for gradients below 4%.
  • Curve shape: simple parabola with equal tangents is standard for summit and valley curves.
  • Sight distance formulas: SSD = 0.278V·t + V²/(254f) with t = 2.5 s and f = 0.35–0.4; eye height 1.2 m and object height 0.15 m (IRC). OSD = d₁ (reaction, 0.278Vb·t, t ≈ 2 s) + d₂ (overtaking manoeuvre, 0.278Vb·T with T = √(14.4A/a), a in km/h/s — equivalently √(4A/a) with a in m/s²) + d₃ (0.278V·T — the oncoming vehicle's travel during the manoeuvre; the initial spacing A ≈ 0.2Vb+6 belongs in d₂ as +2A) — roughly 2.3–5× SSD; intermediate sight distance = 2×SSD.
Fig 9.4 — Sight distance: stopping (SSD) and overtaking (OSD) — geometry, formulas and controls

C. Hill Roads

  • Design considerations: lower design speeds, sharper curves (hairpin R ≥ 14 m), steeper grades (hill ruling 5%, limiting 6%, exceptional 7% per IRC — Nepal hill practice tolerates ≈ 12% on short exceptional stretches), the resisting length concept (total work against the sum of rise and fall), dense cross-drainage, and slope stability — retaining and breast walls, pitching, hairpin loops, galleries/semi-tunnels in rockfall zones, switchbacks, longitudinal drains on the hill side, catch drains above the cut, and causeways at stream crossings.
  • Special structures: retaining wall (holds fill), breast wall (supports the cut face above the road), toe wall, parapet, catch-water drain above the cut, chutes, culverts and causeways — and alignment kept clear of avalanche and GLOF zones in the alpine reaches.
9.2 must-remember set: e_max = 7%; f_design = 0.15; mixed traffic e = V²/225R; transition Ls = 0.0215V³/CR; We = nl²/2R + V/(9.5√R); SSD = 0.278Vt + V²/254f (t 2.5 s, f 0.35); ISD = 2×SSD; crest L = NS²/4.4; valley L = NS²/(1.5+0.035S); ruling gradient plain 3.3%, hill 5%; min gradient ≈ 0.5%; compensation (30+R)/R % capped at 75/R %.

9.3 Highway Materials (ACiE0903)

A. Aggregate Properties & Tests

Fig 9.5 — Aggregate test map: what each test measures (wear, toughness, strength, shape, adhesion)
PropertyTestTypical requirement
Hardness (abrasion)Los Angeles Abrasion (IS 2386 Pt IV)Bituminous surface ≤ 30%, base ≤ 50%, cement concrete ≤ 16%
Crushing strengthAggregate Crushing Value (ACV)Surface ≤ 30%, base ≤ 45%
Toughness (impact)Aggregate Impact Value (AIV)Surface ≤ 30%, base ≤ 45%
Durability (weathering)Soundness (Na₂SO₄/MgSO₄ cycles)Loss ≤ 12% after 5 cycles (sodium sulphate)
ShapeFlakiness & Elongation IndicesCombined ≤ 30% (prefer < 25%)
Water absorption24-h soak≤ 0.6% preferred, 2% maximum
Polish (skid)Polished Stone Value (PSV)PSV > 55 for wearing course
Adhesion to bitumenStripping value testStripping ≤ 25% (retained coating ≥ 95% with anti-stripping agent)
Deleterious contentClay lumps, dustDust (passing 75 μm) ≤ 4–5%
Property definitions (what each really measures):
Hardness — resistance to progressive surface wear/abrasion by traffic → LA abrasion (500 rev with grading charge; % wear on the 1.7 mm sieve).
Crushing strength — resistance to a gradually applied compressive load → ACV: load raised slowly to 40 t over 10 min; % fines passing 2.36 mm = crushing value.
Toughness — resistance to sudden impact/shock (moving loads, handling) → AIV: 15 blows of a 13.5–14 kg hammer; % fines passing 2.36 mm.
Durability — resistance to weathering (freeze–thaw, wet–dry) → soundness: 5 cycles of Na₂SO₄/MgSO₄ immersion + oven drying; % loss.
Shape — flaky if thickness < 0.6 × mean sieve size (thickness gauge); elongated if length > 1.8 × mean (length gauge, not used below 6.3 mm); excess breaks under rolling and hinders compaction.
Water absorption — pore-volume indicator: (wet − oven-dry)/oven-dry × 100 after 24-h soak; high absorption weakens bitumen adhesion.
Adhesion (stripping) — bitumen-film retention on aggregate under water (static immersion/stripping test; retained coating ≥ 95% desired) — siliceous aggregates strip, calcareous adhere better.
Polish (PSV) — friction retained after accelerated polishing (polishing wheel + pendulum tester) — wet skid resistance of the wearing course.
  • Gradation: sieve analysis (IS 2386 Pt I; sieves 80, 63, 50, 40, 25, 20, 12.5, 10, 6.3, 4.75 mm …); coarse/fine split at 4.75 mm. Gradation types: dense-graded (best interlock + binder economy — bituminous courses), well/continuous, gap-graded, and uniform/open-graded (drainage layers). DBM is dense-graded.
  • Fine aggregate: fineness modulus, silt content (field limit ≤ 5%; IS 383 is tighter for concrete sands), grading Zones I–IV with Zone II the standard for concrete.

B. Binding Materials & Their Tests

  • Penetration grades: 30/40 (hardest), 60/70, 80/100 (softer) — penetration falls as the bitumen hardens. Nepal uses the Indian viscosity-graded system VG-10/20/30/40 (VG-30 for most paving). Emulsions (anionic RS/MS/SS, cationic CRS/CMS) suit sprays and damp-weather surface dressing; cutbacks (RC/MC/SC) suit priming and patches.
  • Bitumen tests (each a favourite one-marker):
TestConditionsTypical value
Penetration25 °C, 100 g needle, 5 s; units 0.1 mmThe grade number itself (60/70 → 60–70 units)
Ductility27 °C, 5 cm/min (briquette)≥ 75 cm for 60/70
Softening pointRing & Ball45–55 °C (60/70 ≈ 47–52 °C); higher = less temperature-susceptible
ViscosityKinematic at 135 °C (VG system)Mixing ≈ 150–200 cSt; compaction ≈ 2000–3000 cSt (equiviscous range)
Flash pointPensky-Martens (closed cup)≥ 175 °C for paving bitumen (safety)
Specific gravity—≈ 1.01–1.03
OthersSolubility in trichloroethylene ≥ 99%; water content ≤ 0.2%; loss on heating ≤ 1%; RTFOT/TFOT aging (retained penetration)
  • Binder family: paving bitumen; cutbacks solvent-diluted (RC rapid — naphtha/gasoline, MC medium — kerosene, SC slow — low-volatile oil); emulsions water-based (RS/MS/SS, cationic versions) breaking by evaporation plus charge attraction; polymer-modified binders (PMB — SBS/SBR) for heavy traffic and hot intersections; coal tar (carcinogenic, rarely used today).
  • Cement in roads: OPC for concrete pavements and structures; rapid-hardening for repairs.

C. Design of Asphalt (Bituminous) Mixes

  • Mix types: bituminous concrete (BC/AC — dense-graded wearing course), dense bituminous macadam (DBM — binder course), bituminous macadam (BM — open-graded base). The Marshall method (IRC / Asphalt Institute MS-2) is the standard mix design.
  • Marshall procedure (step by step): (1) pick 4–5 binder contents around the expected optimum (≈ 4–7% in 0.5% steps), batch ≈ 1,200 g per specimen; (2) heat aggregate to 160–175 °C and bitumen to 150–160 °C; mix at the equiviscous temperature (≈ 150–160 °C) and compact hot (≈ 135–140 °C) into 101.6 mm dia × 63.5 mm high moulds — 50 blows/side (light traffic) or 75 (heavy) with the 4.54 kg hammer falling 457 mm; (3) cool, extrude, weigh in air/water for bulk specific gravity Gmb; (4) run the theoretical maximum gravity Gmm (Rice test) on loose mix for the volumetrics; (5) bath specimens in water at 60 °C for 30–40 min; (6) load diametrally at 50.8 mm/min (2 in/min) until failure — stability = corrected peak load (kN), flow = deformation at peak (mm, or flow units of 0.25 mm); (7) repeat per binder content and plot the classic curves — stability, flow, density, Vv, VMA, VFB vs binder %; (8) read the optimum binder content: binder giving 4% air voids, cross-checked against peak stability and 75–85% VFB (Asphalt Institute averages the three satisfactory values).
  • Marshall criteria (IRC/MS-2, heavy traffic): Stability ≥ 8 kN (course medium-traffic floor ≈ 340 kg ≈ 3.4 kN), Flow 2–4 mm (8–16 flow units of 0.25 mm), air voids Vv = 3–5% (design ≈ 4%), VMA ≥ 14%, VFB (VFA) 65–75% (deck's wide acceptance band 40–85%). Retained stability after 24-h immersion ≥ 75% guards moisture damage. The optimum binder content balances the criteria — usually at peak stability/density with Vv ≈ 4%.
  • Volumetrics: Vv = (Gt − Gb)/Gt × 100; VMA = Vv + effective binder volume; VFB = Vbe/VMA; Gmm (Rice) = theoretical maximum gravity; Gmb = bulk gravity.
  • Mix behaviour: more binder raises stability up to the optimum, then bleeding and rutting take over; too many air voids → ravelling and permeability. Skid resistance comes from surface texture; moisture damage is checked by retained stability ≥ 75% (tensile strength ratio TSR ≥ 80% where specified).

D. Evaluation of Subgrade Soil

  • CBR (California Bearing Ratio) — a penetration test compared against standard loads: 1370 kg at 2.5 mm and 2055 kg at 5.0 mm; CBR = (test load ÷ standard load) × 100, taking the greater of the two values — but if the 5 mm value is the greater, the test is repeated. Design uses the soaked CBR (4-day soak). Typical specification floors: sub-base (GSB) ≥ 25–30% (≥ 30% in the top 200 mm), WMM base ≥ 80%, capping layer ≥ 15%.
  • Plate load test — gives the modulus of subgrade reaction k (pressure ÷ deflection at 1.25 mm on a 75 cm dia plate, kg/cm³); DCP correlates field CBR quickly; E from correlations.
  • Other subgrade checks: Atterberg limits (LL ≤ 40, PI ≤ 6 for subgrade fines), Proctor compaction (OMC/MDD — field density 95–100% MDD), free swell index (expansive black-cotton soils need treatment or avoidance), permeability/drainage.
9.3 rapid numbers: CBR standard loads 1370 kg (2.5 mm), 2055 kg (5.0 mm); LA abrasion surface ≤ 30% (CC ≤ 16%); AIV ≤ 30%; Marshall blows 75 (heavy), test temp 60 °C; Vv 3–5%; VFB 65–75%; flash point ≥ 175 °C; ductility ≥ 75 cm; bitumen SG ≈ 1.02.

9.4 Traffic Engineering and Safety (ACiE0904)

A. Human & Vehicular Characteristics

  • Driver: perception-reaction time 1.5–2.5 s (design 2.5 s); vision (acuity, glare recovery, colour) and hearing matter; the PIEV total reaction time — Perception, Intellection, Emotion, Volition.
  • Vehicle: design vehicle 2.5 m wide, 4.75 m high; legal axle loads; braking and acceleration characteristics (acceleration sets overtaking); skid vs slip — skid = wheels locked and sliding, slip = wheels rotating slower than the vehicle moves.
  • Speed statistics: 98th percentile = design speed; 85th percentile = safe speed limit; 50th = median; 15th percentile = minimum speed limit; pace = the 10 km/h band holding the most vehicles.

B. Traffic Studies

  • Volume study: manual or automatic counts (pneumatic tube, induction loop) in PCU/hour/day; AADT built from sample counts with daily/seasonal expansion factors; origin–destination methods — roadside interview, licence-plate, tags, home interview — feed bypass and junction planning.
  • Speed study: radar, enoscope (mirror box), or the floating car — mean stream speed = 2d ÷ (twith + tagainst), times including waits, units consistent; journey speed includes stops, running speed does not.
  • Capacity and flow theory: capacity = max PCU/h/lane under given conditions; level of service A (free flow) → F (breakdown); a two-lane two-way road carries ≈ 2,800 PCU/h combined (design service volumes are lower, ≈ 1,500 PCU/h/dir in Indian conditions). Fundamental relation q = k·v (flow = density × speed); Greenshields' linear v–k model puts maximum flow at v/2 and k/2; jam density kj.
  • Parking study: accumulation, turnover and load factor; on-street types — parallel (least space), angle 30/45/60° (most convenient), perpendicular (most cars per kerb length); off-street lots and multi-level; parking index = occupied ÷ supply.
  • Accident study: rates per veh-km and per population, collision diagrams, spot maps, black spots (locations where counts significantly exceed the average — e.g. ≥ 5 accidents a year or top-ranked sites), causes ≈ 80–90% human; countermeasures are the 3E — engineering, enforcement, education.

C. Traffic Control Devices & Intersections

Fig 9.6 — Intersection types: rotary, signalized, channelized — reducing the 32 conflict points
  • Devices: signs — regulatory, warning, informatory; shapes are a language: octagon = STOP, triangle = give-way/warning, circle = prohibitory, rectangle = informatory. Markings (centre line, lane lines, stop line, zebra, chevron) in paint or thermoplastic; traffic islands (channelizing, pedestrian refuge); signals; and speed enforcers (rumble strips, humps, cameras).
  • At-grade intersections: uncontrolled, priority (stop/give-way), signalized, rotary (roundabout), channelized; grade separation (flyover; interchanges — cloverleaf, diamond, trumpet) removes conflicts entirely.
  • Rotary design: entry width, circulating width, central island 20–40 m dia in urban settings; weaving length L = 2.68·w·(1 + e/w), practically 30–60 m; capacity comes from the weaving section. Rotaries suit 4+ legs with moderate, balanced flows and few pedestrians — they break down beyond ≈ 3,000 PCU/h or with very unequal legs. Signals suit heavy or unbalanced flows with pedestrians.
  • Traffic signals (Webster): cycle C₀ = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y), where L = lost time per cycle (all-red + startups), y = q/s per phase and Y = Σy; green splits proportional to y. Amber = reaction + braking time (≈ 2–4 s); all-red clears the box. Saturation flow s ≈ 1,900 PCU/h/lane (base).
  • Pedestrian facilities: zebra crossings, footpaths (≥ 1.2–1.5 m; 1.8 m urban), FOB/subway by warrant (ped volume × traffic); walking speed 1.2 m/s sets crossing time, and signal timing must give pedestrians at least width/1.2 + startup seconds of green.
  • Night visibility and safety: headlight range, glare (dip rules), retroreflective signage/markings (glass beads), street lighting levels; safety = 3E plus vehicle inspection, road safety audits, black-spot treatment and speed management. Nepal follows IRC-style sign conventions.
9.4 must-knows: PIEV reaction 1.5–2.5 s (design 2.5); speed percentiles — design 98th, safe limit 85th, minimum 15th; PCU: car 1, bus/truck 3, motorcycle 0.5–0.75; q = k·v, Greenshields max flow at v/2 & k/2; two-lane two-way ≈ 2,800 PCU/h; LOS A (free) → F (breakdown); floating-car mean speed = 2d/(t_with + t_against); skid = wheels locked, slip = rotating slower; accidents 80–90% human, countermeasures = 3E; signs: octagon = stop, triangle = give-way, circle = prohibitory, rectangle = informatory; 4-leg junction = 32 conflicts (16 crossing + 8 merging + 8 diverging); rotary weaving L = 2.68w(1 + e/w) ≈ 30–60 m, breaks down ≈ 3,000 PCU/h; Webster C₀ = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y), saturation flow ≈ 1,900 PCU/h/lane; pedestrian walking speed 1.2 m/s.

9.5 Road Pavement (ACiE0905)

A. Pavement Types

Fig 9.7 — Flexible (layered, grain-to-grain) vs rigid (slab action) pavement cross-sections
  • Flexible (bituminous/gravel): a layer system distributing load grain-to-grain; it deflects under load, is temperature- and moisture-sensitive, and can be built stage by stage; the ESWL concept converts dual wheels to an equivalent single wheel. Rigid (cement concrete slab): slab/beam action spreads load over a large area; designed with the modulus of subgrade reaction k; long life, high first cost. Composite/semi-rigid sits between.
  • Flexible layers (top down): wearing course (BC) → binder course (DBM) → base (WMM/crushed stone) → sub-base (GSB) → subgrade — spreading load, draining, smoothing.
  • Rigid components: slab 200–350 mm thick over a granular or cement-treated base; joints: expansion joints (with dowel bars transferring load), contraction joints (grooved, may be dowelled, ≈ 4.5 m spacing), warping joints, and longitudinal joints held by tie bars. Classic MCQ: dowels transfer load across transverse joints; tie bars hold longitudinal joint faces together.
Fig 9.8 — Rigid-pavement joints: dowels across transverse joints, tie bars along longitudinal joints

B. Design Methods

  • Flexible — IRC 37 / DoR guideline: design by subgrade CBR + design traffic in msa; cumulative traffic N = 365 × A × [(1+r)ⁿ − 1]/r × D × F (A = initial commercial ADT, r = growth, n = design life 10–15 yr, D = lane distribution, F = vehicle damage factor).
  • Vehicle Damage Factor: the fourth power law — damage ∝ (P/Pstd)⁴ against the 8.16 t (≈ 80 kN) standard axle; a 1.5× overloaded axle does ≈ 5× the damage.
  • Flexible design inputs: effective subgrade CBR (representative/characteristic value), layer CBRs, traffic in msa; failure criteria — subgrade rutting strain and bituminous fatigue cracking; IRC 37-2018 is mechanistic-empirical (IITPAVE), with catalog thickness tables for lower traffic.
  • Rigid — IRC 58: slab thickness from flexural stress under wheel load (edge/corner cases) plus temperature stresses. Modulus of rupture fcr = 0.7√fck ≈ 4.5 MPa for M40. Radius of relative stiffness l = [Eh³/(12k(1−μ²))]^¼; Westergaard analysis for corner/edge/interior loading; warping stresses by Bradbury; friction stress σ = W·L·f/2 sets the contraction-joint spacing (≈ 4.5 m).
  • Stress summary: wheel-load stress is critical at the edge (corner worst for thin slabs); warping peaks interior/edge; the critical combination is load + warping (day — bottom fibre at interior/edge; night — top).
  • Design drivers: wheel load and contact pressure (tyre pressure ≈ 0.56–0.7 MPa), load repetitions (ESALs), ESWL (Boyd's dual-wheel formula), temperature (rigid warping; flexible stiffness loss), moisture (soaked subgrade design), and subgrade support (k for rigid, CBR for flexible).

C. Pavement Failures (quick list — MCQ)

Fig 9.9 — Pavement distress map: fatigue cracking, rutting, pothole, bleeding — plus rigid-slab failures
  • Flexible: alligator (fatigue) cracking, rutting, potholes, ravelling, bleeding, corrugations, depressions, edge cracking, reflection cracking over underlying joints.
  • Rigid: structural cracking (corner/edge), faulting (step at joints), pumping (subgrade slurry ejected at joints), scaling, spalling, D-cracking, blowups.
Fig 9.10 — Traffic sign shapes: octagon stop, circle prohibitory, inverted triangle give-way, triangle warning, rectangle informatory
9.5 rapid numbers: standard axle 8.16 t (≈ 80 kN); fourth-power law; VDF & lane distribution D ≈ 0.75 (two-lane single carriageway); design life flexible 10–15 yr, rigid 20–30 yr; dowels transverse (load transfer), tie bars longitudinal (hold faces); slab M40, fcr ≈ 4.5 MPa; contraction joints ≈ 4.5 m; expansion joints only every 30–60 m (structures).

9.6 Road Construction & Maintenance (ACiE0906)

A. Construction Activities & Equipment

  • Plant: excavators, dozers (clearing/earthmoving), graders (shaping), scrapers, rollers — smooth-wheel (finishing), pneumatic (base), vibratory (granular), sheepsfoot (clay) — water tankers, bitumen pressure distributors, hot-mix plants (batch/drum), paver finishers, wet-mix (WMM) plants, and crushers (jaw primary, cone/roll secondary, impact for cubical shape).
  • Bituminous temperatures (BC/DBM): aggregate heated 160–175 °C, bitumen 150–160 °C, mixing ≈ 150–160 °C, laying 120–150 °C, and compaction completed while the mat is still above ≈ 90–100 °C.
  • Coats between layers: tack coat — RS/CRS emulsion ≈ 0.25–0.3 kg/m² residual between bituminous layers (the 9.6 deck quotes the spray rate as 4.9–9.8 kg/10 m² ≈ 0.5–1.0 kg/m² — the same coat weighed wet); prime coat — MC cutback or slow-setting emulsion ≈ 0.9–1.8 kg/m² penetrating a granular base; seal coat — premix or liquid seal protecting the surface.

B. Subgrade Preparation & Compaction

  • Subgrade: strip topsoil 15–20 cm; fill in 150–200 mm compacted layers at OMC ± 2%; 95–100% MDD (modified Proctor for heavily trafficked roads); proof-roll to verify. Field control: sand-replacement or core-cutter densities, speedy/oven moisture — acceptance > 95% MDD.
  • Stabilization: mechanical (gradation blending), chemical — lime 2–5% for clays (cuts PI and swell), cement 2–6% for granular soils (adds strength) — flyash/lime-flyash, and geosynthetics (geotextile separation, geogrid reinforcement); WMM as granular stabilization.

C. Construction of Pavement Layers

  • GSB: 200 mm compacted layers, CBR ≥ 30% in the top 200 mm, camber maintained. WMM base: plant-mixed, paver-laid, 100–200 mm layers, ≥ 98–100% MDD. Penetration macadam: hand-packed 75 mm aggregate, compacted, hot bitumen penetrated from top and grit-sealed — the no-plant base still seen on Nepal's rural roads. Bituminous macadam: premixed open-graded binder course. PCC pavement: fixed-form or slip-form paver, dowels/tie bars fixed, joints sawed within 3–6 h (timing critical), broom/tining texture, curing 14–28 days.
  • Asphalt layer sequence: prepare and tack the base → paver lays at a loose factor ≈ 1.2 → breakdown rolling (pneumatic/vibratory) → intermediate → finish rolling (smooth-wheel), passes longitudinal from the edges inward on the crown → longitudinal joints hot-lapped ≈ 150 mm → acceptance: core density ≥ 98% of lab Marshall density (≈ 92–97% of Gmm), plus thickness, level and ride (3 m straightedge).

D. Maintenance, Repair & Rehabilitation

  • Types: routine (daily/seasonal — potholes, drains, verge), periodic (every 4–6 yr — reseal/overlay), special (disaster repairs), rehabilitation (structural overlays, recycling) and reconstruction.
  • Pothole repair: square-cut edges, prime, premix patch, compact, edge-seal — cold-mix throwing is temporary only. Also: edge repair, rut filling, crack sealing before monsoon, surface dressing (single/double chip seal — ≈ 1.3–1.6 kg/m² hot bitumen + 8–14 kg/m² chippings per coat), 50 mm BC overlays, and hot/cold in-place recycling.
  • Pavement management: condition surveys — roughness by bump integrator (BI < 1500 mm/km good; 1500–2500 fair; > 2500 rough; IRI ≈ BI/60–80), PCI, distress mapping, remaining life; prioritise by NPV/rank. DoR Nepal runs its Road Maintenance System (RMS) with periodic and performance-based contracts.
  • Nepal context: the monsoon damage cycle, landslide clearance, regravelling every 3–5 yr, Road Maintenance Groups (RMG/RMGC) on length-person contracts, emergency flood-restoration programmes, and the chronic maintenance funding gap.
9.6 must-knows: bituminous temperatures — aggregate 160–175 °C, bitumen 150–160 °C, lay 120–150 °C, compact above 90–100 °C; tack coat 0.25–0.3 kg/m² between bituminous layers, prime coat 0.9–1.8 kg/m² on granular base, seal coat protects the surface; subgrade in 150–200 mm layers at 95–100% MDD; lime 2–5% for clays, cement 2–6% for granular soils; GSB 200 mm layers (CBR ≥ 30% top 200 mm), WMM ≥ 98–100% MDD; paver loose factor ≈ 1.2, rolling edges inward, core density ≥ 98% of lab Marshall; pothole repair = square-cut → prime → premix → compact → edge-seal; roughness BI < 1500 mm/km good (IRI ≈ BI/60–80); maintenance classes routine / periodic (4–6 yr reseal) / special / rehabilitation; joints sawed within 3–6 h of PCC paving.

Deeper Concept Discussions (Chapter 9)

Why superelevation and transition curves are designed this way (logic, not formula cramming)

  • Superelevation tilts the pavement so part of the centripetal force comes from the road's tilt (the weight component) instead of pure friction — safer on wet days. It is capped at 7% because a slow, heavily-laden vehicle would slide sideways toward the centre on steep crossfall.
  • The mixed-traffic compromise (e = V²/225R) uses 75% of design speed with zero friction, so cyclists and rickshaws feel no side thrust at normal speeds; fast vehicles take up the remainder within the safe friction limit.
  • Transition (spiral): curvature and superelevation change gradually — comfort (rate of change of centripetal acceleration C ≈ 0.5–0.8 m/s³), aesthetics (the curve matches the steering path), and no sudden crossfall "break" at the tangent point.

Flexible vs rigid design philosophy comparison

AspectFlexibleRigid
Load transferLayer system (grain contact), stress coneSlab beam/plate action (wide spread)
Design basisSubgrade CBR + traffic (msa); fatigue & ruttingFlexural stress (load + temperature), k
Temperature roleStiffness/binder behaviourWarping + friction stresses (joints)
JointsNoneTransverse/longitudinal + dowels/ties
Life & staging10–15 yr, stage construction easy20–30 yr, hard to stage
Initial costLowerHigher

Webster's signal worked micro-example

  • Two phases: q₁ = 800, q₂ = 400 PCU/h; s = 1800 each → y₁ = 0.444, y₂ = 0.222, Y = 0.667; L = 12 s → C₀ = (1.5×12 + 5)/(1 − 0.667) ≈ 69 s → adopt 70 s; green split ∝ y: g₁ = (0.444/0.667)×(70−12) ≈ 39 s, g₂ ≈ 19 s.

Rotary vs signal decision logic

  • Rotary: no signal hardware, smooth for balanced multi-leg flows — but needs land and weaving discipline; breaks down above ≈ 3,000 PCU/h or with heavy pedestrians. Signal: handles heavy/unbalanced flows and pedestrians — but stops traffic (delay, fuel).
  • Weaving length L = 2.68w(1 + e/w) with 30–60 m practical; island dia ≈ 25–40 m standard urban, ≈ 1.3–1.5× the circulating width for mini-roundabouts.

20 More Rapid Numericals (answers inline)

  • SSD: V = 50, t = 2.5, f = 0.35: 0.278×50×2.5 = 34.8 + 2500/(254×0.35) = 28.1 → ≈ 63 m.
  • Radius: V = 60, e = 0.07, f = 0.15: R = 3600/(127×0.22) = 129 m.
  • Mixed-traffic e: V = 60, R = 160: e = 3600/(225×160) = 0.10 → capped at 0.07; friction carries the rest.
  • Transition length: V = 80, R = 250, C = 80/(75+80) = 0.516: Ls = 0.0215×80³/(0.516×250) = 85 m.
  • Extra widening: 2 lanes, R = 100, V = 50: We = 2×6.1²/(2×100) + 50/(9.5×10) = 0.372 + 0.526 = 0.9 m.
  • Grade compensation: R = 100: (30+100)/100 = 1.3%, but the cap 75/R = 0.75% governs → 0.75%.
  • Crest curve: N = 0.03 (a 3% deviation), SSD = 60 m: L = 0.03×3600/4.4 = 24.5 m — N enters as a decimal, so writing N = 3 would inflate the answer 100×.
  • Valley curve: N = 0.04 (4% deviation — N is dimensionless!), S = 60: L = 0.04×3600/(1.5+0.035×60) = 144/3.6 = 40 m.
  • CBR: load 1100 kg at 2.5 mm: CBR = 1100/1370 = 80%.
  • ESAL: axle 12.2 t vs 8.16 std: (12.2/8.16)⁴ ≈ 5.0 — overloading multiplies damage 5×.
  • Traffic: A = 800 CV/day, r = 6%, n = 15 yr: N = 365×800×((1.06)¹⁵−1)/0.06 = 365×800×23.28 ≈ 6.8 msa (before D and F).
  • Webster: as above → C₀ ≈ 69–70 s.
  • Marshall check: Vv = (2.51−2.40)/2.51 = 4.4% ✓ (3–5 band).
  • Rotary weaving: w = 10, e = 10: L = 2.68×10×(1+1) = 53.6 m (within 30–60 ✓).
  • Amber time: V = 50 km/h, a = 3.3 m/s²: 1 + 13.9/6.6 ≈ 3.1 s.
  • Friction stress in slab: γ = 24 kN/m³, L = 4.5 m, f = 1.5: σ = 24×4.5×1.5/2 = 81 kPa.
  • Radius of relative stiffness: l rises with h³ — doubling slab thickness scales l by 2^(3/4) ≈ 1.68×.
  • Chip seal binder: single surface dressing ≈ 1.4 kg/m² hot bitumen + chips ≈ 8–14 kg/m².
  • Compaction: a 200 mm layer at 98% of MDD 2.0 g/cc needs field dry density 1.96 g/cc.
  • Hill climb check: ruling gradient 5% over a 60 m rise needs 1200 m < the 2000 m available — OK; at the 8% limiting grade only 750 m is needed; resisting length = total rise + fall work along the profile.

Highway Cross-Section Design Walkthrough (Two-Lane NH in Plain Terrain)

  • Inputs: NH, plain terrain, design speed 100 km/h, AADT 12,000 PCU.
  • Cross-section: carriageway 7.0 m (2×3.5), paved shoulders 2×1.5 m, formation ≈ 10–12 m; ROW 45 m (IRC); camber 2% bituminous → 70 mm crown rise on the 3.5 m half-width; fill slopes 1H:2V for a 3 m embankment; median barrier provided where traffic demands.
  • Horizontal geometry: minimum radius R = 100²/(127×0.22) = 358 m; transition Ls = 0.0215×100³/(0.457×358) ≈ 130 m with C = 80/175 = 0.457; superelevation attained with 2/3 on the straight approach and 1/3 on the curve (IRC), rotating about the centre line.
  • Vertical: ruling gradient 3.3%; crest curve for N = 0.03 with SSD ≈ 180 m at 100 km/h → L = 0.03×180²/4.4 ≈ 221 m; flat summit curves (K > 51) need a drainage check — keep ≥ 0.3–0.5% grade in sags.
  • Pavement (IRC 37 style): growth 6%, 20 yr → N ≈ 30+ msa after D and VDF; subgrade CBR 8% → granular thickness ≈ 650–700 mm (GSB 200 + WMM 250) with DBM 140 mm + BC 40–50 mm per the catalog.
  • Drainage: median drains; shoulders 0.5% steeper than the carriageway; kerb and gutter in built-up stretches; sub-surface drainage with a capillary cut-off ≥ 0.5–1.0 m above the groundwater level.

Rigid Pavement Design Walkthrough (IRC 58 Logic)

  • Inputs: M40 concrete (fcr = 0.7√40 ≈ 4.5 MPa), E = 3×10⁴ MPa, μ = 0.15, k = 6 kg/cm³ (≈ 60 MN/m³), slab trial h = 300 mm, temperature differential per zone (≈ 17 °C).
  • Radius of relative stiffness: l = [Eh³/(12k(1−μ²))]^¼ ≈ 800–900 mm for a 300 mm slab.
  • Stresses: edge wheel-load stress (Westergaard) ≈ 1.5–2.0 MPa for the standard axle; warping (Bradbury, edge) ≈ 0.8–1.2 MPa; friction σ = 24×4.5×1.5/2 = 81 kPa (small).
  • Check: combined load + day-warping (edge case) ≤ fcr/SF with SF ≈ 1.5; if overstressed, increase h (the h³ lever is strong) or improve k with a treated base.
  • Joints: contraction every 4.5 m (plain, dowelled); expansion only at structures or ~30–60 m on plain runs; longitudinal at the lane line with tie bars 12 mm @ 750–900 mm; dowels 32–38 mm × 500 mm @ 300 mm centres — greased on one half to allow slip (tie bars are the bonded ones).
  • Dowel design: check bearing on concrete, shear and moment — standard tables handle it.

Traffic Study Field Notes (how each study is actually done)

  • Volume: 7-day counts (weekend included), classified manual tallies, automatic counters for continuous data; expand ADT → AADT with monthly/weekday factors; apply the PCU table.
  • Speed: spot-speed sample ≥ 50 vehicles per point; radar gun angled ≤ 20°; enoscope for budget studies; time-stamp plate matching at two points for journey speed.
  • O&D: roadside interview at a 5–10% sample with queue management; licence-plate pairing over 24 h; postcard method (historic); tags — outputs: desire lines, bypass justification, diversion effects.
  • Parking: hourly accumulation patrols, in–out surveys; turnover = vehicles per space per day; parking index > 85% signals capacity strain.
  • Accident: police FIR mapping plus hospital data (correct for under-reporting); collision diagram per intersection; black-spot significance by Poisson test; before–after studies with control sites (empirical Bayes is the modern standard).

Bitumen & Binder Selection Logic (why grades differ)

  • Penetration grade: the number is the penetration at 25 °C (100 g, 5 s, 0.1 mm). Hot climate/heavy traffic → harder (30/40, VG-30/40); cold/light traffic → softer (80/100, VG-10) — balancing rutting (want stiffness) against cracking (want flexibility).
  • VG system (IS 73:2013): viscosity-graded at 60 °C — VG-10 for spraying/cold climates, VG-20 for recycling and hot regions, VG-30 the general paving grade (replaces 60/70), VG-40 for heavy traffic and hot climates. Nepal imports the Indian grades.
  • Emulsions (RS/MS/SS and cationic CRS/CMS/CSS): water-based, usable damp, no heating; RS for tack coats (fast set), MS for patches/premix, SS for prime/slurry seals — they break by water evaporation plus attraction to the aggregate charge.
  • Cutbacks (RC/MC/SC): solvent-fluxed — MC-30/MC-70 common primes, RC for fast repairs; solvents evaporate leaving the bitumen film; flammability is why flash-point rules exist.
  • Modified binders (PMB): SBS/SBR/EVA polymers — softening point ≥ 60 °C, better elasticity, for heavy traffic and hot intersections; CRMB (crumb rubber) is used in India; cost 1.3–1.8× but longer life.

Aggregate Production & Quality Control Flow

  • Quarry → primary jaw crusher (150–200 mm feed → 40–75 mm) → secondary cone/roll (→ ~20 mm) → tertiary/impact for cubical shape → vibrating screens to stockpiles (20, 13.2, 6.7 mm bins); grading controlled by feeder ratios; dust < 0.075 mm washed or air-separated; shape matters — roll crushers tend to flaky particles; stockpiles kept separated, uncontaminated and tested per lot.
  • WMM: crusher-run blended with fines and water at the plant, CBR ≥ 80–100, compacted 98%+ — the modern base standard; CRS and WMM gradings per MoRTH/IRC with the Nepal DoR Standard Specifications running parallel.

Nepal Road Construction Practice Notes

  • DoR Standard Specifications (IRC/MoRTH-based) + Nepal Road Standard 2070; source approvals (quarry and borrow permits, EPA compliance, explosive licences); bituminous works scheduled in the dry season (Oct–May); labour-based vs equipment-based — LRN uses LBT (DoLIDAR manuals), SRN is equipment-based.
  • Stage construction: earthen → gravel → bitumen as traffic grows — the flexible pavement's advantage; between stages evaluate by Benkelman Beam deflection (overlay design per IRC 81, deflections corrected for temperature and moisture).
  • Contractor QC: densities (cores/sand cone), thickness (cores), level, ride (bump integrator — spec commonly BI ≤ 2000 mm/km), bitumen extraction (binder ± 0.3%), gradation — acceptance per lot on statistical percent-defective limits.

Geometric Design of Junctions & Access (brief but examinable)

  • Principles: minimise conflict points (crossing → merging → diverging, in descending severity); channelization islands guide paths; corner radii by design vehicle (cars 6–9 m, trucks 9–12 m); sight triangles (approach and departure — ISD at uncontrolled junctions); grade-separate when entering volumes and pedestrian conflicts exceed what a rotary/signal can serve.
  • Channelized turns: speed-change lanes (acceleration/deceleration lengths and tapers by speed); lane balance Nout = Nin + 1; auxiliary lanes at major accesses (50–100 m pocket + taper).
  • Access management: control direct access on NH (service roads); median openings ≈ 250–500 m on urban arterials; consolidate driveways; corner clearances — access control cuts accidents ~30–50%.

Pavement Surface Characteristics (texture, skid, roughness, unevenness)

  • Skid resistance: wet friction by pendulum skid tester — SRV ≥ 55 desirable (50–60 band) — and sideways-force coefficient; governed by aggregate PSV plus macrotexture (sand-patch texture depth ≥ 0.55 mm on wearing courses); polishing lowers it — remedy with grit retexturing or overlay.
  • Unevenness: bump integrator mm/km — < 1500 good, 1500–2500 fair, > 2500 rough; IRI ≈ BI/60–80; roughness drives speed, fuel and comfort, and is the ride criterion in DoR contracts (BI ≤ 2000 mm/km typical spec).
  • Night visibility: bright vs dark surfaces, wet-night glare; road studs (cat's eyes) and delineators on curves; rut depth by straightedge — > 20 mm triggers treatment.
  • Structural deflection: Benkelman Beam on the wheel path under the 8,170 kg standard axle — mean rebound deflection corrected for temperature and moisture; corrected BBD above the allowable (≈ 1.0–1.5 mm by traffic) → overlay per IRC 81; the FWD back-calculates layer moduli.

More Rapid Numericals (another 10, answers inline)

  • Min radius at V = 100 (e = 0.07, f = 0.15): R = 10000/(127×0.22) = 358 m.
  • Transition for V = 100, R = 400, C = 80/175 = 0.457: Ls = 0.0215×10⁶/(0.457×400) = 117.6 → 120 m.
  • OSD components: Vb = 30 km/h; A = 0.2×30 + 6 = 12 m; T = √(14.4×12/0.92) = 13.7 s; d₁ = 0.278×30×2 = 16.7 m; d₂ = 0.278×30×13.7 + 2×12 = 138.3 m; d₃ = 0.278×30×13.7 = 114.3 m (oncoming at V = 30) → OSD ≈ 269 m.
  • Setback: R = 150, d = 8 m, sight line s = SSD 60 m: β = 180×60/(π×150) = 22.9°; m = 150 − (150−8)cos(11.45°) = 10.8 m — a large cut-slope setback.
  • CBR check: 2.5 mm reads 1250 kg (91%), 5 mm reads 1900 kg (92.8%) — the 5 mm value is greater → retest; if confirmed, the 2.5 mm value governs the design CBR.
  • Marshall: stability 12 kN, flow 3.5 mm, Vv 4.2%, VFB 70 — all pass (≥ 8 kN, 2–4 mm, 3–5%, 65–75%).
  • Density: core 2.33 g/cc vs Gmm 2.45 → %Gmm = 95.1% ✓ (92–97 acceptance).
  • Overlay by BBD: mean corrected 1.8 mm > the ≈ 1.0–1.5 mm allowable → overlay 50–75 mm BC (IRC 81 chart by deflection and traffic).
  • Signal y-ratio: q = 1200 PCU/h, s = 1900×2 = 3800 (2 lanes): y = 0.316.
  • Parking: 100 m kerb — parallel (5.7 m per car incl. gap) ≈ 17 cars; perpendicular (2.5 m + manoeuvre ≈ 3 m) ≈ 33 cars — double the density.

Worked Walkthrough: Design Traffic Computation (IRC Flexible Design)

  • Given: two-lane single-carriageway NH; initial commercial ADT = 1,200 CVPD; growth 6%/yr; construction 2 yr; design life 15 yr after completion; VDF = 3.5; D = 0.75.
  • Step 1 — traffic at completion: A = 1200 × (1.06)² ≈ 1,348 CVPD.
  • Step 2 — repetitions: N = 365 × 1348 × [(1.06)¹⁵ − 1]/0.06 = 365×1348×23.28 ≈ 11.46 msa (unadjusted).
  • Step 3 — adjust: Ndesign = 11.46 × 0.75 × 3.5 ≈ 30 msa → pick the IRC 37 catalog row for 30 msa at CBR 8% (GSB 200 + WMM 250 + DBM ≈ 140 + BC 40–50 mm — illustrative; the exam tests Steps 2–3 and reading the catalog).
  • Common traps: forgetting the (1+r)² growth to completion; using n measured before completion; swapping D and VDF; the msa definition (million standard axles of 8.16 t).

Worked Walkthrough: SSD + OSD Application on Two-Lane Hill Section

  • Given: V = 40 km/h hill road, f = 0.37, t = 2.5 s.
  • SSD = 0.278×40×2.5 + 40²/(254×0.37) = 27.8 + 17.0 = 44.8 → 45 m (round up; used for curve setbacks and vertical curves).
  • Overtaking is rarely warranted on hill single lanes — provide intermediate sight distance = 2×SSD = 90 m where possible; where even ISD fails, one-way traffic regulation or passing bays every 300–500 m (the rural single-lane standard) takes over.
  • Curve setback check: R = 40 m, cut face at d = 10 m: β = 180×45/(π×40) = 64.5° → m = 40 − (40−10)cos(32.2°) = 14.6 m — impossible in the cut → bench the cut wider, reduce speed, add a mirror, or realign; this is why hill hairpins carry warning signs and speed tables.

Intersections & Grade Separation Details

  • Conflict points: a 4-leg intersection has 32 — 16 crossing + 8 merging + 8 diverging; a 3-leg (T) junction has 9 — 3 crossing + 3 merging + 3 diverging. Signals or channelization eliminate/relocate most; a rotary reduces them to weaving conflicts. Memorize 32 and 9!
  • Interchanges: cloverleaf (loop ramps all directions — land-hungry, weaving between loops is its weakness; collector–distributor roads fix it), diamond (simplest, ramp terminals signalized on the crossroad — most common), trumpet (3-leg T), directional/semi-directional (highest capacity, costliest — expressway junctions).
  • Ramp design: 40–60 km/h, curvature to match, grades ≤ 4–5% (flatter uphill for trucks); acceleration lanes 200–300 m to merge into 100 km/h mainline traffic.
  • Rotary checks (IRC): weaving length L, weaving ratio, island size — capacity collapses when the weaving ratio exceeds 1 or L < 30 m; the exam tests the L formula and island sizing, not edition-specific capacity constants.

Road Safety Audit & Safety Management (modern syllabus touch)

  • Road Safety Audit (RSA): an independent, formal check at each stage (feasibility → detailed design → pre-opening → existing road) by auditors not involved in the design; findings go to the designer for a formal response.
  • Safe System approach: humans err — the system (road + vehicle + speed + user + post-crash care) must absorb the error: forgiving roadsides (clear zones, breakable poles), speed matched to environment (≈ 90% pedestrian survival at 30 km/h impact vs < 10% at 70 km/h), and separation of vulnerable users.
  • Common audit findings: inadequate curve signing/delineation, insufficient intersection sight distance, roadside hazards (trees, open drains), missing pedestrian facilities, speed limits mismatched to environment, poor work-zone traffic management.
  • Work-zone safety: advance signage, taper lengths (merge tapers L = W·S²/155 with W in m, S in km/h), cones, flaggers and night lamps — Nepali contracts increasingly require traffic-management plans.
  • Nepal institutionally: the Nepal Road Safety Council (under MoPIT) leads; DoR runs black-spot programmes; helmet/seatbelt laws and vehicle inspection are enforced with an ageing fleet; first-responder gaps persist on hill highways.

Last-Mile Memory Hooks (Chapter 9)

  • Percentile ladder: 98% design speed, 85% speed limit, 15% minimum — "design high, limit one notch lower, minimum at the floor".
  • Dowels vs tie bars: Dowels = Diesel (drive loads across transverse joints); Tie = Tight (hold longitudinal faces together).
  • N-dimensionless trap: L = NS²/4.4 uses N as a decimal — a 4% grade deviation is N = 0.04, NOT 4. The #1 numerical blunder.
  • Tack vs prime: Tack = Thin (between bituminous layers); Prime = Penetrates (granular base).
  • IRC magic numbers: e_max 7%, f 0.15 (design)/0.35 (SSD), V²/225R, 0.0215V³/CR, t = 2.5 s, crest 4.4, valley (1.5+0.035S), (30+R)/R capped at 75/R.
  • Fourth-power law story: overload a truck 20% → damage ×2; 50% → ×5 — axle-load control is the cheapest road investment.
  • Sign shapes: octagon stop, triangle yield/warning, circle prohibitory, rectangle informatory — universal shape language.
  • Rotary formula trio: L = 2.68w(1+e/w), island 25–40 m urban, capacity ceiling ≈ 3,000 PCU/h — a question touches one of the three.
  • Conflict-point counts: 4-leg = 32 (16+8+8); 3-leg = 9 (3+3+3) — the most quotable intersection numbers.
  • Survival-speed insight: pedestrian hit at 30 km/h ≈ 90% survival; at 70 ≈ 10% — urban speed management is life-safety, not convenience.

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (9.1–9.6)

Planning, Alignment & Geometric Design (9.1–9.2) — Course Tables

Class I1201008060

  • Camber by surface: cement concrete 1.5–2%, bituminous 2–2.5%, gravel/WBM 3–4%, earthen 4–5%.
  • Lane widths: single lane 3.75 m (Nepal practice 3.5 m carriageway + shoulders); multiple lanes n × 3.5 m. Minimum shoulder widths by class: 3.75 / 2.5 / 2.0 / 1.5 m (Class I–IV). Right of way: highway 50 m, feeder 30 m, district 20 m (Nepal hierarchy).
  • Design vehicle: max width 2.5 m, height 4.75 m, length 18 m; maximum legal single axle load ≈ 10.2 t (≈ 100 kN); the design standard axle is 8.16 t (≈ 80 kN, dual wheels).
  • Capacity C (veh/h) = 1000V/S (V km/h, S average space headway m — the 1000 is the km/h → m/h conversion); level of service A–F; PCU values — car 1, bus/truck 3, cycle 0.5, motorcycle 0.75.
  • Alignment: obligatory controls — positive (industrial area, tourist spot, hill pass — must connect) and negative (marshy, waterlogged, heritage, defence zones — must avoid); evaluate alternates on length, earthwork, drainage, land cost.
  • SSD = vt + v²/2gf (v m/s; t = 2.5 s; f ≈ 0.35–0.4); OSD = Vb·t + Vb·T + 2s + V·T; minimum overtaking zone = 3×OSD, desirable = 5×OSD; intermediate sight distance = 2×SSD; valley-curve headlight sight distance = night SSD.
  • Extra widening: We = nl²/2R (mechanical) + V/(9.5√R) (psychological), l = 6.1 m; superelevation e = V²/225R capped at 7%; gradient plains ≈ 1 in 30 (3.3%); DoR maximum gradients by design speed (4–12%) with 0.5% minimum for drainage; grade compensation = (30+R)/R %, max 75/R %.

Highway Materials (9.3) — Course Limits (with NEC-asked questions)

  • Aggregate sizes: coarse — passing 80 mm, retained 4.75 mm; fine — passing 4.75 mm, retained 0.075 mm.
  • Los Angeles abrasion (most popular; abraded material sieved on 1.7 mm): ≤ 16% for cement concrete, ≤ 30% bituminous surface course, ≤ 50% bituminous base.
  • Aggregate crushing value = (W₂/W₁)×100 under gradual load: ≤ 30% surface, ≤ 45% base. Aggregate impact value (13.5–14 kg hammer, 380 mm fall, 15 blows): ≤ 30% surface, ≤ 45% base.
  • Flakiness index = % by weight with least dimension < 0.6 × mean size (thickness gauge); elongation index = % with length > 1.8 × mean (length gauge) — not applicable below 6.3 mm; angularity number measures voids above 33% (rounded = 0).
  • Cutbacks: Rapid Curing = bitumen + naphtha/gasoline; Medium Curing = bitumen + kerosene (NEC asked); Slow Curing = bitumen + low-volatile oil. Emulsion = bitumen + water + emulsifier (cationic RS/MS/SS); tar RT-1 to RT-5, RT-1 lowest viscosity (NEC asked); coal tar superior to wood tar for roads.
  • Bitumen tests: penetration — 100 g needle, 5 s, 25 °C, in 0.1 mm units (80/100 soft; 60/70 hot climates); ductility — briquette 27 °C, 5 cm/min, min 75 cm; softening point — Ring & Ball (≈ 35–70 °C by grade); viscosity — 10 mm orifice at 25/40 °C; flash & fire point (Pensky-Martens); loss on heating < 1%.
  • Marshall mix design: strength = Marshall Stability (max load at 60 °C — NEC asked, Mangsir 2080); flexibility = flow value (mm at max load); OBC from stability/density/air-voids curves (air voids 3–5%, VMA, VFB 65–75%); specimens 101.6 mm × 63.5 mm, 50 blows/side (75 heavy).
  • Subgrade evaluation: CBR (standard loads 1370 kg at 2.5 mm, 2055 kg at 5 mm — use the 5 mm value only if greater); Group Index GI = 0.2a + 0.005ac + 0.01bd — GI 0–20; DoR subgrade compaction 95–100% MDD.

Traffic Engineering & Safety (9.4) — Course Formulas

  • Studies: volume (manual/mechanical counters, PCU/hour/day), speed (spot — radar, enoscope; journey speed), origin-destination (roadside interview, licence-plate, tag-on-vehicle), parking, accident, flow (fundamental diagram).
  • Speed statistics: 85th percentile = safe speed limit; 98th = design speed; 15th = minimum speed limit; time-mean vs space-mean speed.
  • Traffic signals: trial-cycle method G = 2.5n·C/900 (n phases); Webster optimum C₀ = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y) [course form C = (1.5L + S)/(1 − Y)]; green time G = (y/Y)(C − L); y = q/s; Y = Σy; lost time L per phase; all-red clearance.
  • Road lighting: spacing = (lamp lumen × CoU × MF)/(average lux × road width); mounting heights 15 ft to 100+ ft; staggered/opposite/median layouts.
  • Load equivalence: E = (L/Ls)⁴ fourth-power law — one 10.2 t axle ≈ 2.4× the 8.16 t standard axle's damage; cumulative standard axles = 365 × A × ((1+r)ⁿ − 1)/r.
  • Intersections: at-grade (uncontrolled, rotary, signalized) vs grade-separated (overpass, interchange); rotary design — entry width, weaving width, radii by 40/30/20 km/h; channelization islands; traffic calming; night visibility factors (glare, headlight beam, retroreflective signage/markings, pavement colour); accident study — collision diagrams, black spots, before-and-after studies.

Road Pavement (9.5) — Course Facts

  • Flexible (bituminous): load grain-to-grain through layers — surface, binder, base, sub-base, subgrade; deflects under load; designed by CBR (IRC 37 / DoR guideline); failure = rutting, fatigue cracking, potholes.
  • Rigid (CC): slab action by beam/plate flexure (Westergaard), modulus of subgrade reaction k; failure by cracking, faulting, pumping; temperature stresses: warping (day/night gradient — Bradbury) and friction in long slabs (σ = WLf/2 — sets contraction-joint spacing); dowel bars transfer load, tie bars hold lane continuity.
  • DoR Nepal guideline: traffic classes (AADT/ESA), design CBR, standard axle 8.16 t, design life 10–15 yr flexible / 20–30 yr rigid; gravel-road standard for LRN.
  • Stress under load (flexible, Boussinesq): σz = (3P/2πz²)·[1/(1+(r/z)²)]^(5/2) under a point load; ESWL for dual wheels; tyre pressure ≈ 0.5–0.8 MPa.

Construction & Maintenance (9.6) — Course Facts

  • Subgrade preparation: clearing/grubbing, cut/fill to grade, compaction in 150–200 mm layers at OMC ± 2% (sand cone, core cutter, Proctor needle, nuclear gauge), 95–100% MDD subgrade, 98% base.
  • Soil stabilization: mechanical (gradation), lime (clayey — reduces PI), cement (granular, 2–6%), flyash, bituminous, geotextiles.
  • Layers: WBM (crushed stone 90 mm, screenings, binding; camber maintained), WMM (pre-mixed, better control); penetration macadam (compacted stone + hot bitumen grouted from top); bituminous macadam (pre-mixed); asphalt concrete (batch/drum mix, laying 120–150 °C, breakdown rolling 80–100 °C pneumatic, finish steel-wheel); PCC — fixed/slip form, textured finish, curing 14–28 days.
  • Equipment: dozer, scraper/grader, rollers (smooth-wheel, pneumatic, sheepsfoot, vibratory), paver, bitumen pressure distributor, hot-mix plant.
  • Maintenance: routine (potholes, drains, verge), periodic (surface dressing/overlay 4–5 yearly), special (flood/slip damage), rehabilitation (structural overlay, recycling), strengthening (overlay by Benkelman-beam deflection); evaluation — unevenness (bump integrator), roughness (IRI), rut depth, skid (pendulum tester); defect chain: cracking → ravelling → pothole → edge break → rutting.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps — NEC-asked): MC cutback = kerosene; RT-1 = lowest viscosity; Marshall stability temperature = 60 °C; LA abrasion surface-course limit 30% (CC 16%); penetration unit = 0.1 mm; 85th percentile = speed limit, 98th = design speed; flakiness 0.6× vs elongation 1.8× mean size; overtaking zone minimum 3×OSD.
