Chapter 10: Project Planning, Design and Implementation (AALL10)

NEC License Exam (1-Mark MCQ Focus) | NEC prep-course edition — v5.5

This web is vibe coded by Abhishek Gubhaju from Nepal Engineering College, Pokhara University. Note this is just a refresher pack only — please read more from other sources for more knowledge. Wherever this pack cites a course book or any course material, it means the notes and course content of the 4-year Bachelor of Engineering (Civil, Civil & Rural) programme — the full undergraduate syllabus these notes were drawn from.

10.1 Engineering Drawings and its Concepts (AALL1001)

A. Standard Drawing Sheets

A drawing is the engineer's contract language: the builder works from the drawing, not from spoken words, so every convention on it is examinable. Sheets follow the ISO A-series, where each size has an aspect ratio of 1:√2 and each step down halves the sheet: A0 = 841 × 1189 mm, A1 = 594 × 841, A2 = 420 × 594, A3 = 297 × 420, A4 = 210 × 297. The title block (the information panel that identifies the sheet) conventionally sits in the bottom-right corner and carries the name, title, scale, date, drawing number and revision.

Fig 10.1 — ISO A-series sheets: each halving keeps the 1:√2 ratio; the title block sits in the bottom-right corner
  • Scales: a scale tells you how drawing size compares with real size — reducing (1:10, 1:100, drawing smaller than reality), full (1:1) and enlarging (10:1, drawing bigger than the part). The representative fraction (RF) is drawing distance ÷ actual distance, so 1:100 means 1 cm on paper equals 1 m on the ground. Typical uses: site plans 1:500–1:1000, building plans 1:50–1:100, details 1:5–1:20.
  • Line conventions: each line type has a fixed meaning, so a reader never has to guess: thick continuous — visible outlines; thin continuous — dimension, extension and hatching lines; short dashes — hidden edges; long-dash-dot — centre lines; long-dash-double-dot — adjacent or alternative positions; wavy continuous — short break; zig-zag — long break.
  • Dimensioning rules: engineering drawings dimension in mm (no unit symbol needed); survey plans may use metres. Arrowheads or oblique strokes terminate dimension lines; dimensions sit outside the views where possible, with the smallest nearest to the view. Two "never" rules a checker enforces: never dimension to hidden lines, and never duplicate a dimension.
  • Lettering: all text is single-stroke, vertical or inclined at 75°; height series 1.8–14 mm (3–5 mm for notes); height:width ratio 7:5 — the point is that lettering stays legible even at photocopy size.
Fig 10.2 — The drawing language: the seven standard line types and 45° material-hatching symbols for steel, brick, concrete, earth, water and timber

B. Projections

Fig 10.3 — First vs third angle projection: where the plane sits, view placement, and the cone symbols
  • Orthographic projection uses parallel projectors perpendicular to the plane. First angle (Nepal/India/ISO-Europe): the object sits between the observer and the plane — the top view is placed below the front view and the left-side view appears on the right. Third angle (US): the plane sits between observer and object — the top view goes above the front view. Both are identified by the truncated-cone symbol: locate the circle-view relative to the trapezoid view.
  • Isometric projection: the "3D-looking" view in which all three axes are equally inclined at 120° to each other (30° to the horizontal); the isometric scale factor is √(2/3) ≈ 0.816 of true length (isometric drawing conventionally uses full scale). Foreshortening is equal on all axes, and circles appear as ellipses (four-centre approximation).
  • Pictorial family: all pictorial views show the object in 3D — isometric (axes 120°), dimetric (two equal axes), trimetric (all different), and oblique — cavalier (45° receding axis at full scale) and cabinet (receding axis at half scale).
  • Sectional drawings: imagine slicing the object open — the cutting plane and its arrows show where and which way the object is cut; cut faces are hatched at 45° with spacing/symbols by material (steel close lines, brick masonry, concrete with aggregate symbol, earth, water). Section types: full, half, offset, revolved, removed and broken-out. Hidden lines behind the cutting plane are usually omitted.
  • View selection: the front view is the most informative face; use the minimum number of views that fully define the object; auxiliary views serve inclined faces; developments (surfaces unfolded flat) of prisms, cylinders and cones serve sheet-metal work.
10.1 must-knows: A-series halving ratio 1:√2; A0 = 841×1189 mm; first angle — top view below front; third angle — top above; isometric axes 120°/30° to horizontal, scale 0.816; hatching at 45°; dimensions in mm.

10.2 Engineering Economics (AALL1002)

A. Cash Flow & Time Value of Money

A cash-flow diagram plots time horizontally; arrows up are income, arrows down are cost, all at end-of-period. Two ground rules: sunk costs are ignored (money already spent cannot come back, so it must not influence a future decision), and every use of money has an opportunity cost.

The six interest formulas (i per period, n periods) — every exam numerical comes from these. The letter you solve for leads: P = present sum (value today), F = future sum (value at year n), A = equal annual amount; each formula simply converts one into another:

F = P(1+i)ⁿ [single payment compound amount, (F/P, i, n)]
P = F/(1+i)ⁿ [single payment present worth, (P/F)]
F = A[((1+i)ⁿ−1)/i] [uniform series compound amount, (F/A)]
A = F[i/((1+i)ⁿ−1)] [sinking fund, (A/F)]
P = A[((1+i)ⁿ−1)/(i(1+i)ⁿ)] [uniform series present worth, (P/A)]
A = P[i(1+i)ⁿ/((1+i)ⁿ−1)] [capital recovery, (A/P)]
Arithmetic gradient: P = G[((1+i)ⁿ − in − 1)/(i²(1+i)ⁿ)]; geometric gradient series for inflation-linked flows
  • Nominal vs effective rate: the nominal rate is the advertised yearly rate; the effective rate is what compounding really delivers. With nominal annual rate r compounded m times a year, the effective rate i = (1 + r/m)^m − 1; continuous compounding gives i = e^r − 1. More frequent compounding → higher effective rate.
  • MARR (Minimum Attractive Rate of Return) is the owner's hurdle rate — a project must beat it to be worth doing: cost of capital + risk premium + inflation. Accept projects with IRR ≥ MARR or NPV(MARR) ≥ 0.

B. Evaluation Methods

Fig 10.4 — Cash-flow diagram and the decision rules: NPV, IRR, B/C, payback
  • NPV (net present value): all future benefits and costs brought to today and netted — NPV = Σ(Bt − Ct)/(1+r)ᵗ; accept NPV ≥ 0. The best single measure for mutually exclusive alternatives (an absolute value).
  • IRR (internal rate of return): the interest rate the project effectively earns — the rate that makes NPV = 0; compare against MARR. Watch the failure modes — multiple IRRs when signs change more than once, and scale blindness between alternatives (use incremental IRR: take the higher-cost alternative only if ΔIRR ≥ MARR).
  • Payback period: how many years it takes to recover the investment; discounted payback uses discounted flows. It is a liquidity indicator (how fast cash comes back) — it ignores everything after payback.
  • Benefit-Cost Ratio: BCR = PV(benefits)/PV(costs) — rupees gained per rupee spent; accept ≥ 1; for alternatives use the incremental ΔB/ΔC. The public-works ranking tool.
  • Comparing alternatives: equal lives → NPV; unequal lives → annual worth (AW/EUAC — equivalent uniform annual cost) or the LCM of lives; capitalized cost = perpetual annual worth ÷ i (for long-lived assets like roads and dams that are renewed forever).
  • Depreciation (Nepal): depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its working life. The Income Tax Act 2058 uses the reducing-balance method (each year's charge = rate × remaining book value, so early years cost more) with prescribed rates by asset class (buildings ≈ 5%, machinery ≈ 15%, vehicles ≈ 20%, computers higher — Schedule 2 of the Act); no salvage in tax books. For comparison, other methods: straight line D = (P−S)/n, sum-of-years-digits, sinking fund, double-declining balance (rate = 2/n).
  • Nepal taxation: corporate income tax 25% standard (20% for special industries/infrastructure concessions; banks 30%); VAT 13%; customs per tariff. Tax depreciation is reducing-balance. Depreciation is a non-cash cost but a tax shield: after-tax cash flow = (Rev − Cost − Dep)(1 − T) + Dep — the depreciation "expense" cuts the tax bill even though no cash leaves the site.
  • Inflation: Fisher — nominal ≈ real + inflation (exact: (1+nom)/(1+inf) − 1). Use constant prices with a real discount rate, or current prices with a nominal rate — never mix.
Fig 10.5 — Depreciation: the front-loaded reducing-balance curve (Nepal IT Act 2058) against the straight line to salvage
10.2 rapid numbers: effective i = (1+r/m)^m − 1; accept NPV ≥ 0, IRR ≥ MARR, BCR ≥ 1; EUAC for unequal lives; Nepal tax depreciation = reducing balance (IT Act 2058); CIT 25%, VAT 13%; sunk cost ignored.

10.3 Project Planning and Scheduling (AALL1003)

A. Project Classifications & Life Cycle

  • Project: a temporary endeavour with a unique output, a defined start/end, and the triple constraint — scope, time, cost (plus quality/safety). Change one leg and the other two move.
  • Classification: by sector (building, infrastructure, industrial), owner (public/private/PPP), nature (greenfield/brownfield/retrofit), size. Nepal adds National Pride Projects (Melamchi, Fast Track, international airports, Budhigandaki HPP) and the development portfolio tracked in the RED BOOK (the government's National Projects Bank of approved projects).
  • Life cycle: identification/pre-feasibility → preparation (feasibility & design) → tendering/procurement → implementation/construction → commissioning/handover → O&M → evaluation. The cost-influence curve is the exam favourite: decisions made early cost little to change, but the same change during construction is expensive.
  • Planning outputs: scope (WBS — work breakdown structure, the project sliced into manageable work packages), organization (responsibility matrix RAM/RACI — who does, who checks, who approves), schedule (activities, logic, durations), resources and budget, risk, quality and communication plans — together the baseline for monitoring.

B. Scheduling Techniques

Fig 10.6 — AOA network with dummy activity and highlighted critical path (CPM/PERT)
  • Bar (Gantt) chart: each activity drawn as a bar against a time scale — simple and visual, but shows no logic dependencies (which job must finish before which); good for presentation and small works.
  • CPM (Critical Path Method) — deterministic durations (each activity gets one "most likely" duration):
    • Network in activities and events (AOA arrows or AON nodes); forward pass gives ES and EF = ES + d; backward pass gives LF and LS = LF − d. Floats: total float TF = LS − ES = LF − EF — the days an activity can slip without delaying the whole project; free float FF = min(ES of all immediate successors) − EF (with one successor: ES(next) − EF) — the days it can slip without delaying even the next activity, so always FF ≤ TF; independent float subtracts head-event slack (rarely positive).
    • Critical activities have TF = 0; the critical path is the longest chain through the network and equals the project duration — delay any critical activity and the project slips day for day.
    • Crashing: deliberately shortening durations by spending money — cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost)/(normal time − crash time); crash the cheapest-slope critical activity first, stopping at a path split or the crash limit. Direct costs rise as duration falls, indirect (overhead) costs fall — the optimum duration is where total cost bottoms out.
    Fig 10.7 — Crashing trade-off: direct rises as duration falls, indirect rises with time — total cost bottoms at the optimum
  • PERT — probabilistic (for research/uncertain work where a single duration cannot be trusted): three estimates a (optimistic), m (most likely), b (pessimistic); te = (a + 4m + b)/6 and σ = (b − a)/6; the path variance is the sum of critical-activity variances; probability of finishing by T is Z = (T − Te)/σpath (Z = 1 → ≈ 84.1%, Z = 2 → 97.7%). CPM suits repetitive construction; PERT suits new, uncertain work.
  • Precedence (PDM): the modern network style where relationships can be finish-to-start (FS), start-to-start (SS), finish-to-finish (FF), start-to-finish (SF) with lags — the default in MS Project/Primavera.
  • Line of Balance: schedules repetitive work by matching production rates (roads, housing rows) — each crew's output pace sets the flow.

C. Resource Levelling & Smoothing

  • Resource levelling: resource limits are fixed (only so many crews exist) — the project duration may extend as non-critical work is rescheduled within — or beyond — its float.
  • Resource smoothing: the finish date is fixed — peaks in resource demand are shaved by shifting work within available floats only.
  • The MCQ favourite: levelling may change the duration; smoothing never does.
  • Monitoring & control: progress by physical %, S-curves and milestones; Earned Value Management (EVM) compares three money curves — PV/BCWS (planned value: what you should have done), EV/BCWP (earned value: what you actually did, valued at plan), AC/ACWP (actual cost). CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV (above 1 = ahead, below 1 = behind); EAC = BAC/CPI forecasts the final bill; corrective actions flow through change control (variation orders) and monthly reporting.
  • Nepal context: National Planning Commission periodic plans; Public Procurement Act 2063/Regulations 2064 for works; departmental monitoring; social audits for community projects; the project cycle follows NPC's Project Preparation & Approval Process (PAPP) manual.
Fig 10.8 — Earned Value Management: three money S-curves and the variances read between them at today's date
Fig 10.9 — Anatomy of total float: the early and late schedules of one 5-day activity, on a true day scale
10.3 must-knows: critical path = longest chain, TF = 0; TF = LS − ES; FF ≤ TF; crashing = cheapest slope first; PERT te = (a+4m+b)/6, σ = (b−a)/6; levelling may extend duration, smoothing never; EVM: CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV, EAC = BAC/CPI.

10.4 Project Management (AALL1004)

A. Project Information System (PMIS)

  • Components: planning baselines (schedule/cost), execution records (daily logs, quality tests, payment certificates), communication protocols (drawing registers, RFIs — requests for information, correspondence), document control (revisions), and reporting dashboards. Software: Primavera P6, MS Project, cost/QA tools. Document control ensures only the current revision reaches site — building from a superseded drawing is a classic and costly site error; as-built drawings close the loop at handover.

B. Risk Analysis & Management

  • Process: identification (checklists, brainstorming, HAZOP — a structured hazard-hunting review, lessons learned) → qualitative analysis (probability–impact matrix, risk register — the living list of risks with owners) → quantitative (Monte Carlo, sensitivity/tornado, decision trees, EMV = probability × impact) → response planning → monitoring.
  • Responses: four ways to handle a threat — avoid (change the plan so the risk cannot occur), mitigate (lower its probability or impact), transfer (insurance, subcontract, bonds — shifted, not eliminated), accept (contingency reserve for known risks; management reserve for unknowns). For opportunities: exploit, share, enhance, accept.
Fig 10.10 — Probability–impact heat map: where each response lives (transfer = rare but severe), and the tools (EMV, register, reserves)
  • Construction risks (Nepal): geological (landslides, GLOF), hydrological (monsoon flooding), price escalation (steel/fuel), currency, land acquisition and social issues, contract disputes, workforce, quality/technology, force majeure (the 2015 Gorkha earthquake is the standing lesson).
  • Contractual risk allocation: lump sum (contractor bears cost risk), remeasured/BOQ (shared), cost-plus (owner), target cost with incentives; escalation clauses (price-adjustment formulas) protect long contracts.

C. Project Financing

  • Sources: government budget (RED BOOK), multilateral loans (World Bank, ADB), bilateral (JICA, Exim China), domestic banks, equity, bonds. PPP models (public–private partnership): BOT (build–operate–transfer), BOOT (build–own–operate–transfer), DBFO (design–build–finance–operate), BLT (build–lease–transfer), management contract, lease; Viability Gap Funding supports marginal PPPs. Hydropower examples: Upper Tamakoshi (government + citizens' shares), Khimti/Rasuwagadhi (IPP BOT-style with PPAs to NEA).
  • Financial close: the moment all contracts and security packages are signed and money can flow — PPA signed (the power purchase agreement with NEA), security in place (escrow, DSRA); debt:equity typically 70:30 (Nepal HPP norm); lenders require DSCR ≥ 1.2–1.5 (debt service coverage ratio — cash available per rupee of loan repayment due).

D. Tender & its Process (Nepal — PPA 2063)

  • Methods: ICB (international competitive bidding), NCB (national), restricted/national shopping, direct procurement/negotiation (limited justified cases), framework contracts; two-envelope (technical and financial bids sealed separately) for consultants and complex works; e-GP (electronic government procurement, bolpatra.gov.np) is the mandatory electronic portal.
  • Process: procurement planning → prequalification (optional) → bidding documents (invitation, forms, specs, BOQ, GCC/SCC, drawings) → public notice (bid period 30 days NCB, 45 days ICB; 15 days sealed quotation — PPA Sec 15) → pre-bid meeting → addenda → submission with bid security (earnest money) — stated in the bidding document, up to 5% of the estimate (PPA Sec 14 ceiling; the course decks and PANA quote actual practice as 2–3% of the estimate) → public opening → evaluation (responsiveness → technical → financial; lowest evaluated substantially responsive bid wins) → performance guarantee 5% (PPR Rule 68) → letter of acceptance → contract agreement → advance payment against bank guarantee (up to 20% — PPR Rule 71), recovered from running bills.
  • Bid evaluation: check substantial responsiveness, apply arithmetical corrections, and select the lowest evaluated (not merely lowest arithmetic) price. Abnormally low bids — well below the engineer's estimate — must be justified and may attract additional security, protecting the project from mid-way abandonment.
  • Contract management: types — lump sum (one fixed price for the whole job), remeasured (BOQ unit rate — Nepal's most common: pay for measured quantities at bid rates), cost-plus (actual cost plus fee — owner bears the risk), turnkey/EPC (contractor designs and delivers the complete facility), small-works quotation; standard conditions from FIDIC (Red Book construction, Yellow design-build) and Nepal's PPA/PPR standard documents (GCC/SCC). Roles: Employer (owner), Engineer/PM (certifies what is due), Contractor (builds). Payment cycle: monthly running bills with retention ≈ 5% (money withheld as security against defects, released at completion and after the DLP of 365 days — 1 year), then the final certificate.
  • Variations and claims: scope changes priced at BOQ rates, pro-rata or new rates; EOT (extension of time) for delays not the contractor's fault (weather, late drawings, land) with prompt notices (28 days FIDIC-style); claims stand on contemporaneous records. Dispute ladder: amicable settlement → Engineer's determination / DAB (Dispute Adjudication Board) → arbitration (Arbitration Act 2055) → court last.
  • Suspension & termination: by owner (public interest, default) or contractor (non-payment — 56 days FIDIC-style); force majeure gives relief and possible termination if prolonged; delay damages (LD — liquidated damages) 0.05% per day, capped at 10% (PPR Rule 73) of contract value — a pre-agreed price for lateness, not a punishment.
Fig 10.11 — The tender-to-handover journey under PPA 2063: where every exam percentage sits
10.4 must-knows: bid security 2–3% typical (5% ceiling) at tender; performance security 5–10% at award; retention 5% during execution; DLP = 1 year; LD 0.05–0.1%/day capped 10%; EOT for non-contractor delays; disputes: amicable → DAB → arbitration (Act 2055); DSCR ≥ 1.2–1.5; debt:equity 70:30; risk responses = avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept.

10.5 Engineering Professional Practice (AALL1005)

A. Environment & Society

  • Sustainable development (Brundtland): meeting present needs without compromising future generations — the triple bottom line of economic, social and environmental (profit, people, planet). Engineers deliver it through EIA compliance, green materials, energy efficiency and climate adaptation (Nepal: climate vulnerability, GLOF, water security).
  • Social dimensions: resettlement and livelihood restoration (LARAP — land acquisition and resettlement action plan: what happens to displaced families), gender equality and social inclusion (GESI), indigenous peoples' plans, mandatory public consultation in EIA/IEE, and benefit sharing — hydropower royalties shared among federal, provincial and local governments per Natural Resources & Fiscal Commission recommendations (earlier Electricity Act provisions channelled a share to district/local bodies).

B. Professional Ethics

  • Canon of ethics: hold paramount the public safety, health and welfare; practise only within competence; be honest and objective; act as a faithful agent (no conflicts of interest); refuse bribery and fraud; keep learning; treat colleagues fairly.
  • Ethics dilemmas on site: tender collusion (bid rigging), substandard materials and fake tests, covered-up defects, environmental shortcuts, kickbacks. Whistle-blowing (reporting wrongdoing outside the chain of command) is the last resort after internal escalation; conflicts of interest are disclosed and recused (step aside from the decision).
  • Codes: the NEC Code of Conduct for registered engineers, with ASCE/ICE as international references. Discipline: under the NEC Act the council can suspend or cancel registration for professional misconduct.

C. Regulatory Environment

  • Key Nepal statutes: Public Procurement Act 2063, Environment Protection Act 2076 (& Rules 2077), Building Act 2055 (NBC via municipalities), Labour Act 2074, Arbitration Act 2055, Electricity Act 2049, Water Resources Act 2049, Land Acquisition Act 2034, Forest Act 2076, Nepal Engineering Council Act 2055 — plus the Nepal Engineers' Association as the voluntary professional body.
  • Contemporary issues: urban sprawl and informal settlements, seismic risk in pre-1998 non-engineered buildings, climate adaptation, Kathmandu's air and water pollution, the solid-waste crisis, the energy deficit-to-surplus transition (export potential), engineer brain drain, engineering-education quality, contractor fragmentation, construction corruption, and technology adoption (BIM, e-GP, digital survey).

D. Occupational Health & Safety (OHS)

Fig 10.12 — Site safety in two pictures: hierarchy of controls (eliminate first, PPE last) and the Heinrich pyramid — near misses are free lessons
  • Site hazards: falls from height (the leading killer), struck-by (loads, plant), electrocution, trench collapse, confined spaces, scaffolds and ladders, silica dust, noise, heat, manual handling. Hierarchy of controls: eliminate → substitute → engineering controls → administrative → PPE last — always attack the hazard itself before relying on worker behaviour or protective gear.
  • Key measures: safety plan and officer, inductions and toolbox talks, PPE (helmet, boots, harness with 100% tie-off, hi-vis), scaffolds with guardrails/toe boards and inspections, shoring for trenches deeper than ≈ 1.2–1.5 m (soil-dependent), lifting plans with certified operators, lockout-tagout, housekeeping, first aid and emergency response, and incident/near-miss reporting.
  • Legal frame: Labour Act 2074 (occupational safety duties and safety committees), Building Act, factory rules; internationally, ILO conventions and ISO 45001 OHS management systems.
  • Statistics concept: the accident pyramid (Heinrich) — 1 major : ~30 minor : ~300 near misses — reporting near misses prevents majors.

E. Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA) & Professional Bodies

  • NEA (established 1962 / 2019 BS): the professional society — CPD, conferences and journals, advocacy, international relations, member welfare. It is not a regulator — that role belongs to NEC.
  • NEC (statutory, under the NEC Act 2055): registers engineers (General via the licensing exam — this one; Professional for experienced engineers), requires CPD for renewal, disciplines misconduct, sets the code of conduct and runs the syllabus and exams.
  • NEA roles: professional development and networking, technical discourse, policy input, ethics promotion, scholarships and relief, representation in national/international forums. NEC registration is legally separate and mandatory for practice; NEA membership is voluntary.
10.5 must-knows: hierarchy of controls — eliminate → substitute → engineering → administrative → PPE last; Heinrich pyramid 1 : 30 : 300; public safety, health and welfare held paramount; NEA = professional association (voluntary, est. 1962/2019 BS); NEC = statutory regulator (Act 2055) — registration is legally mandatory for practice.

10.6 Engineering Regulatory Body — Nepal Engineering Council (AALL1006)

A. NEC Act & Regulations

Fig 10.13 — The NEC registration ladder: General Engineer → Professional Engineer, with renewal rules and the foreign-engineer side track
  • Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998) established NEC as an autonomous statutory body (it regulates the profession on its own legal authority); the NEC Regulation 2057 operationalizes registration, categories, code of conduct and exams.
  • Objectives (Act preamble): mobilize the engineering profession — orderly, responsible and efficient; register qualified engineers; maintain standards of engineering education and practice; safeguard professional rights and discipline.
  • Structure: the Council (chairperson and members drawn from government bodies, universities and registered engineers), the registrar's office, and committees for education, discipline/conduct and registration.
  • Registration: General Engineer (GE) — fresh graduates through the licensing exam (this one!); Professional Engineer (PE) — master's degree + 7 years as GE; temporary registration for foreign engineers (project-specific, up to 2 years, renewable 1 year at a time). Registration is renewed periodically with CPD points (continuing professional development — documented learning after graduation) — general engineers annually, professional engineers on a 5-year cycle.
  • Powers/functions: recognize degrees and institutions, conduct licensing exams, maintain the public register, set the code of conduct, hear misconduct complaints (warning → suspension → cancellation), and advise government.
  • Discipline: misconduct (fraudulent registration, negligence causing harm, bribery, serious code breach) → council inquiry with natural justice (show cause, hearing) → penalties, with appeal provisions.
  • Key MCQ facts: Act year 2055 BS (1998 AD); NEC = regulator, NEA = professional association; the 10-chapter general exam syllabus; a licence is required for engineering consultancy (Consultancy Act 2056 also requires licensed professionals in consultancy firms).
10.6 must-knows: NEC Act 2055 BS (1998), Regulation 2057; GE via licensing exam, PE = M.Sc. + 7 years as GE; GE renews yearly, PE every 5 years with CPD; foreign temporary registration ≤ 2 years; discipline ladder = warning → suspension → cancellation; practice without registration — fine up to Rs 10,000 / 3 months / both.

Deeper Concept Discussions (Chapter 10)

Economic comparison worked example (choose between two dozers)

  • Dozer A: cost Rs 80 lakh, annual O&M Rs 8 L, life 8 yr, salvage Rs 8 L. Dozer B: Rs 1.1 crore, O&M Rs 5 L, life 8 yr, salvage Rs 15 L. i = 10%.
  • EUAC_A = 80L×(A/P,10%,8) + 8L − 8L×(A/F,10%,8) = 80L×0.1874 + 8L − 8L×0.0874 = 15.0 + 8 − 0.70 = Rs 22.3 L/yr.
  • EUAC_B = 110L×0.1874 + 5L − 15L×0.0874 = 20.6 + 5 − 1.31 = Rs 24.3 L/yr → choose A — capital dominates at 10% despite B's lower running cost.
  • Break-even: B wins only if its O&M falls below Rs 3.0 L/yr (20.6 + x − 1.31 = 22.3 → x = 3.0).

CPM worked example (small network)

  • Activities (days): A(4), B(6) from start; C(3) after A; D(5) after B; E(4) after C & D. Paths: A-C-E = 11, B-D-E = 15 → critical path B-D-E = 15 days; TF(A) = 4, TF(C) = 4; FF(C) = ES(E) − EF(C) = 11 − 7 = 4 = TF here; project = 15 d.
  • Crash example: D normal 5 d @ Rs 2 L, crash 3 d @ Rs 3.2 L → slope = Rs 0.6 L/day; E normal 4 @ 1.6 L, crash 3 @ 2.5 L → slope 0.9 L/day; indirect cost Rs 1 L/day → crash D first (its 0.6 slope is cheaper than the 1 L/day saving) until D reaches its 3-day crash limit; net saving = 2×(1 − 0.6) = 0.8 L.

PERT probability micro-example

  • Critical path: te = 20 months, Σσ² = 4 (σ = 2). Probability of finishing ≤ 23 months: Z = (23−20)/2 = 1.5 → ≈ 93.3%; by 18 months: Z = −1 → ≈ 15.9%.
  • Remember: expected time = (a+4m+b)/6 — the "4m" beta-distribution weight; variance from range/6.

EVM status micro-example

  • BAC = Rs 100 L; at month 6: PV = 60, EV = 45, AC = 55 → CV = −10 (over cost), SV = −15 (behind); CPI = 45/55 = 0.82; SPI = 45/60 = 0.75; EAC = 100/0.82 ≈ Rs 122 L; the time forecast extends by ≈ 1/SPI (≈ 8 months' equivalent) — a classic dashboard reading.

Tender process chain (memorize the sequence)

Procurement plan → DPP (Durgasana Praastuti Pratibedan — project preparation report per PAPP) → estimate & sanction → bidding doc → notice (e-GP) → pre-bid & addenda → bid + bid security (5%) → public opening → evaluation (responsive, L1) → recommendation/award notice → performance security (5–10%) → contract → advance vs guarantee → works + running bills (retention 5%) → completion → DLP 1 yr → final payment & security release
  • Bid security vs performance security: bid security protects the tender process (bidders' seriousness); performance security protects contract execution — different stages, similar percentages.
  • LD vs bonus: LD penalizes delay (0.05–0.1%/day, cap 10%); bonus rewards early completion (some contracts).

Extended Concept Bank — Chapter 10 (High-Yield Depth)

A. Engineering Drawing Practice — Extra Facts Examined in NEC Papers

  • Sheet margins & frames: trimming edge vs frame — 20 mm on the left edge (binding/filing), 10 mm on the others; grid-reference letters/numbers along margins locate details on large sheets; centring marks align reproduction/printing.
  • Scale accuracy rule: never measure from a scaled drawing on site — use the dimensioned figures; every scale used must be stated. The "Do not scale" note is a legal protection on construction drawings.
  • Material hatching (BS/IS convention): section steel — close 45° lines one direction; brick masonry — 45° double/alternate lines; unreinforced concrete — 45° with dots/aggregate; reinforced concrete — concrete hatch with heavier cover indication; earth — short 45° dashes; water — horizontal wavy lines; timber end grain — annual rings; insulation — zig-zag; glass — long thin diagonals. Conventional symbols are favourite 1-mark items.
  • Developments of solids: cylinder = rectangle of width πD; cone = sector of radius = slant height L with angle θ = (D/L)×180°; prism & pyramid need true lengths by rotation/auxiliary views — sheet-metal and fabrication staples.
  • CAD to BIM: CAD layers (structure, architecture, services) evolve into BIM — clash detection, quantities, 5D (cost) and 6D (sustainability); Nepal's major projects increasingly mandate BIM, but the legally issued set remains the 2D IFC drawings under revision control.
  • Common drawing errors ("spot the wrong statement"): dimensioning to hidden lines (wrong); repeating one size in two dimension chains (wrong); hatching crossing dimension lines (wrong — break the hatch); leader lines crossing (avoid); section-plane arrows point in the direction of sight.

B. Money Mathematics — Worked Conversions You Must Do in 20 Seconds

  • Factor relationships (memorize three, derive all):
(A/P) = (A/F) + i → 0.16275 = 0.06275 + 0.10 ✓ (10%, 10 yr)
(P/A) = 1/(A/P) → 6.1446 = 1/0.16275 ✓
(F/A) = (P/A)×(F/P) → 15.937 = 6.1446 × 2.5937 ✓
  • Sample factor values (10%): (F/P,10%,10) = 2.5937; (P/F) = 0.3855; (P/A,10%,10) = 6.1446; (A/P,10%,10) = 0.16275; (A/F) = 0.06275; (P/A,10%,∞) = 10 (= 1/i).
  • Sample values (12%, 5 yr): (F/P) = 1.7623; (P/A) = 3.6048; (A/P) = 0.27741; (A/F) = 0.15741.
  • Worked loan problem: Rs 20 lakh at 11% for 6 years → A = 20L × (A/P,11%,6) = 20L × 0.2364 = Rs 4.73 L/yr; total interest = 28.4 − 20 = Rs 8.4 L.
  • Worked NPV ranking: X: −100, +40/yr×4; Y: −150, +55/yr×4; i = 10%. NPV_X = −100 + 40×3.1699 = +26.8; NPV_Y = −150 + 55×3.1699 = +24.3 → choose X (the incremental ΔIRR of Y over X is below 10%).
  • Breakeven units: Q* = F/(p−v); F = 10 L, p = 500, v = 300 → Q* = 5,000 units/yr.
  • Inflation-adjusted return: nominal 12%, inflation 5% → real = (1.12/1.05) − 1 = 6.67% (Fisher exact), ≈ 7% by approximation.

C. Scheduling — Full Worked Network (AOA) for Practice

  • Activities (duration, predecessors): A(3,—), B(5,—), C(4,A), D(6,A), E(2,B), F(5,C,E), G(4,D), H(3,F,G).
  • Forward pass: ES: A=0, B=0; EF: A=3, B=5; C: ES=3, EF=7; D: ES=3, EF=9; E: ES=5, EF=7; F: ES=max(7,7)=7, EF=12; G: ES=9, EF=13; H: ES=max(12,13)=13, EF=16 → project = 16 days.
  • Backward pass: LF(H)=16 → LS(H)=13; LF(G)=13, LS(G)=9; LF(F)=13, LS(F)=8; E: LF(E)=LS(F)=8 → LS(E)=6 (TF=1); D: LF(D)=LS(G)=9 → LS(D)=3 (TF=0 — critical); C: LF(C)=LS(F)=8 → LS(C)=4 (TF=1); A: LF(A)=min(LS(C),LS(D))=3 → LS(A)=0; B: LF(B)=LS(E)=6 → LS(B)=1 (TF_B = 1).
  • Critical path: A–D–G–H = 3+6+4+3 = 16 d. Floats: B: TF=1, FF = ES(E)−EF(B) = 5−5 = 0; C: TF=1, FF = ES(F)−EF(C) = 7−7 = 0; E: TF = 6−5 = 1, FF = ES(F)−EF(E) = 7−7 = 0.
  • Lesson (classic MCQ): an activity can have TF > 0 but FF = 0 — its delay eats a successor's float. Total float is the network-wide measure.
  • Crashing this network: slopes D = 0.5 L/d (cheapest critical), G = 0.7, A = 0.9, H = 1.2; indirect cost 0.8 L/d → crash D by 1 day, whereupon A–D–G–H = 15 equals the sub-critical A–C–F–H = 15 (path split) → stop. New duration 15 d; net saving = 1×(0.8 − 0.5) = 0.3 L.

D. Nepal Public Procurement — Numbers & Sequence Drill

  • PPA 2063 principles: transparency, competition, economy & efficiency, fairness/non-discrimination, accountability — five pillars; quote any two.
  • Thresholds & methods (course values): competitive bidding is the default; direct procurement ≤ Rs 10 lakh (goods/works) and Rs 5 lakh (consulting); sealed quotation ≤ Rs 20 lakh; NCB from Rs 20 lakh up to Rs 5 billion; ICB above Rs 5 billion; supplementary works permitted up to a fraction of the original contract value at the same rates.
  • Pre-qualification criteria (typical works): similar-works experience (minimum value & count), turnover (average annual ≥ a contract proportion), equipment list, key personnel, financial standing (solvency/credit line), litigation history, no debarment.
  • Bid opening mechanics: single envelope (works/NCB) opened publicly on the due date with rates read aloud and recorded; two envelopes (consultancy) — technical opened first, financial only of qualified bidders; evaluation within the validity period; validity extensions require the bid security to be extended too.
  • Contract signing: LoA → agreement within the bid validity (typically within 15 days of the LoA); failure to sign forfeits the bid security; mobilization time limits (commence within 15/30 days of site handover).
  • Payment cycle discipline: monthly running bill → measurement book (MB) entries → engineer's certificate → payment within the stipulated days (FIDIC 28; Nepal practice 30–45); PPA/PPR provide bank-rate interest on delayed payments.
  • e-GP facts: launched by PPMO (Public Procurement Monitoring Office); all public entities advertise on www.bolpatra.gov.np; digital submission and online bid security — MCQ: PPMO regulates public procurement (standard documents, compliance monitoring, debarment list).
  • Blacklisting/debarment: bid collusion, fake documents, abandonment → debarment (typically 1–3 years) published by PPMO — repeat offenders lose eligibility.

E. Contract Types — Decision Table

TypePrice riskBest useWatch-outs
Lump sum / fixed priceContractorWell-defined scope, complete designContractor prices contingencies high; variations costly
Unit rate (BOQ, remeasured)Shared (quantity vs rate)Uncertain quantities (earthwork, roads)Unbalanced bidding (front-loaded rates)
Cost plus % / fixed feeOwnerEmergency, R&D, undefined scopeNo cost incentive to contractor
Target cost + incentiveShared with gain/painComplex collaborative projectsNeeds open-book cost records
Turnkey / EPCContractor (single point)Plants (hydropower, WTP) with performance guaranteePerformance tests define acceptance
  • Unbalanced bidding: loading early activities and likely-to-increase items — detected by rate-analysis comparison; obviously unbalanced rates may be adjusted.
  • Dayworks: daily rates for labour/materials/plant for unmeasurable extra work — carried in the BOQ as provisional.
  • Provisional sums & prime cost items: allowances for works not yet designed (PS spent on the engineer's instruction) — favourite definitions.

G. Professional Practice — Extra Exam Facts

  • NEA vs NEC division of labour: NEA = professional society, established 1962 (2019 BS), voluntary membership, CPD and advocacy; NEC = statutory regulator (Act 2055), registration mandatory to practise under the title "engineer", licensing exams and discipline. Consultancy Act 2056 additionally grades consultancy firms (with NEC-registered engineers as principals).
  • CPD structure (typical NEC): points per renewal cycle from training, publications, projects and teaching; professional engineers need more — the principle, not exact points, is examinable.
  • Engineers in disaster management: the NRA precedent after the 2015 earthquake — owner-driven reconstruction, seismic retrofitting campaigns, mason training for building permits; engineers in DRR — code enforcement, early warning, damage assessment (Rapid Visual Screening).
  • Occupational health specifics: silica dust → silicosis (wet methods + respirators for stone cutting); noise > 85 dB(A) over 8 h → hearing protection (action levels 85/90); heat stress (work-rest cycles, hydration); vibration white finger (pneumatic tools); manual-lifting guideline ≈ 25 kg with mechanical aids first; welfare facilities — drinking water, latrines, first-aid ratios, crèche for women workers under the Labour Act.
  • Safety statistics & culture terms: LTIFR (lost-time injuries per million hours), OSHA recordables, the training matrix, and PTW (permit-to-work) systems for hot works/confined space/height — one definition each is enough.
  • Ethics codes comparison: all codes (NEC/ASCE/ICE) share public-safety-first, competence, integrity, no bribery, sustainability duty; they differ in jurisdictional detail and disciplinary machinery — the MCQ asks the shared first principle.
  • Contemporary MCQ statements: Nepal now trades electricity with India (export agreements); Kathmandu's dry-season air pollution and construction-dust rules; e-GP reducing tender malpractice; record labour migration of skilled trades; NBC enforcement strengthening via municipality permits (licensed-engineer drawings mandatory above thresholds).

H. Estimating-Economics Cross Link (why Chapter 10 sits last)

  • Life-cycle cost thinking: initial cost vs O&M vs replacement vs salvage — e.g., asphalt overlay every 8 yr vs concrete pavement at 2.5× cost and 25-yr life — decide by EUAC, never by first cost alone.
  • NPV's sensitivity to the discount rate: long-tailed infrastructure (dams) is penalized by high rates — the "discount rate debate"; rankings can flip between alternatives at the crossover (Fisher) rate.
  • Value engineering (VE): function/cost analysis at design — the biggest savings come before construction (cost influence high, cost incurred low — the classic influence curve); value = function ÷ cost.

Grand Revision Drills — Chapter 10

A. One-Line Definitions Rapid-Fire (Definition MCQs come straight from these)

  • WBS: hierarchical decomposition of scope into deliverables/work packages — the basis of estimating and scheduling.
  • Milestone: a zero-duration significant event (start/finish marker).
  • Hammock activity: spans a group of activities; duration derived, not logic-scheduled.
  • Dummy activity: an AOA arrow with zero duration showing logic only.
  • Enterprise Environmental Factors / Organizational Process Assets: PMBOK inputs — external constraints and company templates/lessons.
  • Project charter: the document authorizing the project and empowering the PM.
  • Baseline: the approved scope/schedule/cost used for variance comparison — changed only via change control.
  • Configuration management: controlling document/drawing revisions so construction follows the current issue.
  • Critical chain: the resource-constrained critical path with project buffers (Goldratt) — unlike classic CPM, it respects resource limits.
  • Look-ahead schedule: a 3-week rolling detail plan for site crews.
  • S-curve: cumulative planned vs actual cost/time — slow start, fast middle, tapering end.
  • Float (second pass): total, free, independent, interfering (= TF − FF, consumed by successors).

B. Nepal-Specific Facts Bank (Chapter 10 slice)

  • PPA 2063 + PPR 2064 — the procurement law pair; PPMO (established under PPA) issues standard bidding documents and monitors; e-GP (bolpatra.gov.np) is the mandatory channel.
  • Environment Protection Act 2076 — BES/IEE/EIA thresholds; EIA needs a public hearing and approval before finance release; climate provisions added (climate-risk screening of major projects).
  • Building Act 2055 & NBC: NBC 105 = seismic design; Mandatory Rules of Thumb for low-rise: NBC 201 (RC with masonry infill), NBC 202 (load-bearing masonry), NBC 205 (RC without masonry infill).
  • Labour Act 2074 — employer OHS duties, safety committee, working hours (8/day, 48/week), overtime caps, women's night-work protections with consent and facilities.
  • Arbitration Act 2055 — construction disputes; arbitration awards are binding with limited court challenge.
  • Consultancy Act 2056 — registration/grading of consultancy firms; NEC-registered engineers required as principals — licensing links to market access.
  • Hydropower financing pattern: 70:30 debt:equity, PPA with NEA, capacity + energy royalties to government with local royalty shares, BOT/concession licensing by DOI (survey and generation licenses).
  • National Pride Projects criteria: national significance, multi-sector benefit, time-bound targets — special (PMO-level) oversight.
  • Development budget cycle: Ministry → NPC (RED BOOK inclusion) → annual budget presented Jestha 15 (moved up from Asar 15 in 2075 BS) → releases tracked through PPMIS/LMBIS (Financial Procedures Act/Rules).

C. Mini Case: Small Hydropower Project Development Sequence (integrative)

  • 1) Site identification & hydrology (flow-duration curve) → 2) Survey license (DOI) → 3) Feasibility (topo, geology, energy potential, tariff screen) → 4) IEE/EIA → 5) PPA & connection agreement (NEA) → 6) Financial close (banks, DSCR proofs) → 7) Generation license → 8) Construction (EPC/civil packages, CPM schedules, monsoon windows) → 9) Commissioning tests → 10) Operation (energy royalty, grid export, O&M).
  • Examinable hooks: survey vs generation license (DOI); PPA before financial close; DSCR ≥ 1.2–1.5; 70:30 gearing; energy royalty as % of sales; EIA/IEE by capacity thresholds.

Applied Practice Bank — Chapter 10 (Final)

A. Scenario-Based Application Notes (the way 1-markers are actually framed)

  • Scenario: "A contractor submits a bid 30% below the engineer's estimate." → Recognize an abnormally low bid: require justification (methodology, rate analysis); PPR allows demanding additional security or rejecting unjustified bids — protecting the project from mid-way abandonment.
  • Scenario: "Site hit unexpected rock; contractor claims extra payment & time." → Changed physical conditions: the contractor notifies promptly, the engineer verifies, and time & cost are adjusted at equitable rates — a classic EOT + variation event, not a silent contractor loss.
  • Scenario: "Owner fails to give land for 3 months." → Contractor entitled to EOT + prolongation costs (idle plant/labour records); critical-path proof required (the delay must hit the critical chain).
  • Scenario: "Engineer rejects concrete cubes below strength; retests confirm." → Acceptance criteria fail → investigate the structure (non-destructive tests), then remediate or recast; the ethics canon: safety first — no certification shortcuts.
  • Scenario: "A subcontractor's worker falls from an unbarricaded edge." → Hierarchy breach (engineering control omitted); the main contractor coordinates safety of all personnel on site; report, investigate, correct.
  • Scenario: "Municipality asks drawings for a 5-storey building permit." → Drawings must be prepared/endorsed by an NEC-registered engineer; NBC compliance (seismic NBC 105; MRT rules of thumb for low-rise only); permit process under Building Act 2055 via the municipality.

B. Formula Sheet Consolidated (print this page!)

MONEY: F/P=(1+i)ⁿ | P/F | F/A | P/A | A/P=i(1+i)ⁿ/((1+i)ⁿ−1) | A/F=i/((1+i)ⁿ−1) | (A/P)=(A/F)+i
EFF RATE: i=(1+r/m)^m −1 | REAL: (1+nom)/(1+inf) −1 | CC=A/i | GRADIENT: P=G[((1+i)ⁿ−in−1)/(i²(1+i)ⁿ)]
DECISION: NPV≥0 | IRR≥MARR | B/C≥1 | EUAC= least | EAC=BAC/CPI
SCHEDULE: TF=LS−ES | FF≤TF | te=(a+4m+b)/6 | σ=(b−a)/6 | Z=(T−te)/σ
SLOPE=(crash−normal cost)/(normal−crash time) | OPTIMUM: total cost min (direct↑ indirect↓)
CONTRACT: LD 0.05–0.1%/d (cap 10%) | bid sec 2–3% (≤5%) | perf sec 5–10% | retention 5% | DLP 1 yr
SALVAGE: book value = P − Σdepr | SLM D=(P−S)/n | WDV D=rate×BV

C. Two-Minute CPM Mock (do in your head)

  • Paths: P1 = 4+7+6 = 17; P2 = 5+9+4 = 18; P3 = 4+3+9+4 = 20 → project 20 d; critical = P3; floats: P1 = 3, P2 = 2.
  • If P1's 7-day activity crashes by 3 d → P1 = 14, project still 20 — no gain (it was never critical) → crash only critical activities.
  • Two paths critical (after crashing P3 by 2 d, both = 18) → further crashing needs BOTH shortened — cost doubles — a typical MCQ insight.

D. Exam-Day Last 60 Seconds Checklist (Chapter 10 scope)

  • Sheet sizes & projection conventions — one mark each, seconds each.
  • The factor-family identity (A/P = A/F + i) solves half the economics MCQs without tables.
  • TF=0 = critical; FF≤TF; the PERT Z-formula with σ=(b−a)/6.
  • Levelling vs smoothing direction; the three EVM equations.
  • Security/retention/DLP numbers; LD caps; the dispute ladder order.
  • NEC (regulator, 2055) vs NEA (association, 1962); CIT 25/VAT 13; EPA 2076.
  • Finally: attempt easy factual questions first, mark lengthy numericals for review, and never leave blanks — NEC general papers carry no negative marking, so a calculated guess beats silence every single time.

Closing Enrichment — Chapter 10

A. Decision-Theory & Negotiation Nuggets

  • Decision under uncertainty: optimistic (maximax), pessimistic (maximin — Wald), regret (minimax — Savage), equal likelihood (Laplace), Hurwicz (weighted optimism), and EMV when probabilities are known — one-line recognition of each is enough for a mark.
  • Decision tree mechanics: squares = decisions, circles = chance nodes; roll-back (right-to-left) expected values choose the best branch — used in go/no-go decisions with staged investment.
  • Negotiation (contract phase): negotiation only with the lowest evaluated bidder in Nepal public procurement (post-award clarification of minor matters allowed; no re-pricing of competitive scope — the anti-corruption principle).
  • Partnering/alliancing: relational contracts with shared risk pools and a no-fault culture — contrast with adversarial measured contracts; used on megaprojects to cut disputes.

B. Quality–Cost–Time Triangle in Monitoring

  • Monthly progress = physical + financial + quality indicators: S-curve variance, critical-activity slippage, NCR (non-conformance report) count, safety incidents, resource productivity (m³/day earthwork, m²/day shuttering) — MCQs test which indicator belongs to which dimension.
  • Cause-analysis tools: Pareto (80/20 defect causes), fishbone (Ishikawa), why-why — borrowed from quality management for construction defect reviews.
  • Closing a project: commissioning tests → provisional (practical) completion certificate → DLP → final account (all claims settled) → as-builts, O&M manuals, spares → performance certificate → security release → lessons-learned and post-evaluation (NPC ex-post assessment for large public projects).

C. Ten Numbers You Should Never Miss (Chapter 10 final flash)

  • 0.816 — isometric scale; 45° — hatching; 20/10 mm — sheet margins.
  • 5% — bid security ceiling (2–3% typical in practice); 5–10% performance; 5% retention; 1 yr — DLP.
  • 0.05–0.1%/day LD; 10% LD cap.
  • 70:30 debt:equity; DSCR ≥ 1.2–1.5.
  • 25% CIT; 13% VAT; Acts: NEC 2055, Arbitration 2055, Consultancy 2056, PPA 2063, Labour 2074, EPA 2076.

Last-Mile Memory Hooks (Chapter 10)

  • Angle conventions: First angle → top view BELOW (the object between eye and paper "pushes" the view down); Third → top ABOVE; Nepal/ISO-Europe = first angle.
  • Isometric trio: 120° axes, 30° to horizontal, ×0.816 scale — one question every year.
  • Formula family map: (F/P)(1+i)ⁿ; (P/F) inverse; (F/A) annuity-forward; (P/A) annuity-back; (A/P) recovery = (A/F) + i — derive from two base formulas instead of memorizing tables.
  • Decision rules: NPV ≥ 0 / IRR ≥ MARR / BCR ≥ 1 / payback short — NPV best for mutually exclusive; IRR fails with sign changes.
  • Levelling vs smoothing: LeveLing = Limited resources (duration can stretch); SmoothiNg = Not extending duration.
  • TF = 0 = critical; FF ≤ TF always.
  • PERT trio: te = (a+4m+b)/6; σ = (b−a)/6; Z = (T−Te)/σ — beta distribution.
  • Security chain: bid security 2–3% (≤5%) → performance 5–10% → retention 5% → release after DLP 1 yr.
  • Dispute ladder: negotiate → Engineer/DAB → arbitration (Act 2055) → court last — the award binds (court challenge limited).
  • Regulator vs association: NEC regulates (Act 2055), NEA associates (1962) — never swap them in an MCQ; consultancy firms additionally need Consultancy Act 2056 grading with NEC-registered principals.
  • OHS hierarchy order: Eliminate → Substitute → Engineering → Administrative → PPE — "ESEAP", PPE last resort.
  • Final word: Chapter 10 is the "open" chapter — its MCQs come from definitions, acts, years and small numbers rather than heavy derivations; read this file twice, run the 99-question exam once, and the 15–20 marks this chapter silently contributes are largely yours.

Prep-Course Grounding — Key Facts from NEC License Preparation Materials (10.1–10.6)

Engineering Drawing (10.1) — Course Facts

  • Sheet sizes (mm): A0 = 841 × 1189; A1 = 594 × 841; A2 = 420 × 594; A3 = 297 × 420; A4 = 210 × 297 (each half of the previous).
  • Lettering: height : width = 7 : 5 (ratio 1.4); single-stroke standard; dimensions in mm without the unit symbol.
  • Projection: First angle — object between observer and plane; top view below the front view, right-side view to the left of the elevation (Nepal/IS practice). Third angle — plane between observer and object; top view above the front view; symbol: truncated cone.
  • Lines: thick continuous — visible outlines; dashed — hidden; chain-thin (long-dash-dot) — centre lines; section hatching at 45°; thin dimension lines with arrowheads.
  • Scales: full 1:1, reducing 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, enlarging 10:1; isometric axes at 120° (30° to horizontal); orthographic = multi-view; sectional views reveal interior features.

Engineering Economics (10.2) — Course Formulas

  • Interest: simple I = PiN; compound F = P(1+i)ᴺ; effective annual rate i_eff = (1 + r/n)ⁿ − 1; continuous compounding i_eff = e^i − 1.
  • Factors: F/P = (1+i)ⁿ; P/F = 1/(1+i)ⁿ; F/A = ((1+i)ⁿ − 1)/i (sinking fund A/F = i/((1+i)ⁿ − 1)); P/A = ((1+i)ⁿ − 1)/(i(1+i)ⁿ) (capital recovery A/P = A/F + i); arithmetic gradient (A/G) = 1/i − n/((1+i)ⁿ − 1), so A = A₁ + G(A/G).
  • Payback period: even flows = investment ÷ annual inflow; uneven = cumulative; discounted payback uses present-valued flows; accept below the management standard; ignores post-payback benefits (limitation).
  • NPV: Σ present worth − investment; accept NPV > 0; between alternatives choose the higher NPV. IRR: the rate making NPV = 0 (trial/interpolation); accept IRR > MARR; between alternatives the higher IRR. MARR = hurdle rate = cost of capital + risk premium.
  • B/C ratio: PV benefits ÷ PV costs; accept > 1; incremental B/C for mutually exclusive alternatives. ERR (external rate of return) reinvests cash flows at MARR.
  • Depreciation: straight line Dₙ = (P − S)/N; declining balance — rate = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n) applied to book value; sum-of-years-digits = (remaining life/SOYD)×(P − S); sinking-fund deposit A = (P − S)·i/((1+i)ⁿ − 1); book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.
  • Nepal taxation: Income Tax Act 2058 — corporate 25% (ordinary), 20% special industries/infrastructure, banks 30%; VAT 13% (VAT Act 2052); customs per tariff; tax depreciation rates (building 5%, machinery 15%, vehicles 20%) — declining balance for tax.

Project Planning & Scheduling (10.3) — Course Facts

  • Project classes: private/public; national priority (e.g., Gautam Buddha International Airport); joint venture (domestic/international); bilateral vs multilateral (ADB, World Bank); labour- vs capital-intensive; industrial/agricultural/infrastructure.
  • Life cycle: identification/pre-investment → preparation (feasibility/design) → appraisal → implementation (tender, construction) → evaluation (monitoring, ex-post). Bar chart — timing without interdependencies.
  • CPM (deterministic, activity-oriented) — 1957 DuPont; critical path = longest path = project duration; critical activities have zero float; sub-critical = second longest; a super-critical activity has negative float.
  • Floats: TF = LS − ES = LF − EF (delay without delaying the project; the activity then becomes critical); FF ≤ TF (delay without touching the successor's ES); independent float (predecessor at LS, successor at EF — can be negative); interfering float = TF − FF. Float belongs to the activity, slack to the event.
  • PERT (probabilistic, event-oriented) — 1958 Polaris; te = (to + 4tm + tp)/6; σ² = ((tp − to)/6)²; project σ = √Σσ² along the critical path; probability via Z = (Ts − Te)/σ.
  • Crashing: cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost)/(normal time − crash time); crash cheapest-slope critical activities first, watching parallel critical paths; direct cost falls with time, indirect rises.
  • Resources: levelling = resource-constrained (duration may extend); smoothing = time-constrained (duration fixed, shift within floats); aggregation profiles demand against time.
  • Monitoring vs evaluation: monitoring = continuous data collection/reporting during implementation; evaluation = periodic outcome/impact assessment; controlling = corrective action from variance analysis (time, cost, quality).

Project Management (10.4) — Course Values (PPA 2063)

  • Information systems: MIS for project data flow; risk analysis — identification, qualitative/quantitative (probability-impact matrix), response (avoid/transfer/mitigate/accept); contingency reserve.
  • Financing: equity, loans (ADB/WB/JICA), BOOT/PPP models, bonds, grants.
  • PPA 2063 method limits (course values): direct procurement ≤ Rs 10 lakh (goods/works), Rs 5 lakh (consulting); sealed quotation ≤ Rs 20 lakh; national competitive bidding Rs 20 lakh – 5 billion; international competitive bidding > Rs 5 billion.
  • Tender process: invitation → bid (2-envelope technical/financial for consultants) → evaluation → Letter of Acceptance → contract. Performance security within 15 days of LoA (5%); retention 5% of each bill (50% released at completion, 50% after DLP); advance up to 20% (PPR Rule 71) against bank guarantee; mobilization advance.
  • Delay damages (LD): 0.05% of contract amount per day, capped at 10% (course values). Price escalation clause mandatory for contracts > 12 months, capped at 25% of the original contract price.
  • Earned Value Management: SV = BCWP − BCWS (negative = behind); CV = BCWP − ACWP (negative = over); SPI = BCWP/BCWS; CPI = BCWP/ACWP; EAC = BAC/CPI.
  • Contract types: lump sum, unit rate (measurement — most common works), cost-plus, item rate; dispute ladder: Engineer's decision → DAB/dispute review board → arbitration (Arbitration Act 2055) → court.

Professional Practice & Regulatory Bodies (10.5–10.6) — Capsule Values

  • Society elements: plurality, stability, likeliness, differences, interdependence; social-change theories: evolution, functionalist, conflict, cyclical.
  • Intellectual property: Copyright Act 2059 (Section 14) — economic & moral rights for life + 50 years; infringement fine Rs 10,000–100,000 or 6 months imprisonment; repeat offence double. Patent, Design & Trademark Act 2022 (1965) — trademark registration 7-year terms (renewable); design registration 5 years, renewable twice (up to 15 years total).
  • Company Act 2063: private company ≤ 50 shareholders; public company minimum 7, no maximum. Labour Act 2074 (effective Bhadra 19, 2074; replaced the 2048 Act): 8 hr/day, 48 hr/week; overtime 1.5× pay.
  • NEA (Nepal Engineers' Association): established 1962 (2019 BS), professional association registered under the Social Service Act (not a regulator).
  • NEC (Nepal Engineering Council): statutory regulator — NEC Act 2055: 7 chapters, 38 sections; first chairman Er. Ram Babu Sharma; first registrar Er. Bindeshwor Yadav; council of 21 members (president BE + 15 yrs; vice-president 10 yrs; provincial members 7 yrs with ≥ 3 women; NEA president member; 5 elected; registrar member-secretary); member tenure 4 years; ≥ 2 exams per year; exam committee of 5 (registrar member-secretary). Practicing without registration: fine up to Rs 10,000 or 3 months imprisonment or both. First amendment 2079 (bill 2076).
  • NEC Regulations 2057 (published 2057-03-08, under Act Section 37): 7 chapters, 38 clauses; amendments 2064, 2069, 2080. Registration categories: General Engineer — pass council exam, fee Rs 5,000 (+ Rs 200 ID); Professional Engineer — Master's + 7 years as general engineer, fee Rs 20,000, 5-year validity, renewal Rs 10,000 (apply 2 months before expiry); Foreign Engineer — BE + 10 years, fee Rs 30,000, registered 2 years (renewable yearly). Engineering professions list: 59 (the course also cites 61 professional-engineer categories — mark per course).
  • Ethics & safety: professional ethics codes (integrity, public safety first, competence, confidentiality); OSH — Nepal Labour Act provisions; hazards hierarchy (elimination → substitution → engineering → administrative → PPE); contemporary issues — climate adaptation, urbanization, standards enforcement.
Course-file watch-outs (MCQ traps): PPA ladder 10/20 lakh–5 billion; LD 0.05%/day cap 10%; retention 5%; escalation ≤ 25% (> 12-month contracts); TF ≥ FF ≥ IF formula order; PERT te = (o + 4m + p)/6; NEC (regulator, Act 2055, 21 members, Rs 5,000/20,000/30,000 fees) vs NEA (association 1962); copyright life + 50 years; VAT 13%, corporate tax 25%.
